en: Preface to the Fourth Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery.
Now, as for that which is cognized by consciousness, how could it ever not be consciousness? As for that which is suchness, it has never failed to be suchness.
Thus, when both the agent of practice and the object of practice are simultaneously empty, the principle of grasping is discarded;
when self-nature and the absence of nature are not distinct, the thought of clinging is forgotten.

If one forgets grasping yet harbors reliance, or retains generalizations while falling into karma; if one knows of vigorous cultivation yet fails to practice, thereby vainly emptying oneself to seek victory—fearing that the wild horse of emotion has not been stilled, the discourse of Vulture Peak is once again opened.
Some say:
regarding its names, it constantly urges the admonition of practicing;
regarding its substance, it necessarily warns against the indolence of failing to practice.
If one’s application is occasionally off the mark, where can one find the central mean?
I venture to respond:

All ordinary beings cleave to the tokens of names and forms and preserve the abode of ignorance and craving; thus, their mental preoccupations remain attached to existence, and whatever they deliberate upon inevitably deviates from the truth.
The Perfected Truth is the opposite of this: movement and stillness are here united.
Speaking from this perspective, one practices yet does not practice, and does not practice yet does not practice, and yet one practices perfectly!
It is as if they do not practice at all!

This is because they employ the provisional name "Prajñā" to bestow it upon a provisional name "Bodhisattva. Since this is merely holding a phantom dharma for a phantom person, there is neither action nor attainment.
Does this not further echo the morning mayfly’s discourse on the year, or the dream-butterfly’s deliberation on awakening?
Alas, these [scriptures] have not yet been fully disseminated; joyfully, this teaching is now gradually spreading.
It consists of twenty-nine chapters and eighteen fascicles.

These are the old *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines* (*Xiaopin*) and the *Daoxing Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, as well as the new *Daoxing Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The term "pin" (chapter) signifies a division; since these divisions vary in length, there are thus the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Chapter) and the *Svalpaprajñāpāramitā* (Small Chapter).
The *Dàoxíng* (Practice of the Way) is the first chapter within the [original] division, which the translator selected to circulate as a separate scripture;
*Míngdù* (Clarity-Degree) is a synonym for *Zhìdù* (Wisdom-Degree), adopted here as the title based on the general heading.
This was truly because the teachings were incomplete and deficient, which caused even the titles to be erroneous.
Now that the Great Teaching has reached its perfection and its grand regulations have been duly disseminated, can the essentials of the mind’s workings not be explained once again?
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Thirty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: On Sublime Conduct (Brahmacaryā-varga), Part Four, Section One. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they had attained true mastery, being well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom. They were like well-trained thoroughbred horses and like great dragons; having done what was to be done and accomplished their task, they had laid down the heavy burden and attained their own benefit. Having exhausted all fetters of existence, they were liberated through perfect knowledge, reaching the state of supreme consummation and sovereign mastery of mind—with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remained alone on the stage of training—the venerable Subhūti serving as their leader.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

"By means of your eloquence, you should proclaim, reveal, and explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; you should instruct and admonish those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may swiftly attain the ultimate consummation of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
"Is Subhūti now, by his own power, proclaiming and elucidating the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
"Is it by relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata?
Endowed with the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the Venerable Subhūti knew what was in the mind of Śāriputra and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Whatever disciples of the World-Honored One dare to proclaim, clarify, or reveal, all do so by relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata."

Why is this so? Śāriputra, it is because the Buddha has previously proclaimed, clarified, and revealed the essential points of the Dharma for others. Those who, relying on the Buddha’s teaching, practice with diligence until they realize the true nature of all phenomena, subsequently turn around to proclaim, clarify, and reveal them for others. If what they teach does not contradict the nature of phenomena, it is entirely due to the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power and is the natural outflow (*nisyanda*) of the realized nature of phenomena. Therefore, I shall now proclaim and reveal the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, instructing and admonishing them so that they may swiftly attain its ultimate realization; all of this is sustained by the Buddha’s power, and is not something I could accomplish through my own eloquence alone.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, you have commanded me to proclaim and reveal the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and to instruct and admonish those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may swiftly attain the ultimate consummation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
"Bhagavān!
Regarding those called 'bodhisattvas,' of what dharma is this a designation when one speaks of a 'bodhisattva'?
Bhagavān!"
"I do not perceive any dharma that can be named 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva,' nor do I perceive any dharma that can be named 'prajñāpāramitā.
World-Honored One!"

I neither see nor find the bodhisattva or the qualities of a bodhisattva, nor do I see or find the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). How then can I proclaim and reveal the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
"Bhagavān!
By means of what profound *prajñāpāramitā* do I instruct and admonish which assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that they may swiftly attain the ultimate consummation in the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
"Bhagavān!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such words, does not become despondent nor feel discouraged, and is neither startled nor terrified, but dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and practices the *prajñāpāramitā* until it reaches its ultimate consummation—then one should know that this is precisely the instruction and admonition for all bodhisattva mahāsattvas, enabling them to swiftly reach the ultimate consummation of the *prajñāpāramitā*. This is also called the proclamation and revelation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to them."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should train in this way: namely, by not clinging to the mind of great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta)."
"Why is this? Because the nature of the mind is not mind; its intrinsic nature is pure.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Is there a nature that is not the nature of mind?
Subhūti asked Śāriputra in return:
"Can a nature that is not the nature of mind be apprehended as either existing or non-existing?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
Subhūti then said to Śāriputra:
"Since neither the existence nor the non-existence of the nature of mind can be apprehended, how can one ask whether there is a nature of 'non-mind'?"
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
"What is meant by 'the nature of mind that is not mind'?
Subhūti replied:
"If there is neither transformation nor conceptualization, this is what is called 'the mind that is not mind.
Then, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying, "Excellent!"
Excellent!
It is truly as you have said.
The Buddha declared that among those who dwell in the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), you are the foremost; this is indeed in accordance with the words of the Noble One.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such words, does not become despondent nor feel discouraged, and is neither startled nor terrified, one should know that they have already attained non-retrogression regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes the mind in this way as being neither mind nor non-mind, one should know that they do not depart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

If good sons or good daughters wish to diligently train in the stages of the śrāvakas, the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, or the stage of the bodhisattvas, they should all, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, and diligently train in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, employing skillful means so that their practice may swiftly reach its ultimate consummation.
Why is this so? Because within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, all dharmas that ought to be studied are extensively expounded.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seeks unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; desires to correctly practice the various bodhisattva deeds; and wishes to fully accomplish skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and all the Buddha-dharmas, they should, with a sincere mind, listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, master thoroughly, and practice according to the instructions of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, all the dharmas that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ought to study are explained in detail.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to apply themselves with diligence to training in this, they will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and all that they seek will be fulfilled without exception.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! I observe that a bodhisattva exists only as a provisional name; I do not know, do not obtain, and do not see any real entity. I observe that the *prajñāpāramitā* also exists only as a provisional name; I do not know, do not obtain, and do not see any real entity. For what kind of bodhisattva-mahāsattva should I proclaim and reveal which profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
"World-Honored One, which bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be instructed and exhorted, so that they may swiftly reach the ultimate consummation in this prajñāpāramitā?"

I observe that both the bodhisattva and the profound perfection of wisdom possess only provisional names; they do not know, cannot be attained, and are not seen as substantial realities. Yet, when one speaks of a "bodhisattva" and a "profound perfection of wisdom" within this context, doubt and regret arise.
"Bhagavān!
Both the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the name 'bodhisattva' are neither determinate nor have they any place of abiding. Why is this so?"
Thus, both these names are non-existent; that which is a non-existent dharma has no fixed nature and no abiding place.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their mind does not sink, nor do they feel discouraged; they are not startled and not terrified, but believe and understand it with deep resolve.

It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom, never departing from it; by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, they dwell securely on the stage of the bodhisattva’s non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not dwell in form (rūpa), nor should they dwell in feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna)."
Why is this? If one dwells in form, one performs activities regarding form and does not practice the perfection of wisdom;

if one dwells in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one performs activities regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness and does not practice the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? One who acts or practices cannot grasp the *prajñāpāramitā*; if one does not grasp the *prajñāpāramitā*, one cannot cultivate it; if one cannot cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, one cannot bring it to fulfillment; if one cannot bring the *prajñāpāramitā* to fulfillment, one cannot attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*); and if one cannot attain the knowledge of all modes, one cannot gather those beings who are to be gathered. Therefore, one should not grasp at form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Form cannot be grasped within the perfection of wisdom;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be grasped within the perfection of wisdom. Because form cannot be grasped, it is not form; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be grasped, they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Furthermore, because the profound perfection of wisdom itself cannot be grasped, it is not the perfection of wisdom.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. If they practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is called the bodhisattva’s concentration that is non-appropriating regarding all phenomena—vast, unopposed, and immeasurable—which is definitively unique to them and not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and which likewise does not appropriate the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).”
Why is this so? This knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is not attained through the cultivation of grasping at signs; indeed, all grasping at signs is affliction (*kleśa*).

If the knowledge of all modes were attained through the cultivation of grasping at signs, then the brahmin Jayasena would not have been able to have faith and resolve in the knowledge of all modes. Although the brahmin Jayasena entered the Buddha-dharma by the power of faith and resolve—being termed a "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārī*)—he was nonetheless able, through a small portion of wisdom, to contemplate the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena and thereby awaken to and enter the knowledge of all modes.

Having thus entered into realization, one does not grasp at the marks of form (*rūpa*), nor does one grasp at the marks of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).

One does not view this wisdom through the lens of joy or delight; one does not view this wisdom by means of internal form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; one does not view this wisdom by means of external form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; one does not view this wisdom by means of both internal and external form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; nor does one view this wisdom apart from form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.

Through such gateways of detachment as these, the brahmin Jayasena conceived deep faith and understanding in the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), and he was entirely without grasping or attachment toward any phenomena (dharma).

Thus, having attained faith and understanding in the knowledge of all modes of knowledge through the gateway of detachment from signs, the brahmin does not grasp at signs in any phenomena, nor does he conceptualize signless dharmas.
Thus, by the power of his resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), that brahmin neither grasps nor rejects any phenomena, and neither attains nor realizes them.
At that time, even regarding his own conviction up to *nirvāṇa*, he does not cling to it, because he takes the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as the definitive standard.
“World-Honored One!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as not grasping even at form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Although they do not grasp at any phenomena, if they have not yet perfected the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth, they will never enter parinirvāṇa midway.”
It should be known that although this profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is free from grasping, it is nevertheless capable of accomplishing all supreme activities.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should observe in this way:
'What is the perfection of wisdom?'"
For what reason is it called "Prajñāpāramitā"?
And what does this Prajñāpāramitā accomplish?
World-Honored One!
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should observe in this way:
"If dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, then within this non-existence of the perfection of wisdom, what is there to be questioned or challenged?"
"Bhagavān!

If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva examines such matters with careful scrutiny, their mind does not sink, nor does it feel despondent; if they are neither startled nor terrified, one should know that they are not separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If form is separated from the intrinsic nature of form, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are separated from the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; if the perfection of wisdom is separated from the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, and the knowledge of all modes is separated from the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all modes—for what reason is it known that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not depart from the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra! All forms are devoid of the intrinsic nature of form; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are devoid of the intrinsic nature of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the perfection of wisdom is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom; and the knowledge of all modes is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all modes.

The self-characteristic of the perfection of wisdom is also devoid of its own characteristic; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is also devoid of its own intrinsic nature. Characteristics are devoid of intrinsic nature, and intrinsic nature is devoid of characteristics. Characteristics are devoid of characteristics, and intrinsic nature is devoid of intrinsic nature. The defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is devoid of the characterized (*lakṣya*), and the characterized is devoid of the defining characteristic. The defining characteristic is devoid of the defining characteristic, and the characterized is devoid of the characterized. The defining characteristic is devoid of the defining characteristic, and the characterized is devoid of the characterized.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know such meanings as they truly are, they will never be separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, will they swiftly be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, they will swiftly be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Why is that?
Śāriputra! This is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing. Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner, they will be in close proximity to the knowledge of all modes.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice with the form of form as their mental object; or practice with the characteristics of form as their mental object; or practice with the characteristic of the signlessness of form as their mental object; or practice with the arising of form as their mental object; or practice with the cessation of form as their mental object; or practice with the destruction of form as their mental object; or practice with the emptiness of form as their mental object; or if they take the thought "I am able to practice" as their mental object; or if they take the thought "I am a bodhisattva who is able to perform actions" as their mental object; or if they take the thought "I am a bodhisattva who is able to attain something" as their mental object.

If one practices with the perception of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signs; if one practices with the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signs; if one practices with the signless characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signs; if one practices with the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signs; if one practices with the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signs; if one practices with the disintegration of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signs; if one practices with the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signs; if one considers "I am able to practice" as a sign; if one considers "I am a bodhisattva who is able to perform actions" as a sign; or if one considers "I am a bodhisattva who is able to attain something" as a sign.
If one forms the thought, "If one can practice in this way, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)," this too becomes a conceptual sign (*nimitta*).
One should know that such a bodhisattva lacks skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); although they engage in practice, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"In what manner should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice so that it is called 'practicing the perfection of wisdom'?"
Subhūti replied:

"If bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not practice with regard to form, do not practice with regard to the signs of form, do not practice with regard to the signlessness of form, do not practice with regard to the arising of form, do not practice with regard to the cessation of form, do not practice with regard to the destruction of form, and do not practice with regard to the emptiness of form—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the characteristic of signlessness in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the disintegration of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and do not practice with regard to the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at practice, does not grasp at non-practice, does not grasp at both practice and non-practice, and does not grasp at neither practice nor non-practice, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Why is this? Śāriputra, because all dharmas are ungraspable, cannot be followed, cannot be appropriated, and are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics, this is called the concentration of non-appropriation regarding all dharmas by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; it is vast, unrivaled, immeasurable, and definitively uncommon to all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Then, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, the Venerable Subhūti spoke again to the Great Virtuous Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, it should be known that they have already received a face-to-face prophecy from the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past."
Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, he does not perceive this samādhi, nor does he cling to the name of this samādhi; furthermore, he does not think:
"I have entered, am entering, or shall enter this samādhi."
Nor does he think:
"Only I can enter this concentration, not others.
All such discursive thoughts and conceptualizations do not arise at all due to the power of this concentration.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by abiding in this samādhi, has already received a face-to-face prophecy from the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is that bodhisattva mahāsattva able to manifest such a samādhi?"
Subhūti replied, “No, Śāriputra!”
"Why is this? Because these sons of good family have neither understanding nor conceptualization regarding such a concentration.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable One, do you say that those sons of good family have neither understanding nor perception regarding such a concentration?
Subhūti replied,
"I certainly say that those sons of good family have neither understanding nor perception regarding such a concentration."
Why is this? Because such meditative concentrations are non-existent.

Those sons of good family have neither understanding nor conceptualization regarding these concentrations; likewise, these concentrations have neither understanding nor conceptualization regarding any phenomena.
"Why is this? It is because all dharmas are non-existent.
At that time, the Bhagavat praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
It is just as you have said.”

Therefore, I declare that you are foremost among those who dwell in the concentration of non-contention; it is by receiving the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power that you are able to speak thus. It is so, Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should study it in this manner. Why is that?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can study in this way, they are said to be truly studying the profound perfection of wisdom.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this way, may they be said to truly train in the profound perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this manner, it is called true training in the profound perfection of wisdom, because they employ the method of non-apprehension.”
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to train in this way, does he do so by taking non-apprehension as his expedient means?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they take non-apprehension as the skillful means regarding all phenomena."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, in what dharma do they train?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not train in dharmas.
Why is that? Śāriputra!"
"It is because all phenomena do not exist in the manner that foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp them.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If that is so, in what manner do all phenomena exist?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“It exists in such a way that it is non-existent.
If one cannot thoroughly comprehend this dharma of non-existence, it is called ignorance.”

Foolish worldlings, regarding the non-existent nature of all phenomena, through the predominant power of ignorance and craving, conceptually discriminate and cling to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Consequently, they neither know nor see the non-existent nature of all phenomena; they discriminate among phenomena, and because of such discrimination, they give rise to clinging. Because of this clinging, they discriminate that the nature of phenomena is non-existent, and thereby they neither see nor know phenomena as they truly are.
Because they neither see nor know all phenomena, they discriminate between the past, future, and present.

Due to this discrimination, they become attached to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because of attachment to name-and-form, they discriminate and cling to non-existent phenomena. Because they discriminate and cling to non-existent phenomena, they neither know nor see the path as it truly is, and are unable to escape the cycle of birth and death within the three realms. They do not believe in the Dharma of the Truths and do not awaken to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); for these reasons, they fall among the ranks of the foolish.
"Therefore, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no attachment whatsoever to the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, do they not also train in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not even seek to train in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Nevertheless, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, although there is nothing to be learned, it is called truly training in the knowledge of all modes; they are thus able to draw near to the knowledge of all modes and swiftly accomplish the knowledge of all modes."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Suppose someone were to come and ask this question:

‘If there are those who are illusory transformations and they cultivate and study the knowledge of all modes, would they be able to draw near to the knowledge of all modes and be able to swiftly accomplish the knowledge of all modes?’”
"If I were to receive this question, how should I answer it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall now ask you a question in return; answer as you see fit."
What do you think?
Is an illusion different from form?
Is an illusion different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Subhūti replied: "An illusion is not different from form; form is not different from an illusion. An illusion is itself form, and form is itself an illusion.

An illusion is not different from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not different from an illusion. An illusion is itself feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves an illusion."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Based on the five aggregates of clinging, does one give rise to a perception and a conceptualization, and then designate and speak of them with the conventional name 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva'?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and cultivate the perfection of wisdom are all training like those who study illusory transformations.”
Why is this? Because illusion is itself the five aggregates of clinging. Why is that so?
"I have taught that the five aggregates and the six sense faculties, such as the eye, are all like magical illusions and are not at all substantially real.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle hears such a teaching, will his mind not become terrified, alarmed, or disheartened?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle associates with evil friends and hears such teachings, his mind will become terrified and he will give rise to despondency; however, if he associates with virtuous friends, although he hears these teachings, he will not be terrified and will have no despondency."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is called a bodhisattva’s evil friend?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Those who are evil friends to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are as follows: those who instruct and admonish the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to cause them to abandon the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; those who cause them to abandon the pursuit of all-knowledge (sarvajñājñāna); those who cause them to study worldly scriptures that grasp at signs; those who cause them to study the sūtras and dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and furthermore, those who do not explain the deeds and faults of Māra, thereby preventing what they have undertaken to practice from reaching fulfillment—such persons are called the evil friends of bodhisattvas.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is called a bodhisattva’s virtuous friend?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The spiritual friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are those who instruct and admonish the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to train in the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; causing them to train in the sought-after knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); causing them to distance themselves from worldly scriptures that involve grasping at signs; causing them to distance themselves from the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; explaining to them the various works and faults of Māra so that they may recognize them and skillfully abandon them; and causing what they have undertaken to train in to be swiftly accomplished. These are called the spiritual friends of the bodhisattvas who are adorned with the great vow and who proceed upon the path of the Mahāyāna."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding what has been called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' what is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"To train in all phenomena without attachment or obstruction, to awaken to all phenomena without attachment or obstruction, and to seek the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the benefit of sentient beings—this is the meaning of a bodhisattva."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason is a bodhisattva called a mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because these bodhisattvas shall become the leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings, they are further called ‘mahāsattvas.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By means of my eloquence, I wish to explain why a bodhisattva is called a mahāsattva according to this meaning; I only pray that you will grant me leave to speak!”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Now is the very time; speak according to your own intention. Śāriputra said:

“By means of their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), bodhisattvas proclaim the essential teachings of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to sever the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a person (*pudgala*), the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of nihilism, the view of eternalism, the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and various other views involving grasping. It is on the basis of this meaning that they are called ‘Great Beings’ (*mahāsattva*).”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By means of my eloquence, I would like to joyfully explain why a bodhisattva is called a mahāsattva on account of this meaning; I only pray that you will grant me leave to do so!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “Now is the right time; speak as you wish.
Subhūti addressed him, saying:

“Because bodhisattvas, desiring to realize the knowledge of all modes, give rise to the mind of enlightenment—the untainted mind, the unequaled mind, and the mind not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and yet do not even cling to such a mind; it is by virtue of this meaning that they are called ‘mahāsattvas.’”

Why is this? Because the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is truly without outflows (anāsrava) and does not fall within the three realms; the mind that seeks the knowledge of all modes is likewise truly without outflows and does not fall within the three realms. One should not cling to such a mind; for this reason, a bodhisattva is called a mahāsattva.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason and by what causal condition does one not even cling to such a mind?
Subhūti replied:
"Since all such minds lack the nature of mind, one should not cling to them.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Does this mind possess the nature of non-mind?"
Subhūti asked Śāriputra in return:
"Is this nature of mind, whether existent or non-existent, apprehendable?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! Subhūti replied:
"Since this 'non-mind-nature' cannot be apprehended as either existent or non-existent, how can one ask:
'Does this mind possess the nature of non-mind?
At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:"
“Excellent! Excellent! It is so!”
"So it is! That which the Buddha has said—that you, O Venerable One, are foremost among those who dwell in the concentration of non-contention—is indeed true, just as the Noble One has spoken.
Then, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By means of my eloquence, I delight in explaining why a bodhisattva is called a ‘mahāsattva’ on account of this meaning; I only pray that you will grant me leave to speak!
The Buddha told Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“Now is precisely the right time; speak according to your own intention.”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

"Because all bodhisattvas don the great armor of merit for the universal benefit of all sentient beings, because they set out upon the Great Vehicle, and because they ride the Great Vehicle, they are called 'mahāsattvas' (Great Beings)."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has spoken of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas donning the great armor of merit, to what extent may it be said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have donned the great armor of merit?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas form this thought:

‘I shall deliver immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder. Although they thus deliver immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings into the realm of nirvana without remainder, there is no dharma whatsoever, nor any sentient being, that attains nirvana.”
Why is this? Because the *dharmatā* of all phenomena ought to be thus.
For example, suppose a magician or his apprentice were to conjure a great multitude at a crossroads and have them inflict mutual harm upon one another. What do you think?
"In this place, is there any actual occurrence of mutual injury, harm, death,
or wounding? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is likewise for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; although they lead immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings across [to liberation] and cause them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, there is no dharma and no sentient being that attains nirvana.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such matters, is not startled, not terrified, and does not feel any retreat or discouragement, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not don the armor of merit, it is precisely this that constitutes donning the great armor of merit."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not don the armor of merit, one should know that this is precisely what it means to don the armor of great merit. Why is this?

Because omniscient wisdom (sarvajñajñāna) is neither created nor conditioned, and all sentient beings are likewise neither created nor conditioned; yet, for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the armor of merit.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason is the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) uncreated and unconditioned, and all sentient beings likewise uncreated and unconditioned, yet the bodhisattva mahāsattvas don the armor of merit out of a desire to benefit those sentient beings?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because no agent can be apprehended. Why is that?
Form is neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
"Why is this? Because form, up to and including consciousness, cannot be apprehended.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is neither defilement nor purification. Why is this?

Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness are likewise neither bound nor liberated. The suchness (*tathatā*) of form is neither bound nor liberated; the suchness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is also neither bound nor liberated."
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Subhūti:

"Venerable One, do you say that form is neither bound nor liberated? Do you say that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also neither bound nor liberated? Do you say that the suchness of form is neither bound nor liberated, and that the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also neither bound nor liberated?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"What kind of form do you say is neither bound nor liberated?
What kind of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do you say are likewise neither bound nor liberated?"
What kind of suchness of form is said to be neither bound nor liberated?
What kind of suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also said to be neither bound nor liberated?

Subhūti replied, “I say that for an illusory person, form is neither bound nor liberated; I say that for an illusory person, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also neither bound nor liberated. I say that for an illusory person, the suchness of form is neither bound nor liberated; I say that for an illusory person, the suchness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is also neither bound nor liberated.”

Why is this? Because from form (*rūpa*) through consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as their suchness (*tathatā*), they are non-existent and thus neither bound nor liberated; they are remote and thus neither bound nor liberated; they are quiescent and thus neither bound nor liberated; they are signless (*animitta*) and thus neither bound nor liberated; they are unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and thus neither bound nor liberated; they are without arising or ceasing and thus neither bound nor liberated; they are without defilement or purity and thus neither bound nor liberated. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle and donning the armor of merit.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having heard these words, received them with joy and faith, and remained silent.
Then, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, donned the armor of merit, and mounted the Great Vehicle—”
What is the Great Vehicle?
To what extent may one say that one has set out toward the Great Vehicle?
From where does such a Great Vehicle emerge, and to where does it abide?
"In this way, where does this Great Vehicle abide?
And who, moreover, rides upon this Great Vehicle and departs?
The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
“The Mahāyāna is a synonym for the immeasurable and the incalculable, because it is accomplished through the convergence of boundless merits.
As for your subsequent question, ‘To what extent may one be said to have set out upon the Mahāyāna?’”
"Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, proceeding from one bodhisattva stage to another bodhisattva stage, it may be said that they have set out upon the Great Vehicle."
"As for your subsequent question, 'From where does such a Great Vehicle emerge, and where does it abide?', Subhūti, you should know this:
Such a Great Vehicle emerges from within the triple world and abides within the knowledge of all modes; yet, because it employs non-duality as its means, there is neither emergence nor abiding."
"As for your subsequent question, 'In what does such a Great Vehicle abide?', Subhūti, you should know this:
such a Great Vehicle abides nowhere at all, because all phenomena abide nowhere; nevertheless, this Great Vehicle abides in non-abiding."
“Regarding what you later asked— ‘Who, moreover, sets out by means of this Great Vehicle?’—
Subhūti, you should know that there is absolutely no one who sets out by means of this Great Vehicle.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the vehicle that is mounted upon, the one who mounts it, the means by which, the purpose for which, the place where, or the time when—none of these exist and are entirely unobtainable. Since all phenomena (dharmas) are non-existent and unobtainable, what phenomenon could mount what other phenomenon to go forth to what place or abide where? How, then, can one speak of "mounting"?
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As for the 'Great Vehicle'—the Great Vehicle universally transcends all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras; it is most honored and most supreme. Such a Great Vehicle is equal to space."

Just as space can universally contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, so too does the Mahāyāna universally contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.
Furthermore, just as space cannot be seen to come, go, or abide, so too is the Mahāyāna: it cannot be seen to come, go, or abide.
Furthermore, just as space cannot be apprehended in its prior, posterior, or middle limits, so too it is with the Mahāyāna; its prior, posterior, and middle limits are all unapprehendable.

Thus, this Mahāyāna is most honored and most supreme, equal to space; it accommodates much, is unshakeable, and is without abiding. It is equal throughout the three periods of time and transcends the three periods of time; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.
“The Bodhisattva Mahāyāna is endowed with such boundless merits as these.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, you previously instructed the Venerable Subhūti to proclaim and reveal the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas; why is it that you now speak of the Mahāyāna?”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the various meanings of the Great Vehicle that I have previously explained, do they not perhaps contradict the Perfection of Wisdom that has been taught?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All the various meanings of the Great Vehicle that you have previously expounded are in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā and do not deviate from it."
"Why is this? Because there are no wholesome dharmas whatsoever that are not subsumed within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“The prior limit of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended; their posterior limit cannot be apprehended;
their middle limit cannot be apprehended. Why is this so?

Because form is boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also boundless; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also boundless.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Within form itself, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not exist and cannot be apprehended; within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not exist and cannot be apprehended;
apart from form, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not exist and cannot be apprehended."
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not exist and cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!

Regarding all these dharmas, in every way, in every place, and at every time, I have sought a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva but have seen none at all and can find none; I have sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* but have seen none at all and can find none; I have sought the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) but have seen none at all and can find none. How then am I to instruct and admonish the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas so that they may swiftly reach the ultimate in the *prajñāpāramitā*, namely, quickly realize the knowledge of all modes?"
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature at all.

Just as it is said that 'self' and so forth are ultimately unarisen, possessing only provisional names and having no intrinsic nature at all, so too are all phenomena: they are ultimately unarisen, possessing only provisional names and having no intrinsic nature at all."
In this context, what is form that is ultimately unarisen?
If it is ultimately unarisen, it is not called form.
What are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are ultimately unarisen?
If there is ultimate non-arising, then it is not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
World-Honored One!

Form is unattainable as a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unattainable as a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; even this unattainability is itself unattainable.
Regarding all such phenomena, I seek for them—in every manner, in every place, and at every time—the bodhisattva and so forth, yet they are entirely unfindable; what dharma, then, should I teach?
"What dharmas are cultivated?
In what place and at what time are they cultivated, and what dharmas are realized?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha, the Bhagavān, exists as a mere designation; all bodhisattvas exist as mere designations; and the profound perfection of wisdom exists as a mere designation.

As it is said, "We" are ultimately unarisen; they exist only as provisional designations and possess no intrinsic nature. All phenomena are likewise: they exist only as provisional designations and possess no intrinsic nature.
What is this form that is neither graspable nor subject to arising?
What are these feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses that are neither graspable nor subject to arising?

Since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is neither graspable nor subject to arising, and since that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot arise, and even this non-arising phenomenon cannot arise, how could I, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā which is ultimately non-arising, instruct and admonish the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—who are themselves ultimately non-arising—in order to bring them to final realization?
"Bhagavān!
Apart from dharmas that are unarisen, no dharma can be apprehended, nor is there any bodhisattva mahāsattva who can practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Bhagavān!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such an exposition, does not sink in spirit nor feel discouraged, and is neither startled nor terrified, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and contemplates all phenomena, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any form (*rūpa*) whatsoever; there is no feeling, no grasping, no dwelling, and no attachment, nor is it designated as form.

They do not apprehend any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness whatsoever; there is no feeling, no grasping, no dwelling, and no attachment, nor are they designated as feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Why is this? Because the nature of form is empty, without arising and without ceasing; the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty, without arising and without ceasing.
"World-Honored One!..."

Form that is without arising and without cessation is not form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are without arising and without cessation are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this so? Form, up to and including consciousness, is non-dual and indivisible from non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is that?

Because the dharmas of non-arising and non-ceasing are neither one, nor two, nor many, nor different, therefore form up to consciousness are without arising and without ceasing; that is to say, they are not form up to consciousness.
World-Honored One!
That form is non-dual is itself not form; that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual are themselves not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
World-Honored One!
The aggregate of form enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness enter into the category of non-dual dharmas.
If one speaks of form, one speaks of non-dual dharmas; if one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one speaks of non-dual dharmas.
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"As I understand the meaning of what you have said, the self and sentient beings are ultimately unarisen; from form up to consciousness, they are ultimately unarisen; and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are ultimately unarisen."

If this is so, for what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in order to deliver immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, practice hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities and undergo immeasurable great sufferings that are hard to endure?

Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra, it is not that I admit that within those dharmas of non-arising there exists a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for the sake of liberating immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, practices hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities and undergoes immeasurable great sufferings that are hard to endure. Rather, although bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice immeasurable kinds of difficult and painful austerities for the sake of sentient beings, they harbor no conception of such austerities within themselves.”
Why is this? If one perceives ascetic practices as mere ascetic practices, one will ultimately be unable to bring great benefit to immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.

Nevertheless, the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, by employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, conceives the thought of joyful practice regarding all ascetic disciplines, the thought of easy practice regarding difficult deeds, and the thought of sentient beings being like their own parents, brothers, wives, children, and their own bodies; thus, for the sake of delivering them, they resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and are thereby able to bring great benefit to immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas conceive of all sentient beings as their parents, brothers, wives, children, or their own selves, they form this thought:

'I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them to be free from all the sufferings of birth and death; I shall undertake hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful practices, preferring to sacrifice my own body rather than abandon them.'"
"Yet, regarding the suffering of sentient beings and their ascetic practices, I do not give rise to the notion that these are the suffering or ascetic practices of sentient beings.
Furthermore, he thinks:

"I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them to be free from the boundless great aggregates of suffering; even if for their sake my body were cut into a hundred thousand pieces, I would never retreat or be cowed, yet within this I shall not give rise to the notion that it is a difficult or painful practice."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should form this thought:
'Just as my own intrinsic nature cannot be found when sought through every mode, in all phenomena, at all places and times;'"
"Internal and external phenomena are likewise thus: they are entirely non-existent and utterly unattainable.

If one abides in this perception, one will not perceive any difficult practices or ascetic austerities; by means of this, one is able to perform hundreds of thousands of difficult practices and austerities for the sake of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings, thereby bringing about great benefit.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 538; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 539.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Four, Chapter One on Sublime Conduct, Section Two. At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Are these bodhisattvas truly without birth?"
Subhūti replied,
“These bodhisattvas are all truly non-arisen.
Śāriputra said:
"Is it only that the Bodhisattva is truly non-arisen, or are the dharmas of a Bodhisattva also truly non-arisen?
Subhūti replied,
"The dharmas of all Bodhisattvas are also truly non-arisen."
Śāriputra asked:
"Is it only the dharmas of a bodhisattva that are truly non-arisen, or is omniscience (sarvajñajñāna) also truly non-arisen?
Subhūti replied:
“The knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) is also truly non-arisen. Śāriputra asked:
“Is it only the knowledge of all modes that is truly non-arisen, or is the dharma of the knowledge of all modes also truly non-arisen?”
Subhūti replied,
“The dharma of omniscience is likewise truly without arising.
Śāriputra said:
"Is it only the dharma of the knowledge of all modes that is truly non-arisen, or are the classes of ordinary beings also truly non-arisen?
Subhūti replied,
"The classes of ordinary beings are also truly non-arisen."
Śāriputra asked:
"Is it only that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are truly non-arisen, or are the dharmas of ordinary beings also truly non-arisen?
Subhūti replied:
“Furthermore, all the dharmas of ordinary beings are also truly non-arisen.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

“If all bodhisattvas are truly non-arisen, if the dharmas of bodhisattvas are also truly non-arisen, if the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is truly non-arisen, if the dharmas of the knowledge of all modes are also truly non-arisen, and if the classes of ordinary beings are truly non-arisen and the dharmas of the classes of ordinary beings are also truly non-arisen, then would it not follow that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should realize the knowledge of all modes accordingly? In that case, would a non-arisen dharma attain a non-arisen dharma?”
Subhūti replied:
"In my view, I do not admit that there is any realization or clear observation within dharmas that are unarisen. Why is this? Because..."
"Because all dharmas that are unarisen are unattainable.
Śāriputra asked:
"Do you maintain that one realizes an arisen dharma by means of an arisen dharma, or do you maintain that one realizes an unarisen dharma by means of an unarisen dharma?"
Subhūti replied, “In my view,
it is not admitted that a produced phenomenon realizes a produced phenomenon, nor is it admitted that an unproduced phenomenon realizes an unproduced phenomenon.
Śāriputra said:
“Do you maintain that a dharma that arises realizes a dharma that does not arise, or do you maintain that a dharma that does not arise realizes a dharma that arises?
Subhūti replied, “In my view,
I do not maintain that a dharma that arises realizes a dharma that does not arise, nor do I maintain that a dharma that does not arise realizes a dharma that arises.”
Śāriputra asked:
"If this is so, is there then absolutely no attainment and no clear realization?
Subhūti replied:

"Although there is attainment and there is clear realization, they are not realized by means of these two dharmas; rather, attainment and clear realization are merely designated in accordance with worldly convention, for in the ultimate sense (paramārtha) there is neither attainment nor clear realization."
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Do you assert that an unarisen phenomenon arises, or do you assert that an already arisen phenomenon arises?
Subhūti replied:
"I do not intend to allow that an unarisen dharma arises, nor do I allow that an arisen dharma arises.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Do you allow the arising of what has already arisen, or do you allow the arising of what has not yet arisen?"
Subhūti replied, "In my view,
I do not admit that there is arising, nor do I admit that there is non-arising.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“Virtuous one, regarding the dharmas of non-arising that you have spoken of, do you delight in debating and explaining the characteristics of non-arising?
Subhūti replied,
“Regarding the dharmas of non-arising that have been spoken of, I likewise do not delight in debating and explaining the characteristics of non-arising.”
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"When one gives rise to the expression 'non-arising' regarding dharmas that are non-arisen, is this expression 'non-arising' itself also non-arisen?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

"Regarding the dharma of non-arising, one gives rise to the expression 'non-arising. Both this dharma and this expression share the meaning of non-arising, yet in accordance with worldly convention, we speak of the characteristic of non-arising.
At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Among those who preach the Dharma, you are foremost; no one can equal you except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

Why is this? Because, in accordance with whatever various Dharma-gates they are questioned or interrogated upon, they are able to provide answers without any obstruction, while remaining entirely unmoved and untransgressing the nature of phenomena.
Subhūti replied,

“Those disciples of the Buddhas who have no dependence or attachment toward any phenomena are, by the very nature of things, able to answer each and every question they are interrogated with mastery and fearlessness, yet they remain unmoved and do not transgress the nature of phenomena.”
"Why is this? Because all phenomena have nothing upon which they rely.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"By the power of which perfection (pāramitā) is this profound essential of the Dharma thus taught accomplished?
Subhūti replied,
"This profound essential of the Dharma thus taught is accomplished entirely by the power of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

Why is this? It is because all phenomena are said to be without any basis of reliance; it is precisely through the perfection of wisdom that one realizes that all phenomena are without any basis of reliance.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, has no doubt or confusion in mind and does not become bewildered, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in such a dwelling as never to abandon it—that is, by means of the skillful method of non-apprehension, they constantly and diligently strive to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
"You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such a supreme mental engagement (*manasikāra*), namely, the mental engagement associated with great compassion.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in such a dwelling and never abandons it, accomplishing the mental engagement associated with great compassion, then all sentient beings would also become bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings, through this dwelling and this mental attention, never abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Since the nature of the mental engagement of great compassion is equal, there would then be no distinction between bodhisattva mahāsattvas and all sentient beings.
Subhūti replied, “Excellent!”
Excellent! So it is! So it is!
It is exactly as you have said.
You have understood the intent of my words as they truly are; thus, although it appears that you are challenging me, you have in fact established my own position. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, you should know that such abiding and mental attention likewise lack intrinsic nature;
because sentient beings do not exist, you should know that such abiding and mental attention likewise do not exist.
Because sentient beings are detached, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also detached;
because sentient beings are quiescent, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also quiescent;
because sentient beings are unapprehendable, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also unapprehendable.
Because sentient beings lack conscious awareness, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention likewise lack conscious awareness.

For this reason, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas never abandon such a dwelling and such mental attention; they are no different from all sentient beings, because all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately empty and without distinction.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know in this way, without any obstruction, they are truly practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
You are truly well able to proclaim and elucidate the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is entirely through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
If there are those who wish to proclaim and elucidate the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they should all proclaim and elucidate it just as you have done.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should all study it according to what you have said.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the perfection of wisdom according to what you have said, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.
Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should diligently practice and study this profound perfection of wisdom.

**Chapter 4: Śakra, Part Two.** At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, arrived and sat in the assembly together with forty thousand sons of the gods from the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The Four World-Protecting Kings (Caturmahārājakāyika) arrived and sat in the assembly together with twenty thousand sons of the gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā world-system, arrived and sat in the assembly together with ten thousand Brahmās. In this manner, even up to the gods of the Five Pure Abodes, each arrived and sat in the assembly together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sons of the gods. Although the retributive light of the bodies of these hosts of devas—produced by their pure karma—was capable of illuminating, it was all eclipsed and rendered invisible by the majestic power of the Tathāgata’s own bodily radiance.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:

"Now, immeasurable hosts of devas from this trichiliocosm have gathered here together to hear the Venerable One proclaim and reveal the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and to receive instruction and admonition for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that they may swiftly attain the ultimate consummation of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
I only pray that the Venerable One will take pity on me and explain:
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in the perfection of wisdom?
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom?
At that time, Subhūti addressed Śakra, saying:

"Relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and in accordance with the Tathāgata’s intention, I shall proclaim and elucidate the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may dwell therein in such a manner and train therein in such a manner."
"You hosts of devas, you should all listen attentively and reflect upon this well. Kausika!
You devas who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta should now all resolve to do so."
Those who have already entered the fixed course of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can no longer generate the mind of great enlightenment.
Why is this, Kauśika?
Because they have already established a boundary across the stream of birth and death,
if there are among them those capable of generating the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta,
I likewise rejoice in it. Why is this so?
"All superior persons should seek the supreme Dharma; I shall never obstruct another's pursuit of superior wholesome qualities.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

You have now skillfully proclaimed and elucidated the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and you are also able to exhort and inspire the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, causing them to rejoice deeply and diligently cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since I recognize your kindness, how could I fail to repay it! Why is this so?

The Buddhas of the past and their disciples have, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, proclaimed the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, providing instruction and admonition, and receiving them with care and mindfulness.
World-Honored One, at that time you also trained therein and purified the holy life; now, having realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, you turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma to benefit us.

Therefore, I should now follow the Buddha’s teaching to proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas everything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; I shall instruct, admonish, sustain, and protect them, causing them to diligently practice and study the pure brahmacarya, so that they may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma until the end of the future, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings—this is what is called repaying their kindness and virtue.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, saying: “Regarding what you asked:
‘How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell and how should they train in the perfection of wisdom?’”
"Listen attentively! Listen attentively!
I shall explain to you the manner in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide and train within the profound perfection of wisdom."

“Kauśika! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, donned in the great armor of merit, should abide in the perfection of wisdom through the characteristic of emptiness; they should not abide in form, nor should they abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they should not abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor should they abide in the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; they should not abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor should they abide in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.”

One should not dwell on the thought that "this is form," nor should one dwell on the thought that "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. One should not dwell on the thought that "this is the fruit of stream-entry," nor should one dwell on the thought that "this is the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship. One should not dwell on the thought that "this is the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha," nor should one dwell on the thought that "this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
One should not dwell on whether form is permanent or impermanent; one should not dwell on whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are permanent or impermanent.
One should not dwell on whether form is pleasant or painful; one should not dwell on whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One should not dwell on form as either self or non-self; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either self or non-self.
One should not dwell on form as either pure or impure; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pure or impure.
One should not dwell on form as either empty or non-empty; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either empty or non-empty.

One should not dwell on the fruit of stream-entry as being manifested by the unconditioned; one should not dwell on the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship as being manifested by the unconditioned; one should not dwell on the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as being manifested by the unconditioned; and one should not dwell on the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as being manifested by the unconditioned.

One should not dwell on the fruit of stream-entry as being a true field of merit worthy of receiving offerings; nor should one dwell on the fruit of stream-entry as being subject to at most seven more births before necessarily entering nirvāṇa.

One should not dwell on the fruit of once-returner as being a true field of merit worthy of receiving offerings; nor should one dwell on the fruit of once-returner as being one who has not yet reached the ultimate goal, but will make an end of suffering after returning once more to this world.

One should not dwell on the thought that the fruit of non-returning is a true field of merit worthy of receiving offerings; one should not dwell on the thought that one who has attained the fruit of non-returning goes there to pass into extinction and does not return again.

One should not dwell on the thought that the fruit of arhatship is a true field of merit worthy of receiving offerings; one should not dwell on the thought that one who has attained the fruit of arhatship will certainly enter nirvana without remainder in this very life.

One should not dwell on the thought that a pratyekabuddha is a true field of merit worthy of receiving offerings; one should not dwell on the thought that a pratyekabuddha transcends the stage of the śrāvaka and attains parinirvāṇa without reaching the stage of a Buddha.

One should not dwell on the thought that the Buddha is a true field of merit who should receive offerings; nor should one dwell on the thought that the Buddha has transcended the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, and the stage of bodhisattvas, abiding instead in the stage of a Buddha to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder;

nor should one dwell on the thought that the Buddha delivers immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing each to attain certainty in the three vehicles, and having performed such various buddha-deeds, enters the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:

"If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he should not abide in the state in which a Buddha abides—that is, in the Buddha-ground—in order to benefit and bring happiness to immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings by causing them to enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder; nor should he abide in the state in which a Buddha delivers immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them to attain certainty in each of the three vehicles; and having performed such various buddha-deeds, he enters the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder—nor should he abide in any other dharmas—then in what manner should these bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide?"
The Venerable Subhūti, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, knowing the thoughts in the mind of Śāriputra, said to him:
"What do you think?
"In what does the mind of the Tathāgatas abide?
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"The minds of all Tathāgatas abide nowhere at all."

Why is this? Because the mind has no abiding place, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; that is to say, he does not abide in the realm of the conditioned, nor does he abide in the realm of the unconditioned, yet it is not that he does not abide.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is also like this: just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have no mental dwelling upon any phenomena, nor do they not dwell [upon them]."

Śāriputra! Regarding the profound perfection of wisdom, all bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide and train in this manner, employing the method of non-apprehension, just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do.
At that time, among the assembly there were certain sons of the gods who secretly thought to themselves:
"Although the words, phrases, and mantras of the yakṣas and others differ in various ways and are indeed obscure, we are still able to understand them."
