"Venerable Subhūti, although you have elucidated the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through various modes of expression, we have nonetheless been unable to understand it."
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of those devaputras, addressed them, saying:
"Do you, O devaputras, not understand what I have said?"
The devaputras said: "So it is! So it is!"
“I am entirely unable to understand the profound meaning of the phrases of the *prajñāpāramitā* as explained by the Venerable One.
The venerable Subhūti replied to him:
“I have neither spoken nor indicated anything here regarding the meaning associated with this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; since you have not heard it, what is there for you to understand?”
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
Within the meaning associated with the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), all letters and verbal expressions are utterly transcended.
Then, those sons of the gods again had this thought:

"Although the Venerable Subhūti has used various skillful means to explain this profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* so that it may be easily understood, its underlying significance remains exceedingly deep, even more deep; subtle, even more subtle; and difficult to fathom."
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing their thoughts, addressed them, saying: "O Sons of Heaven, you should know this! Form is neither profound nor subtle;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither profound nor subtle. The fruit of stream-entry is neither profound nor subtle; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship are neither profound nor subtle. The enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is neither profound nor subtle; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is neither profound nor subtle."
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
Because all dharmas are subtle and profound, and neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands them can be apprehended.
Therefore, among all phenomena, you should cultivate profound and firm patience in accordance with what has been taught.

O Son of Heaven, you should know that those who wish to realize or abide in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, must rely upon this patience in order to realize and abide therein.
At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"Venerable Subhūti, for what kind of sentient beings does he now wish to preach what Dharma?
The venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed them, saying:
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
I now wish to teach the Dharma—which is like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream—to sentient beings who are likewise like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream.”
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
Because those who listen in such a manner neither hear, nor understand, nor realize the Dharma that has been taught.
At that time, the devaputras asked Subhūti:
"Is the speaker, the listener, and the Dharma taught all like an illusion, a transformation, or what is seen in a dream?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

Just as illusory sentient beings teach the illusory Dharma to those who are illusory, as conjured sentient beings teach the conjured Dharma to those who are conjured, and as dream-like sentient beings teach the dream-like Dharma to those who are dream-like.

All sentient beings and all phenomena are without exception like illusions, transformations, and dreamscapes, for all phenomena and all sentient beings are non-dual and indistinguishable from illusions, transformations, and dreams.

"O Son of Heaven, you should know! Whether it be those who have entered the stream and the fruit of stream-entry; those who return once more and the fruit of once-returning; those who do not return and the fruit of non-returning; Arhats and the fruit of arhatship; Pratyekabuddhas and the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; or Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas and the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of a Buddha—all these are without exception like illusions, transformations, and dream-visions."
Then, those sons of the gods asked Subhūti:
"Are the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha, also like an illusion, a transformation, or what is seen in a dream?"
Subhūti replied: “So it is! So it is!”
“Even up to nirvāṇa, I also declare it to be like an illusion, like a magical creation, and like what is seen in a dream.
At that time, the sons of the gods asked Subhūti:
“Can even nirvāṇa be like an illusion, a magical creation, or an object seen in a dream?”
Subhūti replied:
"Even if there were another dharma superior to nirvāṇa, I would likewise say that it is like an illusion, like a transformation, and like what is seen in a dream."

Why is this so? Because illusions, transformations, and dream-objects, as well as all phenomena up to and including nirvāṇa, are non-dual and undifferentiated; they are all ungraspable and inexpressible.
At that time, Śāriputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākāśyapa, and others asked Subhūti:
"Who is able to believe and accept this Prajñāpāramitā that you have described as so profound?"
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the great śrāvakas, Śāriputra and the others, saying:

"There are non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to have deep faith and acceptance in this Prajñāpāramitā; furthermore, there are immeasurable great arhats who possess perfect view and whose outflows are forever exhausted, who are likewise able to have faith and acceptance in this Prajñāpāramitā."
The Venerable Subhūti spoke thus:
"This profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been described cannot be believed or accepted. Why is this so?

In this regard, there is no dharma that can be manifested, demonstrated, or designated; since in reality no dharma can be manifested, demonstrated, or designated, even one who accepts it cannot be found.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"The Venerable Subhūti is raining down the great rain of Dharma; I should manifest various exquisite flowers and scatter them as an offering."
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested various exquisite flowers and scattered them over Subhūti.
The Venerable Subhūti thought to himself:

"These scattered flowers have never been seen before among the realms of the devas; these flowers are so exquisite that they certainly were not produced from water, land, grass, or trees, but must have been emanated by the devas from their own minds."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing what Subhūti was thinking in his mind, said to Subhūti:
"These flowers that have been scattered were not actually produced from water, land, grasses, or trees, nor were they emanated from the minds of the devas."
"Why is this? Because these scattered flowers have the nature of non-arising.
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra:
"These flowers are unarisen; they are not flowers at all!
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought to himself:
"The Venerable Subhūti possesses profound wisdom; he speaks of the ultimate meaning without destroying conventional designations."
Having formed this thought, he addressed Subhūti, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is exactly as your venerable instruction says.
Among all dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train accordingly, following the Venerable One’s teaching.
The Venerable Subhūti said to Śakra:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, regarding all phenomena, should train in accordance with my teaching as follows: ‘Kauśika! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not train in form;

they do not train in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. They do not train in the fruit of stream-entry; they do not train in the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship. They do not train in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they do not train in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas. If they do not train in these stages, this is called training in the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes.’”
If one can study the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes, then one studies the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

If one studies the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, then one does not study form as having increase or decrease, nor does one study feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having increase or decrease.

If one does not train in the increase or decrease of form, nor train in the increase or decrease of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, then one does not train in the grasping or relinquishing of form, nor does one train in the grasping or relinquishing of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

If one does not train in the grasping or abandoning of form, nor train in the grasping or abandoning of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, then one does not train in the grasping or abandoning of any phenomena whatsoever.
If one does not train in all phenomena as having grasping and abandoning, then one does not train in phenomena as being subject to appropriation or subject to destruction.

If one does not train in phenomena as being subject to appropriation or subject to destruction, then one does not train in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) as being subject to appropriation or subject to destruction.
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, it is called training truly in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and they are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not train in the idea that any phenomena are to be grasped or destroyed, nor trains in the idea that the knowledge of all modes is to be grasped or destroyed—if a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in this way, is it called training truly in the knowledge of all modes, and is he able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the idea that any phenomena are subject to appropriation or destruction, nor does he train in the idea that the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is subject to appropriation or destruction, then when this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, it is called training truly in the knowledge of all modes; he will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes by means of non-apprehension as his expedient.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"Where should one seek the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train?"
Śāriputra said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train should be sought within what Subhūti has spoken."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"By whose spiritual power do you rely, that you, Venerable One, speak thus?
Śāriputra replied:
“It is by relying upon the Tathāgata’s spiritual power that I speak thus.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
“By whose spiritual power does the Venerable Subhūti rely when he is able to teach the Prajñāpāramitā?”
Śāriputra said:
"It is by relying upon the Tathāgata’s spiritual power that the Venerable Subhūti is able to teach the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Subhūti addressed Śakra, saying:
“Kauśika, as for your question: ‘By whose spiritual power do you, Subhūti, rely upon as support to be able to speak this Prajñāpāramitā?’—”
"You should know that it is because the Tathāgata’s spiritual power serves as the support that I, Subhūti, am able to teach the Prajñāpāramitā. Kausika!"
Regarding your question, "Kauśika, where should one seek the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train?"— it is as follows:
The perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train should not be sought within form, nor should it be sought apart from form;
it should not be sought within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor should it be sought apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Form is not the perfection of wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom exist apart from form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the perfection of wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom exist apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
“The perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is a great perfection, an immeasurable perfection, and a boundless perfection.”
Subhūti replied: "So it is! So it is!"
Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom studied by the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is the great perfection, the immeasurable perfection, and the boundless perfection.
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because form is great, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is also great.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are great, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also great.
Kausika! Because form is immeasurable, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also immeasurable;
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also immeasurable.
Kausika! Because form is boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
"Furthermore, Kausika!
Because the objects of focus are limitless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also limitless. Kauśika,
why is it that because the objects of focus are limitless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also limitless?

It means that because all phenomena (dharmas) cannot be apprehended at their prior, middle, or subsequent limits, they are said to be "boundless. Since phenomena are boundless, their objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are also boundless; for this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also said to be boundless.
Therefore, I say that because the objects of focus are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Because all phenomena are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Kausika, why is it that because all phenomena are boundless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also boundless?
It means that the limits of all phenomena cannot be apprehended. Why is this?

Because the prior, middle, and posterior limits of all form cannot be apprehended; the prior, middle, and posterior limits of all feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended; and by virtue of this, the prior, middle, and posterior limits of the *prajñāpāramitā* also cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, because all phenomena are boundless, I say that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is also boundless.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
Because all sentient beings are infinite, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also infinite. Why is this?
Because a limit of all sentient beings cannot be found.
"Therefore, I say that because all sentient beings are limitless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is also limitless.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"Venerable One!"
"How is it that because all sentient beings are infinite, one should know that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is also infinite?
Subhūti replied, "Kauśika!..."
Because the number of non-sentient beings is so vast that their limit cannot be calculated, it is said:
"Since all sentient beings are limitless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also limitless."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
“For what purpose do you speak thus?
Subhūti replied:
“Kauśika! I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?”
When you speak of "sentient beings," what dharma does the term "sentient being" designate as a metaphorical expression?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:

"When one speaks of 'sentient beings,' the term 'sentient being' is neither a metaphorical expression for a dharma nor a metaphorical expression for a non-dharma; rather, it is comprised of a provisional name, comprised of a name without a real entity, comprised of a name without a master, and comprised of a name without an objective basis."
Subhūti spoke again:
"Kauśika, what do you think?"
"In this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, is there any indication that a real sentient being exists?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied, "No,
[World-Honored One]."
"Venerable One!
Subhūti replied:
"In this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, since no real sentient beings are demonstrated, it is said to be 'boundless,' because neither a middle nor an extreme can be apprehended therein."
“Kauśika, what do you think? If all Tathāgatas, Arhats,

and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were to spend great eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, speaking with boundless voices the infinite names of sentient beings, would there, within this, be any truly existent sentient being who undergoes birth or cessation?”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No,
Venerable Sir!"
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are pure by nature.
Since they have been non-existent from the very beginning, that which is non-existent cannot undergo arising or ceasing.
Subhūti replied:
"For this reason, I say that because all sentient beings are infinite, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also infinite."
Kauśika! By this you should know that the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train should be described as great, immeasurable, and boundless.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas of the Desire Realm; Brahmā, King of the Gods, and the other devas of the Form Realm; as well as Maheśvara, the celestial seers, and the goddesses, leaped for joy and simultaneously cried out three times in a loud voice:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent!

Because the Buddha has appeared in the world, the Venerable Subhūti, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, has well expounded and revealed for our sake the subtle nature of phenomena—namely, the Prajñāpāramitā—thereby bringing great benefit to gods, humans, asuras, and others.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught and never abandon it, we shall honor and make offerings to them as we would to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devas and others, saying: "So it is! So it is!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding this perfection of wisdom, practices as it has been taught by employing the skillful means of non-apprehension and never remains far from it, you gods and others should all make offerings to them as if they were the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
O devas and others, you should know!

In the past, at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, when I was at the crossroads of the capital city of Padmarāja, I beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. I offered him five stalks of flowers and spread my hair over the mud to cover it. Having heard the essential points of the True Dharma, and by taking non-apprehension as my expedient means, I have never been separated from the profound Prajñāpāramitā and the other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara immediately conferred upon me the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, saying: "Good son!

In a future age, after incalculable eons have passed, within this world during the Bhadrakalpa, you shall become a Buddha named Śāntamati Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so forth, up to—Buddha, Bhagavān. You shall proclaim the profound sūtras of the Prajñāpāramitā and deliver immeasurable multitudes."
At that time, the devas all addressed the Buddha together, saying:

“This Prajñāpāramitā is truly rare and extraordinary; it enables the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to swiftly attract and encompass the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), benefiting and bringing joy to sentient beings until the end of the future.”

Chapter 3: Honoring the Stūpa, Part One of the Fourth Section. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the hosts of devas from the desire and form realms, as well as the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, had gathered like clouds to respectfully receive and uphold [the teaching] as witnesses, immediately looked toward Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and addressed him: "Kauśika!..."

If sons or daughters of good family wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, reflect upon according to the principle, and extensively and unerringly expound this profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, you should know that all evil Māras, humans, non-humans, and the like will be unable to find an opportunity against them; no calamities or misfortunes shall reach them, and their bodies and minds will be peaceful and happy, free from illness, and endowed with long life.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there are sons of the gods who have already resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, but have not yet heard, received, upheld, recited, diligently practiced, or reflected upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle of reality, they should all come to where these good men and good women are. There, with a sincere heart, they should hear, receive, uphold, and recite this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and reflect upon its profound meaning and intent according to the principle of reality, so that they may attain ultimate realization and subsequently explain it to others.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if sons or daughters of good family wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the truth, then whether these sons or daughters of good family are in an empty house, in a wilderness, on a perilous path, or in a place of danger, they shall never feel fear, alarm, or horripilation; the devas and benevolent spirits will constantly come to protect them.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings and their celestial hosts joined their palms in reverent salutation and addressed the Buddha together, saying:

“If any sons or daughters of good family are able to hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere heart, we shall constantly follow them with reverence and protection, ensuring that no calamities or afflictions may harm or disturb them.”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the assembly of devas, joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha in unison:

“If any sons or daughters of good family are able to wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, we shall constantly follow them with respect and provide protection, ensuring that no calamities or afflictions may harm or disturb them.”
Then the Brahma King and the assembly of Brahmās joined their palms in reverence and together addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If sons or daughters of good family are able to listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently study, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate the *Prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere heart, we shall constantly follow them with reverence and provide protection, ensuring that no calamities or afflictions may harm or disturb them.”
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!

If sons or daughters of good family should, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the truth, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will thereby acquire such meritorious qualities in the present life."

If sons or daughters of good family embrace the perfection of wisdom, they thereby embrace the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family embraces the perfection of wisdom, they then fully embrace all six perfections.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters are able to listen with a sincere heart to this *prajñāpāramitā*, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to principle, transcribe it, explain it, and cause it to be widely disseminated—the merit they shall obtain, you should listen attentively and reflect upon it most thoroughly!"
"I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "Indeed!"
"Please speak!
We wish to hear it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

“Kauśika! If there are various wicked non-Buddhist brahmins, or wicked Māras and their retinues, or other violent and arrogant individuals who wish to inflict various kinds of harm upon this bodhisattva mahāsattva, as soon as they give rise to such thoughts, they will swiftly meet with calamity; their intentions shall surely be extinguished and their wishes shall not be fulfilled.”
Why is this so, Kauśika?

Because when these sons and daughters of good family wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this profound Prajñāpāramitā, it is by the very nature of things that those who harbor evil intentions will naturally encounter calamities and fail to achieve their desires.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, with sincere hearts, listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, contemplate according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā;

In that place, should there be evil Māras or their retinues, or various non-Buddhist brahmins, or other violent and arrogant individuals who, out of envy for the True Dharma, wish to create obstacles, rebuke, oppose, and cause it to quickly disappear—though they harbor such intentions, they shall ultimately never succeed.

Because they have briefly heard the sound of Prajñā, their manifold evils gradually perish and their merits gradually arise; subsequently, by relying on the Three Vehicles, they attain the end of suffering, or they escape the evil destinies to be reborn among gods or humans.

“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, with a sincere mind, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they shall obtain such meritorious benefits as these.”

“Kauśika! Suppose there were a wondrous medicine called Mākṣī; by its majestic power, it can neutralize all poisons. Wherever this wondrous medicine is located, various venomous insects cannot approach it.”

There was a large venomous snake that, hungry, went about seeking food; encountering a living being, it wished to sting and devour it. That creature, terrified of death, fled toward a potent medicine; upon smelling the scent of the medicine, the snake immediately retreated and ran away.
Why is this? Kauśika!
Such a wondrous medicine possesses great majestic power; it can benefit life and body, and it can subdue and eliminate all poisons.

Kauśika, you should know that the Prajñāpāramitā possesses great majestic power in this very same way. If sons or daughters of good family listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle, copy it, explain it, and cause it to be widely disseminated, then whatever evil deeds the Māras and their like intend to commit against these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall, by the majestic spiritual power of this Prajñāpāramitā, be naturally extinguished in that very place, rendering them powerless to act.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this Prajñāpāramitā possesses great majestic power, being able to destroy all evils and increase wholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā;

The Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, Mahābrahmā Lord of the Sahā World, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens, and other benevolent deities constantly come to provide protection, ensuring that no calamities or afflictions may invade or disturb them, and that whatever they seek in accordance with the Dharma shall be fully satisfied.

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions also constantly protect and keep [this person] in mind, causing evil to gradually diminish and wholesome dharmas to gradually increase.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family are able to wholeheartedly hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this *prajñāpāramitā*, then by virtue of these causes and conditions, the speech of these sons and daughters of good family will be majestic and solemn such that all who hear it respectfully accept it; their words will be measured and their speech free from clamor; they will steadfastly serve virtuous friends and deeply understand how to repay their kindness; and their minds will not be obscured by stinginess, envy, anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, flattery, deception, or hypocrisy.
Why is this so? Kauśika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family, through the superior power of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, have disciplined their bodies and minds, causing them to remain far removed from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*) such as greed, hatred, and delusion.

These sons and daughters of good family, endowed with mindfulness, clear comprehension, and the [four immeasurables] of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, constantly reflect:
"I must not follow the power of stinginess and greed; for if I were to follow that power, I would become poor and lowly, and my perfection of giving would not be fulfilled.
I must not follow the power of breaking the precepts; for if I were to follow that power, I would fall into the various evil destinies, and my perfection of pure morality would not be fulfilled."

I should not follow the power of anger; if I were to follow its force, my faculties would be impaired, my physical appearance would be ugly, I would not possess the perfect body of a bodhisattva, and I would further be unable to fulfill patience.
I should not follow the power of laziness; if I were to follow its force, I would be unable to cultivate the supreme path of a bodhisattva, nor would I fulfill superior diligence.

I should not follow the power of distraction; if I were to follow its force, I would be unable to cultivate the supreme meditative concentration of a bodhisattva, and thus the various dhyānas would not be perfected.

I should not follow the power of delusion; for if I were to follow its power, my supreme wisdom would not reach fulfillment, and I would not transcend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, much less attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
"Therefore, I should not now follow the power of that stinginess, greed, and so forth. Kausika!
By means of this reflection, these sons and daughters of good family always attain right mindfulness, and various evil afflictions do not obscure their minds.

“Kauśika! If any sons or daughters of good family wholeheartedly hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, they shall obtain such meritorious benefits as these.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 539;
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 540.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Part Four: Chapter Three, Part Two, "Offerings to the Stūpa. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is most marvelous and rare; it is able to discipline the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to abandon arrogance and to dedicate themselves toward the attainment of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:

"In what way is the Prajñāpāramitā so marvelous and rare, being able to discipline the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they abandon arrogance and redirect their efforts toward the attainment of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna)?"
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not rely on the perfection of wisdom when practicing from generosity up to wisdom, as well as various other dharmas of the Buddhas, then because they lack skillful means, although they cultivate various virtues, they give rise to a haughty mind and are unable to dedicate them toward the knowledge of all modes."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon the perfection of wisdom and practices generosity up to wisdom, as well as various other dharmas of a buddha, because they possess skillful means, they subdue their arrogant mind regarding all the virtues they cultivate and dedicate them toward the attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. "Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family are able to hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, contemplate according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate the Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, these sons and daughters of good family will experience peace and happiness in body and mind, and shall not be afflicted by any calamities or misfortunes."

If, while in the midst of military conflict on the battlefield, one recites this Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, maintaining compassion and protective mindfulness toward all sentient beings, one shall not be harmed or killed by blades or clubs; all opposing enemies will give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness, and even if they harbor evil intentions, they will naturally retreat and be defeated.

It is impossible that these sons and daughters of good family should lose their lives or have their bodies destroyed by being wounded by swords or arrows in the midst of military campaigns. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because these sons and daughters of good family who practice the perfection of wisdom are themselves able to subdue afflictions, evil karma, and various weapons, and are likewise able to eliminate the afflictions, evil karma, and all weapons of others.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect upon according to principle, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise the Prajñāpāramitā, and copy it, explain it, and cause it to be widely disseminated—then these good sons and good daughters cannot be harmed by any poisons, sorcery, ghosts and spirits, curses, incantations, or spells; they cannot be drowned by water, burned by fire, or injured by blades, weapons, wild beasts, enemies, thieves, evil deities, various heterodoxies, or malevolent specters."
Why is this so? Kauśika!
This Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and a mantra equal to the unequaled.

Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is the king of all mantras; it is the most supreme, the most wondrous, and peerless. Possessing great majestic power, it can subdue all things and cannot itself be subdued by anything.
These sons and daughters of good family who diligently practice and study this King of Mantras shall not be harmed by themselves, nor harmed by others, nor harmed by both.

Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, although they have no attainment of either myself or the Dharma, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By means of this, they obtain the knowledge of all modes; they observe the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and, according to what is appropriate, turn the unexcelled wheel of Dharma, enabling those who practice as taught to obtain great benefit.
Why is this? Kausika!

All bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present study this profound Great Dharani King of the Prajñāpāramitā; there is nothing they do not attain and nothing they do not realize. For this reason, it is called the "knowledge of all modes" (sarvajñajñāna).

“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, with sincere hearts, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect upon according to the principle, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this Prajñāpāramitā, transcribe it, explain it, and cause it to be widely disseminated, they shall obtain such various merits as these in both the present life and future lives.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters write down this Great Divine Mantra King of the Prajñāpāramitā and place it in a pure location, making offerings to it, honoring, respecting, and praising it—even if they do not hear it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle, nor explain or analyze it for others—nevertheless, all humans and non-humans in that dwelling place, kingdom, city, or royal capital shall not be harmed by any calamities, misfortunes, or epidemics."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good men and good women, fearing enemies, wild beasts, calamities, malevolent incantations, epidemics, poisons, spells, and the like, should write down this Great Divine Spell King of the Prajñāpāramitā and place it within a precious tube contained in a small sachet of various fragrances, constantly carrying it with them and making offerings and paying it respect, all matters of fear will be entirely eliminated. Devas, nāgas, and spirits will constantly come to protect them, except for those karmic results from past lives that must be experienced."
Kauśika! For example, if a person or even an animal were to enter the precincts of the Bodhi tree or merely reach its vicinity, neither humans nor non-humans would be able to harm them.
Why is this? Kauśika!

All Buddhas of the past, future, and present sit in this very place and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having attained enlightenment, they bestow upon all sentient beings freedom from fear, freedom from dread, freedom from enmity, and freedom from harm, granting them peace and happiness of body and mind.
It should be known that the Perfection of Wisdom is likewise in every place where it abides; all devas, nāgas, asuras, and others constantly come to protect it.

Kauśika! Wherever this Prajñāpāramitā may abide, you should know that this place is a true caitya; all sentient beings should pay homage to it, and they should honor, revere, respect, and praise it with various kinds of supreme and exquisite offerings.
"Why is this? Because these sentient beings are the objects of refuge.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If good sons and good daughters write down this Prajñāpāramitā and provide it with various adornments, offerings, reverence, respect, and praise; and further offer it various exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, many wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps for illumination;..."

There may be sons of good family, daughters of good family, and others who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, erect stūpas adorned with the seven precious gems, place the Buddha’s śarīra within them contained in jeweled caskets, and offer them worship, reverence, respect, and praise; furthermore, they provide offerings of various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, myriad wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps.
"Of these two, which would yield more merit?
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"I shall question you in return; answer as you see fit."
"What do you think?
By what path did the Tathāgata train in order to attain the omniscience of all-knowledge, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment that he realized, and the physical body upon which it rests?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

"The all-knowing wisdom attained by the Tathāgata, the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by him, and the body upon which it relies—all these are obtained through training in the perfection of wisdom."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Because I have trained in the Perfection of Wisdom, I have attained the knowledge of all modes, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment that was realized, and the body upon which it rests.
Why is this? Kausika!
It is impossible that one who has not studied the perfection of wisdom could obtain the knowledge of all modes, realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, or attain the body upon which it relies.

“Kauśika! It is not merely by attaining the body endowed with the marks and signs that one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; rather, it is by realizing the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) that one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

Kauśika! The omniscient wisdom (sarvajñajñāna) attained by the Tathāgata arises necessarily with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) as its cause; the Buddha’s body of marks and signs (lakṣaṇavyañjana-kāya) serves merely as its basis. If one does not rely upon the Buddha’s body of marks and signs, there would be no means for it to arise. Therefore, while the perfection of wisdom is the direct cause that gives rise to omniscient wisdom, in order to cause this wisdom to manifest and continue uninterruptedly, one further cultivates and accumulates the Buddha’s body of marks and signs.
If this body endowed with the primary and secondary marks were not the basis for omniscience, then all devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others would not offer it sincere worship and respect.
Because this body endowed with the marks and signs serves as the basis for the Buddha’s universal wisdom, it is venerated and honored by devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others.
For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, non-humans, and others shall likewise venerate and honor my śarīra relics.

“Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters write down this Prajñāpāramitā and offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to it, they are thereby making offerings to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), to the Buddha’s body endowed with the marks and signs of excellence upon which that knowledge relies, and to the Buddha’s relics after his parinirvāṇa.”
Why is this? Kausika!
It is because the knowledge of all modes, as well as the body endowed with the marks and signs and the śarīra relics, all have the perfection of wisdom as their root.
For this reason, Kauśika,

if any sons or daughters of good family write down this Prajñāpāramitā, and with various adornments offer it worship, respect, honor, and praise, further making offerings of various exquisite flower garlands up to lamps and lights;

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, erect a stūpa adorned with the seven precious gems; they place the Buddha’s śarīra within a casket made of jewels and enshrine it therein, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising it, further offering various kinds of exquisite flower garlands and even lamps for illumination.
Of these two, the merit obtained by the former is many times greater, immeasurable fold.
Why is this? Kausika!

If sons or daughters of good family make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are thereby making offerings to the reliquaries (śarīra) of the Buddha’s body endowed with the marks and signs of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The people of Jambudvīpa are unable to transcribe this Prajñāpāramitā adorned with various jewels, nor to honor, revere, respect, and praise it; they are unable to hear it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, apply themselves diligently to its study, or contemplate it according to the principle. How is it that they do not know that by transcribing this Prajñāpāramitā adorned with various jewels, and by honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it, and by hearing it with a sincere heart, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, applying themselves diligently to its study, and contemplating it according to the principle, one obtains various meritorious benefits?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?"
Within Jambudvīpa, how many people have attained the verified confidence in the Buddha, the verified confidence in the Dharma, and the verified confidence in the Saṅgha?
How many people have attained the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship?
How many people have resolved their minds to definitely proceed toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?
How many people have resolved their minds to definitely proceed toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

"Within Jambudvīpa, there are few people who have attained pure faith in the Buddha, pure faith in the Dharma, and pure faith in the Saṅgha; even fewer have attained the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; even fewer have resolved their minds to definitely attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and even fewer have resolved their minds to definitely attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Kausika! Within Jambudvīpa, there are only a very small number of people who have attained pure confidence in the Buddha, pure confidence in the Dharma, and pure confidence in the Saṃgha."

Regarding the purities of realization (*avetyaprasāda*): a small number of people attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship;
a small number of people resolve their minds to definitely proceed toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
a small number of people resolve their minds to definitely proceed toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; and a small number...
Once some people have already resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they diligently practice and train in the conduct leading to bodhi;
yet fewer still diligently practice and train in the conduct of bodhi when they come to receive and accept this *prajñāpāramitā* with a profound mind;
and even fewer, having received it with deep faith, actually practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Once a small number of people have practiced, they gradually come to abide in the stage of non-retrogression;
and once a further small number of people abide in this stage, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained abiding on the stage of non-retrogression and seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they will be able to deeply revere, believe in, and accept this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere heart; they will listen to it with all their being, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and reflect upon it according to the Dharma. Furthermore, they will unerringly proclaim it for others, and moreover, honor, respect, venerate, and praise it by making offerings of various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and lights.”

“Kauśika! With my unobstructed, pure Buddha-eye, I survey the boundless worlds of the ten directions. Although there are immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings who have resolved for bodhicitta and practice the bodhisattva path, because they are far removed from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), only one, two, or three sentient beings may attain the stage of non-retrogression as bodhisattvas; for the most part, they fall back into the lower inclinations, lower practices, and inferior stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
Why is this? Kausika!

The merit of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is boundless and extremely difficult to realize; sentient beings with evil wisdom, indolence, inferior diligence, or inferior resolute conviction cannot attain it.
"Therefore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters who have resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and practice the bodhisattva path wish to abide in the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without hindrance, they should repeatedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect according to the principle upon this *prajñāpāramitā*. They should take pleasure in questioning their teachers and delighting in explaining it to others; furthermore, they should write it down, adorn it with various jewels, and offer it worship, respect, honor, and praise."
Why is this? Kausika!
These sons and daughters of good family should form this thought:

"When the Tathāgata formerly dwelt on the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated and studied the profound meaning and intent of this Prajñāpāramitā, thereby realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; we, too, should diligently cultivate and study this Prajñāpāramitā."
"He is my Great Teacher; following his instruction, my aspirations shall be fulfilled. Kausika!
Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always rely upon and diligently train in the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If good sons and good daughters, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth, and extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings; or if they transcribe it, adorn it with various jewels, and further offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to lamps and lights, to honor, revere, respect, and praise it."
“By this cause and condition, how much merit will these sons and daughters of good family obtain?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
“The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable; it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha’s relics (śarīra), construct stūpas out of the seven precious jewels, adorned with various rare and wonderful ornaments, and further offer various celestial flower garlands up to lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them throughout their entire lives."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would those sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha told Kauśika:

“There may be sons of good family or daughters of good family who, with a pure mind, respectfully believe in and understand this profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle, extensively proclaim and explain it for the sake of sentient beings, and examine it with superior wisdom in a thorough and precise manner.”

In order that the True Dharma may long abide in the world; in order that the Buddha-eye may not be severed or destroyed; in order that the True Dharma may not disappear; in order to embrace and cause Bodhisattvas to increase; and in order that the pure Dharma-eye of the world may not be severed or destroyed—one should transcribe this profound *prajñāpāramitā* adorned with various jewels, and further offer it various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, and manifold wonders.
With rare and marvelous objects, music, and lamps, they shall offer worship, respect, honor, and praise.
The merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Let us set aside this one matter.

Suppose good sons and good daughters, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha’s śarīras, erect stūpas made of the seven exquisite precious gems, adorned with various rare and wonderful ornaments. Suppose they fill an entire Jambudvīpa, or the four continents, or a small thousand-world system, or a medium thousand-world system, or even a trichiliocosm with such stūpas, and throughout their entire lives, they offer and revere them, honoring, respecting, and praising them with all kinds of celestial flower garlands up to lamps and lights."
"What do you think?
Would these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said to Kauśika:

“There may be sons of good family or daughters of good family who, with a pure mind, respectfully believe in and understand this profound meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā; seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle, extensively proclaim and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings, and examine it with thorough discernment through superior wisdom.”

In order that the True Dharma may long abide in the world; in order that the Buddha-eye may not be severed or destroyed; in order that the True Dharma may not disappear; in order to sustain bodhisattvas so that they may increase; and in order that the pure Dharma-eye of the world may not be severed or destroyed—one should write out this profound *prajñāpāramitā* adorned with various jewels, and further offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, wonderful and rare treasures, music, and lamps, to worship, revere, honor, and praise it.
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Setting aside this matter for a moment:

suppose that every sentient being within this Jambudvīpa, or every sentient being in the four great continents, or every sentient being in a small thousand-world system, or every sentient being in a medium thousand-world system, or even every sentient being in a great trichiliocosm, were each to erect a single great stūpa made of the seven precious jewels—adorned with various rare and wonderful ornaments—after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha’s śarīra. Suppose they were to offer all kinds of celestial flower garlands and even lamps, and throughout their entire lives, each were to offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise at their respective stūpas.
What do you think?

Would the sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa, or in the four continents, or in a small thousand-world system, or a medium thousand-world system, or a great trichiliocosm, acquire much merit by reason of this cause and condition?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so,
Sugata! The Buddha told Kauśika:

“There may be sons and daughters of good family who, with a pure mind, respectfully believe in and understand this profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*; for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they listen with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, reflect upon it according to the principle, extensively proclaim and reveal it to sentient beings, and examine it with thorough scrutiny through superior wisdom.”

In order that the True Dharma may long abide in the world; in order that the Buddha-eye may never be severed or destroyed; in order that the True Dharma may not vanish; in order to sustain and cause Bodhisattvas to flourish; and in order that the pure Dharma-eye of the world may never be severed or destroyed—one should write out this profound Prajñāpāramitā, adorning it with various jewels, and further offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, myriad wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps, to worship, revere, honor, and praise it.
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Setting aside this matter:

suppose that all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa were to become human beings simultaneously, neither before nor after one another; and suppose that each and every one of them, for the sake of making offerings to the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddha, were to erect a *stūpa* made of the seven exquisite precious substances—adorned and interspersed with various rare and wonderful treasures—after the parinirvāṇa of each Tathāgata, such that these individual *stūpas* filled the entirety of Jambudvīpa.

Or suppose that all sentient beings throughout the four great continents were to become human beings simultaneously, neither before nor after one another; and suppose that each and every one of them, for the sake of making offerings to the *śarīra* of the Buddha, were to erect a *stūpa* made of the seven exquisite precious substances—adorned and interspersed with various rare and wonderful treasures—after the parinirvāṇa of each Tathāgata, such that these individual *stūpas* filled the entirety of the four great continents.

Or suppose that all sentient beings within a small chiliocosm, without one preceding or following another, were all to become human; and each of these individuals, for the sake of making offerings to the *śarīra* of the Buddha, were to erect a *stūpa* out of exquisite seven precious gems—adorned and interspersed with various rare and wonderful treasures—such that each individual filled an entire small chiliocosm.

Or suppose that all sentient beings within a medium dichiliocosm, without one preceding or following another, were all to become human; and each of these individuals, for the sake of making offerings to the *śarīra* of the Buddha, were to erect a *stūpa* out of exquisite seven precious gems—adorned and interspersed with various rare and wonderful treasures—such that each individual filled an entire medium dichiliocosm.

Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were to become human beings simultaneously, neither before nor after one another; and suppose each of these individuals, for the sake of making offerings to the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha, were to erect a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels—adorned and embellished with various rare and wonderful treasures—after the parinirvāṇa of each Tathāgata, such that there was one for every individual filling the entire trichiliocosm.

These people, each holding various kinds of celestial, exquisite flower garlands and even lamps, for one kalpa or more than one kalpa, each made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised at their respective stūpas.
What do you think?

Would the sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa, or the four continents, or a small thousandfold world system, or a medium thousandfold world system, or a great trichiliocosm, acquire much merit by reason of these causes and conditions?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so,
Sugata! The Buddha told Kauśika:

“There may be sons and daughters of good family who, with a pure mind, respectfully believe in and understand this profound meaning and purpose of the *prajñāpāramitā*; seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, reflect upon it according to the principle, extensively proclaim and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings, and examine it with discerning wisdom.”

In order that the True Dharma may long abide in the world; in order that the Buddha-eye may not be severed or destroyed; in order that the True Dharma may not vanish; in order to embrace and cause Bodhisattvas to increase; and in order that the pure Dharma-eye of the world may not be severed or destroyed—one should write out this profound Prajñāpāramitā adorned with various jewels, and further offer it worship, respect, reverence, and praise with all kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps.
"The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is so!"
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"

If sons or daughters of good family offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that they are thereby offering worship, reverence, respect, and praise to the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñājñāna*) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
“Blessed One!

Setting aside for now all the sentient beings in the trichiliocosm whom you have mentioned—each of whom, for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgata’s relics, erects a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.

Suppose that all sentient beings in every world throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were simultaneously to become human beings, neither before nor after one another. Suppose each of these individuals, after the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, were to construct a stūpa for the veneration of the Buddha’s śarīra using exquisite seven precious gems, adorned with various rare and wonderful ornaments. Suppose each of them were to fill the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with such stūpas; and suppose each were to hold various celestial flower garlands, up to lamps and lights, and for one kalpa or more than one kalpa, offer worship, respect, honor, and praise.
Although the mass of merit obtained by these sentient beings through these causes and conditions is immeasurable, it is still surpassed by another.

Any sons or daughters of good family who, with a pure mind, respectfully believe in and understand this profound meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to principle, extensively proclaim and reveal it to sentient beings, and examine it with superior wisdom in a thorough and precise manner—[their merit shall be even greater].

In order that the True Dharma may long abide in the world; in order that the Buddha-eye may not be severed or destroyed; in order that the True Dharma may not vanish; in order to sustain and cause Bodhisattvas to increase; and in order that the pure Dharma-eye of the world may not be severed or destroyed—one should write out this profound *prajñāpāramitā* adorned with various jewels, and further offer it with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, wonderful and rare treasures, music, and lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it.

The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that—immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable; it cannot be reached by calculation, nor can it be approached by analogy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said, Kauśika!

For these sons and daughters of good family, the mass of merit obtained from this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable; it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes; and because the knowledge of all modes of all Tathāgatas can give birth to the *śarīras* of all Buddhas.
"For this reason, Kauśika!

If any sons or daughters of good family, with a pure mind, can respectfully believe in and understand the profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, reflect upon it according to the truth, extensively proclaim and reveal it to sentient beings, and examine it with superior wisdom through careful scrutiny."

In order that the True Dharma may long abide in the world; in order that the Buddha-eye may never be severed or destroyed; in order that the True Dharma may not vanish; in order to embrace and cause Bodhisattvas to increase; and in order that the pure Dharma-eye of the world may never be severed or destroyed—one should transcribe this profound Prajñāpāramitā, adorning it with various jewels, and further offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, wonderful and rare treasures, music, and lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it.

The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family surpasses the merit from constructing the aforementioned stūpas and making offerings a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold more excellent.
At that time, forty thousand devaputras within the assembly raised their voices in unison and addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Great Seer!

Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should hear it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently study and practice it, reflect upon it according to the principle, and extensively analyze and explain it for others, while making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising it."

Why is this so? Because if one can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently study, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the truth, and furthermore extensively analyze and explain it for others, while making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising it, then all unwholesome dharmas will diminish and wholesome dharmas will increase.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:

"You should, with a sincere mind, listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle; furthermore, you should extensively analyze and explain it for others, making offerings to it, honoring, respecting, and praising it."
Why is this? If the asuras and their evil factions should give rise to such a thought:
"We shall wage war against the Trāyastriṃśa gods."

"At that time, you and your retinues of devas should each, with utmost sincerity, recite and contemplate this profound Prajñāpāramitā, making offerings to it, honoring it, respecting it, and praising it."
At that time, the evil intentions arising from the asuras and their factions were immediately extinguished.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The profound Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, an unequaled mantra; it is the king of all mantras, most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most wondrous. It can subdue all things and cannot be subdued by anything."
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can extinguish all evil and unwholesome dharmas, and can fulfill all supreme and wholesome dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said. Why is this? Kausika!

All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have, by relying upon this profound Great Dharani King of Prajñāpāramitā, realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turned the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and delivered the multitudes of sentient beings.

I, too, by relying on this great king of dhāraṇīs, the profound Prajñāpāramitā, have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and I preach the unsurpassed Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.

“Kauśika! By relying on this great king of mantras, the profound Prajñāpāramitā, there come to exist in the world the ten paths of wholesome action associated with the factors of awakening, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six supernormal powers, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.”
Kauśika! To speak briefly, the eighty-four thousand aggregates of all wholesome dharmas have all appeared in the world by relying upon this profound Great Dhāraṇī King, the Prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! All Buddha-wisdom, spontaneously arisen wisdom, and inconceivable wisdom all appear in the world by depending upon this Great Dharani King, the Prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! It is by relying on this great king of spells, the profound Prajñāpāramitā, that Bodhisattvas appear in the world;

and because of the Bodhisattvas, there appear in the world the ten paths of wholesome action associated with the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six supernormal powers, and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

If Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not appear in the world, there are only Bodhisattvas who, through the power of the outflow of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* previously heard, have accomplished sublime skillful means; out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, they establish and institute the ten paths of wholesome action associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
Kauśika! It is like the night, when the light of the full moon shines upon them, causing the stars, medicinal herbs, and other things to flourish according to their respective powers.

Thus, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma has vanished, and before another has yet appeared, all worldly practices of the Dharma and sublime conduct depend entirely upon the appearance of a Bodhisattva.
All the skillful means of a bodhisattva are accomplished by relying upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Therefore, the perfection of wisdom is the root of all excellent and wholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family should, with a sincere mind, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they shall achieve the meritorious benefits of both the present and future worlds, as well as supramundane virtues."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How do these sons and daughters of good family accomplish the benefits and excellences of mundane and supramundane merit in the present and future lives?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

"These sons and daughters of good family shall, in the present life, not be harmed by any poisons, malevolent incantations, or sorcery; fire cannot burn them, water cannot drown them, and various weapons such as swords and staves likewise cannot injure them. They shall not even meet their end through the four hundred and four types of diseases, except for those karmic results of determinate actions from previous lives that must be experienced in the present."

Kauśika! If these sons and daughters of good family encounter legal troubles or are oppressed by enemies and bandits, and they recite and contemplate the profound Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, then when they come before those [oppressors], they will ultimately not be punished or harmed; and though those [oppressors] seek their faults, they shall be unable to find any.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the majestic power and influence of the profound Prajñāpāramitā cause things to be thus.

Kauśika! If these sons and daughters of good family wish to go before kings, princes, ministers, and the like, and recite the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere mind, they will certainly be greeted with joy by those kings and others, who will then offer them sustenance, respect, honor, and praise.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family constantly evoke various acts of compassion toward sentient beings through their recitation of the *prajñāpāramitā*, by virtue of these causes and conditions, those who seek faults—whether in wildernesses, perilous places, or among humans and non-humans—shall find no opportunity.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family shall attain the accomplishment of all such present merits and benefits as these.

“Kauśika! Wherever these sons and daughters of good family are born, they shall never be separated from the various supreme wholesome dharmas; they shall not fall into the evil destinies, shall benefit sentient beings, and will gradually be able to realize the knowledge of all modes.”
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family shall attain the accomplishment of all such future merits and benefits as these.
At that time, a great multitude of non-Buddhist brahmins, wishing to seek out the Buddha, approached the place where he was.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw them, he thought to himself:
"Now these many non-Buddhist brahmins are coming toward this Dharma assembly seeking to find fault with the Buddha; could this not be an obstacle created by Prajñā?"
"I shall recite and contemplate the profound Prajñāpāramitā as I received it from the Buddha, so that those followers of heterodox paths may return whence they came.
Having thought this, he then recited the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Thereupon, the many non-Buddhist brahmins extended their respectful salutations from afar, circumambulated the World-Honored One to the right, and departed by the way they had come.
At that time, having seen this, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"For what reason did they just now come and then depart?"
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, told Śāriputra:
"Those non-Buddhists came seeking my faults; it was through the recitation of the Prajñāpāramitā by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, that they were made to depart."
Śāriputra! I do not see even the slightest trace of white dharma in those non-Buddhists; they have come to me solely out of malice, seeking to find fault with me.

Śāriputra! I do not see anyone in all the worlds—whether among the gods, Māras, or outsiders—who, being a sentient being, could harbor a malevolent mind while the Prajñā is being taught and come seeking an opportunity to find fault; for the power of the Prajñā is such that none can destroy it.
At that time, Māra the Evil One secretly thought to himself:
"Now the Buddha is surrounded by the fourfold assembly before and behind, and the devas of the desire and form realms have all gathered to hear him proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā."

Within this assembly there must surely be great bodhisattvas who have personally received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha, who shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, emptying my domain.
"I shall go there and destroy his eyes.
Having formed this thought, he manifested the fourfold army and, displaying fierce prowess and sharp valor, approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw him and thought to himself:
"Could it not be that Māra has manifested these things, desiring to come and disturb the Buddha and create obstacles for the Prajñāpāramitā?
For what reason?"
These four armies, so magnificently adorned and exquisite, are such that none of the hosts of other kings can equal them; they must surely be an emanation created by Māra, the Evil One.

For a long night, Māra has sought out the Buddha’s vulnerabilities and sought to destroy the sublime accomplishments cultivated by sentient beings. I shall now recite and contemplate the profound Prajñāpāramitā as received from the Buddha, so that this evil Māra may be sent back upon his way.

Then, having thought thus, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, recited the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Thereupon, the evil Māra gradually retreated and departed, compelled by the majestic power of this great king of spells, the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
