At that time, immeasurable devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven simultaneously manifested celestial *divyagandhapuṣpa* (wondrous-scented flowers) and, leaping into the air, scattered them over the Buddha. With palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha in unison:
“May this Prajñāpāramitā long abide among the people of Jambudvīpa, and may the Prajñāpāramitā continue to circulate among the people of Jambudvīpa.”
"You should know that in such a place, the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha shall never perish; it will benefit the world, causing it to obtain supreme benefit, peace, and happiness.
At that time, those devas each further manifested celestial *mañjūṣaka* flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If sentient beings practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, all Māras and their retinues, though seeking to find a flaw, will be unable to gain an advantage."
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If sentient beings merely hear the names and the qualities of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that such beings have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, have formed great vows in the presence of those Buddhas, and have accumulated vast roots of virtue capable of accomplishing this matter; they have not come from meager roots of virtue. How much more so for those who can hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect according to the truth, copy, explain, widely disseminate, and offer worship, respect, honor, and praise!”
It should be known that the merit and wisdom of such sentient beings are inconceivable. Why is this?

Those who seek the omniscient wisdom of all Buddhas must seek it within the principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, just as sentient beings who seek great jewels must diligently seek them in the great ocean through skillful means; likewise, those who seek the omniscient wisdom must seek it within the principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
All the omniscient wisdom attained by the Buddhas is accomplished in reliance upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Therefore, the perfection of wisdom is the most supreme root of all the Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

for what reason do you not praise the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, as well as other virtues, but praise only the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because this prajñāpāramitā serves as the sovereign and the guide for the first five pāramitās and all other merits, I praise it specifically."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
What do you think?

If one practices giving, up to and including wisdom, without dedicating it toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), can this be called truly practicing the perfection of giving, up to and including the perfection of wisdom?"
Ānanda replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

Only by dedicating [the merit] toward omniscience (sarvajñājñāna) while practicing from generosity up to wisdom can it be called the true cultivation of the perfections (pāramitās), from generosity up to wisdom.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“What do you think?

If one practices giving, up to and including wisdom, without dedicating it toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), would such practice be called a perfection (pāramitā) of giving and so forth?”
Ānanda replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

One must practice from generosity up to wisdom by dedicating them toward omniscience; only when practiced in this manner do they receive the name of "perfections" (pāramitās), such as the perfection of generosity and so forth.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What do you think?
If one cultivates roots of goodness without dedicating them toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), will such roots of goodness reach their ultimate consummation?"
Ānanda replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"One must cultivate roots of goodness by dedicating them toward omniscience; only in this way do such roots of goodness reach their ultimate fulfillment.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "What do you think?"
“If one were separated from the perfection of wisdom, would one be able to truly dedicate [merit] toward the knowledge of all modes? Ānanda replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
It is only through the perfection of wisdom that there can be a true dedication toward the knowledge of all modes.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What do you think?
Can the majestic power and meritorious qualities of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* be conceived?
Ānanda replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The majestic power and meritorious virtues of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are inconceivable; all other roots of goodness cannot equal them."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"For this reason, I say that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) serves as the sovereign and the guide for the first five perfections and all other merits; it brings the first five perfections and all other merits to ultimate fulfillment. Therefore, I praise it preeminently."
"If one praises the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one also praises the first five perfections and all other merits.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How does one dedicate [merit] toward omniscience (sarvajñājñāna) while practicing the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, as well as other merits?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"By means of non-duality as the skillful method, non-arising as the skillful method, and non-apprehension as the skillful method, one should dedicate [the merit] toward omniscience and cultivate the perfections from generosity through prajñā, as well as other meritorious qualities."
The Venerable Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“By means of what non-duality, by means of what non-arising, and by means of what non-apprehension should one dedicate toward all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) the practice of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), as well as other meritorious qualities?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“By means of the non-duality of form through to consciousness, by means of non-arising, and by means of non-apprehension, one should dedicate [the merit] toward omniscience and cultivate the perfections from generosity through to wisdom, as well as other meritorious qualities.”

Because phenomena such as form are all empty of intrinsic nature, and because the emptiness of the nature of form and so forth is non-dual with generosity and the other perfections, Ānanda, you should know this:

it is through the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that one can dedicate [merit] toward omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*); and by being able to dedicate it toward omniscience, one brings the boundless merits of generosity and the rest to ultimate fulfillment.
Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the sovereign and the guide for all meritorious qualities such as generosity.
"Ānanda, you should know this:

just as when seeds are sown in the great earth, they grow through the convergence of various conditions, so too should it be understood that the great earth serves as the support and the foundation for the growth of those seeds."

Thus, because this *prajñāpāramitā* and the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) toward which it is dedicated serve as the basis and the support for all merits such as generosity, causing them to grow and flourish, it is said that *prajñāpāramitā* is the sovereign and the guide of all merits such as generosity. Therefore, I specifically praise the profound *prajñāpāramitā* rather than other merits; for if one praises *prajñā*, one praises the others as well.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 540;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 541.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three, Part Three: The Fourth Division, The Chapter on Making Offerings to the Stūpa. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has not yet finished expounding upon the meritorious benefits of the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? The merits and benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā* that I have received from the World-Honored One are exceedingly profound, exceedingly vast, and immeasurable in their extent.

All sons and daughters of good family who, with a sincere heart, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently study, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and further make offerings of various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps and illuminations, shall obtain merit that is likewise boundless.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as you have said, Kauśika!
I do not say that this profound perfection of wisdom possesses only the merits and benefits previously described."
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is endowed with boundless meritorious benefits, such that its detailed exposition can never be exhausted.

Kauśika! I do not say that one who listens to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere heart, upholds, recites, diligently studies, reflects upon it according to the principle, copies it, explains it, causes it to be widely disseminated, and further makes offerings of various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps, [attains the merit].
All sons and daughters of good family shall possess only the aforementioned merits and benefits.
Why is this? Kausika!

If sons or daughters of good family, with a pure mind, reverently accept this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, reflect upon it according to the principle, extensively proclaim and reveal it to sentient beings, and examine it with thorough scrutiny through superior wisdom; [they shall attain great merit].

In order to cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world; in order to ensure that the Buddha-eye is never severed or destroyed; in order to prevent the True Dharma from vanishing; in order to embrace and cause Bodhisattvas to increase in virtue; and in order to ensure that the pure Dharma-eye of the world remains without deficiency—[one] shall transcribe this profound Prajñāpāramitā, adorning it with various jewels, and further offer it various exquisite flower garlands, up to lamps and lights, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it.
"I say that they shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merits and benefits in the present and the future.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We gods will constantly follow and protect these sons and daughters of good family, so that no humans or non-humans, nor any various adverse conditions, shall be able to harm them."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
"If sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, read, and recite the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and extensively proclaim, explain, and reveal it to others."
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras gathered together for the sake of hearing the Dharma; with joyful exultation, they reverently received this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

By their celestial power, these devaputras cause the Dharma-preacher’s eloquence to increase so that his proclamation is inexhaustible; they cause those who do not delight in speaking to find joy in speaking, and they restore the physical and mental exhaustion of the speaker so that he attains vigor and strength.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family who uphold, recite, and extensively explain and reveal this profound Prajñāpāramitā to others shall obtain such present benefits as these.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family, among the fourfold assembly, proclaim this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with hearts free from fear or trepidation, they shall not be overcome by any form of debate or challenge."

Why is this? Because they are protected and sustained by this great king of mantras, the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and because within the secret treasury of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* all phenomena are extensively analyzed and distinguished.

Because these sons and daughters of good family dwell well in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), they do not perceive at all a challenger, an object of challenge, or that which is spoken; nor do they perceive anyone who could seek out flaws in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they perceive any fault in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. For this reason, they cannot be overcome by the polemical challenges of any heterodox schools.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family who proclaim this profound *prajñāpāramitā* to the assembly shall obtain such benefits in the present life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons and daughters of good family, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this profound Prajñāpāramitā;
These sons and daughters of good family do not sink into despondency, nor do they feel regret; they are neither afraid nor terrified. Why is this?
Because these sons and daughters of good family do not perceive any dharma that could cause them to sink, regret, or be terrified; they have no attachment to any dharmas whatsoever.
Kauśika! Because these sons and daughters of good family wholeheartedly listen to, and even propagate, this Prajñāpāramitā, they obtain such benefits in the present life as these.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters are able to listen with a sincere mind to this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently study it, contemplate it according to the principle, copy it, explain it, and cause it to be widely disseminated; and furthermore, offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps as an act of worship."

These sons and daughters of good family will always be held in respect and affection by their parents, teachers, elders, relatives, friends, kings, ministers, and all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; they will also be protected and remembered by the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions; furthermore, they will be guarded by the devas, māras, brahmās, humans, and non-humans of the world; all calamities and misfortunes will naturally vanish, and the heterodox arguments of outsiders shall be unable to overcome them.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family, by listening with a sincere heart to the Prajñāpāramitā and even making offerings to it, obtain such present benefits as these.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā, adorn it in various ways, and place it in a pure location, making offerings to it, honoring, respecting, and praising it."

At that time, all those belonging to the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Broad Fruit—within this trichiliocosm and throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions—who had already resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta, would constantly come to this place to behold and pay homage to, recite and chant, make offerings to, revere, respect, praise, circumambulate to the right, and prostrate before the profound Prajñāpāramitā, and then depart with palms joined.

The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens also constantly come here to behold and pay homage to this profound Prajñāpāramitā; they make offerings, show reverence, honor, and praise it, circumambulate it to the right, prostrate, and depart with palms joined.

Nāgas and yakṣas of great majesty and power, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, also constantly come here to behold and pay homage to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, to read and recite it, and to make offerings, show reverence, honor, and praise it; they circumambulate it to the right, prostrate, join their palms, and depart.
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family should form this thought:

‘Now, all the devas, nāgas, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, from this trichiliocosm and the other infinite worlds of the ten directions, constantly come here to behold and pay homage to, read and recite, and to offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to this profound Prajñāpāramitā which I have written down; they circumambulate it to the right, prostrate, join their palms, and then depart.’”
"In this way, I shall have already bestowed the gift of Dharma.
Having formed this thought, he is filled with joy and exultation, causing the merit he has obtained to increase twofold. Kausika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family are constantly protected by the deities of the Boundless Realm, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others, no humans or non-humans can harm them, except for those karmic causes of fixed evil deeds from past lives that must ripen in the present, or where heavy evils are transformed so they are experienced lightly in this life.
“Kauśika! By the great majestic power of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, these sons and daughters of good family shall obtain such various merits and benefits in the present life.”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“By what signs may these sons and daughters of good family know that there are this trichiliocosm and other boundless worlds in the ten directions, with their devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth, who come to that place to behold and pay homage to, read and recite, and offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to the profound Prajñāpāramitā they have written and upheld, circumambulating it to the right with palms joined, rejoicing and protecting it with mindfulness?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

"Wherever these sons and daughters of good family see this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there will be a wondrous radiance; or they may smell a rare and fragrant incense; or again, they may hear the sound of subtle music."

It should be known that at that time, devas, nāgas, and others of great supernormal power and blazing majesty will come to that place to behold and pay homage to, read and recite, and offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* written and upheld there; they will join their palms, circumambulate it to the right, and joyfully protect and keep it in mind.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
These sons and daughters of good family cultivate pure and fresh conduct to adorn their dwelling place, and with a sincere heart, they make offerings to the profound Prajñāpāramitā."

It should be known that at that time, devas, nāgas, and others of great supernormal power and blazing majesty will come to that place to behold and pay homage to, read and recite, and make offerings to, revere, respect, honor, and praise the profound *prajñāpāramitā* written and upheld there; they will join their palms, circumambulate it to the right, and joyfully protect and keep it in mind.

Kauśika! Whichever gods, nāgas, and others endowed with such great supernormal powers and blazing majesty may come to that place, all the malevolent spirits and heterodox deities therein will be struck with terror and disperse, none daring to remain.

Due to these causes and conditions, the minds of these sons and daughters of good family will become vast and give rise to pure resolve; the wholesome karma they cultivate will double in clarity and brilliance, and all their endeavors will be free from obstacles.

For this reason, Kauśika, wherever this profound Prajñāpāramitā may be located, one should thoroughly clear away all filth and impurities, sweep and scrub the ground, apply fragrant ointments, and sprinkle scented water. One should arrange a precious throne and install it there, burning incense, scattering flowers, and spreading canopies and awnings. Adorn the area with precious banners, pennants, and bells, and embellish that place with various wonderful and rare objects, gold, silver, precious vessels, robes, necklaces, music, lamps, and all kinds of multicolored silks.

If one can make such offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*, then immeasurable devas, nāgas, and others—possessing great supernormal powers and blazing with majestic virtue—will come to that place to behold and pay homage to it; they will read and recite the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it is written and upheld there, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising it, while circumambulating it to the right with palms joined, guarding and mindful of it with joy.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If these sons and daughters of good family can thus make offerings, show reverence, respect, and praise to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will certainly attain a body and mind free from weariness, a body and mind at peace, a body and mind that are supple and compliant, and a body and mind that are light and agile."

With the mind bound to the *prajñāpāramitā*, when sleeping at night, one has no evil dreams but only auspicious ones; that is to say, one sees the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, his body of true golden color adorned with the marks and signs, emitting great radiance that universally illumines all things, surrounded before and behind by śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and while situated among the assembly, hears the Buddha expounding for them the Dharma and meanings associated with the six *pāramitās*, such as generosity, and other roots of goodness.

Or, within a dream, one may see a Bodhi tree, vast in height and breadth and adorned with various jewels; beneath it, a bodhisattva mahāsattva approaches, sits cross-legged, realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turns the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.

Or, within a dream, one may see an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of great bodhisattvas, engaging in discussion and definitive discernment of the various meanings of the Dharma.

Or, within a dream, they may see in each of the ten directions immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and they also hear their voices, saying: "In such-and-such a world, there is such-and-such a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and Śrāvaka disciples who pay him homage, as he teaches such a Dharma."

Furthermore, they may see in a dream that in each of the worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa; after each of those Buddhas has entered parinirvāṇa, there are donors who, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha’s śarīras, each construct immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of great stūpas made of the seven wonderful precious substances.

Furthermore, at each and every stūpa, they shall offer worship, honor, respect, and praise for immeasurable eons, using countless supreme and exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and illuminations.

“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family see such auspicious dream-omens as these, whether asleep or awake, their bodies and minds are peaceful and happy. The various devas and spirits augment their vital energy, causing them to perceive their own bodies as light and agile. By virtue of this cause and condition, they do not become excessively attached to food, drink, medicine, clothing, or bedding; their minds remain detached toward these four types of offerings.”

It is just as when a practitioner of yoga enters a sublime meditative concentration; because their body and mind are nourished by the power of that concentration, even upon emerging from meditation and encountering delicious food, their mind remains light and subtle. This case is likewise so.
Why is this so, Kauśika?

It is because these sons and daughters of good family are protected and mindful of by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others who possess great supernormal powers and supreme majesty, throughout this trichiliocosm and the infinite worlds of the ten directions. Through their compassionate care, they secretly infuse their bodies and minds with wondrous vital energy, causing their resolve to be courageous and their physical strength to flourish.

“Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family wish to obtain such various present benefits and merits, they should constantly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with the truth; they should extensively proclaim and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings, and furthermore, offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps as acts of worship, respect, veneration, and praise.”
Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, although unable to hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, or extensively proclaim and disseminate the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of sentient beings, nevertheless—out of a desire for the true Dharma to abide long in the world, to ensure that the Buddha-eye is not severed or destroyed, to prevent the true Dharma from vanishing, to embrace and cause Bodhisattvas to increase, and to ensure that the pure Dharma-eye of the world does not perish—they transcribe and uphold this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, adorning it with various jewels, and further offer, revere, respect, and praise it with immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps; they too shall obtain the various merits and benefits as previously described.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because these sons and daughters of good family are able to extensively bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
"For this reason, Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family wish to attain various kinds of meritorious benefits in both the present and the future, they should, with a pure mind, reverently accept the Prajñāpāramitā. Seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle, extensively proclaim and explain it to sentient beings, and examine it with profound wisdom through superior insight."

Because they wish to cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world; because they wish to ensure that the Buddha-eye is never severed or destroyed; because they wish to prevent the True Dharma from disappearing; because they wish to embrace and cause Bodhisattvas to increase; because they wish to distribute the meaning of the Dharma to sentient beings so that they may be fully satisfied; and because they wish to ensure that the vast Buddha-eye of all well-disciplined classes of sentient beings remains without deficiency—they write down and uphold this profound Prajñāpāramitā, adorning it with various jewels, and further offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to it with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and lights.
"If one can act in this way, one will certainly attain boundless meritorious benefits in both the present and the future.
Chapter Four: Praising Merit. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose this Jambudvīpa were filled with the relics of the Buddha as one portion, and the profound Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā were written down as another portion; of these two portions, which would you take?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"In my mind, I would rather take up the profound Prajñāpāramitā. Why is that? Because..."

It is not that I lack faith, devotion, worship, or respect for the *śarīra* relics of the Buddhas; rather, it is because the bodies of the Buddhas and their *śarīra* relics are all born from this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and are all cultivated by the power and majesty of the merit of this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that they are thus worshipped, respected, honored, and praised by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.

All the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have diligently practiced and studied this profound dharma-gate of the perfection of wisdom, thereby realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, penetrate suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality, thereby accomplishing the Dharma-body.
It is because of the *dharmakāya* that one is called a Buddha; since the Buddha’s *śarīra* relies upon the *dharmakāya*, it is therefore revered and offered to by the world.
“World-Honored One!

Just as when I am seated upon the throne of Śakra, Lord of Devas, in the Sudharmā Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, proclaiming the True Dharma for the assembly of devas, immeasurable sons of the gods come to my presence to listen to what I say; they pay homage and show respect, circumambulate me to the right, and then depart.

"When I am not present at that Dharma-seat, the sons of the gods will also come to that place; although they do not see me, they will pay homage and make offerings just as they did when I was there, all saying:

'This is the seat where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, preached the Dharma for the sake of the gods; we should all act as if the Lord of the Gods were present, making offerings, circumambulating him to the right, and prostrating before departing.'"

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise so: if anyone writes it down, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, or extensively explains and disseminates it for the sake of sentient beings, one should know that this place will always be visited by the assembly of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others—immeasurable and innumerable—from this land and from the infinite worlds of the ten directions. Even if there is no one speaking it, out of reverence for the Dharma, they will also pay homage and respect at that place, circumambulate it to the right, and depart.
“Blessed One!

This profound perfection of wisdom is the cause, the condition, the basis of reliance, and the means of elicitation for the practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as well as for the omniscient wisdom attained by the Buddhas.”
Therefore, I say:

suppose one portion were filled with the relics of the Buddha throughout this Jambudvīpa, and another portion consisted of the written profound Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā; of these two portions, my inclination would be to take the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One! Let us set aside for a moment the Buddha-relics that would fill this Jambudvīpa as one portion.

Suppose there were another portion consisting of Buddha-relics filling the four great continents; or another portion consisting of Buddha-relics filling a small thousand-world system; or another portion consisting of Buddha-relics filling a medium thousand-world system; or another portion consisting of Buddha-relics filling a great trichiliocosm. And suppose there were yet another portion consisting of the written profound Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā. Between these two portions, my inclination would be to take the profound Prajñāpāramitā."

Why is this? It is not that I lack faith, joy, worship, or reverence for the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddhas; rather, it is because the bodies of the Buddhas and their *śarīra* are all born from the profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and are all perfumed and cultivated by the meritorious power of the profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, they are worshipped, revered, honored, and praised by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.

"Furthermore, Blessed One, if sons or daughters of good family wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, reflect upon according to the principle, write down, explain, and widely disseminate this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they shall not fall into the evil destinies in the future; they shall remain far removed from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they need have no fear of being afflicted by any calamities or epidemics."
Just as a debtor who fears his creditor immediately seeks out and serves a king, relying on the king’s power to escape that fear;

so too, the *prajñāpāramitā* is like the king, and those sons and daughters of good family are like the debtor. By relying upon the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to leave behind the evil destinies and all other fears.
World-Honored One!
It is like a person who, by relying upon a king and being supported by the king, is honored, revered, respected, and praised by all people of the world.

The relics of the Buddha are likewise; because they have been perfumed and cultivated by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are honored, revered, respected, and praised by devas, humans, asuras, and others.
The King is a metaphor for the *prajñāpāramitā*, and the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) is a metaphor for that which relies upon the king.
World-Honored One,
since the omniscient wisdom attained by all Buddhas is also accomplished in reliance upon the *prajñāpāramitā*, I would rather take up this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

This profound Prajñāpāramitā brings great benefit to the trichiliocosm and possesses great supernormal power. In whatever place it resides, there is a Buddha performing the works of a Buddha, namely, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings."
World-Honored One!

It is like a priceless great divine jewel that possesses immeasurable kinds of sublime and wondrous majestic power; wherever this divine jewel resides, humans and non-humans can never cause harm or affliction.

Should there be a man or a woman possessed by a ghost, suffering physical and mental distress, if someone were to show them this divine jewel, the ghost would immediately depart by the power of the jewel.

Whether there be various fevers, or diseases caused by wind, or phlegm, or the combination of heat, wind, and phlegm—if one ties this divine jewel to the body, none of these ailments will fail to be cured.

This jewel can provide illumination in the darkness; it cools in times of heat and warms in times of cold. Wherever this divine jewel is located, the seasons are harmonized such that it is neither too cold nor too hot.
If this divine jewel is present in a locality, venomous creatures such as snakes and scorpions will not dare to remain there.
Should a man or a woman be struck by poison such that the pain is unbearable, if they are made to see this divine jewel, the poison will be instantly extinguished by the power of the jewel.

If any sentient beings suffer from leprosy, malignant sores, swellings, blisters, eye diseases such as vertigo and cataracts, or ailments of the ears, nose, tongue, throat, body, or various limbs and joints, all these illnesses shall be healed by wearing this divine jewel.

If there are ponds, pools, springs, or wells whose water is turbid and foul, or which is on the verge of drying up, when this jewel is cast into them, the water immediately becomes full, fragrant, pure, and clear, endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.

If one wraps this divine jewel in garments of various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, or green—and casts it into water, the water will take on those various colors according to the hues of the cloth.

Thus, this priceless great jewel, the divine pearl, possesses boundless majesty and virtue that cannot be fully described; even when placed within a chest or casket, it causes that vessel to be completely endowed with boundless majesty and virtue.
"Even if an empty box or casket once held a jewel, that vessel will still be cherished and esteemed by all people.
At that time, Ānanda asked Śakra:
"Is such a divine jewel possessed only by the devas, or do humans have them as well?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"This jewel exists both among humans and in the heavens. If it is among humans, its form is small and heavy; if it is in the heavens, its form is large and light.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the jewel among humans are incomplete, whereas those of the one in the heavens are perfectly complete."
"The divine jewels of the heavens possess such extraordinary majesty and power that they exceed those possessed by humans by immeasurable multiples.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise so: it is the source of all virtues and is capable of extinguishing immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas. In whatever place it resides, it causes the physical and mental suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings to be entirely eliminated, and neither humans nor non-humans can cause them harm."
“World-Honored One!

All the omniscient wisdom attained by the Tathāgata, as well as his other immeasurable and boundless merits, are all brought forth and revealed by the Great Divine Mantra King that is the Prajñāpāramitā; its majestic power is profound, vast, immeasurable, and boundless.”

Because the Buddha’s relics have been perfumed by all his meritorious virtues and serve as the vessel that supports those virtues, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Setting aside the Buddha-relics of a trichiliocosm, suppose one portion consists of the Buddha-relics filling as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and another portion consists of the written text of this profound Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Between these two portions, my intention would be to take the profound *Prajñāpāramitā*."

Why is this? It is not that I lack faith, joy, offerings, or reverence toward the *śarīras* (relics) of the Buddhas; rather, it is because the bodies of the Buddhas and their *śarīras* are all produced from the profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and are all cultivated by the power and majesty of the merit of the profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that they are thus honored, revered, respected, and praised by all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). The knowledge of all modes attained by the Tathāgata can, in turn, give birth to the Buddha-body and the *śarīra*. Therefore, to make offerings to this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is to make offerings to the knowledge of all modes and the *śarīra* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
"Furthermore, Blessed One,

if good sons and good daughters wish to constantly behold the infinite and incalculable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions, they should practice the perfection of wisdom and cultivate the perfection of wisdom."
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said,
Kauśika! All the Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom."
All future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom;

all present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions are currently realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom.
Now, I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, have likewise realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“The profound perfection of wisdom is the great perfection, the unsurpassed perfection, and the unequaled perfection.”

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, all rely upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā to know the distinctions in the mental activities of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said,

Kauśika! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have practiced the profound perfection of wisdom for a long night are able to see, according to reality, the differences in the mental activities of all sentient beings."
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas only practice the perfection of wisdom, or should they also practice the other five perfections?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: “Kauśika!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the six pāramitās in their entirety; however, when practicing generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration while contemplating all phenomena, they must take the perfection of wisdom as their foremost guide.”

Kauśika! Just as all the trees in Jambudvīpa—though their branches, trunks, flowers, leaves, and fruits differ in various forms and kinds—their shadows are entirely without distinction; they possess great merit and are a refuge for all beings.

Although these six perfections are each distinct, through the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, they are embraced and dedicated toward omniscience; thus, no differentiated characteristics can be apprehended at all, and they possess great merit as the refuge of all beings.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* accomplishes vast and sublime merit; it accomplishes all sublime merit; it accomplishes perfect and sublime merit; it accomplishes immeasurable sublime merit; it accomplishes boundless sublime merit; it accomplishes innumerable sublime merit; it accomplishes incomparable sublime merit; it accomplishes inexhaustible sublime merit.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Chapter Five: The Gateways to Merit, Part One. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If sons or daughters of good family, with a pure mind, respectfully accept this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, listen to it with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, reflect upon it according to the principle, and extensively explain and reveal it to sentient beings, examining it with superior wisdom through careful and precise observation.

Desiring that the True Dharma may long abide in the world, desiring that the Buddha-eye may never be severed or destroyed, desiring that the True Dharma may not vanish, desiring to sustain and cause Bodhisattvas to flourish, and desiring that the pure Dharma-eye of the world remain free from deficiency or decline, one should transcribe this profound *prajñāpāramitā* adorned with various jewels, and further offer it worship, respect, reverence, and praise with diverse, exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and lights;
and one should think:

"This profound *prajñāpāramitā* accomplishes vast merit and benefits; it is extremely difficult to encounter and should not be abandoned; one should personally protect, worship, respect, recite, and contemplate it."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā* adorned with various jewels, and who honor, revere, respect, and praise it, and bestow it upon others so that they may receive, uphold, and widely disseminate it;

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who receive from others a portion of the Buddha’s *śarīra* relics and distribute even as much as a mustard seed to another, causing them to receive it with reverence and enshrine it according to the Dharma; they further honor, respect, revere, and praise it with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and illuminations.
"What do you think?
Of these two accumulations of merit, which is superior?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, of these two accumulations of merit, the latter is superior.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

"Furthermore, Kausika!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, transcribe it, adorn it, and bestow it upon sentient beings, their merit will surpass the previous accumulation of merit by an immeasurable and boundless amount.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, transcribe it, adorn it, and bestow it upon sentient beings."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, well understand its meaning and intent, and are able to explain it to others through various skillful words and meanings, the mass of merit they obtain will surpass the previous mass of merit by being immeasurable and boundless.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Should sons and daughters of good family expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others using various skillful words and meanings?"
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika, it is so!
It is thus!”
It is so! If good sons and good daughters can expound the profound Prajñāpāramitā for others using various skillful words and meanings, they will immediately obtain a boundless mass of great merit.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what kind of sentient beings should one proclaim the profound meaning and intent of the Prajñāpāramitā?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who do not understand the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should proclaim the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of such sons and daughters of good family."
Why is this? Kauśika!

In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family who seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet upon hearing others proclaim a counterfeit perfection of wisdom, their minds will become deluded and they will fall away from the Middle Way.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called 'semblance prajñāpāramitā,' and why is it called the teaching of semblance prajñāpāramitā?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:

"In future ages, there will be certain bhikṣus who are unable to properly cultivate their body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; their wisdom will be as narrow and inferior as that of oxen or sheep. Although they wish to proclaim the true Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of sentient beings, they will instead perversely teach a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā."
How does a bhikṣu perversely proclaim a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*?

It is when that bhikṣu, for the sake of those who have generated the mind set on unsurpassed bodhi, says that form is called impermanent because it is subject to destruction, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called impermanent because they are subject to destruction;
furthermore, he makes this statement:
If one seeks in such a manner, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Kauśika!
This is called the perverted teaching of a counterfeit perfection of wisdom.

Kauśika! One should not contemplate the impermanence of form by means of its disintegration; one should not contemplate the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness by means of their disintegration. If one contemplates form through to consciousness as being impermanent in such a manner, you should know that they are practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the practices from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, saying:
'Come!'"
"Son of good family!
I shall instruct you in the practice and study of the perfections, from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.

If you practice and study according to my instructions, you will swiftly abide in the first bodhisattva ground through to the tenth ground; you will attain all other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, quickly enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty beyond regression, and transcend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

"Kauśika! Because they employ signs (*nimitta*) and the apprehension of objects (*upalambha*) as their means, they teach the cultivation of everything from the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) based on the perception of temporal divisions. This is called the perverted teaching of a counterfeit perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should say to those of the bodhisattva lineage:
'If one listens to, receives, upholds, recites, diligently studies, and reflects upon the Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, one shall obtain boundless and supreme merit.'"
"Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, they speak in this way; this is called a perverted teaching that resembles the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should say to one who belongs to the lineage of the bodhisattva vehicle:

'Regarding all the roots of goodness of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until their ultimate perfection—you should rejoice in them all, collect them together, and dedicate them for the sake of all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.'"

"Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, they speak in this way; this is called a perverted teaching that resembles the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
"For this reason, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, correctly expounds the profound meaning and intent of the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all sentient beings, the mass of merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless, and they will be able to bring about the benefit and happiness of sentient beings."

Part Four, Chapter Five on the Gate of Merit, Section Two. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters were to instruct all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, causing them all to abide in the fruit of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), or the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of an Arhat (*arhat*)."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:

“If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, with a pure mind, reverently accept this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, transcribe it, bestow it upon others, and further explain it for them—causing them to have no doubt regarding its profound meaning—and instruct and admonish all sentient beings, saying:”
"You should diligently cultivate the path of the true Bodhisattva, namely the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

If you can apply yourself with vigor to training in this path, you will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), thereby rescuing and delivering infinite sentient beings, enabling them to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) where all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted, and enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder."
The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former.
Why is this? Kausika!
All those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship do so because these states flow forth from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

When those sons and daughters of good family hear this profound perfection of wisdom and, through its instructions and admonitions, apply themselves with diligence to its cultivation, they will gradually fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas, even attaining the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*). They then transform sentient beings, enabling them to attain the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha-bodhi*), to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and ultimately to realize the enlightenment of a Buddha.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Setting aside all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa,

All Tathāgatas and their noble disciples, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, employ skillful means to encourage, sustain, and assist bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that they may swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
Why is this? All the supreme matters of the world—whether pertaining to all Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas—are brought forth by means of the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Why is this? Kauśika!

If there were no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who had resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), then there would be no bodhisattva mahāsattvas capable of training in the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If there were no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who could train in the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, then there would be no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who could realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas did not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, then there would be no such superior worldly phenomena as the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

Therefore, one should encourage, embrace, and assist all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to train in the six perfections until they reach ultimate perfection, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 542; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 543.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Four, Chapter Six: Rejoicing and Dedication (The First of Two Parts). At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Virtuous One!"

All the meritorious deeds associated with the sympathetic joy and dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed—equal to the unequaled—compared to the meritorious deeds of other sentient beings, such as those consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"The mind of sympathetic joy and dedication generated by the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas universally takes as its object the infinite, countless, inconceivable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions; in each and every world, there are infinite..."
Countless, inconceivable, and boundless Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas— who have severed all paths of existence,
cut off the way of conceptual proliferation, and have already entered the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder—

from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attained the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and so on, up until their entry into nirvāṇa without remainder.
Based upon the realm of parinirvāṇa, extending successively until the extinction of the True Dharma,
all the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation that exist within that interval;
as well as the roots of virtue associated with the six pāramitās, or the roots of virtue associated with the Buddha’s perfected qualities.
The roots of goodness associated with the faculties, or the powers, or the fearlessnesses; the roots of goodness associated with the supernormal knowledges and the *pāramitās*;
the roots of goodness associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; the roots of goodness associated with the *pāramitā* of great vows;
and the roots of goodness associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Whether it be the great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings;
or the immeasurable and innumerable merits of the Buddhas; or the sublime bliss of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
or the perfection of attaining great mastery over all phenomena; or that which is invincible—
It is able to subdue all immeasurable and most extreme supernormal powers and wondrous practices;
it is the unobstructed, unimpeded, peerless, incomparable, and limitless true heroic power of the Tathāgata;
it is the Buddha’s wisdom and vision, the Buddha’s ten powers and perfections (pāramitās), and the most supreme among the four fearlessnesses.
the fulfillment of the realized qualities of a Buddha;
if one can bring forth the realization of the ultimate truth of all phenomena;
if one turns the wheel of Dharma, holds aloft the torch of Dharma, beats the drum of Dharma, blows the conch of Dharma, rains down the rain of Dharma, or provides...
In this Dharma assembly, if one satisfies all sentient beings with the flavor of the Dharma according to their inclinations and desires,
and if, regarding such unsurpassed teachings— the teachings of the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, or the Śrāvakas—
one possesses the discipline and resolute conviction that leads definitely toward the three types of enlightenment, then [it is] as if the Buddha...
Whatever supreme roots of goodness the Blessed One has bestowed as the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for all bodhisattvas— namely,
the roots of goodness associated with the perfections from generosity up to wisdom—
and whatever [roots of goodness] he has bestowed as the prediction of the enlightenment of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas for those individuals who are pratyekabuddhas— all of them...
Exalted roots of goodness—namely, the roots of goodness associated with the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination;
or if one were to bestow upon a śrāvaka person the prediction of awakening through the Śrāvakayāna;
or all those exalted roots of goodness, namely the three bases of meritorious action consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation; or [the roots of] training...
The untainted roots of goodness of those beyond training; the roots of goodness planted by ordinary worldlings in those various dharmas;

and all that is of the nature of giving and the nature of morality belonging to the fourfold assembly of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—namely, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
The three types of meritorious actions consisting of cultivation and nature;
the roots of virtue planted by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, regarding the Dharma teachings spoken by the Buddhas;
the roots of virtue planted after the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas; and whatever [roots of virtue] sentient beings have planted toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and others...
The noble person, with a profound mind of faith and delight, gives rise to various kinds of excellent roots of goodness.

Having gathered together all these roots of goodness and other merits, and having observed and weighed them, they manifest before them a mind of sympathetic joy that is most honored, most supreme, most exalted, and most wondrous.

Furthermore, with these various meritorious deeds accompanied by such sympathetic joy, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, vowing that these roots of virtue may jointly bring about the sought-after unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for all classes of sentient beings.

This rejoicing and dedication thus generated is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all other meritorious deeds that have been generated.
"What do you think?

Regarding such an object, does that bodhisattva mahāsattva have any such object of focus obtainable, corresponding to the mental state of rejoicing and dedication characterized by the marks they have grasped?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya replied to the Venerable Subhūti:

"When those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication based on such objects and with such mental aspects, there is in reality no such object to be apprehended as the mark grasped by those bodhisattvas."
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

"If there are no such objective referents for those signs as they are grasped by those bodhisattvas, would not the sympathetic joy and dedication of those bodhisattvas all constitute perversions of perception, mind, and view?"

Why is this so? Because if one is greedily attached to non-existent things, perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure, one immediately gives rise to perversions of perception, thought, and view.
Just as the objective referent (ālambana-vastu) does not exist in reality, so too it is with bodhi and the mind; all phenomena (dharma) and all realms (dhātu) should likewise be understood.
If, in every respect, they are all non-existent and without distinction, what then is this objective referent?
What is the mind of sympathetic joy? What is bodhi?
And what is dedication?
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking such matters as an object, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Bodhisattva Maitreya replied to Subhūti:
“Such giving of rise to sympathetic joy and dedication should not be spoken of in the presence of a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva who has recently set out in the Mahāyāna.”
Why is this? Because upon hearing such rejoicing and dedication, all their faith, delight, and reverent mind will surely vanish.

This method of rejoicing and dedication should be explained and revealed only for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive, or those who have made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, have long since made great vows, have planted many roots of goodness, and are sustained by many virtuous friends.
Why is this? Because upon hearing such rejoicing and dedication, they are not startled, not terrified, do not retreat, and do not sink in despair.

"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dedicate these meritorious deeds accompanied by such rejoicing toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; at that time, they should form this thought:"

"The mind that is employed for sympathetic joy and dedication, this mind is exhausted, extinguished, detached, and transformed; and these objects of focus as well as all roots of goodness likewise become exhausted, extinguished, detached, and transformed, just like that mind."
In this context, what is the mind that is employed?
Furthermore, by means of what objects of focus and what roots of goodness does one speak of sympathetic joy and the dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
In this regard, it is logically untenable for a mind to rejoice in or dedicate itself to another mind, because two minds cannot arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, a mind cannot rejoice in or dedicate itself, as that would be its own intrinsic nature. Therefore, both the mind that rejoices in or dedicates and the object upon which it focuses are ultimately unattainable.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
"When the assembly of bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna hears such matters as these, will their minds not become terrified, alarmed, or discouraged?"
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the objects of their focus?

And how do they embrace those meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy, dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) without contradicting the principle of reality?
At that time, Subhūti, relying upon the majestic power of the Bodhisattva Maitreya, addressed Śakra, saying:

"All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas universally take as their object of focus all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions—
those who have severed all paths of existence and eliminated all conceptual play."
Discoursing on the Path, they dispel all clouds and mists and crush all thorns; having laid down all heavy burdens, they attain their own benefit;
exhausting all fetters of existence, they achieve liberation through right knowledge;

reaching the sovereign mastery of mind and the supreme ultimate, they enter the realm of nirvana without remainder—from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the realization of the sought-after unsurpassed state.

All the various roots of merit and virtue from the time of attaining perfect enlightenment, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings, until the final nirvana and the subsequent disappearance of the Dharma;
as well as the roots of merit planted by the assembly of disciples in the teachings of all Buddhas, and all other various virtues that have arisen— [all these]...
Having gathered together these observations and deliberations, one manifests a mind of sympathetic joy that is most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime. Furthermore,
one takes all such meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"At that time, through skillful means, he is able to avoid falling into the perversions of perception, thought, and view.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the mind that arises from their own rejoicing and dedication, does not form the conceptual notion of ‘rejoicing’ or ‘dedication’; regarding the merits of the Buddhas and their disciples, does not form the conceptual notion of ‘the merits of the Buddhas and their disciples’; and regarding the roots of goodness planted by gods, humans, asuras, and others, does not form the conceptual notion of ‘the roots of goodness of gods, humans, asuras, and others,’ yet is able to rejoice and dedicate these toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—then the mind of rejoicing and dedication arising from this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not fall into the perversions of perception, mind, or view.”

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding the mind that arises from their own practice of sympathetic joy and dedication, must form the conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*) of sympathetic joy and dedication; and regarding the merits of the Buddhas and their disciples whom they recollect, must form the conceptual thought of the merits of those Buddhas and disciples; and regarding the roots of goodness planted by gods, humans, asuras, and others, must form the conceptual thought of the roots of goodness of those gods, humans, asuras, and others—only then can they dedicate [the merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication arising from this bodhisattva-mahāsattva then falls into the perversions of conceptualization, mind, and view.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with such a mind, recollect the merits and roots of goodness of all Buddhas and their disciples; they correctly know that this mind is exhausted, ceased, detached, and transformed, and thus it is not that which rejoices. They correctly know that the nature of those dharmas is likewise so, and thus they are not that which is rejoiced in.

Furthermore, they correctly and thoroughly realize that the dharma-nature of the mind capable of dedicating is also thus—it is not that which dedicates—and they correctly and thoroughly know that the nature of the dharmas to be dedicated is also thus—they are not that which is dedicated.”

If there are those who can rely upon this aforementioned rejoicing and dedication, it is correct and not erroneous; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to such rejoicing and dedication for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva [recalls] all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past— who have severed the paths of existence and cut off the ways of conceptual proliferation—
from their first generation of the mind until their realization of the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

Successively, up until entering the realm of nirvana without remainder, and thus even until the extinction of the True Dharma—in this interval, all the roots of goodness associated with the *pāramitās* of all Buddhas;
or the roots of goodness associated with the *pāramitās* when a Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows a prophecy upon a bodhisattva; or the roots of goodness of a Buddha...
When the World-Honored One bestows the prediction of enlightenment upon a pratyekabuddha, he observes the roots of goodness associated with dependent origination;
or when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows the prediction upon a śrāvaka, [he observes] the roots of goodness consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation that have been initiated by him,

as well as all the contaminated and uncontaminated roots of goodness belonging to those in the stage of training (śaikṣa), and the uncontaminated roots of goodness belonging to those in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).

The roots: whether it be the Buddha, the World-Honored One’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*);
or his great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings;
or his other immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-dharmas; or that which the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has proclaimed...
The preaching of the true Dharma; the roots of goodness of those who, through diligent cultivation and study of the true Dharma, abide with resolute conviction;
the roots of goodness planted by various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) regarding the true Dharma;
and the roots of goodness planted by gods, nāgas, asuras, and others upon hearing the true Dharma, as well as after having heard it—these, indeed...
Regarding the hearing of the true Dharma by those in the animal realm, and the roots of goodness planted after hearing that Dharma,
as well as all the roots of goodness planted by humans, devas, and others after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the World-Honored One—
if one were to gather and weigh all such things together, one would manifest the most honored, the most supreme, the highest, and the most wondrous rejoicing.
With a mind [free from stinginess], he further takes these various meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings,
dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"At such a time, if one correctly understands that all dharmas which can be rejoiced in and dedicated are exhausted, ceased, detached from, and transformed, then the intrinsic nature of all those dharmas of rejoicing and dedication is empty."

Although one knows this, one is able to rejoice and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; furthermore, at that time, if one correctly understands that there is no dharma whatsoever that can rejoice or dedicate itself to any dharma.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and within emptiness there are no phenomena of either agent or object for rejoicing or dedication.

Although they know this, they are able to rejoice and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not fall into errors of perception, mind, or view.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to attachment toward the mind of sympathetic joy or the roots of merit and goodness that are rejoiced in; nor does he give rise to attachment toward the mind of dedication or the unsurpassed enlightenment to which they are dedicated. By being without attachment, he does not fall into perversion.
The mind of sympathetic joy and dedication thus aroused by a bodhisattva is called the correct and unsurpassed dedication of sympathetic joy; it is far removed from all false conceptualization.

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding the dharmas that can be rejoiced in and dedicated, gives rise to the notion that they are 'dharmas that can be rejoiced in and dedicated,' and regarding the dharmas that are rejoiced in and dedicated, gives rise to the notion that they are 'dharmas that are rejoiced in and dedicated,' yet proceeds to rejoice in and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—then the mind of rejoicing and dedication produced by this bodhisattva-mahāsattva falls into the perversions of notion, mind, and view; all such rejoicings and dedications are erroneous, and the bodhisattva should know how to skillfully distance themselves from them."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva considers all the roots of virtue associated with the *pāramitās* belonging to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—who have universally severed the paths of existence and cut off the way of conceptual proliferation in the future—from their first generation of the mind until they realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and continuing through their successive stages until they enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, and even until the extinction of the True Dharma;
as well as the roots of virtue associated with the *pāramitās* when those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow predictions upon bodhisattvas;..."
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows a prediction upon a pratyekabuddha, it concerns the roots of goodness associated with the contemplation of dependent origination;

if the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows a prediction upon a śrāvaka, it concerns the roots of goodness consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation that he has initiated, as well as all the tainted and untainted roots of goodness belonging to those in the stage of training (śaikṣa),
and the untainted roots of goodness belonging to those in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Whether it be the Buddha, the World-Honored One’s aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
or his great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings;
or any other immeasurable and innumerable qualities of a Buddha;
Whether it be the True Dharma proclaimed by the Buddha, the Blessed One;
or the roots of goodness cultivated by those who diligently train in and dwell with resolute conviction in that True Dharma;
or the roots of goodness planted by ordinary worldlings within the True Dharma.
Whatever roots of goodness planted by gods, nāgas, asuras, and others upon hearing the true Dharma, and even those planted by animals upon hearing the true Dharma;
as well as whatever roots of goodness planted by humans, gods, and others after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Having thus gathered and weighed all these together, one should manifest a mind of sympathetic joy that is most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime.

Furthermore, taking these various meritorious deeds associated with such sympathetic joy, one should share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"At such a time, if one correctly understands that all phenomena which can be rejoiced in and dedicated are exhausted, ceased, detached from, and transformed, and that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena of rejoicing and dedication is empty, yet one is still able to rejoice and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, at that time, if one correctly understands that there is no dharma whatsoever that can be rejoiced in or dedicated toward a dharma.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty; within emptiness, there is neither a subject nor an object of rejoicing or dedication.

Although they know this, they are able to rejoice in it and dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not fall into the perversions of perception, mind, or view.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not give rise to attachment toward the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*) or the roots of merit and goodness that are the object of that joy; nor do they give rise to attachment toward the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) or the unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) to which it is dedicated. By being without attachment, they do not fall into inverted views (*viparyāsa*).
The mind of sympathetic joy and dedication thus aroused by a bodhisattva is called the correct and unsurpassed dedication of sympathetic joy; it is far removed from all false conceptualization.
