'How does that scripture differ from this one?'"
"What use is that to him?
For this reason, he will certainly be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Why is this so?

The sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* manifest through various skillful means, exhorting, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening those sons of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle, causing them to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One who abandons [the Mahāyāna] to seek and study the sūtras of the two vehicles should be known to be just like that person. Why is this?
Because by diligently practicing and studying the sūtras of the two vehicles, one will certainly be unable to realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a hungry person who, having obtained food of a hundred flavors, cast it aside to seek out and eat two-month-old grain porridge.
What do you think?"
"Is that person wise?
Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“In a future age, there will likewise be sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to seek and study scriptures associated with the two vehicles. Desiring to find the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatājñāna*) therein, they will labor in vain and ultimately be unable to attain it.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a poor man who, having obtained a priceless jewel, cast it away and instead took up a glass trinket.
What do you think?"
"Is that person clever?
Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“In a future age, there will likewise be sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who, seeking to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead seek to study the sūtras associated with the two vehicles. Desiring therein to find the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), they will labor in vain and ultimately be unable to attain it.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are correctly copying, upholding, reciting, contemplating, or cultivating a sūtra associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if various forms of eloquence suddenly arise and they take pleasure in expounding diverse and differentiated dharma-gates, thereby preventing the completion of the copying and other such tasks, you should know that this is a work of Māra for the bodhisattva."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Can this profound *prajñāpāramitā* be written down?
The Blessed One replied:
"No, Subhūti! If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle,
while copying such a sūtra associated with this profound perfection of wisdom, should form such a thought as this:"

"To write down the Prajñāpāramitā in letters—these very letters are the Prajñāpāramitā"—or to rely on letters and become attached to the Prajñāpāramitā: know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate,
and expound the profound sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom, or..."
One may contemplate the land, or contemplate cities and towns, or contemplate the royal capital, or contemplate regions and locations,
or contemplate teachers and friends, or contemplate parents, or contemplate wives and children,
or contemplate brothers, or contemplate sisters, or contemplate relatives, or contemplate companions, or contemplate kings and ministers, or...
One may think of thieves, or wild beasts, or wicked people, or malevolent spirits;
one may think of crowds, or of play, or of music; one may think of seeking revenge, or of repaying kindness;
or one may think of food, clothing, bedding, or various other requisites.
Whether they think of their own bodies and belongings; or think of composing literary verses, treatises, or commentaries; or think of the seasons, cold and heat, or abundance and scarcity;
or think of matters such as elephants, horses, water, and fire; or think of various other tasks and activities—one should know that all these are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Māra uses these matters to disturb and vex the Bodhisattva, causing such tasks as copying [the scriptures] to fail; the Bodhisattva, becoming aware of this, should distance himself from them all.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they may obtain great fame, profit, honor, and offerings. One should know that if they, on account of these conditions, neglect their spiritual practice, this is also a work of Māra for a bodhisattva; the bodhisattva should recognize it and abandon it with detachment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, Māra will manifest in the guise of bhikṣus and the like, carrying various worldly treatises or even sūtras associated with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). He will falsely appear as a friend and bestow them upon the bodhisattva, saying:
'The meaning and flavor of these sūtras are profound and subtle; you should apply yourself diligently to their study and abandon the sūtras you have been practicing.'"

These sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, through their skillful means, should not accept or become attached to worldly treatises bestowed by Māra, nor to scriptures associated with the two vehicles.

Why is this? Because worldly treatises and the scriptures of the two vehicles cannot give rise to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); they are not the unerring means for proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but rather constitute a profound obstacle to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Subhūti, you should know that within the sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ path is extensively explained; if one diligently trains therein, one will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, due to a lack of skillful means and because of associating with evil friends, abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to study the worldly treatises of Māra and the scriptures of the two vehicles, you should know that this constitutes a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who listen to the Dharma take pleasure in hearing it, taking pleasure in questioning it, copying it, receiving and upholding it, reciting it, and practicing it, yet those who preach the Dharma are attached to pleasure and indolence, having no desire to preach it, nor do they bestow this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma is not attached to pleasure nor is indolent, but delights in preaching and bestowing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and through skillful means encourages [others] to copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who listens to the Dharma is indolent and attached to pleasure, having no desire to listen, receive, or even cultivate it—know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to hear the Dharma possess the power of mindfulness and wisdom, and delight in hearing, questioning, copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the one who is able to preach the Dharma intends to go to another region and is unable to provide instruction, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma delights in preaching and bestowing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and through skillful means encourages [others] to copy, uphold, recite, and practice it, yet the one who wishes to hear the Dharma is unable to receive it because they must go to another region—know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma possesses great evil desires, cherishing fame and profit, and is never satiated in his mind with offerings and respect—such as robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites—while the one who listens to the Dharma has few desires, is easily contented, practices seclusion, is courageous and diligent, and is endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, yet detests and fears gain, honor, and reputation; or if [the preacher] is possessed of jealousy and stinginess and cannot practice giving—then these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who preaches the Dharma has few desires, is easily contented, practices seclusion, is courageous and diligent, possesses mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and feels aversion toward and fear of gain, honor, and fame; yet he is either possessed of envy and stinginess and unable to practice giving, or the one who listens to the Dharma possesses great and wicked desires, craving and valuing fame, profit, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other material goods, never being satisfied with offerings, honor, or respect. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain instruction, listening, receiving, writing, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who preaches the Dharma possesses faith and ethical discipline, practices the twelve dhūta qualities, and delights in expounding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, skillfully encouraging them to copy, uphold, read, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who listens to the Dharma lacks faith, lacks ethical discipline, and likewise lacks the twelve dhūta qualities. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reading, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose those who listen to the Dharma possess faith and ethical discipline, and practice the twelve dhūta-guṇas, delighting in hearing, questioning, copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and cultivating the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Yet, the one who preaches the Dharma lacks faith and ethical discipline, and likewise lacks the twelve dhūta-guṇas, having no desire to provide instruction. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to achieve the hearing, copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has a mind free from stinginess and is able to relinquish everything, while the one who listens to the Dharma has a mind possessed by stinginess and is unable to give or sacrifice—or if it is the reverse of these two—and thus they do not harmonize, such that they fail to obtain instruction, listen to, receive, transcribe, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who wish to listen to the Dharma desire to provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities to those who preach the Dharma, yet the preachers do not wish to accept them—or conversely—if the two are at odds and fail to reach harmony, such that they do not obtain the opportunity to teach, listen to, write down, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma possesses the wisdom of exposition yet does not delight in extensive explanation, while the one who listens to the Dharma possesses the wisdom of elucidation yet does not delight in concise summary—or if it is the reverse of these—and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma is exclusively devoted to extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelvefold teachings, while the one who listens to the Dharma does not take pleasure in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelvefold teachings—or vice versa—and thus the two do not harmonize, such that they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has accomplished the six perfections and attained dhāraṇīs through skillful means, while the one who listens to the Dharma lacks such virtues—or conversely—if the two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma wishes to have the profound *prajñāpāramitā* respectfully copied, received, upheld, recited, and practiced, but the one who listens to the Dharma does not follow their intent—or conversely, if they act contrary to it—and thus the two do not harmonize, such that they fail to obtain instruction, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has already abandoned the stain of stinginess and the five hindrances, while the one who listens to the Dharma has not yet abandoned the stain of stinginess and the five hindrances—or vice versa—and thus the two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose there is a listener who possesses a mind of faith and joy and desires to understand the profound meaning, yet the teacher of the Dharma is not yet fully proficient in this sūtra and is unable to provide a definitive explanation. Consequently, the listener takes no pleasure in hearing it. Due to these causes and conditions, they are unable to copy, receive and uphold, read and recite, contemplate, or cultivate [the teaching]. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who can preach the Dharma delights in preaching it, while the one who can listen to the Dharma does not delight in listening, or if the opposite occurs such that the two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the opportunity for the preaching and listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It may be that the one who can preach the Dharma delights in preaching it, yet their body is heavy and burdened by various ailments such that they are unable to preach; or it may be that the listener delights in hearing the Dharma, yet their body is heavy and burdened by various ailments such that they are unable to listen and receive it. When these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain instruction, listening, receiving, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and explaining sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if someone should come and describe the various sufferings of the evil destinies, they might further say to them:

'You should apply yourself with diligence in this very body to quickly reach the end of suffering and enter parinirvāṇa. Why do you linger in the great ocean of birth and death to undergo hundreds of thousands of kinds of unbearable sufferings for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?'"

Because of these words, they will fail to reach the ultimate goal in the writing, receiving, upholding, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and explaining this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding the profound sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom, if someone should come and praise the various superior matters of the human realm, or praise the long life and happiness of the devas, and say to them: "

"Although you experience the pleasures of desire in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the pleasures of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the pleasures of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all of these are impermanent, suffering, empty, selfless, impure, subject to transformation and decay, subject to passing away, subject to separation, subject to exhaustion, and subject to cessation. Why, with regard to this body, do you not apply yourself with diligence to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), and proceeding further up to the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*), enter parinirvāṇa for ultimate peace and happiness? What is the use of remaining long in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), undergoing various hardships for no purpose on behalf of others, merely seeking to advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)?"

Because of these words, they will fail to reach the ultimate goal in the copying, upholding, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and explaining of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has no attachments in his own person, devotes himself exclusively to his own affairs, and does not concern himself with the work of others, while the one who listens to the Dharma delights in leading a following, enjoys managing the affairs of others, and does not concern himself with his own work—or if it be the reverse—such that the two are not in harmony and fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma does not delight in noisy commotion, while the one who listens to the Dharma delights in staying in noisy commotion—or vice versa—and thus the two are not in harmony, such that they fail to obtain instruction, listen and receive [the teaching], copy and uphold it, read and recite it, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma desires that the listener provide full assistance in all that he does, yet the listener does not comply with his wishes—or conversely—if the two are at odds and do not harmonize, such that they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a teacher of the Dharma, for the sake of gain and fame, desires to speak it to others and further wishes to cause them to write down, receive, uphold, recite, and practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; yet the listener, knowing his motive, does not wish to receive it from him.

Or suppose the listener, for the sake of gain and fame, desires to request the teacher to speak it and further wishes to employ skillful means to have this profound *prajñāpāramitā* written down, received, upheld, recited, and practiced; yet the teacher, knowing his motive, does not comply with the request. Since these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, receiving, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If the one who can preach the Dharma wishes to go to another region where life and limb are in danger, but the one who can listen to the Dharma fears for their life and does not wish to go along;

or if the listener wishes to go to another region where life and limb are in danger, but the preacher fears for their life and does not wish to go with them—where the two are thus not in harmony and fail to obtain instruction, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who can preach the Dharma wishes to go to another land that is full of bandits, pestilence, hunger, and thirst, while the one who can listen to the Dharma fears those hardships and is unwilling to go with him;

or suppose the listener wishes to go to another land full of bandits, pestilence, hunger, and thirst, while the preacher of the Dharma fears those hardships and is unwilling to go together with him. Because the two are not in harmony, they do not obtain the opportunity to teach, listen, copy, uphold, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 546;
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 547.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Four, Chapter Eleven: On the Deeds of Māra (2).

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to go to another region that is peaceful, prosperous, and free from difficulties, and a listener of the Dharma wishes to follow him. The teacher of the Dharma then uses skillful means to say: "
"Although you have followed me out of desire for gain, will your wishes necessarily be fulfilled upon reaching that place?
You should reflect well and not harbor grief or regret later.
At that time, the listeners, having heard this, thought to themselves:
"This teacher does not wish for me to leave his presence; even if I were to go with him by force, would I necessarily hear the Dharma?

For this reason, he does not follow him away. Because the two are not in harmony, he fails to receive instruction, listen to, write down, uphold, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to travel to another region, and the road he must traverse passes through a wilderness that is desolate and perilous, filled with many dangers from bandits, as well as fears of caṇḍālas, wild beasts, hunters, venomous snakes, and the like. A listener of the Dharma wishes to follow him, but the teacher of the Dharma uses skillful means to test him, saying:
'For what reason do you now follow me without any business of your own, wishing to go to such dangerous and difficult places?'"
"You should reflect well upon this and not later feel sorrow or regret.
The one capable of hearing the Dharma, having heard these words, thinks to himself:
"The teacher likely does not wish for me to follow him; even if I were to insist on following, how could I possibly hear the Dharma?"

For this reason, if one does not follow them and the two parties do not reach harmony, such that one fails to obtain instruction, listen to, write down, uphold, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this constitutes a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It may happen that the teacher of the Dharma has many donors who follow him constantly, while the listener comes to request the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, or requests that it be written down, upheld, recited, or practiced according to the instructions. Because of these many obstacles, the teacher lacks the leisure to provide instruction. The listener then gives rise to feelings of resentment; subsequently, even when instructed, they do not listen or accept the teaching. Since the two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the instruction, the listening, the writing, the upholding, the recitation, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are various evil Māras who assume diverse forms and approach the Bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy him, so that he may not copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others the sūtras associated with the Prajñāpāramitā."
Therefore, Subhūti,

you should know that all obstacles encountered by sons of good family who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle when they are copying or otherwise engaging with this profound perfection of wisdom are all the deeds of Māra.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason do evil Māras assume various forms and go to where Bodhisattvas dwell, employing skillful means to destroy them, so that they may not transcribe, nor even expound, the sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: “The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the all-knowing wisdom (*sarvajñājñāna*) of all Buddhas; from the all-knowing wisdom of all Buddhas, the Buddha-teachings (*buddhadharma*) are produced; from the Buddha-teachings, the *prajñā* of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings is produced; and through the *prajñā* of sentient beings, the severance of boundless afflictions (*kleśa*) is realized. Those who have severed their afflictions cannot be taken advantage of by any evil Māras. Because they cannot be taken advantage of, many evil Māras give rise to grief and suffering as if an arrow had pierced their hearts, thinking:
‘May I not be deprived of this realm of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* because of them.’”

For this reason, Māra the Evil One assumes various forms and approaches the bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy [their practice], so that they may not copy, nor even expound, the sūtras associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what manner does Māra, the evil one, manifest various forms and approach the bodhisattva in order to skillfully destroy them?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are certain evil Māras who take the form of śramaṇas and approach the bodhisattvas with skillful means to destroy them, causing them to disparage and become weary of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. They say such things as:
'The formless sūtras that you study and recite are not the true *prajñāpāramitā*; the sūtras with forms that I study and recite are the true *prajñāpāramitā*.'"

When these words were spoken, there were certain bodhisattvas who had not yet received their prediction, being beginners in the Mahāyāna with narrow and inferior wisdom. They then gave rise to doubt and confusion regarding the sūtras associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because of this doubt and confusion, they developed revulsion and disdain for the *prajñāpāramitā*. Due to this revulsion and disdain, they consequently did not copy, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a demonic activity (*mārakarman*) of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are certain evil Māras who, assuming the guise of bhikṣus, approach a bodhisattva and say to him:

'If a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they will only realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they will never be able to realize unsurpassed buddhahood. For what reason, then, do you exert yourself in vain in this regard?'"

When a bodhisattva hears this and consequently fails to write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice it, contemplate it, or explain it in detail to others, one should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for the bodhisattva.
"In this way, Subhūti!

When the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being transcribed and so forth, many demonic obstacles (*mārakarman*) will arise; the bodhisattva should recognize them, and having recognized them, should diligently apply right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samyaksmṛti-samprajanya*) to skillfully distance himself from them."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Sugata!
When the profound perfection of wisdom is being written down and so forth, there will be many demonic obstacles."
For example, just as a priceless great jewel, a divine pearl, possesses superior powers yet encounters many enemies and thieves;
so too, although this Prajñāpāramitā possesses supreme virtues, it encounters many obstacles and hindrances.

Because those sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle possess little merit, various evil Māras create obstacles when they engage in activities such as copying [the scriptures]; thus, although they have the aspiration, they are unable to achieve success.

Why is this? There are those who are deluded by Māra; when sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle engage in such acts as transcribing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they create obstacles for them.
"Bhagavān!

Those who are foolish possess dull and obscure wisdom; they are unable to conceive of the vast Buddha-dharma. They themselves are incapable of writing down, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, practicing, contemplating, hearing, or explaining the Prajñāpāramitā, and furthermore, they take pleasure in obstructing others from performing such acts as writing it down."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

There are foolish people who are incited by Māra; they have not planted roots of goodness, their merit and wisdom are meager and inferior, they have not yet made great vows before the Buddha, and they have not been taken under the care of virtuous friends. Such individuals are unable themselves to copy, or even to expound, the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, when newly initiated sons of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna are copying and so forth this profound *Prajñāpāramitā*, these [foolish ones] create obstacles for them.

In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family whose merit and wisdom are meager and whose roots of goodness are slight; they will have no joy in the vast merits of the Tathāgatas, and they themselves will be unable to write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, hear, or explain the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, they will delight in obstructing others from writing it down and so forth. You should know that such individuals will incur boundless transgressions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle engage in activities such as copying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, many demonic obstacles (*mārakarma*) arise to create hindrances, causing these activities—such as copying—to fail to be accomplished. Consequently, they are unable to fulfill their merits, because their roots of goodness are not yet matured and their merit and wisdom are meager."

When sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle engage in such acts as transcribing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if no demonic interference occurs, one should know that this is entirely due to the spiritual power, compassion, and protective mindfulness of all Buddhas.

Why is this? Although the retinues of Māra exert themselves with skillful means wishing to destroy the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise exert themselves with skillful means, protecting and mindful of them with compassion, so that sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle may encounter no obstacles when copying and otherwise engaging with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
12. Chapter on Manifesting the World, Part Four, Chapter Twelve: Manifesting the World.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is as if there were a woman who had many sons—perhaps five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred or a thousand."
When his mother fell ill, each of her sons diligently sought out physicians and medicines, all thinking to themselves:

"How may we cause our mother’s illness to be cured? How may she be free from obstacles, so that her life and reputation shall not perish? How may she dwell long in peace and happiness, with no painful sensations arising, and how may all exquisite articles of enjoyment come to our mother?"
"Why is this? To give birth to us and show us the ways of the world was exceedingly difficult and arduous.

Having formed this thought, they vied with one another to employ skillful means to seek peaceful conditions for the protection of their mother’s body, ensuring she was not touched by mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, wind, rain, humans, non-humans, or other unpleasant things; they diligently attended to her needs so that she might be free from all illnesses, her six sense faculties purified, and devoid of all sorrow and suffering.
Furthermore, they made offerings and paid homage with various kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of enjoyment, saying:
"Our mother, out of compassion, gave birth to us and instructed us in all worldly affairs; how could we fail to repay our mother's kindness?"
"In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, constantly protects and keeps in mind the Prajñāpāramitā through various skillful means."

If sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle are able to write down, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and explain this Prajñāpāramitā without weariness, the Tathāgata will likewise diligently protect and mindfully sustain them through various skillful means, so that they may remain free from harm and affliction.

Furthermore, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in other worlds throughout the ten directions—who out of compassion seek to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings—likewise employ various skillful means to protect and mindfully attend to this Prajñāpāramitā, ensuring that no evil Māras can destroy it, so that it may long endure for the benefit and happiness of the entire world.
In this way, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas all protect and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā through various skillful means. Why is this so?

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it can correctly manifest the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and it can demonstrate the true reality of all phenomena in the world; furthermore, that knowledge of all modes also arises from it.
“Subhūti, you should know that all the Buddhas,

the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, have all relied upon this very profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to diligently practice and train, thereby realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
In the past, I too relied upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, diligently practicing and training in it, thereby realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it can correctly manifest all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*), and it can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the perfection of wisdom can give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) as well as other merits, it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"One who can demonstrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world" means one who can demonstrate the true reality of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the world.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"In what way does the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) demonstrate the true reality of the five aggregates in the world?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate that the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), possess no characteristic of transformation or decay, it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world."

Why is this so? Because the five aggregates, such as form and the rest, lack intrinsic nature, they are said to be empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, uncreated, unborn, and unceasing. Since the true dharma-realm itself cannot undergo transformation or decay through such qualities as emptiness, it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all worldly phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to universally realize and know the distinctions in the designations of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the perfection of wisdom to realize, as they truly are, the distinctions in the mental activities of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings, they declare that the perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the intrinsic nature of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings does not exist; therefore, they declare that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings have no abiding place, because they are like space, having nothing upon which to rely. Therefore, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the abbreviated minds of all immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are exhausted, detached, and lack the intrinsic nature of abbreviation; therefore, they say that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, all the distracted minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. Because of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and because of the non-distracted nature of mind, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, the defiled minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—because they cannot be demonstrated and because the nature of the mind is undefiled—they say that the Prajñāpāramitā can demonstrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the perfection of wisdom to realize, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are unstained, because their intrinsic nature is pure and they lack a nature of defilement; thus they proclaim that the perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, all the inferior dispositions of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings; because these cannot be concealed and because there is no nature of inferior disposition, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the perfection of wisdom to realize, as they truly are, all the mental stirrings of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings; because these are unfathomable and because they lack the nature of mental stirring, the perfection of wisdom is said to be able to reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, the finite, infinite, and boundless defiled minds of sentient beings—because they lack intrinsic nature, because they are without conceptual differentiation, and because they lack the nature of outflows. Therefore, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings—because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because they are without objective apprehension (*anupalambha*), and because they do not possess the nature of being untainted. Thus, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings possess greed; because the true nature of those minds is not one that possesses greed, they declare that the prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings that are free from desire; because the nature of these minds as they truly are is not a mind free from desire, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the various states of anger in immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are, in their true nature, not states of anger; therefore, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings that are free from hatred; because the true nature of those minds is not something apart from being free from hatred, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the deluded minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings are, by their very nature, not deluded minds; therefore, they say that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings that are free from delusion; because the true nature of those minds is not something separate from being free from delusion, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, all the small minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—minds that neither come nor go and have no attachment, because they lack the intrinsic nature of a small mind. For this reason, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, the great minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—minds whose self-nature is equal and which accord with the nature of equality because they lack the nature of a 'great mind. For this reason, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that all immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings possess narrow minds—minds that do not give rise to skillful means, are without attachment, and lack the nature of narrowness. For this reason, they declare that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the vast minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings—minds that neither increase nor decrease and are not separate [from suchness], because they have already transcended them and possess no nature of vastness. Thus, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, that the finite minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are empty of intrinsic nature and do not possess a finite nature; thus, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless minds of sentient beings—minds that are without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without differentiation; which have no point of reliance, being like the great void; and which are not 'immeasurable minds' [in a conventional sense]. For this reason, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the minds of all immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings that perceive phenomena. Because their intrinsic nature is equal, because the five eyes do not function therein, and because it is not a mind that perceives phenomena, the Prajñāpāramitā is said to be able to demonstrate the true reality of all dharmas in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the non-perceiving minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings—because no marks can be apprehended therein, because they are free from various objective spheres, and because they are not [simply] non-perceiving minds. Thus, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true nature of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are characterized by opposition; they are falsely discriminated because they lack mastery over their objects of perception and are not non-oppositional minds. For this reason, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true nature of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the non-obstructed minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—realizing them as truly inexhaustible and without arising. Because these are not non-obstructed minds [in the sense of being mere negations], it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true nature of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the various states of superior mind of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—their true nature being devoid of volitional thought. Because there is no state of superior mind, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the unsurpassed minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—minds that are free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and wherein even a fraction of a mental nature cannot be found. Because it is not [a mind] that is 'unsurpassed,' the Prajñāpāramitā is said to be able to reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the indeterminate minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings—because their true nature is equal to the unequaled and not because they are indeterminate minds—they say that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the concentrated minds of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. Their true nature is equal and uniform, just like space; because there is no inherent nature to concentration, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings are not liberated—because their intrinsic nature is remote, because their nature is the absence of nature, and because they are not non-liberated minds—and thus the Prajñāpāramitā is said to be able to reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the minds of liberation of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings. Because the true nature of these minds is the non-nature of mind, they cannot be apprehended through investigation throughout the three periods of time; because they are not [substantial] minds of liberation, the Prajñāpāramitā is said to be able to reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless minds of sentient beings as being invisible. Because they lack intrinsic nature, because they are invisible, because they are not real, because they transcend the faculties and their objects, because they cannot be discerned, and because they are not fully established, they are not even apprehended by the wisdom-eye or the divine eye, much less by the fleshly eye!"

Because all eyes are unable to see it, it is called "unseeable. Since this unseeability is itself unattainable, and because one cannot speak of a mind that is unseeable, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena in the world.
"So it is, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom can reveal to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas the true reality of the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the emergence and disappearance of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings."

“Subhūti! How is it that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the perfection of wisdom, realize as they truly are the emergence and submergence of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings?”

It means that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, realize and know as they truly are the minds and mental factors of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—all of which arise in dependence upon form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;

likewise, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, realize and know as they truly are the emergence and disappearance of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings.
“Subhūti! In what way do the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings arise and subside, all depending on form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness for their birth?”

That is to say, regarding the minds and mental factors of sentient beings, there are those who, based on form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing away, he either exists, or does not exist, or both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist—and that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish and false;

or there are those who, based on form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, cling to the view that the self and the world are either eternal, or non-eternal, or both eternal and non-eternal, or neither eternal nor non-eternal—and that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish and false.

There are those who, relying on form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, cling to the self and the world as being either finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite, asserting: "This alone is the truth; all else is foolish and false.

There are others who, relying on form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, cling to the idea that the life-principle is identical to the body or that it is distinct from the body, asserting: "This alone is the truth; all else is foolish and false."
"So it is, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the perfection of wisdom to realize, as they truly are, the emergence and disappearance of the minds and mental factors of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings; all of which arise based on the differentiated perceptions of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the emergence and submergence of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings."

“Subhūti! How is it that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the perfection of wisdom, realize as they truly are the emergence and disappearance of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings?”

It means that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, know form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are—identical with suchness, non-dual and undifferentiated.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the five aggregates; the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of the world. Why is that?
As the Blessed One has said, the name "world" is established in dependence upon the five aggregates. Therefore, Subhūti, the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of the world;

the suchness of the world is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry; the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning, and so on in succession until the suchness of the conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the suchness of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; the suchness of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is the suchness of all sentient beings.
Subhūti, you should know this:

whether it be the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; the suchness of all sentient beings; or the suchness of all phenomena—such suchnesses are not separate from one another. Because they are neither identical nor different, nor both identical and different, they are inexhaustible, non-dual, and without division, and cannot be conceptually differentiated.
“Subhūti, you should know that all Tathāgatas,
Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the perfection of wisdom to realize the ultimate suchness of all phenomena and thereby attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
For this reason, it is said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas; she is the mother of all Buddhas, capable of revealing to all Buddhas the true reality of the world.
Subhūti, you should know that all Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to be able to realize, as they truly are, the suchness of all phenomena, their non-falsity, and their immutability.
"Because he has realized the characteristic of suchness as it truly is, he is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The suchness, the non-falsity, and the non-alteration realized by the profound Prajñāpāramitā are extremely profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize."
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas reveal and distinguish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas by means of suchness (*tathatā*).
Suchness is so profound and so sublime—who could believe and understand it?

Only irreversible bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, great arhats whose vows are fulfilled, and sons of good family who possess right view can, upon hearing the Buddha speak of this profound suchness, give rise to faith and understanding.
“The Tathāgata, for their sake, reveals and distinguishes them based on the characteristics of the suchness (tathatā) realized by himself.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “It is so! It is so!”
So it is! It is as you have said. Why is this so?

Because suchness is inexhaustible, it is profound; only the Tathāgata, having attained manifest and perfect enlightenment regarding the profound characteristic of inexhaustible suchness, proclaims and reveals it for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that they may give rise to faith and understanding.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, leading ten thousand devaputras of the desire realm, and Mahābrahmā, King of the Great Brahmās, leading twenty thousand devaputras of the form realm, together approached the Buddha’s dwelling. They prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha in unison, saying:
“Regarding the various profound dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata, what are their characteristics?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying:
"The Dharma I teach has emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-formation, non-arising, non-ceasing, quiescence, nirvana, and the dharma-realm as its characteristics."
Why is this? The Dharma taught by the Buddha has no point of reliance; it is, for example, like space, which cannot be pointed out.
"Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The profound characteristics of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata do not fall within the category of form, nor do they fall within the categories of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they do not rely upon form, nor do they rely upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

"Son of Heaven, you should know that the profound characteristics of phenomena taught by the Tathāgata cannot be established nor can they be subverted by the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others."

Why is this? Because the world—including gods, humans, and asuras—is entirely characterized by marks (*nimitta*); and that which possesses marks can neither establish nor destroy the mark of the markless (*animitta*).
"Son of Heaven, you should know!
The profound characteristics of phenomena taught by the Tathāgata cannot be established or destroyed by means of the hand, nor can they be established or destroyed by means of any other phenomena."
“O Son of Heaven, you should know!
Suppose there were this question:
‘Who established space?’”
"Who, moreover, could destroy it?
Is one who asks this question asking correctly?
The devaputras replied:
"That is not a correct question.
Why is this? Because space has no substance, no characteristics, and is unconditioned; it cannot be established, nor can it be destroyed."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
O Devaputra, you should know that the profound nature of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) which I proclaim is likewise thus: it cannot be established, nor can it be destroyed."

Whether a Buddha exists or not, the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is such; the Buddha awakens to these characteristics as they truly are, and for this reason is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the sons of the gods again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The various characteristics awakened to by the Tathāgata are exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize.”
Because the Tathāgata has realized such characteristics through manifest awakening, unimpeded wisdom operates regarding all phenomena.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas abide in such characteristics, analytically revealing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for the sake of all sentient beings, they skillfully reveal the characteristics of all phenomena, causing them to attain unimpeded wisdom regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*.

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the constant sphere of activity for all Tathāgatas; because all Tathāgatas practice within this sphere, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and then analyze and reveal it for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Son of Heaven, you should know that the Tathāgata has realized the characteristics of all phenomena, exactly as they are, to be signless."
"For this reason, I say that the Buddhas have attained unimpeded wisdom, and there is no one equal to them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
"The profound Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas; it can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."

Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha dwells in accordance with the Dharma; he honors, reveres, respects, praises, upholds, and protects that Dharma upon which he relies and abides—this Dharma is none other than the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not fail to rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, honoring, revering, respecting, praising, embracing, and upholding it.

Why is this so? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas, serves as the locus of reliance for all Buddhas, and can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.
“Subhūti, you should know that all Tathāgatas,
Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are those who recognize kindness and are able to repay kindness.
If someone were to ask:”
"Who is it that knows gratitude and is able to repay kindness?
One should answer correctly:
"The Buddha is the one who knows gratitude and is able to repay kindness."
"Why is this? Because among all those in the world who recognize kindness and repay it, none surpass the Buddha.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s knowing gratitude and repaying kindness?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have mounted such a vehicle and traversed such a path to arrive at unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.”

Having attained awakening, at all times one shall offer worship, respect, honor, praise, embrace, and protection to this vehicle and this path, never ceasing for even a moment; know that this vehicle and this path are none other than the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s knowing of kindness and repaying kindness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are no Tathāgatas, Arhats,
or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to realize that all phenomena lack real activity, because an agent does not exist."

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, without exception, rely upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā to awaken to the fact that all phenomena are not established as real entities, because no substantial form can be apprehended.
Subhūti, you should know that because the Tathāgatas, Arhats,

and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* to realize that all phenomena are devoid of activity and lack anything to be accomplished, and because they have at all times— without interruption— made offerings, shown reverence, honored, praised, accepted, and protected it, they are therefore called those who truly know gratitude and repay their debt of gratitude.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are no Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to turn the wheel of wisdom regarding all phenomena as being without action, without accomplishment, and without arising; furthermore, they are able to know the causes and conditions for this non-turning."
Therefore, one should know that the profound Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and can also manifest the characteristics of the world as they truly are.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata has constantly taught that the nature of all phenomena is without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision.”
How can it be said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is also able to reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning. It is so! It is so!"
It is as you have said:
the nature of all phenomena is without arising, without origination, without cognition, and without vision;

yet, according to worldly convention, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and can also reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are.
"Subhūti! Why is it that the nature of all phenomena is without arising, without origination, without cognition, and without vision?
Because all phenomena are empty, non-existent, without basis, and without attachment; for these reasons, they are without arising, without origination, without cognition, and without vision."
Subhūti, you should know this:
although the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to Buddhas and manifest the characteristics of the world, there is nothing that is born, nor is there anything that is manifested.
Subhūti, you should know this:

because the profound perfection of wisdom does not perceive form, it is called the demonstration of the characteristic of form; because it does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, it is called the demonstration of the characteristics of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
"By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom is able to reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying,

"In what way does this profound perfection of wisdom reveal the characteristics of form by not seeing form, and reveal the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by not seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not give rise to consciousness by taking form (*rūpa*) as its object; this is called ‘showing the characteristic of form’ because form is not seen.

It does not give rise to consciousness by taking feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its objects; this is called ‘showing the characteristics of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness’ because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are not seen.”
By virtue of this meaning, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal that the world is empty, that the world is secluded, that the world is pure, and that the world is tranquil, it is called 'that which reveals the true reality of the world. It is thus that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is said to teach the Dharma."
Why is this? Because emptiness, detachment, purity, and tranquility are the true characteristics of all these worlds.
Chapter Thirteen: On the Inconceivable and Other Qualities, Part Four. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Bhagavān, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world for a great purpose; it appears in the world for an inconceivable purpose; it appears in the world for an immeasurable purpose; it appears in the world for an incalculable purpose; it appears in the world for a purpose that is unequaled.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said, Subhūti!
In what way does the profound perfection of wisdom appear in the world for the sake of a great task?"

It is said that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas take as their great task the rescue and deliverance of all sentient beings, never abandoning them for even a moment; it is for this purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
Subhūti!
How is it that the profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of inconceivable matters, immeasurable matters, incalculable matters, and matters equal to the unequaled?

That is to say, the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and omniscient nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are all inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; it is for this purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it only the Buddha-nature, Tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and all-knowledge nature of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha that are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; or are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—even all phenomena likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Not only are the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and omniscient nature of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and peerless; but form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even all dharmas—are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and peerless.”
Why is this so? Because within the true nature of all phenomena, both the mind and its mental factors are unapprehendable.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"
Because all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as all phenomena, cannot be designated, they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and peerless.
Why is this? Because these dharmas lack intrinsic nature, are unapprehendable, and are empty of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because all forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, are unapprehendable, they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are immeasurable, non-existent, and empty of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because all forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, are without limit, they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions are all forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, without limit?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is it possible for the mind or mental factors to measure or limit space?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, are likewise so; because their intrinsic nature is empty, the mind and mental factors cannot measure them.”

For this reason, because all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as all phenomena, are limitless, they are all inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
“Subhūti, you should know that because all phenomena are inconceivable,

immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.”
"Subhūti, you should know that all such dharmas are inconceivable, because conceptualization has ceased;
they are immeasurable, because measurement has ceased."
It is immeasurable because all measure has ceased;
it is unequaled because all equality has ceased.
Subhūti, you should know this!
Thus, all these dharmas are inconceivable, for they transcend conception;
they are immeasurable, for they transcend measurement;
they are incalculable, for they transcend calculation.
"Unequaled, because it transcends all that is equal.
Subhūti, you should know that 'inconceivable,' 'immeasurable,' 'incalculable,' and 'unequaled' are merely designations; they possess no reality whatsoever."
"Subhūti, you should know that that which is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled— all these are like space, being utterly non-existent."

For this reason, all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; for Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the world with its gods, humans, and asuras are all unable to conceive of, measure, calculate, or equalize these dharmas.

When the Buddha had spoken these inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled dharmas, five hundred bhikṣus and two thousand bhikṣuṇīs among the assembly attained liberation of mind through the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*). Furthermore, sixty upāsakas and thirty upāsikās gave rise to the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, becoming free from dust and defilement. Additionally, twenty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); the World-Honored One prophesied that they would receive the irreversible prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment within this Bhadrakalpa.

Regarding those laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*) previously mentioned who, amidst all phenomena, have become free from dust and free from defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye—the Buddha has likewise prophesied that before long they shall realize the liberation of mind and wisdom through the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Forty-seven;
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Forty-eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 14: Parables, Part Four, Chapter Fourteen: Parables. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is this profound perfection of wisdom indeed a great matter appearing in the world?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!"
So it is! This profound Prajñāpāramitā has indeed appeared in the world for a great purpose. Why is this so?
The profound perfection of wisdom truly accomplishes the knowledge of all modes; it truly accomplishes the stage of the solitary buddhas; and it truly accomplishes the stages of the śrāvakas.
Subhūti, you should know this!

Just as a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration, possessing majestic power and sovereignty, subdues all and entrusts all affairs of state to his ministers, remaining at ease with hands folded, free from exertion, and dwelling in peace and happiness—so too are the Buddhas. As Great Dharma Kings, they possess majestic power and sovereignty, subduing all, and entrust all the Buddha-dharmas, whether those of Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas, entirely to the profound Prajñāpāramitā, causing them all to be fully accomplished.
Therefore, Subhūti,
this profound perfection of wisdom has truly appeared in the world as a great matter.
Subhūti, you should know this!

The profound perfection of wisdom does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to form; it does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
