It does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the fruit of stream-entry; it does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship.

It does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor does it appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the knowledge of all modes.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way does this profound perfection of wisdom also not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do you perceive any fruit of arhatship that can be grasped or clung to?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"I do not see any fruit of arhatship that can be grasped or clung to therein.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
I, too, do not perceive any dharma of the Tathāgata within which one could grasp or become attached.
Therefore, Subhūti!
“Furthermore, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the knowledge of all modes, then when the assembly of bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle hear such a teaching, their minds will be struck with alarm and fear, and they will be unable to believe or accept it.”

If the causes are complete—having made great vows in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the past and having accumulated sublime roots of goodness throughout the long night—then the assembly of Bodhisattvas, upon hearing such a teaching, will be able to believe and accept it.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
For this reason, the profound perfection of wisdom should not be taught indiscriminately to those bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound; it is difficult to see and difficult to realize, and extremely difficult to believe and understand."

If there are sentient beings who, in the past, have made great vows before immeasurable Buddhas, cultivated various roots of goodness, and served many virtuous friends, they will be able to believe in and understand this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

Even if all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were to become followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and so forth, and those beings were to practice the conduct of their respective stages for an eon or more than an eon, it would not equal the merit obtained by someone who, for a single day, endures, delights in, contemplates, weighs, and examines this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; the latter’s merit is infinitely superior to that of the former.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

O Devaputra, you should know that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will swiftly attain *nirvāṇa*. This is superior to what was previously described regarding those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and others who practice their respective stages for an eon or even more than an eon—how much more so for those who possess patience and delight!

At that time, the sons of the gods, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. They prostrated themselves before the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and took their leave of the Buddha to return to their palaces. Not long after they had departed from the assembly, they suddenly vanished; each returned to his own palace within his respective realm and exhorted the gods there to cultivate supreme practices.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is able to give rise to faith and understanding, without sinking, without being submerged, without confusion, and without despondency; without doubt, without uncertainty, without grasping, and without attachment; and listens to and receives it with joy, honoring and making offerings to it—from where did such a person pass away to be reborn here?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, is able to give rise to faith and understanding,
and does not sink, does not drown, is not confused, and is not despondent, being without delusion, without doubt, and without..."
Grasping it without attachment, they joyfully listen and receive it, honoring and making offerings to it; they delight in seeing and hearing it, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it.

They are never separated from this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and its associated sublime mental engagements (*manasikāra*), and they cherish and follow those who can preach the Dharma, like a calf following its mother.

Following his mother, he never for a moment departed from her until he had attained a profound mastery of all the meanings and principles of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and was able to explain them to others;
until then, he never remained separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or his Dharma teacher for even a brief instant. This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
“A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who passes away from among humans and comes to be born here is able to accomplish such a feat by virtue of superior causes from former lives.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Are there any Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who, having accomplished such meritorious qualities and having made offerings to and served Buddhas in other directions, pass away from those places and come to be born here?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having made offerings to and served Buddhas in other directions, pass away from those places and are reborn here, having accomplished such sublime merits.”

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have previously, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in other directions, heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and were able to give rise to faith and understanding; they have venerated and made offerings to it, copied it, received and upheld it, inquired about its most profound meanings, practiced it, contemplated it, and extensively explained it to others. Having passed away from those places, they have been reborn here, and by virtue of their past roots of goodness, they are able to accomplish these deeds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, passing away from the common assembly of the Tuṣita heaven, are reborn among human beings; they, too, are endowed with such meritorious qualities."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in previous lives, having heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya in the Tuṣita Heaven, were able to give rise to faith and understanding, and they honored and made offerings to it; they inquired into its profound meanings and purports, practiced it, contemplated it, and extensively explained it to others. Having passed away from that place, they have been reborn here, and by means of those past roots of goodness, they are able to accomplish these matters.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, did not inquire about its profound meaning and intent. Now born among humans, when they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds become confused, perplexed, and despondent; or else they give rise to erroneous interpretations that are difficult to rectify."
Why is that? Because those who do not understand the provisional meaning are frequently plagued by mental confusion, doubt, and despondency.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

There are sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives and even inquired about its profound meaning for one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days, did not practice with diligence according to the teaching.

Having been born among humans in this life, although they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and their minds remain firm and indestructible for a short time, if they depart from what they have heard of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the Dharma teacher, and fail to inquire about its deep meaning, they will soon fall away and their minds will become hesitant.

Why is this? Although these sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle heard the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives and were even able to inquire about its profound meaning, they did not practice with diligence according to the teachings. Consequently, in this present life, regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, at times they delight in hearing it and at times they do not; at times their resolve is firm and at times they regress. Their minds are light and fickle, fluctuating between progress and retreat like *tūla* cotton drifting and turning with the wind.

It should be known that such sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and are newly trained in the Mahāyāna, although they possess faith, it is not firm or pure; they are unable to maintain their joyful confidence in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a long time, and consequently, they will either follow after two stages or fall into one of them—namely, the stage of the Śrāvaka or the stage of the Pratyekabuddha.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

it is like a ship upon which people have embarked to cross the great ocean; if those on board do not take hold of timber, vessels, floats, planks, or even a corpse to rely upon, it is certain they will drown and fail to reach the other shore.”

If one can take hold of wooden vessels, flotation bags, planks, or a corpse as something to rely upon, you should know that such a person will ultimately not drown, but will reach the peaceful far shore of the great ocean, remaining unhurt and unharmed while experiencing all manner of happiness.

It is the same for sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle: although they may have attained a small measure of faith, respect, and affection for the Mahāyāna, they do not embrace the profound Prajñāpāramitā as their point of reliance.

It should be known that such individuals fall away from the middle way and fail to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), meaning they descend to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

However, those who possess faith, patience, delight, aspiration, diligence, superior resolve, heedfulness, excellent intention, equanimity, reverence, joy, gladness, and a pure mind; who do not abandon the yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and who are further able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as their support—[they shall succeed].

It should be known that such individuals will never midway fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; they are certain to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a man or a woman who, taking an unbaked clay jar, went to a river, a pond, a well, a spring, or a canal to fetch water; you should know that this jar will soon rot and break."
Why is this? Because this jar is not yet fired; it cannot hold water and will ultimately return to earth.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

There are sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they possess faith, patience, delight, aspiration, diligence, superior resolve, heedfulness, superior intention, equanimity, reverence, joy, gladness, a pure mind, and do not relinquish the yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in regard to the Great Vehicle, yet fail to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means—it should be known that such individuals will fall away midway and be unable to realize the knowledge of all aspects (sarvajñajñāna), meaning they will fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose there were a man or a woman who, taking a well-fired jar, went to a river, or a pond, or a well, or a spring, or a canal to fetch water; you should know that this jar would never break or dissolve.
Why is this? Because this jar is well-fired, capable of holding water, and extremely durable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

There are sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith and patience toward the Mahāyāna, and so forth, up to those who do not abandon the noble yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they are able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). It should be known that such individuals will never regress midway to enter the stage of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha; they are certain to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and will be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings until the end of the future.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose there is a merchant who lacks skillful wisdom;

while his ship is still at the shore and not yet securely prepared, he loads his goods upon it, hauls it into the water, and sets sail immediately. You should know that this ship will break apart and sink midway, and the people, the ship, and the goods will all be scattered to different places. Thus, because this merchant lacks skillful wisdom, he loses both his life and all his wealth."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

There are sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they possess faith and forbearance regarding the Great Vehicle—and as has been explained at length, even possess the non-abandonment of the noble yoke toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—yet do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means. You should know that such individuals will fall away midway and fail to realize the knowledge of all modes; that is to say, they will fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a merchant possessed of skillful wisdom who, having first thoroughly repaired a ship at the seashore, then towed it into the water to ensure it was free of leaks, and subsequently loaded his goods upon it before departing; you should know that this ship will certainly not be wrecked or sink, and both the people and the goods will reach their destination in safety."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons of good family who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle have faith and patience regarding the Great Vehicle—and as has been explained at length, up to not relinquishing the noble yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—and furthermore are able to embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that such individuals will never fall back midway into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; they are certain to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings until the end of the future.

Why is this? If sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle possess faith in the Great Vehicle and possess patience—expanding this description up to not relinquishing the yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—and further are able to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), then by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), they will not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas in the interim; they will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and constantly bring benefit to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, decrepit and worn out by age, further afflicted by various diseases—namely, wind disorders, bile disorders, phlegm disorders, or combinations of these three."
"What do you think?
Would this old and sick man be able to rise from his bed by himself?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Even if someone were to support this person and help them stand up, they would not have the strength to walk even one *krośa*, or two, or three.
Why is this? Because they are extremely old and sick."

In this way, Subhūti, there may be sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith in the Great Vehicle and possess receptivity, and so forth, up to not relinquishing the noble yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet, if they do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, you should know that such individuals will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but will instead fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? It is because it is the natural order of things for those who are devoid of skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

Suppose there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, aged, decrepit, and worn out, further afflicted by various ailments—namely, disorders of wind, heat, or phlegm, or a combination of these three—and this aged and sick person, wishing to rise from his bed or seat to go elsewhere, was unable to do so himself.
Two strong men each supported one of his armpits, slowly assisting him to rise and said to him:
"Do not hesitate; go wherever you wish. We two shall never abandon you; you will surely reach your destination in safety and without harm."
"In this way, Subhūti!

If there are sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who have faith and patience regarding the Great Vehicle—and as has been explained at length—up to those who do not relinquish the noble yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and who are further able to embrace the skillful means of the profound perfection of wisdom, you should know that such individuals will never fall away midway into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; they are certain to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings."
Chapter 15: Praise by the Gods, Part Four. Chapter Fifteen: Praise by the Gods. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
How should the newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwelling in the Mahāyāna abide in the profound perfection of wisdom?
How should they train in the profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to abide in and train in the profound perfection of wisdom should first draw near to, serve, and make offerings to true and pure spiritual friends."
If one can proclaim the profound Prajñāpāramitā and provide instruction and admonition to bodhisattvas, know that such a person is a true, pure, and virtuous friend.
That is to say, they are able to proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instruct and admonish those bodhisattvas who have newly entered the Mahāyāna,
saying: "Come,
son of good family!..."
You should diligently cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

When you practice diligently, you should do so with the skillful means of non-apprehension, dedicating [the merit] together with all sentient beings equally toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

When you dedicate [merit], do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by way of form; do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Son of good family!
If there is nothing to be grasped, one is able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"O son of good family!
Do not give rise to craving or attachment for the stage of the śrāvaka or the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
Thus it was said, Subhūti!

The true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friend provides instruction and admonition to the newly initiated bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the Mahāyāna, causing them to gradually enter the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“These bodhisattva mahāsattvas perform what is difficult; relying upon such characteristics as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet they do not wish to attain parinirvāṇa through their own power.”

Contemplating the realm of sentient beings undergoing extreme suffering, he seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to deliver them through skillful means throughout the future, yet without fear of the cycle of birth and death.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult: for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all the world, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, making this vow:

"For the sake of rescuing and uplifting the world, for the sake of being a dwelling place for the world, for the sake of being a refuge for the world, for the sake of showing the ultimate path to the world, for the sake of being an island for the world, for the sake of being a light for the world, for the sake of being a leader for the world, and for the sake of being a destination for the world, I shall exert diligent effort and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
“What is it that constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s solemn vow:
‘For the sake of rescuing and delivering all the world, I shall arouse diligent vigor and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment’?”
"Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see that all beings in the world are transmigrating through birth and death, undergoing various sufferings and unable to escape them, they rouse diligent vigor in order to sever those sufferings and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is what it means for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to make this vow:
'For the sake of rescuing and delivering all the world, I rouse diligent vigor and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of acting as a shelter for all the world, exert diligent effort and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
“Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to teach all phenomena to the world as being entirely non-composite, they exert diligent effort and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to exert diligent effort and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a dwelling place for all the worlds.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in what way are all phenomena not in conjunction?”

The Buddha told Subhūti: "All forms are non-composite; that is, forms are not mutually connected. If forms are not mutually connected, then forms have no arising or ceasing. If forms have no arising or ceasing, then forms are non-composite. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to explain to the world that all phenomena possess such a characteristic of non-composition should exert diligent effort and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of becoming a refuge for all the world, exert diligent effort and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
"Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to cause all those in the world who are oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, grief, and despair to swiftly attain liberation from these manifold sufferings such as birth and so forth, and to enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, exerts diligent vigor and advances toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva exerting diligent vigor and advancing toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of providing a refuge for all the world."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva exert diligent effort and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of demonstrating the ultimate path to the world?"
“Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to teach such a Dharma to the world declares: ‘The further shore of form is itself not form; as is the further shore, so too is form.

The further shore of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is itself not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; as is the further shore, so too are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.’”
"Just as with form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, so it is with all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If, as with form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, all phenomena are likewise the "other shore," then has the bodhisattva mahāsattva not already attained manifest, complete enlightenment regarding all phenomena?
"Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no matter of conceptual discrimination.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So it is! So it is! Within that other shore there is no conceptual differentiation; because there is no conceptual differentiation, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained manifest, complete enlightenment regarding all phenomena."

"Subhūti, you should know that it is a most difficult task for bodhisattva mahāsattvas: although they are able to contemplate all phenomena in this way, they do not realize them as a final attainment, nor do they become discouraged. They form this thought:
'Having attained manifest perfect awakening regarding these phenomena, I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and proclaim and reveal them to all the worlds.'"
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of demonstrating the ultimate path to the world, exerts diligent effort and advances toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of becoming an island for all the world, exert diligent effort and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
“Subhūti!
It is just as, for example, when there is high ground that can be inhabited amidst the great oceans, rivers, and ponds, and because it is surrounded by water on all sides, it is called an island.
In the same way, Subhūti!”

From form up to consciousness, the prior and posterior limits are severed; because these are severed, all phenomena are severed. This severance of the prior and posterior limits of all phenomena is itself the quiescent, sublime nirvāṇa, and it is also the nature of reality as it is, free from inversion.
"Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, desiring to preach such a Dharma for sentient beings so that they may swiftly enter such nirvāṇa, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to exert diligent vigor toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as an island for all the world."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva exert diligent effort and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a light for all the worlds?"

"Subhūti! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek to shatter the heavy darkness of sentient beings who have been covered by the eggshell of ignorance throughout the long night; because they seek to cure the cataracts of ignorance in sentient beings so that their vision may become clear and bright; and because they seek to provide the light of wisdom to all sentient beings who are mired in folly and obscurity, they exert diligent vigor and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is what it means for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to exert diligent vigor and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a light for all the world."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to act as a leader for all the world, arouse diligent vigor and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to proclaim and reveal to the world that the intrinsic nature of all forms is without arising or cessation; wishes to proclaim and reveal to the world that the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is without arising or cessation; wishes to proclaim and reveal to the world that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena of ordinary beings is without arising or cessation; wishes to proclaim and reveal to the world that the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas is without arising or cessation; and wishes to proclaim and reveal to the world that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is without arising or cessation—then they exert diligent effort and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to exert diligent effort and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a leader for all the worlds.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of becoming a destination for all the world, exert diligent vigor and advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to proclaim and reveal to the world that form has space as its destination, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have space as their destination; that all phenomena have space as their destination; and who wishes to proclaim and reveal to the world that form has no destination and is equal to space, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no destination and are equal to space, and that all phenomena have no destination and are equal to space—[this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva]."

Just as the great void has no coming, no going, no action, no abiding, no establishment, no arising, and no cessation, so too are all phenomena; for they are all like space, and because they are without discrimination, there is nothing to be discriminated.

Why is this? Because all forms (*rūpa*) are empty, they neither come nor go; because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are empty, they likewise neither come nor go; and because all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, they are all without coming or going.
Why is this so? Because all dharmas take emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as their destination, and they cannot transcend that destination;
all dharmas take non-creation and non-action as their destination, and they cannot transcend that destination.
All phenomena have non-arising and non-origination as their ultimate destination, and they cannot transcend that destination;
all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their ultimate destination, and they cannot transcend that destination;
all phenomena have being like a dream as their ultimate destination, and they cannot transcend that destination.
All phenomena have selflessness as their ultimate destination, and they cannot transcend that destination;
all phenomena have the boundless as their ultimate destination, and they cannot transcend that destination;
all phenomena have tranquility, nirvana, non-grasping, non-rejection, no coming, no going, the ultimate limit, and cessation as their ultimate destination, and they cannot transcend that destination.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to expound such a Dharma for the sake of the world, they exert diligent effort and advance toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is what is meant by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exerting diligent effort and advancing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as a destination for all the world.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Who will be able to give rise to faith and understanding in such a profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has long cultivated the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, has formed great vows in the presence of those Buddhas, has brought the roots of goodness he has planted to full maturity, and has been sustained and protected by immeasurable spiritual friends, then he will be able to give rise to faith and understanding in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to give rise to faith and understanding in such a profound prajñāpāramitā, what constitutes their intrinsic nature?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva has taming and seclusion as his intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Where will this bodhisattva mahāsattva go?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva shall go toward the knowledge of all modes.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva proceeds toward omniscience, they are able to realize this path and are also able to proclaim it, and they serve as a refuge for sentient beings."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva proceeds toward omniscience, they are able to awaken to that path and are also able to proclaim it, and they serve as a refuge for sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform what is difficult, in that he dons such firm armor as this:
‘I shall deliver immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings and lead them into nirvāṇa,’ yet no sentient beings at all can be apprehended.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.

Furthermore, Subhūti, this armor donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not belong to form, nor is it for the sake of form; it does not belong to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it for the sake of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It does not belong to the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor is it for the sake of the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it does not belong to the level of bodhisattvas, nor is it for the sake of the level of bodhisattvas; it does not belong to the level of buddhas, nor is it for the sake of the level of buddhas."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without ownership and without purpose.
It is for this reason that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing profound prajñāpāramitā are able to don such firm armor.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to don such firm armor and practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they will have no dwelling or attachment toward three things.”
What are the three?
First, the stage of the śrāvaka;
second, the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
"Third, the stage of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In view of what meaning do you speak thus?"
Subhūti replied:

"The profound perfection of wisdom has no place of attachment; there is no one who can practice it, no dharma that is practiced, no time or place for its practice, nor is there anything by means of which it can be cultivated."
Why is this? Because within this profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is not even the slightest portion of a real dharma that can be designated as "one who practices" and so forth.

"Bhagavān! If one cultivates space, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; if one cultivates all phenomena, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; if one cultivates non-attachment, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; if one cultivates non-existence, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; if one cultivates non-appropriation, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; if one cultivates the elimination of phenomena, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
one should observe non-regressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas by relying upon such a supreme practice and dwelling within this profound perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound perfection of wisdom while remaining without attachment to this profound perfection of wisdom, one should know that they are a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Those non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not grasp at the words or instructions of others as being the ultimate truth; they do not act merely out of faith in others. Upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, do not sink, do not despair, and are without doubt, regret, or confusion. Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they joyfully delight in hearing it, receive it with deep faith, write it down, uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to the principle, and explain it to others without ever becoming weary. You should know that such non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already heard the meaning and intent of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives."

Why is this? Because when these non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear the teaching of such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; as it is extensively explained, they even teach it to others without weariness.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid—and as has been explained at length, they constantly preach it to others without weariness—how should such a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the profound perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva, whose continuum conforms to, tends toward, and approaches the knowledge of all modes, should practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously, in accordance with, and tending toward, enter into the practice of profound prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all-knowledge?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously, conformably, progressively, and with full engagement practices the profound perfection of wisdom as if moving through space, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who continuously, conformably, progressively, and with full engagement practices the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects."

Why is this? Because the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is immeasurable and boundless. That which is immeasurable and boundless is neither form (*rūpa*), nor feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is without attainment, without clear realization (*abhisamaya*), without realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), and without the fruits of the path. It is without cognition (*jñāna*), without consciousness (*vijñāna*), without arising, and without cessation. It is without formation, without destruction, without origination, and without exhaustion. It is without cultivation, without action, and it neither comes from anywhere nor goes anywhere. It has no direction, no domain, and no place of abiding; it can only be described as immeasurable and boundless.

“Subhūti, you should know that because space is immeasurable and boundless, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is also immeasurable and boundless. Because the knowledge of all modes is immeasurable and boundless, there is no one who can realize it; it cannot be realized by form, nor can it be realized by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It cannot be realized by the perfection of generosity, nor can it be realized by the perfections of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? Form is itself the knowledge of all modes;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves the knowledge of all modes; the perfection of generosity is itself the knowledge of all modes; and the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom are themselves the knowledge of all modes.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, leading the host of devaputras of the desire realm, and Mahābrahmā, King of the Great Brahmās, leading the host of devaputras of the form realm, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side. With palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound, difficult to see, and difficult to fathom."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said. O Devaputra,

you should know that when I first attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I sat in meditation and reflected, having no desire to preach the Dharma, and my mind formed this thought:"
"The Dharma I have realized is subtle and profoundly deep; it cannot be easily believed or accepted by the world.

O Son of Heaven, you should know that the Dharma I have realized is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā. This Dharma is exceedingly profound: it is neither the subject that realizes nor the object that is realized; there is no place of realization and no time of realization.

"O Son of Heaven, you should know! Because space is profound, this Dharma is profound; because the self is profound, this Dharma is profound; because all dharmas neither come nor go, this Dharma is profound; because all dharmas are immeasurable and boundless, this Dharma is profound; because all dharmas are without arising or ceasing, this Dharma is profound; because all dharmas are without defilement or purity, this Dharma is profound."
At that time, the sons of the gods again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
"How rare!
Well-gone One!
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is subtle and profoundly deep; it is difficult for all the world to believe and difficult to understand."

Why is this? The Dharma taught by the Buddha is neither for the sake of grasping nor for the sake of abandoning; yet sentient beings in the world mostly practice grasping or abandoning. For this reason, those in the world are unable to have faith and understanding in what the Buddha has taught.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Chapter Sixteen: Suchness, Part Four, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is subtle and profound; it is able to accord with all phenomena without any obstruction.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha has the characteristic of non-obstruction, being entirely without trace, like empty space.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha has no characteristic of opposition, for there is no second.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha has no equal mark, for it is without adversary;
the Dharma taught by the Buddha leaves no trace, for it is without arising or ceasing;
the Dharma taught by the Buddha is entirely without arising or ceasing, for all arising and ceasing are unattainable.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is entirely without tracks or paths, for no such tracks or paths can be apprehended;
the Dharma taught by the Buddha is entirely without conceptual proliferation, for all discursive speech cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Venerable Subhūti is a true son of the Buddha, born after the Tathāgata."
"Why is this? Because, Venerable Subhūti, all the teachings you have expounded are entirely in accord with emptiness.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms, saying:
“You have said that you are true sons of the Buddha, born after the Tathāgata.
In what way, Subhūti, are you born after the Tathāgata?
It is because you are born after the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata, for no dharma of birth can be apprehended.”

Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata’s true suchness (tathatā) neither comes nor goes, and its intrinsic nature is unborn; Subhūti’s true suchness likewise neither comes nor goes, and its intrinsic nature is unborn. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is the suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of all phenomena is the Tathāgata’s suchness. Such suchness has no nature of being suchness, nor does it have a nature of not being suchness; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata’s true suchness (tathatā) has permanence as its characteristic; Subhūti’s true suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s true suchness is without change, without discrimination, and pervades all phenomena; Subhūti’s true suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s true thusness is without obstruction, and the true thusness of all phenomena is likewise without obstruction. Whether it be the true thusness of the Tathāgata or the true thusness of all phenomena, they are a single true thusness—non-dual, undifferentiated, uncreated, and unconditioned.

Thus, suchness is the eternal characteristic of suchness; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of suchness. Because it is the eternal characteristic of suchness and there is no time when it is not the characteristic of suchness, it is non-dual and undifferentiated. Subhūti, suchness is likewise; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is without recollection and without discrimination regarding all phenomena; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata’s suchness is without distinction and is ungraspable; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is not separate from the suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of all phenomena is not separate from the Tathāgata’s suchness. Such suchness is eternally the characteristic of suchness; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of suchness. Subhūti’s suchness is also like this; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
Although it is said that he is born in accordance with [the Tathāgata], there is nothing with which he is born in accordance, because Subhūti’s suchness is not different from the Buddha’s.

The suchness of the Tathāgata is neither past, nor future, nor present; the suchness of all phenomena is likewise neither past, nor future, nor present; and the suchness of Subhūti is also thus. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

Subhūti’s suchness conforms to the Tathāgata’s suchness; the Tathāgata’s suchness conforms to the suchness of the past; the suchness of the past conforms to the Tathāgata’s suchness; the Tathāgata’s suchness conforms to the suchness of the future; the suchness of the future conforms to the Tathāgata’s suchness; the Tathāgata’s suchness conforms to the suchness of the present; the suchness of the present conforms to the Tathāgata’s suchness; the Tathāgata’s suchness conforms to the suchness of the three periods of time; and the suchness of the three periods of time conforms to the Tathāgata’s suchness. The suchness of the three periods of time and the Tathāgata’s suchness are non-dual and without distinction; the suchness of all dharmas and Subhūti’s suchness are likewise non-dual and without distinction. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.
The suchness of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself the suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
It is by virtue of this suchness that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and are thus designated as Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Because I have developed profound faith and understanding in the suchness (*tathatā*) of all these dharmas, I say that Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.

When this characteristic of suchness was being taught, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; it was no different from when the Buddha realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, I say that Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.

“Son of Heaven, you should know this! However, I, Subhūti, do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by way of form; I do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. I do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by way of the fruit of stream-entry; I do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by way of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship. I do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by way of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; I do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by way of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. Rather, it is solely by way of suchness that I follow the Tathāgata’s birth.”
“Son of Heaven, you should know this! However, I, Subhūti, am not born following form;

I am not born following feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. I am not born following the fruit of stream-entry; I am not born following the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship. I am not born following the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; I am not born following the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas. Rather, because I am born following true suchness (tathatā), I, Subhūti, am born following the Tathāgata.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Such *tathatā* (thusness) is profoundly deep and subtle.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said;
such is the profound and subtle nature of true thusness (*tathatā*).

When this description of the characteristics of true thusness was spoken, three hundred bhikṣus were forever freed from all outflows (*āsrava*), their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
five thousand devaputras, whose past karma had reached maturity, simultaneously realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
and sixty bodhisattvas, no longer subject to outflows, attained liberation of mind.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"In this assembly, there are sixty bodhisattvas who have already drawn near to and made offerings to five hundred Buddhas in the past. Although they have practiced generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they did not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and skillful means (upāyakauśalya). Because they gave rise to divergent conceptions and engaged in divergent practices, they did not enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktvaniyāma). Therefore, although they have now heard the Great Dharma, by the power of their past causes, they do not experience the outflows (āsrava), and their minds have attained liberation."
Therefore, Śāriputra,

although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the bodhisattva path, if they do not embrace the skillful means of profound prajñāpāramitā, they will realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

“Śāriputra! It is as if there were a bird whose body was vast, measuring one hundred yojanas, or perhaps two hundred, even up to five hundred yojanas, yet its wings and feathers were either not yet formed or had already decayed.”
Suppose this bird were to leap down from that Trāyastriṃśa Heaven toward Jambudvīpa, and while on its way, it should suddenly think:
"I shall now return to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
"What do you think?
Would that bird be able to return to the Heaven of the Thirty-three?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If this bird were to form this aspiration midway:
'Upon reaching Jambudvīpa, may my body be without injury or suffering,' what do you think?"
"Will this bird's wish be fulfilled?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"World-Honored One!
When this bird reaches Jambudvīpa, its body will certainly suffer injury and pain; it will either meet its end or be near death."
"Why is this? Because this bird’s body is large and it falls from a great distance; its wings and feathers have not yet developed, or they are worn out and decayed.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

It is the same for sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle: although they have generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and have diligently practiced generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and have also cultivated the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—if they do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they will realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and consequently fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

“Śāriputra! Although these sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle recollect the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the three periods of time, their minds grasp at signs. They neither know nor see the true merits of these five aggregates of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; rather, hearing only an empty sound, they grasp at signs and become attached to them. When they dedicate this toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they fall instead into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because these bodhisattvas,

by not embracing the skillful means of the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), lack the power to dedicate the various roots of virtue they have cultivated toward enlightenment, despite their efforts to maintain them.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle are devoid of skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom, then even though they possess immeasurable accumulations of merit, they may or may not attain awakening.”
Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must certainly not distance themselves from the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 548 (and Fascicle 504).
19. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Part Four, Chapter Sixteen on Suchness (Tathatā), Section Two. At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is most profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand.
World-Honored One!”
"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is also most profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand,
World-Honored One!
Since unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is so difficult to believe and understand, it is also difficult to realize."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

If sentient beings possess corrupted wisdom, inferior diligence, and inferior resolve, lack skillful means, and are influenced by evil companions, it is truly difficult for them to have faith and understanding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and it is also difficult for them to have faith and understanding in the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; because of this, that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is also difficult to realize.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the World-Honored One has said, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is both difficult to believe and understand, and difficult to realize. In what way is this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment so extremely difficult to believe and understand, and so difficult to realize?"
Within this, there is absolutely nothing that can be realized.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are ultimately empty; within emptiness, there is no phenomenon capable of realizing another phenomenon.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; if one were to teach such a phenomenon for the sake of permanently severing such phenomena, that teaching itself is also empty.
For this reason, regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, that which realizes it, the phenomena realized, that which knows it, and the phenomena known—all are empty.
For this reason, I have formed this thought:

"The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is easy to believe and understand, and easy to realize; it is not difficult to believe and understand, nor is it difficult to realize, because there is no phenomenon that is not empty, and by believing and knowing this, one realizes it."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because those who can believe and understand, as well as those who can realize, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, it is said to be difficult to believe and understand, and difficult to realize;
because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is not a real existent, it is said to be difficult to believe and understand, and difficult to realize."
"Because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is not something that can be accumulated, it is said to be difficult to believe and understand,
and difficult to realize. At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti,

"Because all phenomena are ultimately empty, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to attain."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and are all like space.
For example, space does not form such a thought:
"I shall give rise to faith and understanding regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and I shall realize it.

All phenomena are likewise; they are all like space, entirely devoid of intrinsic nature. Therefore, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha were easy to believe and understand, or easy to realize and attain, then there would not be such a multitude of bodhisattvas—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—who, having set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, subsequently regress. Therefore, one should know that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize and attain.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think?
Does form regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
"Is there any phenomenon apart from form that regresses from unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that regresses from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Does the suchness of form ever regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
“Does the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied, “No, it does not.”
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Apart from the suchness of form, is there any dharma that regresses from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that regresses from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
“Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what do you think?
Can form realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
“What do you think?
Can feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
"Apart from form, is there any dharma that can realize unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
“What do you think?
Can the suchness of form realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
“Can the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness realize unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Apart from the suchness of form, is there any dharma that can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what do you think?
Does suchness ever regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“What do you think?
Apart from suchness, is there any dharma that can regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
Can suchness realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?..."
"Apart from suchness, is there any dharma that can realize unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Excellent, Subhūti! Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what do you think?"

Is there any dharma that is neither identical to form and so forth nor separate from form and so forth, neither identical to suchness nor separate from suchness, which could regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what do you think? Is there any dharma that—
neither identical to nor separate from form and so forth, neither identical to nor separate from suchness— is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"If all dharmas, by virtue of their truth and their stability, are entirely non-existent and unapprehendable, what dharma could be said to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"According to what you have said, within the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there is no phenomenon whatsoever, nor is there any bodhisattva who could be said to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
If that is so, why did the Buddha speak of three types of individuals who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle? He should have spoken of only one.
Furthermore, according to your explanation, there should be no distinction between the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles; there should be only a single vehicle of perfectly complete enlightenment.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"One should ask Subhūti:
'Do you admit that there is a single vehicle of the bodhisattvas?'"
Thereafter, one may raise this objection:
"There should be no establishment of distinctions among the three vehicles; there should be only the single vehicle of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“Do you admit that there is such a thing as the single Bodhisattva Vehicle?
Subhūti replied, “What do you think?”
"Is there any distinction between the three vehicles within True Suchness?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti!
Since even true suchness cannot be apprehended as having three characteristics, how much less could there be within it the three separate vehicles!
What do you think?"
"Is there, within suchness, any vehicle of the One Vehicle that can be apprehended? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Since even suchness has not even a single characteristic that can be apprehended, how much less could there be a Single Vehicle within it!
What do you think?"
“Is there, within true thusness, to be seen even a single dharma or a single bodhisattva?
Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Subhūti! At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"If all dharmas, by virtue of their truth and their abiding nature, are entirely non-existent and utterly unapprehendable, and the Bodhisattva is likewise so, how can you, Venerable One, entertain such a thought?"
"Is this a śrāvaka, this a pratyekabuddha, and this a bodhisattva? Are they thus three, or are they thus one?
"Śāriputra! [the Buddha said.]

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing at all to be apprehended among all phenomena, finds nothing to be apprehended in the suchness of phenomena, finds nothing to be apprehended in the various bodhisattvas, and finds nothing to be apprehended in the various Tathāgatas, one should know that this is a true bodhisattva.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing it said that suchness has no differentiated characteristics, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not become despondent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and in the interval there will certainly be no regression.
At that time, the Blessed One praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
That you are now able to skillfully expound the essential points of the Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas—what you have spoken is entirely through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Subhūti, you should know this!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva deeply gives rise to faith and understanding regarding the mark of the non-apprehensibility of the suchness of phenomena, knowing that all phenomena have no mark of differentiation, and upon hearing the teaching of such a mark of the non-apprehensibility of the suchness of all phenomena, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not become despondent—this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these dharmas, will they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these dharmas, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and shall not fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening that they seek, in what manner should they abide?"
"How should one train?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should dwell with equanimity toward all sentient beings; they should give rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of equality, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of equanimity, a mind of benefit, a mind of happiness, a mind of gentleness, a mind of respect, a mind free from malice, a mind free from harm, a mind of straightforwardness, a mind like that of a father, a mind like that of a mother, a mind like that of a brother, a mind like that of a sister, and a mind that acts as a protector. Furthermore, they should address them with such a mind."
"Subhūti, you should know this!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening that they seek, they should abide in this manner toward all sentient beings and should train in this manner."
Chapter 17: Signs of Non-Retrogression, Part Four. At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what conduct, characteristics, and signs shall we recognize a bodhisattva mahāsattva as one who is non-retrogressive?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know, as they truly are, the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, the stage of bodhisattvas, or the stage of tathāgatas—though these stages are said to be distinct, within the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, they are without change and without differentiation; they are all non-dual and indivisible.”

Although this bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly awakens to and enters into the suchness of all phenomena, they also truly abide in the suchness of all phenomena without conceptual differentiation, because they employ the method of non-apprehension.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having truly awakened to and entered into the suchness of all phenomena, hears that suchness and all phenomena are non-dual and indistinguishable, yet remains free from doubt or obstruction.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having truly dwelt in the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena and having emerged from that suchness, hears of the various different characteristics of all phenomena; yet, therein he has no attachment and no hesitation, nor does he form the thought:
"This is as it truly is; this is not as it truly is."
Although they do not harbor such thoughts, they are able to know all phenomena as they truly are.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never utter words lightly; whatever they say leads to meaningful benefit, and if it lacks meaning or benefit, they never speak at all.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva never observes the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others, but preaches the Dharma with impartial compassion.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they will certainly never again regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained non-retrogression never take pleasure in observing the physical appearances or listening to the discourses of non-Buddhist śramaṇas, brahmins, and the like."
It is impossible that those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas could truly know and truly see the phenomena to be known, or be able to establish a gateway to the Dharma of right view.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva will never pay homage to other celestial deities as those practiced by the non-Buddhists of the world; nor will they ever offer various flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, music, or lamps to such deities or non-Buddhists.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certainly no longer subject to regression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive do not fall into the evil destinies, do not receive a female body, nor are they born into lowly or base lineages—except when, for the purpose of liberating those sentient beings, they manifest birth among them as a skillful means of gathering them in."

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva always delights in practicing the ten paths of wholesome action; they themselves abstain from taking life up to and including wrong view, and they also exhort others to abstain from taking life up to and including wrong view. They themselves practice the ten paths of wholesome action and also exhort others to practice them. They demonstrate, encourage, inspire, gladden, and sustain sentient beings, causing them to become firm in their resolve.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not engage in the ten paths of unwholesome action even in dreams, nor does he give rise to evil or unwholesome thoughts even in dreams; rather, even in dreams, he constantly trains in and practices the ten paths of wholesome action.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they will certainly never again regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive thoroughly master the various sūtras they receive, uphold, contemplate, and recite, doing so solely for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. They constantly maintain this thought:
'I shall proclaim and reveal these dharmas to all sentient beings, and thereby cause the aspirations of all regarding the dharmas to be fulfilled.'"
Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such giving of the Dharma, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certain not to regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All non-regressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never give rise to doubt, hesitation, or confusion regarding the profound Dharma-gates spoken by the Buddha; they accept them with joy and faith.
Whatever they utter is for the benefit of others; they speak with moderation and their words are gentle."
In sleep and rest, afflictions are few and do not arise; in coming and going, entering and exiting, the mind is never deluded or mistaken.

At all times, one dwells securely in right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*). Whether advancing or halting, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—even when lifting or setting down the feet—it is likewise so.

Wherever one travels, one necessarily observes the ground; with composure and focused attention, one walks while gazing straight ahead. In movement and speech, one is always free from abruptness or violence.
All bedding and clothing they use are always fragrant and clean, free from any foul odors or impurities; they are likewise free from filth, grease, lice, nits, and other such insects.
They constantly delight in purity and are forever free from illness, for within their bodies there are no eighty thousand families of parasites.

Why is this so? Because these bodhisattvas’ roots of goodness have increased to such an extent that they transcend the world; as their roots of goodness gradually grow, so too do their bodies and minds become purified.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, the bodies and minds of these bodhisattvas become as firm and solid as vajra, such that they cannot be harmed or disturbed by adverse conditions.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certain never again to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand that the mind is eternally pure?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As these roots of goodness of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gradually increase, so too do all forms of flattery, crookedness, and deceit cease to function within their mind forever."

By virtue of these causes and conditions, all afflictions and other unwholesome states are forever extinguished; one also transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, swiftly proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one should know that the mind is eternally pure.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive do not value gain and offerings, nor do they pursue fame and reputation.
Their minds are free from envy and stinginess, and their bodies are without fault. Regarding food and drink, clothing, bedding..."
They do not give rise to attachment toward requisites, medicines, or material wealth; their minds are not confused when hearing the profound Dharma;
their wisdom is deep and firm as they respectfully believe and accept it; whatever they hear, they are able to integrate into the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
and all worldly activities they undertake are likewise based upon *prajñāpāramitā*.
The *Pāramitā-upāyakauśalya-parivarta* enters into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); not a single thing is seen to transcend the nature of phenomena.

Even if there were something that did not accord with the nature of phenomena, one would still be able to skillfully bring it into accord with the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, whereby nothing is seen to transcend the nature of phenomena.
