If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certainly non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose an evil Māra were to manifest before all non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and conjure up eight great hells; furthermore, within each of these great hells, he would conjure up immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, all of whom are being scorched by intersecting fierce flames and each undergoing bitter, painful, and agonizing suffering.
Having performed such a conjuration, he would address the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, saying:"

"These bodhisattvas have all received the prediction of non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore, they have fallen into such a great hell and constantly undergo these various kinds of intense suffering."
"Since you Bodhisattvas have received the prediction of non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, you too shall fall into this great hell and undergo various intense sufferings."

The Buddha has granted you the prediction that you shall undergo extreme suffering within the great hells; he has not granted you the prediction of non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, you should swiftly abandon the mind of great bodhicitta, so that you may escape the suffering of these hells and be reborn among the gods or among humans to experience various sublime pleasures.
At that time, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive sees or hears this matter, his mind remains unmoved and he is neither startled nor doubtful; he simply thinks:

"It is absolutely impossible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has received the prediction of non-retrogression would fall into the evil destinies and undergo various sufferings from which he could not escape."
"What we have now seen and heard must surely be the work and speech of an evil Māra; none of it is real.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they will certainly never again regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose an evil Māra, assuming the guise of a śramaṇa, should come to a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva and say these words:

'All those profound sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom that you have previously heard, upheld, read, and recited are all false teachings; you should quickly abandon them and not consider them to be true.'"
If you can swiftly renounce these, I shall teach you the truly pure Buddha-dharma and cause you to quickly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
What you have previously heard is not the true word of the Buddha; it is a deceptive compilation by a poet. That which I speak is the true word of the Buddha.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such words, experiences agitation, alarm, or doubt, you should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such a teaching, remains unmoved and free from alarm or doubt, but dwells in accordance with the nature of phenomena that is unconditioned, signless, and unborn, then whatever this bodhisattva mahāsattva undertakes, they do not rely on the words of others nor do they waver following the instructions of others. Just as an arhat, in all that they do, does not rely on the words of others and has directly realized the nature of phenomena without confusion or doubt, such that no evil māras can shake them, so it is for this bodhisattva.

Thus, these non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be undermined by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, followers of external paths, or various evil māras, such that they would give rise to retreat or despondency regarding awakening.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they will certainly never again regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose an evil Māra should come to where all non-retrogressive Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas dwell, falsely manifesting himself as a friend and saying:

'The practices you are engaged in are the dharmas of birth and death, not the conduct of a Bodhisattva. You should now cultivate the path that exhausts suffering; quickly exhaust all sufferings and attain parinirvāṇa.'"
At that time, Māra the Evil One immediately expounded to the Bodhisattva a counterfeit path of the cycle of birth and death, saying to him:
"This is the true path; by practicing this path, you shall swiftly bring an end to all birth, old age, sickness, and death, and attain parinirvāṇa."
"If one should now feel revulsion toward and abandon even this present suffering body, how much more so should one not seek to receive a future suffering body!
You ought to reflect carefully for yourself and renounce what you previously believed.
When that bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears these words, his mind remains unmoved and free from alarm or doubt; he simply thinks to himself:
"One who speaks thus must surely be an evil Māra.
Then, that evil Māra spoke again to the Bodhisattva:
"Do you wish to hear of the bodhisattva’s unbeneficial practices?"

This means that for bodhisattvas, throughout great eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have made offerings to the Buddhas with immeasurable kinds of sublime and excellent requisites; furthermore, in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have practiced immeasurable kinds of difficult and arduous austerities; they have approached and served Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and inquired about the immeasurable and boundless paths to be cultivated by bodhisattvas;
and these Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have explained them in successive order according to those inquiries.

Even those assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, following the Buddha’s instructions and exhortations, practiced with diligent application for immeasurable eons were still unable to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they sought; how much less can you now possibly attain it!
At that time, although the Bodhisattva heard these words, his mind remained unmoved and he was without doubt.
Then, at that very spot, the evil Māra further manifested the forms of immeasurable bhikṣus and said to the Bodhisattva:

"All these bhikṣus practiced immeasurable kinds of difficult and ascetic austerities throughout countless kalpas in the past, yet they were unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi; they have all now regressed and abide in the fruit of arhatship. How then can you possibly realize bodhi?"
When those bodhisattvas have seen and heard this, they immediately form this thought:

"This must certainly be a wicked Māra who, in order to disturb us, has performed such deeds. There is certainly no bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who reaches the stage of fulfillment, nor does he realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; rather, he regresses and dwells on the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
He further thought:
"If bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path as taught by the Buddha, it is absolutely impossible that they would not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"You should know that what you have now seen and heard is certainly the work and the speech of an evil Māra.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, marks, and characteristics, they will certainly never again regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose an evil Māra were to come to an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the guise of a bhikṣu, wishing to cause him to become weary of and turn away from unsurpassed enlightenment, and were to say:

'The knowledge of all modes is equal to space; its nature is the absence of intrinsic nature, for its own-characteristics are fundamentally empty. All phenomena are likewise equal to space; their nature is the absence of intrinsic nature.'"

Within the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics, there is not a single dharma that can be called the "realizer," nor is there a single dharma that can be called the "realized. Neither the locus of realization, the time of realization, nor that by which one realizes can be apprehended.

Since all phenomena are equal to space, having non-existence as their nature and being empty of intrinsic characteristics from the very beginning, why do you undergo such toil and hardship in vain to seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"All that you have previously heard regarding how the assembly of bodhisattvas should seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is the speech of Māra, not the true word of the Buddha.

You should abandon the resolve to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; do not undergo diligent suffering for the sake of sentient beings throughout the long night. Though you may practice various difficult and painful austerities, you will ultimately be unable to attain enlightenment."
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears such words of reproach and admonition, they are able to examine them carefully, thinking:

"This is the work of Māra, seeking to cause me to retreat from and destroy my great bodhicitta. I must not now believe or accept his words and lose the great bodhicitta I have already generated; rather, I should become even more firm and resolute, never wavering again."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certain not to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive, when they wish to enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, are able to enter them at will."
Although this bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the four dhyānas, he does not experience their fruits.

For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, he assumes whatever body is appropriate to be assumed according to his wish; he is able to assume it exactly as he intends. Having performed what was to be done, he is then able to relinquish it. Therefore, although he is able to enter the various dhyānas, he does not undergo rebirth under the influence of their power.
In order to deliver sentient beings, he returns to birth in the desire realm; yet, though born in the desire realm, he is not defiled by desire.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certain never again to regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive do not prize fame or renown, nor do they cling to praise. Toward sentient beings, they harbor no ill will or resentment, but always desire to bring them benefit and happiness.
Whether coming or going, entering or exiting, they possess no distracted mind; in all their movements and deportment, they constantly abide in right mindfulness."

For the sake of sentient beings, although he dwells in a household, he does not give rise to greedy attachment therein; though he manifests the enjoyment of desires, he is always weary of and terrified by them, like one traversing a perilous path whose mind is constantly filled with alarm and fear. Though he has food to eat, he is apprehensive and uneasy, thinking only of when he might emerge from this dangerous difficulty.

Though he manifests the use of various precious wealth, he does not give rise to craving or love for it, nor does he sustain himself through wrong livelihood or unrighteous means; rather, he would sooner perish than harm others.
Why is this? These bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;

they are the most honored among humans, the virtuous sages among humans, the noble and distinguished among humans, the bull-kings among humans, the lotuses among humans, the dragon-elephants among humans, the lions among humans, the courageous and valiant among humans, the tamed and disciplined among humans, and the heroic elites among humans. Having originally acted for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, they now dwell in the household life as a skillful means to provide abundant benefit; how could they ever harm others for the sake of their own livelihood?
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are sustained by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they will certainly never again regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas are constantly followed on their left and right by Vajrapāṇi yakṣa kings who secretly provide protection for them, so that they cannot be harmed in body or mind by the power of any humans, non-humans, or malevolent spirits."

By virtue of these causes and conditions, these bodhisattvas, until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, remain serene in body and mind, ever free from disturbance. They possess the marks of a great man with fully perfected faculties; their mental conduct is harmonious and virtuous as they constantly cultivate a pure livelihood. They do not practice illusionist arts, divination, prognostication of good or bad fortune, incantations, exorcisms, or the compounding of medicinal decoctions. They do not employ base and deceptive means to entice others, nor do they cultivate intimacy with the noble and powerful, show contempt for sages and worthies, or form close attachments to men and women. They do not praise themselves or disparage others for the sake of fame or profit, nor do they look about with stained minds or engage in frivolous laughter. Their precepts and views are pure, and their nature and character are sincere and honest.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certainly non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, though they have attained skill in the various worldly arts and crafts, do not become attached to them, because they realize that all phenomena are ungraspable and that they are all subsumed under frivolous speech and wrong livelihood;
though they also thoroughly know the secular treatises of the non-Buddhists, they do not delight in or cling to them, because they realize that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness."
Furthermore, the principles and phenomena taught in the secular and non-Buddhist treatises often involve exaggerations and omissions; therefore, they do not accord with the path of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, marks, and signs, they will certainly never again regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are yet other practices, tokens, and signs of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive, which I shall analyze and explain for you."
That is to say, when that bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and realizes the emptiness of all phenomena,
they take no pleasure in examining or discoursing upon various matters, such as affairs of kings, thieves, military affairs, battles, cities, towns,
villages, elephants, horses, chariots, clothing, food and drink, or bedding.
They do not delight in observing or discoursing upon matters such as the fragrance of flowers, men and women, the beautiful and the ugly, gardens, groves, ponds, mountains, and seas;
they do not delight in observing or discoursing upon matters concerning yakṣas, rākṣasas, and other spirits;
nor do they delight in observing or discoursing upon matters concerning streets, marketplaces, pavilions, and merchants. They do not delight in...
One observes and discusses matters such as singing, dancing, music, acrobatics, and jesting;
one does not delight in observing and discussing matters such as continents, islands, bridges, rafts, or precious jewels;
one does not delight in observing and discussing matters such as the stars, wind and rain, cold and heat, or auspicious and inauspicious omens. One does not delight in...
They examine various discourses on the meanings of phenomena that appear contradictory, as well as prose and verse compositions;
they take no pleasure in examining discourses associated with ordinary beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas,
but instead delight in examining discourses associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the mental attention associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and is never separated from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). He does not delight in discord but rejoices in harmony; he constantly aspires for the True Dharma and does not love what is contrary to the Dharma; he always yearns for virtuous friends and does not take pleasure in evil friends; he delights in uttering words of the Dharma and avoids words contrary to the Dharma; he rejoices in seeing the Tathāgatas and takes joy in the community of renunciants.

Wherever in the lands of the ten directions there are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma, he vows to be reborn there to attend upon them, make offerings to them, and hear the True Dharma.”

“Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas mostly pass away from the heavens of the desire realm or the form realm and are reborn in the central lands of the human realm in Jambudvīpa; they are skilled in the arts, incantations, scriptures, geography, astronomy, and the meaning of all dharmas;
or they are born in great kingdoms and great cities in the borderlands, bringing great benefit to sentient beings.”
"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will never doubt:
'Am I regressing, or am I non-regressing?'"
Regarding the phenomena of their own stage, they do not give rise to doubt as to whether they exist or do not exist;
they are well able to discern and understand all demonic activities.

Just as a stream-enterer never gives rise to doubt regarding the dharmas of their own stage, and even if an evil Māra were to employ various forms of delusion and confusion, he could not shake them; likewise, a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva Mahāsattva never gives rise to doubt regarding the dharmas of their own stage, and though they may encounter the deeds of Māra, they do not succumb to the power of Māra.

For example, if one has committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), that mind of immediacy constantly pursues them until the end of life, such that it cannot be abandoned; even if other thoughts arise, they cannot suppress it.

These bodhisattvas are likewise: their non-retrogressive mind constantly follows them as they dwell securely in the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression. Neither the gods, humans, nor asuras of the world can shake or destroy the Dharma they have attained. They are well able to recognize all demonic activities and remain forever free from doubt regarding the Dharma they have realized.
Even when born in other worlds, they do not give rise to minds associated with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they harbor self-doubt, thinking:
"Will I be able to realize unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment in a future life?"
"Not abiding in their own stage and not following the conditions of others, there is no one who can destroy them regarding the dharmas of their own stage. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattvas have accomplished unshakable and non-retrogressive wisdom; all adverse conditions cannot incline or move them, for their minds are as firm and solid as adamant."
Suppose an evil Māra were to assume the form of a Buddha, come to that person's location, and speak these words:
"You should now seek the fruit of Arhatship, exhaust all outflows forever, and enter parinirvāṇa."
"You are not yet fit to receive the prediction of great enlightenment, nor have you yet realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

You do not yet possess the practices, characteristics, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression; therefore, the Tathāgata should not grant you the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva hears those words, his mind remains unshaken; he does not retreat, nor does he sink into despondency; he is without alarm and without fear, but thinks only this:

"This must be a wicked Māra, or a member of Māra’s retinue, who has conjured the form of a Buddha and come to me to speak these words; if it were the true Buddha speaking, there would be no difference."
“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears those words, they should be able to observe and reflect thus:

‘This must certainly be a wicked Māra who has transformed himself into the likeness of a Buddha, seeking to cause me to distance myself from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and to abandon the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening I seek; therefore, I should not follow what he says.’”
At that time, Māra, struck with fear and alarm, immediately vanished.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has certainly established himself in the stage of non-retrogression; long ago, the Buddhas of the past have already bestowed upon him the prophecy of great enlightenment.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have fully accomplished the practices, characteristics, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression; they are thus able to recognize the activities of Māra and cause them to vanish so that they no longer appear.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certainly non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All those non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice profound prajñāpāramitā protect and uphold the true Dharma, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives, let alone other treasures, wealth, friends, or kinsmen!"
To protect the true Dharma with courageous diligence, they constantly maintain this thought:
"This true Dharma is the pure Dharmakāya of all Buddhas, which all Tathāgatas revere and make offerings to."

I now uphold and protect the Buddha-dharma of the past, future, and present; because this constitutes upholding and protecting the pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, I should now, without begrudging my body, life, wealth, or kinsmen, uphold and protect this Dharma.
Again, he reflects:
"Such True Dharma belongs universally to the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time; I, too, am included among the number of future Buddhas.

Since the Buddha has already bestowed upon me the prediction of Great Bodhi, by this cause and condition, the True Dharma of all Buddhas is my own Dharma. I should protect and uphold it, not sparing even my body, life, wealth, or kinsmen."
"When I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I too shall proclaim this Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Seeing such benefit and purpose, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas uphold and protect the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, not sparing even their own bodies or lives, remaining ever free from weariness until they reach enlightenment.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certainly non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive hear the sublime Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas without confusion or doubt; having heard it, they receive and uphold it so as not to forget it, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, because they have already attained the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva merely hear the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and thus remain without confusion or doubt, never forgetting it until reaching awakening;

or does he also, upon hearing the true Dharma spoken by bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, likewise remain without confusion or doubt regarding them, never forgetting it until reaching awakening?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva universally hears the speech, sounds, letters, and meanings of all sentient beings; he is able to penetrate them all, remaining without confusion or doubt, and never forgetting them.”

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having attained the patience toward the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), have thoroughly mastered the true nature of all phenomena; upon hearing them, they accord with them entirely and harbor no doubt.
Furthermore, because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, they are always able to recollect and never forget.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, they will certainly never again regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know that these are the practices, tokens, and signs of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva. Chapter 18:
Characteristics of Emptiness, Part Four, Section One of Chapter Eighteen: Characteristics of Emptiness. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Such non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish rare and vast merit.

World-Honored One, you could for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges expound upon the practices, marks, and signs of non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; through the practices, marks, and signs thus spoken by the Buddha, one reveals that non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished immeasurable and preeminent merit.”

I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will further proclaim the points of meaning associated with the profound Prajñāpāramitā, so that all bodhisattvas may dwell therein and cultivate various merits until they are swiftly perfected.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

It is well that you are now able, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound points of meaning associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), so that all bodhisattvas may dwell therein and cultivate various merits until they are swiftly and fully perfected.

Subhūti, you should know that the thematic domains associated with the profound perfection of wisdom are: emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, effortlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-existence, tranquility, detachment, and nirvāṇa.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it only this dharma that is called a locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, or are all dharmas likewise called loci of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All other dharmas may also be called the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this so?
That is to say, all form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also called the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Subhūti!..."
Why are all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also said to be the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
Subhūti, you should know this:

because suchness is profound, form is also profound; because suchness is profound, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also profound. Therefore, all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also designated as the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Just as the suchness of form is profound, so too is form profound; just as the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is profound, so too are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness profound. Therefore, all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness may also be called the 'locus of meaning associated with the profound Prajñāpāramitā.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Where form and name are non-existent, that is the profound depth of form and name; where feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent, that is the profound depth of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness may also be called the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, how marvelous! With subtle and wondrous skillful means, you negate all forms and reveal nirvāṇa; you negate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and reveal nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.

Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, regarding such points of meaning associated with this profound perfection of wisdom, reflect with careful discernment and form this thought:"
"I should now abide in accordance with what is taught in the profound Prajñāpāramitā; I should now train in accordance with what is explained in the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
"Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thoroughly contemplate the meaning associated with such profound prajñāpāramitā, and abide as taught in the profound prajñāpāramitā, and train as explained in the profound prajñāpāramitā."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by being able to rely thus upon the profound perfection of wisdom, reflects with discernment and trains with diligence for even a single day, the mass of merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless.

"Suppose, for example, a person of greedy temperament who is also prone to discursive thought makes an appointment with a beautiful woman; if that woman is obstructed and fails to arrive at the appointed time, this person's lustful mind will burn intensely and flow forth."
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Where does that person's desire-thought arise?"
“World-Honored One!
This person’s mind turns toward a woman with desire, thinking:
‘When will she come so that we may meet here and enjoy ourselves in pleasure and sport?’”
"Subhūti! What do you think?
How many thoughts of desire arise in that person during a day and night?"
“World-Honored One!
This person has many thoughts of desire day and night.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, reflects with careful discernment and diligently practices for even a single day, the number of kalpas of cyclic existence they transcend is equal to the number of desire-thoughts arising in a person of greedy temperament over the course of one day and night."

“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and reflects with discernment while training with diligence, they are able to liberate themselves from all faults that obstruct unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Therefore, by relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, reflecting with discernment, and training with diligence, the bodhisattva swiftly realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, reflects with discernment and trains with diligence, the merit obtained in a single day and night surpasses the immeasurable and boundless merit of all bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practice giving for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, reflects with discernment and trains with diligence, the merit obtained in a single day and night surpasses that of all bodhisattvas who, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, offer all manner of requisites to stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas; the merit of such giving would be immeasurable and boundless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and diligently practices generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for even a single day and night, the merit they obtain surpasses that of all other bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, diligently practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; the merit [of the former] is immeasurable and boundless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for even a single day and night, the merit they obtain by giving the sublime Dharma to all sentient beings surpasses the merit obtained by other bodhisattvas who, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, give the sublime Dharma to all sentient beings while remaining apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; [the former's merit] is immeasurable and boundless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for even a single day and night, the merit obtained from cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and other roots of goodness will surpass the merit obtained by all other bodhisattvas who, separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and other roots of goodness for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—its merit being immeasurable and boundless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for even a single day and night, practicing various kinds of material giving and the giving of Dharma, dwelling in a secluded place with focused mindfulness and reflection, and dedicating the merit obtained from those previously practiced various meritorious deeds—shared equally with all sentient beings—toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, their merit shall surpass that of all other bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practice various kinds of material giving and the giving of Dharma, dwell in secluded places with focused mindfulness and reflection, and dedicate the merit obtained from those previously practiced various meritorious deeds—shared equally with all sentient beings—toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, even if they do so for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; the former’s merit is immeasurable and boundless.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for even a single day and night, universally taking as their object the roots of virtue and merit of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their disciples throughout the three periods of time, and having combined and weighed them, rejoices therein in the presence [of the Buddhas], and dedicates that merit—shared equally with all sentient beings—toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; the merit thus obtained is infinitely and boundlessly superior to the merit obtained by bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, dwell for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, universally taking as their object the roots of virtue and merit of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their disciples throughout the three periods of time, and having combined and weighed them, rejoice therein in the presence [of the Buddhas], and dedicate that merit—shared equally with all sentient beings—toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 549.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 550.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The Fourth Division, Chapter Eighteen on the Characteristics of Emptiness, Part Two. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has said:"
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are produced by conceptualization; arising from false imagination, they do not exist as reality at all.
By what causes and conditions do the merits obtained by these bodhisattvas become immeasurable and boundless?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

However, when bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they also explain that all conditioned phenomena are produced by conceptual differentiation, being empty, non-existent, false, and unreal.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas, having thoroughly studied the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are nothing other than the products of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), being empty, non-existent, false, and unreal.

To the extent that this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are merely products of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), empty and non-existent, false and unreal, to that same extent they are able not to be separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. To the extent that they are not separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, to that same extent the merit they obtain is immeasurable and boundless.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the difference between 'immeasurable' and 'boundless'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"To say 'immeasurable' means that in this regard, all measure has forever ceased;
to say 'boundless' means that within this, numbers cannot be exhausted.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is there any cause or condition by which form (*rūpa*) may also be said to be immeasurable and boundless, and feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) may also be said to be immeasurable and boundless?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There are reasons why form may also be said to be immeasurable and boundless, and why feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness may also be said to be immeasurable and boundless.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions can form also be said to be immeasurable and boundless, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also be said to be immeasurable and boundless?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because the nature of form is empty, it may also be said to be immeasurable and boundless;
because the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, they may also be said to be immeasurable and boundless.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it only form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are empty, or are all phenomena likewise empty?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
"Have I not previously taught that all phenomena are empty?
Subhūti replied:
"Although the Buddha has constantly taught that all phenomena are empty, sentient beings do not know, see, or realize this; therefore, I now ask this question once again."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is not only form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are empty; I say that there are no dharmas whatsoever that are not empty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the designation for ‘immeasurable and boundless’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“‘Immeasurable and boundless’ is a designation for emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are 'immeasurable,' 'boundless,' and so forth merely emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, or do they have further meanings?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Have I not taught that among all dharmas, there are none that are not empty?"
Subhūti replied,
“The Tathāgata has always taught that there is no dharma-door whatsoever that is not empty.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Emptiness is inexhaustible; emptiness is immeasurable; emptiness is boundless; emptiness is the ultimate meaning.
Therefore, Subhūti, although all dharma-gates have various distinctions in their verbal expressions, their meaning is no different."

“Subhūti, you should know that the principle of the emptiness of all phenomena is ultimately ineffable; yet through the skillful means of the Tathāgata, it is described as inexhaustible, or as immeasurable, or as boundless, or as empty, or as signless, or as wishless, or as unconditioned, or as non-arising, or as non-ceasing, or as non-existent, or as quiescent, or as free from defilement, or as nirvāṇa.”

All such immeasurable Dharma gates as these are in truth without difference in meaning; they are all expediently expounded by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, your skillful means are truly marvelous; although the true nature of all phenomena cannot be expressed in words, you have skillfully revealed it for the sake of sentient beings."
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the true nature of all phenomena is ultimately ineffable.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is!"
It is so! The true nature of all phenomena is entirely ineffable. Why is this?
"The nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, and there is nothing that can be proclaimed as 'ultimately empty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Is there any increase or decrease in the meaning of that which is ineffable?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the meaning that cannot be expressed has neither increase nor decrease, then the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom should likewise have neither increase nor decrease;
and if these six perfections also have neither increase nor decrease, then all six perfections should be non-existent."

If these six perfections are all non-existent, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and be able to draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

The six pāramitās, beginning with generosity, are all without increase or decrease and are non-existent; nevertheless, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the prajñāpāramitā, they employ skillful means and do not form the thought:
"There is increase or decrease in these [perfections] from generosity up to prajñāpāramitā."
They should simply form this thought:
"There is only a name and a conceptualization which we call 'generosity' up to and including 'perfection of wisdom.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom, they take up this mental engagement (*manasikāra*) that accompanies generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom; and, based upon this, they dedicate their thoughts and roots of virtue to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, sharing them equally with all sentient beings.

Just as the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is subtle and profound, one should perform dedication in that same manner; by the superior power of this skillful means of dedication, one is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The suchness of all phenomena is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, you should know that because the suchness of all phenomena neither increases nor decreases, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas likewise neither increases nor decreases."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva frequently dwells in such mental engagement associated with thusness, they will draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Although the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, one does not lose the mental attention directed toward true suchness; although the perfections neither increase nor decrease, one does not lose the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that is sought.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in such mental attention to true thusness and practices from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they will draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Chapter 19: Profound Merit, Part Four. Chapter 19: Profound Merit. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the arising of the initial thought, or does he realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the arising of the final thought?"

If the initial thought could realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then at the time the initial thought arises, the subsequent thoughts have not yet arisen, and thus there is no sense of conjunction.

If the final thought could realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then at the time the final thought arises, the preceding thoughts have already ceased, and thus there is no sense of conjunction.

In this way, when one examines the preceding and succeeding moments of mind and mental factors from every perspective, there is no sense of their combination; how, then, can roots of virtue be accumulated?
If roots of virtue cannot be accumulated, how can a bodhisattva’s roots of virtue become perfected so as to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think?
When a lamp is lit, is it the initial flame that burns the wick, or is it the final flame that burns the wick?”

Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning, it is not by the first flame that the wick is burned, yet it is not apart from the first flame; nor is it by the last flame that the wick is burned, yet it is not apart from the last flame."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Does the wick burn?"
Subhūti replied,
“In the world it is clearly seen that the wick is indeed scorched.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also like this: it is not by the arising of the initial mind that they can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet it is not apart from the initial mind; it is not by the arising of the final mind that they can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet it is not apart from the final mind. Rather, through the skillful means of practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cause all roots of goodness to increase and reach fulfillment, thereby enabling them to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The principle of dependent origination is thus profound: namely, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial thought-moment, yet they do not realize it apart from the initial thought-moment; they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final thought-moment, yet they do not realize it apart from the final thought-moment. It is not because of the arising of these very thought-moments that they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor is it because of being apart from the arising of these very thought-moments that they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—and yet, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Once the mind has ceased, can it arise again?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"This mind has already ceased and cannot arise again.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?"
"If a mind has already arisen, does it have the nature of cessation?
Subhūti replied, "It is so!"
“World-Honored One!
If a mind has already arisen, it is certain to possess the nature of cessation.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is a mind subject to cessation not destined to cease?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
A mind subject to cessation is certain to cease."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Can a mind that is of a nature not to cease be produced?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"The mind that is not subject to cessation has no sense of being produced.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?"
“Can the mind of the non-arising dharma be extinguished? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
The mind of non-arising dharmas has no meaning of extinction.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Can a mind that is without the nature of arising and ceasing undergo arising and ceasing?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
A mind that is without the dharma of arising and ceasing has no meaning of arising or ceasing."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
If a dharma has already ceased, can it cease again?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"If a phenomenon has already ceased, it cannot cease again.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?"
"If a dharma has already arisen,
can it arise again? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
If a dharma has already arisen, it cannot arise again.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Does the true nature of all phenomena have arising and ceasing?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The true nature of all phenomena is without arising and without cessation."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does the mind abide in the same manner as the true suchness of the mind?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"Just as the suchness of the mind is, so does the mind abide.
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
"What do you think?"
"If the mind abides as suchness, does that mind abide eternally as the nature of suchness and the limit of reality?
Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
This mind is not like true thusness or the limit of reality; its nature is not eternally abiding.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What do you think?
Is the suchness of all phenomena extremely profound?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The suchness of all phenomena is exceedingly profound."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is that very suchness the mind?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is there a mind apart from suchness?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is the mind itself suchness?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is there suchness apart from the mind?"
Subhūti replied:
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is it possible for suchness to see suchness?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do you perceive any truly existent suchness?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, is he practicing the profound perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, this is practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, where does he practice?
Subhūti replied,
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, there is no place at all where he practices.”

Why is this? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they do not perceive at all a practitioner, an object of practice, a time of practice, or a place of practice, because all dharmas of manifest activity do not arise.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, what is it that he practices?"
Subhūti replied,
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), because within it all conceptual constructions are absent.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, does he apprehend signs within the ultimate truth?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, does he practice by taking signs within the ultimate truth?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva, with respect to ultimate truth, destroy signs?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva, in terms of ultimate truth, eliminate signs?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if he neither destroys nor dispels marks (lakṣaṇa) within the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), how can he eliminate the perception of grasping at marks?”
Subhūti replied:
"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, he does not form such thoughts as:
'I am now destroying signs,' 'I am now dispelling signs,' 'I am severing the perception of signs,' nor does he train in the path for severing the perception of signs."

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while diligently training in the bodhisattva practices, cultivates the path of the perception of abandonment, at that time, because all the Buddha-dharmas are not yet fulfilled, they would fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most supreme skill in means; although they deeply understand the faults of all marks and the perception of grasping at marks, they do not destroy or sever them, yet they swiftly realize the signless.
"Why is this? Because all the Buddha-dharmas have not yet been perfected.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."
At that time, Śāriputra asked the venerable Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—in a dream, does this bring any increase to the profound perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied,

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates these three doors of liberation while awake and thereby gains progress in the profound perfection of wisdom, he will likewise gain progress by cultivating them even in a dream.”
Why is this? Because the Buddha has taught that there is no distinction between dreaming and waking. Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and practices the profound perfection of wisdom while awake—thereby being said to dwell securely in the profound perfection of wisdom—that bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom even in a dream, is likewise said to dwell securely in the profound perfection of wisdom.
The three gates of liberation likewise provide augmentation for the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; whether in a dream or while awake, their meaning is without deficiency or diminution.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family performs an action in a dream, does it result in any increase or decrease [of karma]?"

Subhūti replied, “The Buddha has taught that all phenomena are like what is seen in a dream. If karma created in a dream neither increases nor decreases, then karma created while awake should likewise neither increase nor decrease.”

However, the various karmas created within a dream do not undergo any increase or decrease; it is only when one reaches the waking state and engages in conceptualization and discrimination regarding what was done in the dream that those karmas come to undergo increase or decrease.

Suppose a person, while dreaming, takes the life of another; later, upon waking, they engage in conceptualization and discrimination, feeling deep self-congratulation—then that karma increases. If, however, they feel deep remorse and shame, that karma decreases.
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"If a person, having taken the life of another while awake, later experiences either self-congratulation or deep remorse in a dream, does this cause the karma of the waking state to increase or decrease?"
Subhūti replied:
"There is indeed increase and decrease;
however, that increase and decrease does not equal the clarity experienced during the waking state, because what is performed within the mind is superior."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If there is no objective referent, neither volition nor karma can arise; it is only when there is an objective referent that volition and karma originate."
"From what causes and conditions do the mental activities within a dream arise?
Subhūti replied, "It is so!"

It is so! Whether in a dream or while awake, volitional karma does not arise without an object of perception; it is only when there is an object of perception that volitional karma arises. Why is this?
Śāriputra! It is only when there is the engagement of discerning wisdom (*buddhi*) regarding phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or known that defilement or purification arises.
If there were no seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, then among all phenomena there would be no engagement of discerning wisdom, nor would there be defilement or purification.

"From this it is known that whether in a dream or while awake, volitional karma arises only when there is an object of perception; volitional karma does not arise in the absence of an object of perception.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"The Buddha has taught that all objects of perception are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); how then can it be said that volitional karma arises when there is an object of perception, and does not arise when there is no object of perception?"
Subhūti replied:

“Although all volitional actions and their objective referents are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are conventionally designated as having objects of perception due to the conceptualization of signs by one's own mind.”

Based on these objects of perception, various volitional actions arise; as it is said that ignorance is the condition for the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*), and formations are the conditions for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, all of which are described as having objects of perception due to the conceptualization of signs by one's own mind, yet they do not possess a real intrinsic nature.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving while dreaming, and having given, dedicates it toward unexcelled enlightenment, does that bodhisattva mahāsattva truly dedicate the gift toward unexcelled Buddha-enlightenment?"

Subhūti replied, “The Bodhisattva Maitreya has long ago received the prophecy of great enlightenment; bound by only one more birth, he is certain to become a Buddha. He is perfectly capable of answering all difficult questions. It is fitting that you inquire of him here in this assembly; as the Regent, the Compassionate Honored One will surely provide the answer.”
Then, Śāriputra, following the words of Subhūti, respectfully questioned the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya turned back to interrogate Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable One, you say that the Bodhisattva Maitreya can answer this meaning; what is it that is called 'the Bodhisattva Maitreya'?"
Is it name that can answer?
Is it form that can answer?
Or is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that can answer?
Is it the capacity to answer that is manifested?
Is it the form that answers?
Or is it the emptiness of form that answers?
Can emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness provide an answer?

Furthermore, even the name "Maitreya" cannot provide an answer; form cannot provide an answer; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also cannot provide an answer; visibility cannot provide an answer; shape cannot provide an answer; the emptiness of form cannot provide an answer; and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also cannot provide an answer.
Why is this? Because I do not perceive any dharma that can answer, nor any dharma that is answered; nor do I perceive the place of answering, the time of answering, or that by which one answers.

I do not perceive any dharma that can grant a prediction, nor any dharma that is predicted; I likewise do not perceive the place of prediction, the time of prediction, or that by which the prediction is made. Why is this?
"Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty and non-existent, being neither dual nor distinct, and because upon ultimate investigation they cannot be apprehended.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Is the Dharma you have taught as it was realized?"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya said:
"The Dharma that I have taught is not as it was realized. Why is this so?"
The Dharma realized by me is ineffable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
I do not perceive any realized dharma that possesses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that can be apprehended, such as that which is conceived by the mind or expressed by words.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The self-nature of all phenomena cannot be touched by the body, cannot be expressed by speech, and cannot be conceived by the mind. Why is this?
"Śāriputra, it is because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
“Maitreya Bodhisattva’s awakened wisdom is profoundly deep; having practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a long night, he is able to speak thus.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“The thought in your mind is: ‘Maitreya Bodhisattva’s awakened wisdom is profoundly deep; having practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a long night, he is able to speak thus.’”
"Thus it is, Śāriputra! It is just as you have conceived.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
By means of this dharma have you become an arhat; do you perceive this dharma as something that can be expressed?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, the nature of phenomena realized therein is likewise ineffable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form this thought:
"By means of this dharma, I have already received, am now receiving, or shall receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
They do not form this thought:
"By means of this dharma, I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they will not give rise to doubt or uncertainty, thinking:
"Shall I attain or not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
They should simply think:
"I am diligent and energetic; I shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, for I have already attained superior power regarding enlightenment."
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, upon hearing the most profound Dharma, they are not startled, not terrified, not frightened, not afraid, do not sink, and do not despair; nor do they have any fear regarding the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, because they know with certainty that they shall realize it.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If these bodhisattvas are in a wilderness inhabited by fierce beasts, they have no fear. Why is this? "
These bodhisattvas, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, are able to relinquish all that they possess, both internal and external, constantly reflecting:
"Should any malevolent spirits or ferocious beasts wish to devour my body, I shall give it to them so that they may be fully satisfied."

By means of these roots of goodness, may I swiftly bring the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) to fulfillment and quickly draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that, when I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, there shall be no animals or hungry ghosts at all within my buddha-field.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
These bodhisattvas have no fear even when in wilderness regions where there are evil bandits. Why is this? Because..."

These bodhisattvas, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, are able to relinquish all internal and external possessions and diligently cultivate various virtues. They have no regard or stinginess for their bodies, lives, or wealth, and they constantly reflect:
"If sentient beings should come in competition to plunder my various requisites, I shall respectfully and joyfully bestow them upon them;
or if, because of this, they should harm my body or life, I will ultimately harbor no anger or resentment toward them, nor will I give rise to any evil of body, speech, or mind."

By this cause and condition, may my perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience be swiftly brought to fulfillment, and may I quickly draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that, when I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there shall be no calamities from the elements or hostile thieves within my buddha-field; for because my buddha-field is utterly pure, there shall be no other evils either.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If these bodhisattvas are in a wilderness where there is no water, they likewise have no fear. Why is this? Because..."
It is the natural law for Bodhisattvas to be free from all fears; they constantly reflect:

"I shall seek to learn the Dharma that severs the thirst and craving of all sentient beings; I should not give rise to fear on this account. Even if my life should end through such thirst and exhaustion, I must never abandon the mental engagement of great compassion toward sentient beings, but shall instead bestow the water of the sublime Dharma."
"How wondrous that these sentient beings,
possessing such meager merit, dwell in a world such as this, devoid of water!

I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that, when I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there shall be no such parched wildernesses lacking water within my buddha-field."
"I shall employ skillful means to exhort all sentient beings to cultivate supreme meritorious deeds, causing them to possess the water of eight virtues wherever they may be.
Through such firm and fierce diligence, I shall skillfully transform and teach all sentient beings."

"By this causal condition, may my perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) be swiftly fulfilled, and may I quickly draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
These bodhisattvas also have no fear when in a land of famine. Why is this?
These bodhisattvas have donned the armor of merit and, with courageous diligence, purify buddha-fields, making this vow:

"When I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may there be no such famines in my buddha-field; may all sentient beings be endowed with happiness, and whatever they require shall arrive immediately upon their thought, just as everything desired is obtained in the celestial realms."

I shall arouse firm and fierce diligence so that the dharma-aspirations of all sentient beings may be fulfilled, and that at all times and in all places, all sentient beings may lack nothing in any kind of life-sustaining requisites.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When these bodhisattvas encounter times of pestilence, they likewise have no fear. Why is this? Because..."
These bodhisattvas constantly and carefully observe:
"There is no dharma named 'sickness,' nor is there any dharma that can be called 'sick'; all things are empty and should not be feared."

I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that, when I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all sentient beings within my buddha-field shall be free from all calamities and epidemics, and shall energetically cultivate sublime, correct practice.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If these bodhisattvas contemplate unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should not feel fear, even though it will be attained only after a long time."

Why is this? Although the kalpas of the past limit are immeasurable, they are formed by the accumulation of recollections and conceptualizations within a single moment of thought; one should know that the kalpas of the future are likewise so. Therefore, a bodhisattva should not conceive the notion of vast duration therein, nor say that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment can only be realized after a long time, thereby giving rise to fear.
Why is this? Because the length of kalpas in both the past limit (*pūrvānta*) and the future limit (*aparānta*) are all associated with a single moment of mind (*ekakṣaṇacitta*).
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva may hear the sūtras for a long time before realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they do not give rise to fear when examining them with precise scrutiny.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If bodhisattvas do not give rise to fear toward any other phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or known as being terrifying, it should be known that they will swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek."
Therefore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek should don the armor of merit and train with diligent application according to the Tathāgata’s teaching on true, pure emptiness, and should not feel fear toward any phenomena.

Chapter 20: The Devī Gaṅgā, Part Four, Chapter Twenty. At that time, there was a goddess in the assembly named Gaṅgā. She rose from her seat, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, bared her right shoulder, placed her right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I have no fear in this regard, nor do I have any doubt concerning all phenomena; in future ages as well, I shall preach the Dharma that is fearless and free from doubt for the sake of sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his face issued forth a golden light that universally illuminated the boundless worlds of the ten directions. It returned to the Brahma world to manifest great supernormal powers, gradually approaching the Buddha and circling him three times to the right. Having performed these miraculous transformations, it entered into the crown of the Buddha’s head.

At that time, having witnessed this event, the goddess Gaṅgā was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; she took exquisite golden flowers and, with reverent sincerity, scattered them over the Tathāgata.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, these golden flowers leaped up into the air and remained there, shimmering in profusion.

At that time, having seen and heard this, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?
It is not without cause or condition that the Buddha manifests a smile!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"This goddess shall, in a future age, become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; the eon shall be named Star-like (Tārakopama), and the Buddha’s name shall be Golden Flower (Suvarṇapuṣpa)."

Ānanda, you should know that this goddess has received her female body for the very last time; once she has cast off this body, she will receive a male body and shall never again be female until the end of the future.

After passing away from here, she will be reborn in the delightful world of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya in the eastern direction; there, under that Buddha, she will diligently cultivate the holy life, and in that realm, this woman shall be named Suvarṇapuṣpā.

Having passed away from the world-system of Akṣobhya Buddha, they are reborn again in other world-systems where Buddhas reside; passing from one buddha-field to another, they are never separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Just as a wheel-turning monarch, from one palace terrace to another, enjoys pleasures and delights until the end of his life without ever setting foot upon the ground, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Golden Flower: from one buddha-field to another, until he attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he never leaves the Buddha wherever he is born.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought to himself:
"When the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
"The assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in that gathering shall be as numerous as the assembly of the Buddha’s bodhisattvas here now.
Knowing his thought, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying: "It is so!"
"It is so! It is as you have conceived.

When the Bodhisattva Golden Flower attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim this profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly; the number of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in that assembly shall also be equal to the number in the present assembly of the Buddha and his Bodhisattvas."

Ānanda, you should know that when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, the number of his śrāvaka disciples who attain nirvāṇa will be so vast as to be beyond calculation; it cannot be reckoned by hundreds, thousands, or koṭis, but can only be described in general terms as immeasurable and boundless.

Ānanda, you should know that when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, his land will be free from wild beasts and evil spirits; it shall also be without the calamities of hostile robbers, water shortages, famine, or epidemics.

Ānanda, you should know that when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the sentient beings in his land will be free from all fears, as well as various calamities, misfortunes, and faults.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, under which Buddha did this goddess first resolve her mind toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, planting various roots of goodness and dedicating them through the making of vows?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, at the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, this goddess first gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, planted various roots of goodness, and dedicated them through making vows."
At that time, he also scattered golden flowers over the Buddha, seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Ānanda, you should know:

in the past, at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I offered five stalks of flowers to that Buddha, dedicating them and making a vow; at that moment, I attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, knowing that my faculties were mature, bestowed upon me this prophecy:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni, the realm shall be named Sahā, and the eon shall be called Bhadrakalpa."

At that time, having heard the Buddha bestow upon me the prediction of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), the goddess leaped for joy. She immediately scattered golden flowers over the Buddha and gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhicitta*). Planting various roots of goodness, she dedicated them toward her vow:

"May I, in a future life when this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, likewise receive the prediction of great enlightenment from him in his very presence, just as the present Buddha has now bestowed it upon me."
"Therefore, I now bestow this prediction upon her.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"This goddess has long since resolved her mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having planted various roots of goodness and dedicated them through the making of vows, they have now reached maturity; for this reason, the Tathāgata has bestowed this prediction upon her."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Because their roots of goodness have ripened, I bestow upon them the prediction of great enlightenment.
Chapter 21: Awakening to the Deeds of Māra, Part 4, Section One. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How do Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cultivate emptiness?
How do they manifest entry into the *samādhi* of emptiness?
The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate form as empty; they should contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty. When performing this contemplation, they must not allow the mind to become distracted. If the mind is not distracted, one does not perceive dharmas; if one does not perceive dharmas, one does not realize them.”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the World-Honored One has taught, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) without realizing it.
