How is it that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abide in the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) yet do not realize it?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom and contemplate the emptiness of phenomena, they first form this thought:
'I should contemplate that all characteristics of phenomena are empty, but I should not realize [this emptiness as a final limit].'"
‘I contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena for the sake of training, not for the sake of realization; now is the time for training, not the time for realization.

Thus, when this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet entered meditative concentration, he binds his mind to the object and takes up the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), rather than binding his mind to the object and taking up the perfection of wisdom at the time of having entered meditative concentration.”

At such a time, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not regress from any of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), nor does he realize the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya). Why is that?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such vast wisdom and being well-established in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as well as all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), constantly reflects:
"At this time, I should practice; I should not realize [the ultimate fruit]."

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the samādhi of emptiness yet does not realize emptiness, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva also dwells in the samādhi of signlessness yet does not realize signlessness."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished exceptionally superior, firm, and pure roots of goodness, and they constantly maintain this thought:
"At this time, I should practice; I should not realize [the fruit]."

Now you should embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, contemplate all phenomena as empty and signless, and bring all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) to fulfillment; you should not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) at this time.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

“Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who was brave, robust, and majestic; whose resolve was firm and difficult to shake; whose physical form was upright and dignified, such that all people delighted in seeing him;
who possessed many supreme qualities of ethical discipline (śīla); and who was wise and eloquent.”
He is well able to respond, possessing eloquence and discernment, knowing the proper place and time;
he has reached the ultimate mastery in military arts and techniques, his defenses are firm and he can destroy many enemies;
all his skills are perfectly accomplished, and he has mastered every field of craftsmanship; he possesses mindfulness, wisdom, conduct, and heroic discipline. In...
They attain fearlessness regarding all the sūtras; they are endowed with compassion and righteousness and possess great power.
Their limbs are without defect and their faculties are complete; their retinue and resources are fully provided.

All people revere and submit to them, looking up to them with admiration. Whatever they undertake, they are able to accomplish; because of their virtuous deeds, their effort is small while their benefit is great.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, they become abundant in wealth and treasures, and are well able to provide for many kinds of sentient beings: they are able to make offerings to those worthy of offering, show reverence to those worthy of reverence, honor those worthy of honor, and praise those worthy of praise.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Would that person, on account of this,
experience an even greater surge of joy, a profound delight in his heart, and take comfort in himself?”
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"That courageous man has accomplished such a great and magnificent feat.

For a certain reason, he set out for another region with his parents, wife, children, and kinsmen; on the way, they passed through a perilous wilderness filled with many fearsome occurrences, such as predatory beasts, hostile bandits, and lurking enemies, so that none among his kinsmen, whether young or old, were without alarm."
That man, relying on his many arts and skills, was fierce and courageous, with a mind at ease; he comforted his parents, wife, children, and kinsmen, saying:
"Have no fear or anxiety!"
"I shall certainly ensure that they suffer no hardship, but swiftly cross the wilderness to reach a place of peace and security. Furthermore,
Subhūti, what do you think?

In this wilderness, where threats and harms manifest, if that person possesses courage and skill, is endowed with loving-kindness and respect for his kin, and is equipped with all manner of weapons, would he not abandon his parents, wife, children, and retinue to carry himself alone across the perilous difficulties?
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because although he possesses many skills and can conjure weapons in the wilderness, being brave, robust, and more formidable than his enemies, it is impossible for him to see them naturally retreat and disperse, and thus abandon his loved ones to carry himself alone across the perilous wilderness. It cannot happen.
Yet, in that wilderness, those warriors had no intention of harming wild beasts or hostile bandits. Why was this?
Because they relied on their own prowess, possessed various skills and arts, and were free from fear.
"Bhagavān!

By means of skillful arts, that person will lead his retinue across the perilous wilderness without any harm, and they will surely reach a place of peace and security, such as a village, a city, or the capital of a great king."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Out of compassion for sentient beings suffering in saṃsāra, they fix their mindfulness and abide in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they gather the sublime roots of goodness of the prajñāpāramitā and, through skillful means as authorized by the Buddha, dedicate all these merits toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.”

Although you cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, do not give rise to the mind of realization regarding the limit of reality, lest you fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?

These bodhisattvas possess great power and firm diligence; they embrace the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), excellent roots of goodness, and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Vowing never to abandon any sentient being, they will thereby certainly attain peace and security without hindrance, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
“Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva, out of a mind of loving-kindness, takes pity on all sentient beings and, taking those beings as an object, desires to bestow peace and happiness upon them—at that time, the bodhisattva transcends the category of afflictions, and also transcends the category of Māra and the stages of the two vehicles. Although they abide in samādhi, they do not reach the exhaustion of outflows; although they are well-practiced in emptiness, they do not realize it as a final attainment.”
Subhūti, you should know this:

when a bodhisattva is able to dwell securely in the door of liberation that is emptiness, at that time the bodhisattva is also able to dwell in the concentration of signlessness; yet, through skillful means therein, they do not realize signlessness. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they transcend the stages of the two vehicles and will certainly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

Just as a bird with strong wings soars through the void, flying freely for a long time without falling, though it sports within the sky, it does not dwell in the sky, nor is it obstructed by the sky; you should know that the bodhisattva is likewise. Although they practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not dwell in emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness. Until the Buddha-dharma is fully perfected, they will never rely on those [gates] to permanently exhaust all outflows.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

Suppose there were a strong man, well-versed in the art of archery, who, wishing to display his skill, shot an arrow upward into the air. To prevent the arrow from falling to the ground, he shot a subsequent arrow into the notch of the preceding one; thus continuing in succession for a long time, each arrow supported the next so that none fell. If he wished for them to fall, he would simply cease shooting further arrows, and only then would all the arrows suddenly drop down.

One should know that it is likewise for the bodhisattva: practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and embracing superior skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), as long as the roots of virtue that serve as the causes for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment have not yet all matured, the bodhisattva will never realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway. Only when the roots of virtue that serve as the causes for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment have all matured does the bodhisattva then realize the limit of reality and attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Therefore, Subhūti, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and embrace superior skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they should all thus scrutinize the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) with careful attention: as long as the qualities of a Buddha are not yet fully perfected, one should not realize [the ultimate fruit]."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The bodhisattva mahāsattvas are truly rare and perform what is difficult to do; for although they practice emptiness, they do not dwell in emptiness, and although they manifest entry into the concentration of emptiness, they do not realize the limit of reality.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. Why is this?
These bodhisattvas vow never to abandon sentient beings, having made such sublime and wondrous aspirations:
"If there are sentient beings who have not yet attained liberation, I shall never abandon my application of the roots of virtue.

Subhūti, you should know that because these bodhisattvas give rise to such a vast mind, they desire to liberate all sentient beings; thus, although they induce the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) due to their embrace of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are sustained by skillful means, they constantly maintain this thought:
"I shall never abandon any sentient being in order to enter parinirvāṇa."
"Because he gives rise to this thought through skillful means, he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas have already examined,
or shall examine, the profound state— the sphere of activity of the three gates of liberation, namely the concentrations on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
These bodhisattvas constantly reflect:

"Sentient beings, throughout the long night, give rise to the notion of a sentient being and engage in grasping at attainments; they produce various wrong views and wander through birth and death, suffering endlessly."

In order to sever those wrong and evil views, I should seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and preach the profound Dharma of emptiness for all sentient beings, so that they may abandon their attachments and bring an end to the suffering of birth and death.
"Therefore, although they study the gate of liberation that is emptiness, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) midway. Subhūti,

you should know that by means of this skillful means arising from such a thought, these bodhisattvas, while not realizing the limit of reality midway, do not fall away from the four immeasurable concentrations.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are sustained by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their pure dharmas increase manifold, their faculties gradually become sharper, and their powers, factors of enlightenment, and branches of the path further increase.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas constantly reflect:
'Sentient beings have for a long night wandered among various signs, giving rise to manifold attachments; because of this, they transmigrate and undergo suffering without end.'"

In order to sever their attachment to signs, I should seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall preach the Dharma of signlessness so that they may sever their attachment to signs and emerge from the suffering of birth and death; it is for this reason that I frequently enter the meditative absorption of signlessness.

"Subhūti, you should know that because these bodhisattvas have previously accomplished skillful means and the mindfulness they have generated, although they repeatedly enter the meditative absorption of the signless, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim."

Although they do not realize the limit of reality during this interval, they do not fall away from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, nor from any other meditative concentrations. Why is this?

Because these bodhisattvas are sustained by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their pure dharmas increase manifold, their faculties gradually become sharper, and their powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path further increase.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas constantly reflect:

'Sentient beings, throughout the long night, have their minds constantly give rise to the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of self, and the perception of purity; because of this, they produce inverted attachments, transmigrating through birth and death and undergoing suffering without end.'"

In order to sever those four inversions, I should seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment so that I may preach the non-inverted Dharma for all sentient beings; that is to say, I shall preach that saṃsāra is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity, and that only nirvāṇa is subtle, tranquil, and endowed with various kinds of true merits.
"By means of this, they repeatedly enter the concentration of wishlessness.
Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattvas,

by virtue of having previously perfected skillful means and the mindfulness they have generated, repeatedly manifest entry into the concentration of wishlessness, they do not, until all the Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected, realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim.

Although they do not realize the limit of reality during this interval, they do not fall away from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, nor from any other meditative concentrations. Why is this?

Because these bodhisattvas are sustained by the skillful means of this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), their pure qualities (*śukladharma*) increase manifold, their faculties (*indriya*) gradually become sharper, and their powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) further increase.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! These bodhisattvas constantly reflect: 'Sentient beings have for a long night already practiced with apprehension, and now they still practice with apprehension;

they have for a long night already practiced with signs, and now they still practice with signs; they have for a long night already practiced with perversions, and now they still practice with perversions; they have for a long night already practiced with notions of combination, and now they still practice with notions of combination; they have for a long night already practiced with false imaginings, and now they still practice with false imaginings; they have for a long night already practiced with wrong views, and now they still practice with wrong views. Because of this, they transmigrate and undergo suffering without end.'"

In order to sever such faults as these, I should seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and preach the profound Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, so that those faults may be forever eliminated, they no longer transmigrate through the suffering of birth and death, and they may swiftly realize the eternal, blissful, true, and pure nirvana.

"Subhūti, you should know that because these bodhisattvas, out of deep compassion for all sentient beings, have accomplished sublime skillful means and are sustained by the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),

they constantly delight in observing the profound nature of phenomena— namely, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of effort, non-arising, non-cessation, non-origination, inexhaustibility, absence of intrinsic nature, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."

"Subhūti, you should know that for these bodhisattvas who have accomplished such sublime wisdom and vision, it is impossible for them to fall into the dharmas of signlessness and non-action, or to abide within the triple world."

Subhūti, you should know that it is absolutely impossible for these bodhisattvas— who have accomplished such sublime merit— to abandon all sentient beings and proceed toward parinirvāṇa, rather than realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to benefit sentient beings.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 550; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 551.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Four, Chapter Twenty-one, "Awakening to the Deeds of Māra," Section Two: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should carefully inquire of other bodhisattvas:

"How does a bodhisattva cultivate all the factors conducive to enlightenment and give rise to what kind of mind, so that while practicing emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of effort, non-arising, non-cessation, non-origination, inexhaustibility, absence of intrinsic nature, and the reality-limit, they do not realize them [prematurely], yet continue to cultivate the perfection of wisdom?"
"Subhūti, you should know that if other bodhisattvas, when asked this question, were to answer thus:
'Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should only contemplate:'"

Whether it be emptiness, signlessness, or even the limit of reality, one should not manifest them; rather, one should maintain mindfulness of never abandoning any sentient being and embrace superior skillful means.
It should be known that those bodhisattvas have not yet received from the Buddhas the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?

Because those bodhisattvas have not yet been able to reveal, declare, or clarify the unique characteristics of the bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression; they do not know, as it truly is, the practices, signs, and marks of the stage of non-retrogression when questioned by others, nor can they provide an answer.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any causal basis by which one may know whether bodhisattvas are non-retrogressive?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There are also causes and conditions by which one knows that various bodhisattvas are non-retrogressive. That is to say, there are bodhisattvas who, whether they have heard or not heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are able to answer as they truly are regarding previous questions, and are able to practice the conduct of bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression as it truly is; by these causes and conditions, one knows that those bodhisattvas are non-retrogressive.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions is it that while many bodhisattvas seek to study for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, few are able to provide a response in accordance with reality?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Although many bodhisattvas seek to train for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, few bodhisattvas receive such a prediction of the subtle wisdom of the stage of non-retrogression."
If there are those who receive such a prophecy, they will all be able to provide a response to this in accordance with reality.

Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas possess roots of goodness that are bright and pure, and wisdom that is profound and vast; neither gods, humans, nor asuras of the world can destroy them, and they will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas, even in their dreams, take no delight in any phenomena of the three realms, nor do they praise any dharmas of the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and although they contemplate all phenomena as being like what is seen in a dream, they neither realize nor grasp at the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)—you should know that this is the mark of a bodhisattva on the stage of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva sees in a dream the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a respectful retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bhikṣus as he teaches the Dharma, or if they see themselves in such a situation, you should know that this is a mark of a bodhisattva on the stage of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva, in a dream, sees a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—perfectly adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, with a constant light extending one fathom illuminating all around, amidst an immeasurable assembly, leaping into the air and manifesting great supernormal powers while preaching the essentials of the True Dharma; or sees him manifest emanations who go to other boundless buddha-fields to perform the work of a Buddha; or sees his own self performing such deeds—one should know that this is a sign of a bodhisattva on the stage of non-retrogression."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva sees in a dream mad bandits destroying a village or city; or sees a fire breaking out and burning down a settlement; or sees lions, tigers, wolves, fierce beasts, venomous snakes, or vicious scorpions about to come and harm his body; or sees an enemy wishing to cut off his head; or sees his parents, wife, children, or kinsmen on the verge of death; or sees himself being oppressed by other painful matters—even upon seeing such terrifying events, he is neither startled nor afraid, nor does he feel anxiety or distress.

Having awakened from the dream, he is immediately able to reflect: "The Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are like a dream. Therefore, these phenomena are not real, they are not false, and they are not different from a dream. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this manner, he should be known as one who dwells in the perfection of wisdom."

"The three realms are not real; they are all like dreams. When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall teach sentient beings that all phenomena of the three realms are false and entirely like dream-objects."
"You should know that these are the marks of bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas—
even in their dreams— should see sentient beings in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, they should then form this thought:"

"I shall diligently cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, so that in my buddha-field there shall not even be the name for the evil destinies of hell-beings, animals, or the realm of hungry ghosts."
Upon awakening from the dream, they likewise form this thought.

Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattvas attain buddhahood, their buddha-fields will be pure; there will certainly be no evil realms nor even the names of evil realms. You should know that this is the mark of bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva, in a dream, sees sentient beings in the hells and other realms being burned by fire, or sees cities, towns, and villages being consumed by flames, they should then make this vow:

'If I have already received the prediction of non-retrogression and shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may these great fires be instantly extinguished and transformed into coolness.'"
"If this bodhisattva, having made such a vow, sees fire in a dream that is immediately and instantly extinguished, one should know that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression;

if this bodhisattva, having made such a vow, sees fire in a dream that is not immediately and instantly extinguished, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva, while awake, sees a great fire suddenly break out, burning cities or villages, they should then think:
'Whether in a dream or while awake, have I ever seen the practices, marks, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression belonging to myself? I do not yet know whether these are real or false.'"
"If what I perceive is truly existent, may this great fire be instantly extinguished and transformed into coolness.

Subhūti, you should know that if this bodhisattva makes such a vow and utters these words of truthful resolve, the great fire will then be instantly extinguished; you should know that he has already received the prediction of non-retrogression.
If this bodhisattva makes such a vow and utters these words of truth, yet the fire does not immediately go out, you should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva, while awake, sees fire burning various cities or villages, they then form this thought:
"Whether in a dream or in the waking state, I have previously seen the practices, characteristics, and signs of my own stage of non-retrogression."
If what I have seen is certainly real and true, and I am destined to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may this great fire be instantly extinguished and turn into coolness.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Once these bodhisattvas have made such vows and uttered these words of truth, at that time the great fire does not suddenly go out; rather, it burns one house and then skips over one house before burning another, or it burns one alley and then skips over one alley before burning another. In this manner, the fire gradually subsides. These bodhisattvas have certainly received the prediction of non-retrogression."

However, as for those who are burned, it is because those sentient beings have created and accumulated karma that destroys the True Dharma; by virtue of this karma, they first fell into the evil destinies and underwent the full fruit of suffering for immeasurable eons. Now, having been born in the human realm, they undergo the remaining retribution of that karma. Alternatively, by virtue of this karma, they are destined to fall into the evil destinies and undergo the full fruit of suffering for immeasurable eons, yet now, while in the human realm, they first manifest a small portion of that retribution. One should know that this is the mark of Bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are yet other practices, characteristics, and signs by which one knows a bodhisattva mahāsattva to be non-retrogressive; I shall analyze and explain them for you. You should listen attentively and reflect upon them very well."
Subhūti replied,
“Indeed! I pray that you will speak.”
“We would delight to hear it.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If any bodhisattva sees a man, or a woman, or a boy, or a girl who has been possessed by a non-human spirit and is undergoing various sufferings from which they cannot escape, that bodhisattva then thinks:”

"If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know that I have attained pure intention and have conferred upon me the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

if I have long since developed pure intention seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, remaining far removed from the mental orientations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and not seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the mental orientations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

and if I shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the future, being able to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all classes of sentient beings until the end of time;"

If there are currently present in the worlds of the ten directions immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who proclaim the essentials of the True Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings—those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who see nothing unseen, know nothing unknown, understand nothing uncomprehended, and realize nothing unrealized; who presently know, see, and awaken to the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings—I pray that you will examine my thoughts and my sincere words:

if I am truly able to cultivate the bodhisattva practices and shall certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, then may this man, or this woman, or this boy, or this girl not be disturbed or harassed by non-human spirits; following my words, they shall immediately depart.
When these bodhisattvas speak these words, if that non-human being does not depart, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression;
if that non-human being immediately departs, one should know that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattvas who have not yet fully practiced all the Buddha-dharmas, have not yet entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), have not yet escaped the disturbances caused by Māra, and have not yet recognized the works of Māra. They have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression from enlightenment, cannot personally examine the depth of their own roots of goodness, and give rise to overweening pride regarding their meager cultivation. While training as bodhisattvas, they utter words of solemn truth and are thereby deceived and deluded by Māra."

That is to say, when that bodhisattva sees a man, or a woman, or a young boy, or a young girl who has been possessed by a non-human spirit and is undergoing various sufferings, unable to escape them, he immediately utters a solemn word of truth with ease:

"If I have already received from the Buddhas of the past the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment as one who is irreversible, let this man or woman not be troubled by the non-human spirit; following my words, it shall quickly depart."
After these bodhisattvas had spoken these words, at that time the evil Māra, for the sake of deception and delusion, immediately drove away the non-human beings. Why was this?
The power of Māra was superior to that of the non-human beings; therefore, at Māra’s command, the non-human beings immediately departed.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Bodhisattva leaped for joy and thought to himself:
"That the non-human beings have now departed is due to my own power."
"Why is this? It is because no non-human being has released these men and women simply by following the vow I have made; there is no other cause.

These bodhisattvas fail to realize that this is the work of Māra, and instead, falsely giving rise to joy by attributing it to their own power, they rely on this to treat other bodhisattvas with contempt, saying:
"I have already received from the Buddhas of the past the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; thus, the vows I have made shall not be in vain."

"Since you have not yet received the prophecy from the Buddhas, you should not emulate one another by making solemn declarations of truth; even if you make such commitments, they will surely be empty and bear no fruit.

Because these bodhisattvas treat other bodhisattvas with contempt and derision, and because they falsely rely on their meager abilities to give rise to various forms of overweening pride regarding their merits, they distance themselves from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and are unable to realize the knowledge of all modes.

Because these bodhisattvas lack the power of skillful means, because they give rise to many forms of overweening pride, and because they disparage and despise other bodhisattvas, they fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha despite their diligent exertion.
Because these bodhisattvas have meager merit, all the virtuous deeds they perform and the truthful words they utter stir up the works of Māra.

These bodhisattvas are unable to draw near to, make offerings to, revere, respect, or praise true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); they are unable to inquire about the characteristics of the bodhisattva practices that lead to non-retrogression; and they are unable to consult with or receive instruction regarding the activities of the various evil māra armies. Consequently, their bondage by Māra becomes even more firm and solid.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have not practiced the six pāramitās for long and are far removed from the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā; therefore, they are deceived and deluded by Māra, the Evil One.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should skillfully recognize the deeds of Māra and diligently cultivate wholesome karma.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who have not long practiced the six pāramitās and are far removed from the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā; consequently, they are deceived and deluded by Māra."
This refers to a wicked Māra who, for the sake of deception and delusion, employs skillful means to manifest various forms and approaches the Bodhisattva, speaking these words: "Ho!..."
"Good son!
Do you know for yourself?
The Buddhas of the past have already bestowed upon you the prediction of great enlightenment; you shall certainly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening and shall never again fall back."

I fully know the names and distinctions of your parents, brothers, sisters, friends, and kinsmen, even down to seven generations; I know that you were born in such a direction, such a country, such a city, such a town, and such a village, and that you were born under the constellation of King [Rājā] on such a year, such a month, such a day, at such a time.
If an evil Māra sees that a bodhisattva is by nature gentle and has dull faculties, he will falsely declare:
"In your previous lives, the nature of your faculties was already like this."
If he sees that a bodhisattva is by nature firm and resolute, with keen and sharp faculties, he then falsely predicts:
"In your previous lives, the faculties you were endowed with were also like this."

"If one sees a bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, or always practicing alms-gathering, or accepting only one meal a day, or eating in a single sitting, or eating from a single bowl; or dwelling among tombs, or in the open air, or at the foot of a tree; or wearing rag-robes, or possessing only the three robes; or constantly sitting without lying down, or using old bedding as it was originally spread; or having few desires, or being easily contented, or delighting in seclusion, or delighting in tranquil concentration; or possessing right mindfulness, or possessing sublime wisdom; or not valuing gain and offerings, or not esteeming fame and reputation; or preferring frugality and not oiling the feet, or reducing sleep, or being free from restlessness, or preferring few words, or delighting in gentle speech."
When the evil Māra sees these various practices of the bodhisattva, he falsely predicts:
"In your previous lives as well, you were just like this. Why is that?"

You have now accomplished such and such sublime merits, as is witnessed by all in the world; therefore, you must certainly have possessed such sublime merits in previous lives as well. You should rejoice and comfort yourself, and never disparage yourself.

At that time, when that bodhisattva heard this evil Māra speak of his past and future merits, as well as the merits of his current friends and his own name, and further praised his various excellent roots of goodness, he was filled with joy and leaped for joy; he then gave rise to overweening pride, looking down upon, despising, and reviling all other bodhisattvas.
At that time, Māra, knowing him to be dull-witted, arrogant, and contemptuous of others, addressed him again, saying:

"You have certainly accomplished supreme merit; the Tathāgatas of the past have already bestowed upon you a prophecy. You shall certainly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and never regress; such auspicious signs as these have now appeared before you."

At that time, for the sake of causing disturbance, Māra the Evil One may falsely manifest himself in the form of a renunciant, or falsely manifest himself in the form of a householder; or he may falsely manifest himself in various forms such as a parent, brother, sister, friend, brahmin, teacher, deva, nāga, yakṣa, human, or non-human. Coming to the place where this bodhisattva dwells, he speaks these words:
"In the past, the Tathāgata long ago conferred upon you the prediction of great enlightenment; you shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and will never again fall back."
"Why is this? Because you possess all the characteristics of a bodhisattva on the stage of non-retrogression; you should respect yourself and not give rise to doubt.
When that bodhisattva heard these words, his mind of overweening pride became even more firmly established.
“Subhūti, you should know that those practices,
tokens, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression which I have described do not actually exist at all in these bodhisattvas.”
"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas are possessed by Māra; they are harassed by Māra and lack self-mastery. Why is this?"

These bodhisattvas do not actually possess any of the practices, characteristics, or signs of non-retrogression; yet, having heard the evil Māra falsely proclaim their virtues, names, and so forth, they give rise to overweening pride and treat other bodhisattvas with contempt, derision, and abuse.
Therefore, Subhūti!
If bodhisattvas wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should skillfully recognize the deeds of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are some bodhisattvas who are possessed by Māra and bewitched by Māra; they merely hear the names [of these teachings] and give rise to false attachments. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattvas have not yet skillfully practiced the six pāramitās and the other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; for this reason, Māra gains an opportunity.
These bodhisattvas are unable to discern the characteristics of the four māras; by this cause and condition, they allow the māras to find an opportunity.

These bodhisattvas are unable to discern the immeasurable dharma-gates such as the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), nor do they discern the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the names of sentient beings and phenomena; by this cause and condition, they allow the māras to find an opportunity. Through skillful means, the māras manifest various forms and say to the bodhisattva: "The practices and vows you have cultivated are already fulfilled;
you shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). When you become a Buddha, you shall obtain such meritorious titles and names."
That is to say, that evil Māra knows this bodhisattva’s long-standing thoughts and vows:
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall obtain such merit and such a name.
Accordingly, he predicts and proclaims it in accordance with those thoughts and vows.
At that time, this bodhisattva, being devoid of skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom, hears the Mara’s prophecy and thinks to himself:
"This person is truly marvelous!
"Please grant me a prophecy regarding the meritorious name and title I shall attain upon becoming a Buddha, so that it may correspond with my long-standing aspirations and vows.

By this, I know that the Buddhas of the past have certainly already bestowed upon me the prophecy of Great Bodhi; I am certain to attain Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment and shall never again fall back. When I become a Buddha, I will surely obtain such a meritorious and noble name and title."

As these bodhisattvas are thus prophesied by Māra, or the retinue of Māra, or by śramaṇas possessed by Māra, regarding their future names upon attaining buddhahood, their pride increases all the more:
"In the future, I shall certainly become a buddha and obtain such meritorious names; no other bodhisattvas are my equal."

"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas have not yet accomplished the practices, characteristics, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression as I have described them. Merely hearing the illusory fame of attaining buddhahood spoken by Māra, they give rise to arrogance and treat other bodhisattvas with contempt and derision."
For this reason, these bodhisattvas distance themselves from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Because these bodhisattvas distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, abandon virtuous friends, and are taken hold of by evil associates, they will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

“Subhūti, you should know that some of these bodhisattvas may regain right mindfulness in this very body, sincerely repent their transgressions, abandon a mind of arrogance, and draw near to, serve, and make offerings to true and pure spiritual friends;

although they may continue to wander through saṃsāra for a long time, they will later rely once more upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to train progressively and shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"Subhūti, you should know this!

If these bodhisattvas possess such a body, yet fail to attain right mindfulness, are unable to repent their transgressions, do not relinquish their prideful mind, and do not delight in personally attending upon true, pure, and virtuous friends;

they will certainly wander through saṃsāra for a long time. Even if they later apply themselves with diligence to cultivate various wholesome deeds, they will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."

For example, if a bhikṣu seeking the fruit of a śrāvaka commits even one of the four pārājika offenses, he is no longer a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya; he will certainly be unable to attain the fruits such as stream-entry (srotāpatti) in this present life.

It is the same for those who falsely cling to the empty title of "Bodhisattva": merely hearing the Māra’s discourse on the hollow name of "becoming a Buddha," they give rise to arrogance and treat other Bodhisattvas with contempt and derision. You should know that this transgression is infinitely greater than the four grave offenses committed by a Bhikṣu.
Setting aside the four pārājika offenses committed by that bhikṣu, this bodhisattva’s transgression is immeasurably many times greater than even the five ānantarya crimes. Why is this?

It is because these bodhisattvas have not actually accomplished any superior merit; yet, upon hearing the evil Māra proclaim their false reputation for attaining Buddhahood, they become conceited and look down upon other bodhisattvas. Therefore, this sin exceeds the five ānantarya crimes by an immeasurable multiple.

"From this it should be known that if bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should skillfully recognize such subtle demonic activities as the prophetic declarations of empty names and titles."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattvas who practice the conduct of seclusion; that is to say, they dwell in mountain forests, empty marshes, and vast wildernesses, residing in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages) to sit in meditation and engage in contemplation."
At that time, an evil Māra came to where he was and, paying respectful homage, praised the merit of seclusion, saying: "Excellent,
Great Being!

One who is able to practice such genuine conduct of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; Śakra, Lord of Devas, and other celestial beings and ṛṣis all protect, make offerings to, and revere them. You should dwell constantly in this place and not go elsewhere.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
I do not praise those bodhisattvas who constantly delight in solitude, dwelling in forest hermitages, wildernesses, or mountain groves, sitting in meditation and practicing the conduct of seclusion."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of practice of true seclusion should the assembly of bodhisattvas cultivate,
when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now speaks thus?"
"I do not praise those bodhisattvas who always delight in tranquility, dwelling in *āraṇya*, wilderness, or mountain forests, sitting in meditation and cultivating the practice of seclusion."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Whether bodhisattvas dwell in mountain forests, empty marshes, wildernesses, or forest hermitages (āraṇya), or whether they reside in cities, towns, royal capitals, or noisy and crowded places, provided they can remain far removed from afflictions, evil karma, and the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) with skillful means (upāyakauśalya) as well as cultivate other various superior merits—this is called the true practice of seclusion for a bodhisattva."
This practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is approved by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

The assembly of Bodhisattvas should constantly train in it; whether by day or by night, they should correctly contemplate and diligently practice this dharma of seclusion. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the practice of seclusion.

This practice of seclusion is unmixed with the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and is unmixed with any afflictions or unwholesome karma; free from all clamor and utterly pure, it causes bodhisattvas to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, enabling them to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings throughout the future.
“Subhūti, you should know this!

That which Māra praises—hiding away in mountain forests, empty marshes, wildernesses, and *āraṇya* dwellings, abandoning superior bedding and seats to sit in meditation and contemplate—is not the true practice of seclusion for bodhisattvas.”
Why is this? Because even that practice of seclusion may still involve distraction;

that is to say, it may be mixed with unwholesome karma and afflictions, or mixed with the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Consequently, one cannot apply oneself with diligence to believe in, accept, and train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful means, and thus one cannot fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*).
"Subhūti, you should know that there are some bodhisattvas who,
though they delight in practicing the dharmas of seclusion praised by Māra, give rise to pride and an impure mind, thereby despising and disparaging other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

This refers to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although residing in cities, villages, or royal capitals, maintain a pure mind untainted by various afflictions, evil karma, or the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they diligently cultivate the pāramitās and other immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment, bringing sentient beings to maturity and purifying buddha-fields. Though they dwell amidst the clamor of the world, their minds remain tranquil, and they always delight in practicing true seclusion.
"Subhūti, you should know that toward such a truly pure assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he gives rise to arrogance, treating them with contempt, disparaging them, slandering them,
and looking down upon them."

These bodhisattvas, being devoid of the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), may dwell in a wilderness extending for a hundred yojanas where there are absolutely no predatory beasts, snakes, scorpions, or thieves; yet, it is only spirits, rākṣasas, and the like who roam and reside therein.

Although he dwells in such a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) for one year, or five, or ten, or even up to hundreds of thousands of koṭis—or more than that number—practicing the conduct of seclusion, he does not understand true seclusion. This is because, while Bodhisattvas may dwell in the midst of bustle and clamor, their minds remain tranquil; they are far removed from various afflictions (kleśa), evil karma, and the mental orientations (manasikāra) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as they set out toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

"Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattvas dwell in the wilderness for a long time, they harbor the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they develop a deep attachment to those two stages, cultivate practices of seclusion based on the dharmas of those two stages, and further become deeply immersed in and addicted to such practices."
Although they practice such conduct of seclusion in this way, it does not accord with the minds of the Buddhas.
"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas do not at all achieve the true conduct of seclusion that I have praised."
Within that truly pure practice of detachment, they do not perceive even a semblance of such conduct. Why is this?
Because they do not find joy in such true practice of detachment; rather, they delight only in diligently cultivating the empty practices of detachment characteristic of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattvas practice the conduct of seclusion for the sake of non-perfect purity, Māra comes through the air, joyfully praising them and saying:
‘O Great Being!’”
Excellent! Excellent!
You are able to diligently cultivate the practice of true seclusion.

This practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; if you diligently train in this practice, you will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas, clinging to such practices of seclusion cultivated by those of the two vehicles as being supreme, will treat with contempt and derision those bhikṣus who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattva—even if they dwell in the midst of bustle—whose minds are tranquil and who have accomplished the dharmas of discipline, saying:
'They do not cultivate the practice of seclusion; though their bodies dwell in bustle, their minds are not tranquil, and they lack the dharmas of discipline.'"

"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas disparage and revile those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the genuine seclusion praised by the Buddha, saying: 'They live in the clamor of the crowd and their minds are not tranquil; they are unable to diligently cultivate the practice of genuine seclusion.'"

Regarding those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whom the Tathāgatas do not praise for dwelling in true worldly bustle, they instead honor and extol them—those whose minds are not distracted by bustle and who are tranquil, being able to correctly practice the genuine conduct of seclusion.

“Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas do not approach, serve, or respectfully make offerings to those who are worthy of being approached, served, and respectfully offered to as if they were World-Honored Ones; instead, they treat them with contempt.”

Regarding those whom one should distance oneself from—whom one ought not to associate with, honor, or make offerings to as one would a bad friend—one instead associates with, makes offerings to, and honors them as if serving the World-Honored One.
"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas,
being far removed from the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, give rise to various false conceptualizations and attachments."
Why is this? They think to themselves:
"The practice I am cultivating is true seclusion; therefore, non-human beings praise and protect me."
"Those who dwell in cities have their bodies and minds disturbed; who would then protect, remember, praise, or respect them?

Due to these causes and conditions, the minds of these bodhisattvas become filled with arrogance; they look down upon, despise, and revile other bodhisattvas, and their afflictions and evil karma increase day and night.

“Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas are outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) among other bodhisattvas; they defile the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Although they possess the outward appearance of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they are great thieves among gods and humans, deceiving gods, humans, asuras, and others. Though their bodies are clothed in the dharma-robes of śramaṇas, their minds constantly harbor the intentions of thieves.”
Those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle should not associate with, make offerings to, honor, respect, or praise such evil persons. Why is this?
These people harbor overweening pride; outwardly they appear to be bodhisattvas, yet inwardly they abound in afflictions.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), does not forsake unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), seeks the knowledge of all modes with a profound mind, desires to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and intends to bring universal benefit, happiness, and peace to all sentient beings, he should not associate with, make offerings to, honor, revere, or praise such evil persons.

“Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always cultivate their own task with diligence; they should be weary of and detached from birth and death, and remain unattached to the triple world. Toward those wicked, murderous cāṇḍālas, they should constantly give rise to the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and should think:

‘I must not give rise to the faults that such evil persons give rise to; even if I should momentarily lose mindfulness and such faults arise as they do, I shall immediately recognize them and swiftly eliminate them.’”

"Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should skillfully recognize the deeds of Māra; they should diligently apply themselves to distance themselves from and eliminate such faults as those arising in bodhisattvas, and strive earnestly for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
“Subhūti, you should know that one who trains in this way possesses the skillful means of a bodhisattva and truly awakens to the deeds of Māra.
Chapter 22: Good Friends (Kalyāṇamitra-varga), Part 4, Section 1. At that time, the Bhagavān again addressed Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with a profound mind, desires to realize unsurpassed enlightenment, they should always draw near to, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise true and pure spiritual friends.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends of these bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
all non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas are likewise the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends of the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas."

Furthermore, if other bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, or other virtuous persons can proclaim and reveal to a bodhisattva dharma-gates associated with the profound perfection of wisdom, and instruct and advise the assembly of bodhisattvas so that they may plant roots of goodness, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and swiftly bring them to fulfillment—these too are the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The sūtras associated with the profound perfection of wisdom are also the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

One should know that the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are likewise the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends of the bodhisattvas.
Subhūti, you should know that these six perfections are also the teachers of bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
these six perfections are also the guides of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; these six perfections—
The *pāramitās* are also the illumination of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; likewise, these six kinds of *pāramitās* are also the radiance of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
likewise, these six kinds of *pāramitās* are also the relinquishment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
likewise, these six kinds of *pāramitās* are also the [protection] of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Guardianship; likewise, these six perfections are also the refuge of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, these six perfections are also the destination of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and these six perfections are also the island of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Thus, these six perfections—
Furthermore, these six perfections are the fathers of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and likewise,
these six perfections are the mothers of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; for it is through these six perfections that the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas attains subtle and wondrous wisdom,
gives rise to realization according to reality, and swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Bodhi. Why is this so?
Because all the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the ultimate perfection of the cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā by means of the six pāramitās.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, who have already realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and have already entered parinirvāṇa—all those Blessed Buddhas gave rise to all-knowledge by relying upon the six perfections.

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future, who shall realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and shall enter parinirvāṇa—all those Blessed Buddhas shall likewise give rise to all-knowledge by relying upon the six perfections.”

All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions—who have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and are currently proclaiming the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings—those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise give rise to all-knowledge by means of the six perfections.

Now, I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, currently proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; likewise, all-knowledge arises in dependence upon the six perfections.

Why is this? These six kinds of pāramitās are universally able to encompass the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, as well as the four divine abodes, the four means of attraction, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; whether it be the wisdom of all Buddhas, the self-arisen wisdom, the inconceivable wisdom, the unopposed wisdom, or the wisdom of all-knowledge—all are entirely contained within these six kinds of pāramitās.

Therefore, I say that these six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are the true, pure, and virtuous friends of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas; they serve as teachers and guides for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as lamps and illuminations, as shelters and protections, as refuges and destinations, as islands and peninsulas, and as fathers and mothers. They enable the bodhisattva mahāsattvas to attain subtle and wondrous wisdom and give rise to realization according to reality, so that they may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, acting as friends to all sentient beings who do not seek any recompense.
Therefore, Subhūti,
bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the six perfections.
Furthermore, Subhūti:

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to study the six perfections should, with a sincere mind, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, examine the meaning and intent, and resolve their doubts regarding this profound sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom.

Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā is able to act as the sovereign, the guide, the indicator, and the transformer for the six perfections, serving as their mother who gives birth and nurtures them.

Why is this? If one is separated from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), then there are no five preceding perfections; although there may be generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they are not called "perfections" that can reach the other shore.

Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to act without following the instructions of others, who wish to abide on the ground of not following the instructions of others, who wish to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, who wish to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, who wish to purify buddha-fields, and who wish to bring sentient beings to maturity, should study the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because within this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, the dharmas that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study are explained in detail.
All the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently train within this.

If they diligently train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they will certainly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-attachment as its characteristic.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is there any reason why, while profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-attachment as its characteristic, all other phenomena could also be said to have the characteristic of non-attachment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

By reason of certain causes and conditions, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of non-attachment; it may also be said that all other phenomena likewise possess this characteristic of non-attachment.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are none other than the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is empty and detached.
Therefore, Subhūti!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is empty and detached by virtue of the characteristic of non-attachment; all other phenomena are likewise empty and detached by virtue of the characteristic of non-attachment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are empty and detached, how can sentient beings be established as having defilement or purification?"
"Bhagavān!
It is not possible to speak of defilement or purification regarding phenomena that are empty and detached.
Bhagavān!"

It is not by means of emptiness or detachment that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; nor is there any other distinct dharma apart from emptiness or detachment that can be found to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!
How may I understand the profound meaning and intent of what the Buddha has spoken?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do sentient beings, throughout the long night, harbor the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and cling with their minds to 'I' and 'mine'?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One! So it is!"
“Sugata! For a long night, sentient beings have held to the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and their minds have been attached to ‘I’ and ‘mine.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What do you think?
Are the self and what belongs to the self, as clung to by sentient beings, empty and devoid?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is! World-Honored One! So it is!"
“Sugata! The self and what belongs to the self grasped by sentient beings are all empty and remote.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What do you think?
Is it not the case that sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death due to the grasping at ‘I’ and ‘mine’?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One! So it is!"
“Sugata! It is because sentient beings grasp at a self and what belongs to a self that they wander through birth and death.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In this way, sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death, and the designations of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) are established.
Because sentient beings falsely cling to a self and what belongs to a self, one speaks of affliction, yet within that there is no affliction;
because sentient beings do not falsely cling to a self and what belongs to a self, one speaks of purification, yet within that there is no purification.”
Therefore, Subhūti!
Although all phenomena are empty and detached, sentient beings can nevertheless be designated as having defilement or purity.
Subhūti, you should know this!
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, it is called practicing the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How extraordinary!”
World-Honored One!
How rare! Sugata!
Although all phenomena are empty and detached, sentient beings still possess defilement and purity.
World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they do not course in form, nor do they course in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, none among the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and so forth, will be able to overcome them.
World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they surpass all practices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, reaching the state where there is no further excellence. Why is this?
Because the nature of all Buddhas, the nature of the Tathāgata, the nature of self-awakening, and the nature of omniscience are all invincible.
World-Honored One!

By means of this mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide day and night in skillful means, proceeding toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
what do you think?"

Suppose that all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa, neither before nor after one another, were all to obtain human bodies; having obtained human bodies, they all gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and having given rise to that mind, they practiced the conduct of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and all realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as their lives last, provide offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise to these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas with all the most excellent and sublime worldly articles of enjoyment.
Furthermore, taking these accumulated roots of goodness and sharing them equally with all sentient beings, they dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By reason of this, would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied,
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Very many,
Sugata! The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If good sons and good daughters, among the great assembly, proclaim such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, establishing, instituting, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and abide in the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) associated with such profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
By this cause and condition, the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
What do you think?

Suppose that all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously, without one preceding another, attain human bodies; having attained human bodies, they were all to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and having resolved their minds, throughout the remainder of their lives, they were to reverently practice generosity toward all sentient beings with every kind of worldly article of enjoyment.
Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such giving and sharing them equally with all sentient beings, they dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By reason of this, would those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied,
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so,
Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells for even a single day in mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, the merit obtained will be far more than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.”

Why is this so? To the extent that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell day and night in mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), to that same extent they become worthy fields of merit for all sentient beings.

Why is this so? Because the mind of loving-kindness generated by this bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be equaled by any sentient beings, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have no equal; because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are beyond analogy; and because the dharmas accomplished by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable.
“Subhūti! How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva can bring forth such a multitude of sublime qualities?
Subhūti, you should know this!”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such a sublime perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); by means of this perfection of wisdom, they perceive all sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and afflictions as if being executed, and thus give rise to great compassion (mahākaruṇā).

Furthermore, observing all worlds with the divine eye, he saw countless classes of sentient beings who, having committed deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), had fallen into states of no leisure (*akṣaṇa*) and were undergoing intense suffering; or those who were shrouded by the net of views and could not attain the right path;
or again, he saw other classes of sentient beings who, having fallen into states of no leisure, were deprived of all opportunities for spiritual freedom.

Having seen such sentient beings as these, one gives rise to great revulsion and fear; then, universally taking all the world of sentient beings as one's object, one arouses a mental orientation associated with great compassion, thinking:
"I shall act as a great refuge and protector for all sentient beings; I shall liberate all sentient beings from the suffering and affliction they endure."
"Although they form this thought, they do not abide in this perception, nor do they abide in any other perception. Subhūti,
you should know that this is called the great light of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, which is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti, you should know that by abiding in this dwelling, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to serve as a field of merit for all the world. Although they have not yet realized the knowledge of all modes, they have attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and are worthy of receiving from donors robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites."

Subhūti, you should know that because this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells well in the perfection of wisdom, they are able to ultimately repay the kindness of their benefactors and are also able to draw near to the knowledge of all modes.
Therefore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes not to receive in vain the faithful offerings of kings, ministers, and all sentient beings; wishes to show sentient beings the true and pure path; wishes to act as a great illumination for sentient beings; wishes to liberate sentient beings from the prison of birth and death; and wishes to bestow upon sentient beings the pure eye of Dharma, they should always abide in a mental orientation associated with the profound perfection of wisdom.
"Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will always maintain mindfulness of this mental attention, not allowing any other mental attentions to arise even momentarily; furthermore, all their speech will also accord with the principles of the perfection of wisdom."

Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva exerts himself with diligence day and night, constantly abiding in mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom, never abandoning it for even a moment.

It is like a person who previously never possessed a maṇi-jewel, but later by chance obtains one and rejoices with self-congratulation; yet, having lost it again due to circumstances, they give rise to great distress and sorrow, constantly harboring lamentation and never ceasing to think of it, wondering what plan they might devise to recover this jewel.
Because of this associated mental attention (*manasikāra*), that person never for a moment relinquishes his focus upon this precious jewel.

In the same way, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should always abide in mental attention associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; if they do not abide in mental attention associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will lose the mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, Subhūti,
bodhisattva mahāsattvas should always abide in mental attention associated with the profound perfection of wisdom, never abandoning it even for a moment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If all phenomena and all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), empty, and non-existent, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena and all mental engagements are devoid of intrinsic nature, empty, and non-existent, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all aspects, which is the perfection of wisdom.”

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), empty, and non-existent; herein there is neither increase nor decrease. If one correctly penetrates this, it is called "non-separation."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the intrinsic nature of the profound perfection of wisdom is eternally empty, neither increasing nor decreasing, how is it that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate and realize this perfection of wisdom, they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate and realize the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there is neither increase nor decrease in any phenomena, nor is there any increase or decrease in the bodhisattva mahāsattvas themselves. Just as the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the profound perfection of wisdom is empty and thus without increase or decrease, so it is with all buddhas and bodhisattvas.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can understand in this way, this is called the cultivation and realization of the *prajñāpāramitā*; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they will be able to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that they seek.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such a teaching on the profound perfection of wisdom being neither increased nor diminished, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, does not become despondent, and remains free from hesitation, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom to its ultimate limit, dwells securely on the stage of non-retrogression, will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings until the end of the future.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 551; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 552.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The Fourth Division, Chapter Twenty-two on Good Friends, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Is it that very prajñāpāramitā which is able to practice the prajñāpāramitā?
“No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma apart from the perfection of wisdom that can practice the perfection of wisdom? “It is not so.”
"Subhūti!
"World-Honored One!
Is it that which is empty of the perfection of wisdom that is able to practice the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, it is not so.
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"If one were to seek any dharma that exists as either empty or existent in order to depart from the perfection of wisdom, would one then be able to practice the perfection of wisdom?
"Not so, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is it that emptiness itself can practice the perfection of wisdom? “No, it is not.”
"Subhūti!
"World-Honored One!
Is it possible to find any dharma apart from emptiness that can practice the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, [it is not so].
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it that one who is emptiness itself can practice emptiness?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
