The Buddha told Ānanda: “Because the nature of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is inexhaustible, it is called immeasurable; because its nature is detached, it is called immeasurable; because its nature is quiescent, it is called immeasurable; because it is like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is called immeasurable; because it is like space, it is called immeasurable; because its merit is vast, it is called immeasurable; because it is without boundary, it is called immeasurable; and because it cannot be measured, it is called immeasurable.”

Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time study the *prajñāpāramitā*, ultimately and perfectly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and proclaim and reveal it for the sake of all sentient beings; yet this *prajñāpāramitā* is eternally without decrease or exhaustion.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is inexhaustible, like the great void.
Ānanda, you should know this!
Whoever wishes to exhaust the profound *prajñāpāramitā* wishes to exhaust the limits of space.
Therefore, Ānanda, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is said to be inexhaustible; because it is inexhaustible, it is said to be immeasurable.
At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"This point is profound; I shall question the Buddha about it.
Having had this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason does the Tathāgata say that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is inexhaustible?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is like the great void; because it cannot be exhausted, it is said to be inexhaustible.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of form; they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

They should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of the sense base of the eye; they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

They should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of the sense base of forms; they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena.”

One should contemplate the inexhaustibility of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) to bring forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements to bring forth the perfection of wisdom;

one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) to bring forth the perfection of wisdom; one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and mental-object-elements (*dharmadhātu*) to bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
and one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) to bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate the inexhaustibility of the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness to bring forth the perfection of wisdom;

one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of eye-contact to bring forth the perfection of wisdom; one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact to bring forth the perfection of wisdom;

one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition to bring forth the perfection of wisdom; and one should contemplate the inexhaustibility of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions to bring forth the perfection of wisdom.

One should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of the earth element; one should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

One should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of causes and conditions; one should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition.

One should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of ignorance; one should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the inexhaustibility of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that form (*rūpa*) is inexhaustible like space; they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are inexhaustible like space.

They should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the eye base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is inexhaustible like space; they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases (*śrotra-, ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāya-, mana-āyatana*) are inexhaustible like space."

One should contemplate the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); one should contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom.

One should contemplate the eye constituent (*cakṣurdhātu*) as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom; one should contemplate the constituents of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind (*manodhātu*) as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom.

One should contemplate the form constituent (*rūpadhātu*) as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom; one should contemplate the constituents of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom.

One should contemplate the eye-consciousness element as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom; one should contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom;

one should contemplate eye-contact as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom; and one should contemplate ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as being like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom.

One should contemplate that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom; one should contemplate that the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom;

one should contemplate that the earth element is like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom; and one should contemplate that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are like space and inexhaustible, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom.

One should contemplate causes and conditions as being inexhaustible like space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); one should contemplate the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition as being inexhaustible like space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom;

one should contemplate ignorance as being inexhaustible like space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom; and one should contemplate volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being inexhaustible like space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom.
“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, you should know this!”

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas thus contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as being free from the two extremes, and when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas thus contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as having neither middle nor end—this is the sublime contemplation unique to the assembly of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. It is only by sitting upon the sublime seat of awakening that one can thus contemplate the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination as it truly is, profound as the great void and inexhaustible; thereby, one is able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom with the mode of practice that is as inexhaustible as space, and observes the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are, they will not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

"Subhūti, you should know that if any bodhisattva mahāsattvas should regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, it is entirely because they do not rely on such mental attention and skillful means, and thus do not know as it truly is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, and how one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom through inexhaustible modes of practice."
How should one observe the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are through the aspect of inexhaustibility?

“Subhūti, you should know that if any bodhisattva mahāsattvas should regress from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, it is entirely due to their distance from the skillful means that induce the perfection of wisdom.”

Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment do so entirely by relying on the skillful means that induce the perfection of wisdom. By relying on such skillful means and practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas observe the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are, through a mode of activity that is inexhaustible like space.
By means of these causes and conditions, one will be able to swiftly fulfill the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate the dharma of dependent origination in this manner, they do not perceive any phenomenon arising without a cause; they do not perceive any phenomenon whose nature or characteristics are eternally abiding; and they do not perceive any phenomenon involving an agent or a recipient.

"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they observe the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are through a mode of activity as inexhaustible as space. By thus engendering the perfection of wisdom and cultivating the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they evoke the perfection of wisdom through the mode of practice that is inexhaustible like space, and thus observe the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are.”
At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the aggregate of form, nor does he perceive the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not perceive the sense-base of the eye, nor does he perceive the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
he does not perceive the sense-base of forms, nor does he perceive the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
One does not perceive the eye-element; one does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
One does not perceive the form-element; one does not perceive the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, or mental-object-element.
One does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element; one does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness-element.
He does not perceive eye-contact; he does not perceive ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.

He does not perceive the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; he does not perceive the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as a condition.
He does not perceive the earth element; he does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
They do not perceive the causal condition; they do not perceive the immediately preceding condition, the objective condition, or the dominant condition.

They do not perceive ignorance; they do not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
They do not perceive the perfection of generosity; they do not perceive the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
They do not perceive internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
they do not perceive suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm;
they do not perceive the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
They do not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they do not perceive the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
they do not perceive the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They do not perceive the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they do not perceive the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
they do not perceive the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud.
They do not perceive any dhāraṇī gates or samādhi gates;
they do not perceive the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
they do not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One does not see the thirty-two marks or the eighty secondary signs;
one does not see the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity;
one does not see all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects.
They do not perceive the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
they do not perceive any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they do not perceive the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
One does not perceive the knowledge of all modes;
one does not perceive this buddha-field, nor does one perceive that buddha-field;
one does not perceive any dharma capable of perceiving this or that buddha-field.
"Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, you should know this!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, at that time Māra the Evil One gives rise to extreme distress and affliction, as if pierced by a poisoned arrow.
Just as a person experiences physical and mental agony when their parents suddenly pass away, so it is with Māra the Evil One.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it because of a single evil Māra that he sees such great distress and affliction, like being struck by a poisoned arrow, upon seeing all the bodhisattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom?"
"Is it only these many evil Māras, or are all the evil Māras throughout the entire trichiliocosm likewise so?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All the evil Māras who fill the trichiliocosm, upon seeing bodhisattvas practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, experience extreme distress as if pierced by poisoned arrows; each is unable to remain at ease in their own seat."

Why is this? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the subtle practice and abiding of profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the gods, humans, asuras, and others of the world may search for their faults, yet they shall find none; nor can they disturb, agitate, or obstruct them.
Therefore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should diligently abide in the subtle practice and dwelling of the profound perfection of wisdom.

"Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can diligently abide in the subtle practice and dwelling of the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will then be able to cultivate and fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."

Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly practice the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, they will be able to fully cultivate and perfect all the perfections, and will be able to truly recognize and distance themselves from any obstacles that arise.
Subhūti, you should know this:
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to correctly embrace skillful means, they should practice the perfection of wisdom and cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and brings forth the perfection of wisdom, at that time all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently teaching the Dharma in immeasurable and incalculable worlds, will all protect and mindfully attend to them."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
"Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise give birth to all-knowledge from the perfection of wisdom."
"Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should further reflect:
'Just as the dharmas to be realized by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, I too shall realize them.'"
"In this way, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom and bringing forth the perfection of wisdom, were to contemplate for even the duration of a finger-snap the mass of merit thus produced, it would surpass the merit obtained by those bodhisattvas who have attained something [conceptually] and have practiced generosity for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. How much more so if they can practice the perfection of wisdom and bring forth the perfection of wisdom for a single day or half a day, recollecting and contemplating the merits of the Buddhas!"

“Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the perfection of wisdom for even a single day, or even for as brief a moment as the snap of a finger, and thereby give rise to the perfection of wisdom while recollecting and contemplating the virtues of the Buddhas, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will before long abide on the stage of non-retrogression; that bodhisattva mahāsattva will always be protected and mindful of by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”

Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is constantly protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and will not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is certain never again to fall into the various evil destinies, is certain never to be born in the states of no leisure, and will always be born in the happy realms, never being separated from the Buddhas.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom and bringing forth the perfection of wisdom, recollects and contemplates the virtues of the Buddhas for even the duration of a finger-snap, they will still obtain boundless merit and benefits; how much more so if they practice the perfection of wisdom, bring forth the perfection of wisdom, and recollect and contemplate the virtues of the Buddhas for an entire day, or more than a day!

Just as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gandhahastin constantly practices the perfection of wisdom, brings forth the perfection of wisdom, and recollects and contemplates the merits of the Buddhas without ever abandoning them, so too this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva now practices the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 554; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 555.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 29: Conforming. Section Four: Chapter Twenty-nine on Conforming. "Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are without conjunction;
they should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are without discrimination;
they should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are without confusion or destruction.
One should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are without transformation;
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are without representation;
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena accord with awakened gnosis.
One should contemplate that all phenomena are merely expressed by provisional names; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that all phenomena are merely verbal designations and conventional constructs; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom.

One should contemplate that all phenomena are merely provisionally established, for there is no place, no time, and no substantial entity that can be proclaimed; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that all phenomena possess only a nature, characteristic, and function that are merely provisional; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
One should contemplate that all phenomena are without limit or obstruction; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is immeasurable; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom.
One should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless;
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the sense base of the eye is limitless;
and one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are limitless.
One should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the sphere of form is limitless;
one should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena are limitless;
and one should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the eye-element is limitless.
One should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind elements are immeasurable;
one should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the form element is immeasurable;
and one should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements are immeasurable.
One should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the eye-consciousness element is immeasurable;
one should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are immeasurable;
and one should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that eye-contact is immeasurable.
One should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the contacts of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are immeasurable;
one should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are immeasurable;

and one should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all feelings produced with the contacts of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as conditions are immeasurable.
One should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the earth element is limitless;
one should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are limitless;
and one should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that causes and conditions are limitless.
One should contemplate the equality and boundlessness of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition, and thereby accord with the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate the boundlessness of ignorance, and thereby accord with the perfection of wisdom;

one should contemplate the boundlessness of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, and thereby accord with the perfection of wisdom.
One should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are without marks;
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena have the characteristic of thorough penetration;
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are pure by nature.
One should contemplate all phenomena as being beyond verbal expression, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate all phenomena as being unarisen and so forth, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate all phenomena as being unceasing and so forth, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom.
One should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are equal to nirvāṇa;
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are equal to suchness (*tathatā*);
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena have neither coming nor going.
One should contemplate all phenomena as being without self or other, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate all phenomena as equal in terms of self and other, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate all phenomena as pure by nature for both ordinary beings and noble ones, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate all phenomena as having cast off the heavy burden because there is no further accumulation; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate all phenomena as being without location or direction; thus one accords with the perfection of wisdom.

"Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form has no direction and no location; the intrinsic natures of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no direction and no location;

the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye has no direction and no location; and the intrinsic natures of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have no direction and no location."

The intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form is without direction and without location; the intrinsic natures of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are without direction and without location.

The intrinsic nature of the eye-element is without direction and without location; the intrinsic natures of the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are without direction and without location.

The intrinsic nature of the form-element is without direction and without location; the intrinsic natures of the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are without direction and without location.
The eye-consciousness element is by nature without direction and without location; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are by nature without direction and without location.
Eye-contact is by nature without direction and without location; ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are by nature without direction and without location.

All sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition are by nature without direction and without location; all sensations produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are by nature without direction and without location.

The intrinsic nature of the earth element is without direction and without location; the intrinsic nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is without direction and without location.

The intrinsic nature of causes and conditions is without direction and without location; the intrinsic nature of the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition is without direction and without location.

The intrinsic nature of ignorance is without direction and without location; the intrinsic nature of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair is without direction and without location.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
One should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are quiescent and blissful;
one should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all phenomena are without craving and without freedom from craving."
One should contemplate all phenomena as being neither defiled nor free from defilement, thereby conforming to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? Because the true nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is neither defiled nor free from defilement; the true natures of the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise neither defiled nor free from defilement.

The true nature of the eye-base is without defilement and without freedom from defilement; the true nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases is without defilement and without freedom from defilement.

The true nature of the form-base is without defilement and without freedom from defilement; the true nature of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases is without defilement and without freedom from defilement.

The true nature of the eye-element is without defilement and without freedom from defilement; the true nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements is without defilement and without freedom from defilement.

The true nature of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is without defilement and without freedom from defilement; the true nature of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (*dharmadhātu*) is without defilement and without freedom from defilement.

The true nature of the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is without defilement and without freedom from defilement; the true nature of the realms of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness is without defilement and without freedom from defilement.

The true nature of eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) is without defilement and without freedom from defilement; the true nature of the contacts of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is without defilement and without freedom from defilement.

The true nature of all sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition is unstained and not free from stain; the true nature of all sensations produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions is unstained and not free from stain.
The true nature of the earth element is unstained and not free from stain; the true nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is unstained and not free from stain.

The true nature of causal conditions is unstained and not free from stain; the true nature of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition is unstained and not free from stain.

The true nature of ignorance is without defilement and without freedom from defilement; the true nature of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair is without defilement and without freedom from defilement.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
One should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by observing that all phenomena are ultimately pure;
one should practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom by observing that all phenomena are unattached and free from attachment."
One should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating all phenomena as awakening to bodhi and buddha-knowledge;
one should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating all phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless;
one should conform to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating all phenomena as excellent medicine, with compassion as the foremost.
One should contemplate all phenomena as abiding in loving-kindness, the Brahma-abodes, being faultless and without grasping, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate all phenomena as being without hatred or anger toward sentient beings, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate the great ocean as being without limit, thereby conforming to the perfection of wisdom.
One should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that space is boundless;
one should accord with the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the aggregate of form is free from all signs;

At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I neither know nor apprehend the mind of a bodhisattva; I do not perceive any real entity to be found among the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas or within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). How, then, am I to proclaim and demonstrate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
“World-Honored One!

When I contemplate all things—whether arising or ceasing, whether defiled or pure—I find them utterly unobtainable; yet, when one speaks of the existence within this of such things as ‘bodhisattva’ or the ‘name of prajñā,’ doubt and regret immediately arise.”
World-Honored One!
Names such as "bodhisattva" are neither determinate nor have they any place of abiding. Why is this so?
The names and so forth of bodhisattvas are entirely non-existent; that which is non-existent has no fixed nature and no abiding place.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, does not sink in spirit nor feel discouraged, and is neither startled nor terrified, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is definitively established in the stage of non-retrogression, dwelling in non-dwelling by means of non-abiding as their skillful method.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on form, nor should they dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? If one dwells in form, one performs activities regarding form, and does not practice the profound perfection of wisdom;

if one dwells in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one performs activities regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and does not practice the profound perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? It is not one who acts or exerts effort who can take up the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). If one cannot take up the perfection of wisdom, then one cannot cultivate the perfection of wisdom; if one cannot cultivate the perfection of wisdom, then one cannot bring it to fulfillment; if one cannot bring it to fulfillment, then one cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*); and if one cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes, then one cannot benefit those sentient beings who are to be benefited.
Why is this? Form should not be grasped;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should also not be grasped. One should likewise not grasp the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor should one grasp form. Because it cannot be grasped, it is not form; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be grasped, they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and because the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be grasped, it is not the *prajñāpāramitā*.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way; if they train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, it is called the bodhisattva’s wheel of samādhi that is without grasping. It is a vast provision, immeasurable and inexhaustible, which cannot be diverted or stolen by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, yet it does not grasp at the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).”
Why is this? This knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is not attained through the cultivation of grasping at signs; indeed, all grasping at signs is affliction (*kleśa*).

If the knowledge of all modes were attained through grasping at cultivation, then the brahmin Jayasena would not have been able to have faith and understanding in the knowledge of all modes. Although the brahmin Jayasena entered the Buddha-dharma by the power of faith and understanding—being termed a "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārī*)—he was nonetheless able to contemplate the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena with even a small portion of wisdom and thereby awaken to and enter the knowledge of all modes.

Having thus entered into realization, one does not grasp at the mark of form (*rūpa*), nor does one grasp at the marks of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*). One does not view this wisdom through the lens of joy or delight; one does not view this wisdom through hearing it; one does not view this wisdom by means of internal form, nor by external form, nor by both internal and external form, nor even apart from form.

One does not view this wisdom by means of internal feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor by external feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor by both internal and external feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor even apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Through such gates of detachment as these, the brahmin Jayasena gave rise to profound faith and understanding regarding the knowledge of all modes of knowledge; he was thus called a "follower by faith," having no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena whatsoever.

In this way, once the brahmin has attained faith and understanding regarding the knowledge of all modes through the gateway of signlessness, he does not apprehend signs in any phenomena, nor does he mentally construct signless phenomena.
In this way, by the power of his resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), the brahmin neither grasps nor rejects any phenomena; he neither attains nor realizes them.
At that time, that brahmin does not even cling to his own conviction up to and including nirvāṇa, because he takes the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as the definitive standard.
“World-Honored One!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at form, nor does it grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Although there is nothing among all phenomena that it grasps, as long as they have not yet perfected the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth, they will never enter parinirvāṇa midway.”

It should be known that this profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, though free from grasping and attachment, is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should contemplate in this way:
What is called the perfection of wisdom?"
To whom does this *prajñāpāramitā* belong?
If phenomena are non-existent and unattainable, is that *prajñāpāramitā* [the same]?
Within non-existence, there is neither "that" nor "this"—to what could it possibly belong?
"Bhagavān!

If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva examines such matters in this way, their mind does not sink, nor do they feel discouraged; if they are not startled and not terrified, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"For what reason is it that form is separated from the nature of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are separated from the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and the perfection of wisdom is separated from the nature of the perfection of wisdom, yet it is said that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

Form is devoid of the nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are devoid of the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and the perfection of wisdom is devoid of the nature of the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, regarding all these phenomena (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and intrinsic nature is also devoid of characteristics; characteristics are devoid of characteristics, and intrinsic nature is devoid of intrinsic nature; neither the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor the characterized object (*lakṣya*) can be apprehended.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know such meanings as they truly are, they do not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, will they swiftly accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatājñāna)?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, they will swiftly be able to accomplish all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).
Why is that? Śāriputra!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing. Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they will be close to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice with the formative aspect of practicing form, or practice with the formative aspect of the arising of form, or practice with the formative aspect of the disintegration of form, or practice with the formative aspect of the cessation of form, or practice with the formative aspect of the emptiness of form, or think 'I am able to practice,' such practice is characterized by apprehension."

If one practices with the perception of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a sign; if one practices with the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a sign; if one practices with the decay of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a sign; if one practices with the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a sign; if one practices with the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a sign; or if one thinks, "I am practicing"—this practice is characterized by grasping.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought as,
"I am a bodhisattva; I am able to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)," this constitutes a mark of practice.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought as,
"One who can practice in this way is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)," this too becomes a conceptual sign (*nimitta*);
it should be known that such a bodhisattva lacks skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“In what manner should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice so that it is called ‘practicing the perfection of wisdom’?”
Subhūti replied, “If bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not course in form,

do not course in the marks of form, do not course in the arising of form, do not course in the disintegration of form, do not course in the cessation of form, and do not course in the emptiness of form, this is the coursing in the perfection of wisdom.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not practice with regard to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the characteristics of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the arising of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the destruction of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; do not practice with regard to the cessation of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and do not practice with regard to the emptiness of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at practice, does not grasp at non-practice, does not grasp at both practice and non-practice, does not grasp at neither practice nor non-practice, and even does not grasp at this non-grasping, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Why is this? Śāriputra, because all phenomena are ungraspable, cannot be followed, cannot be appropriated, and are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ wheel of the certainty of non-arising regarding all phenomena. It is a vast provision, immeasurable and inexhaustible, not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, further addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Even though a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they do not perceive this samādhi, nor do they become attached to it, nor do they think: '...'"
"I have entered, am entering, or shall enter this concentration.

When such thoughts and discriminations do not arise at all due to the power of that concentration, one should know that he has already been granted the prophecy of non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by dwelling in this samādhi, has already received a face-to-face prophecy from the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is that bodhisattva mahāsattva able to manifest such a samādhi?"
Subhūti replied, “No, Śāriputra!”
"Why is this? Because these sons of good family have neither knowledge nor perception regarding such a concentration.
Śāriputra said:
“Venerable One, do you say that those sons of good family have neither knowledge nor perception regarding such a concentration?
Subhūti replied,
“I certainly say that those sons of good family have neither knowledge nor perception regarding such a concentration.”
Why is this? Because such meditative concentrations are non-existent.
That son of good family has neither knowledge nor perception regarding such concentrations, and such concentrations likewise have neither knowledge nor perception regarding all phenomena.
"Why is this? Because all phenomena are non-existent.
At that time, the Bhagavat praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
It is just as you have said.”
Therefore, I declare that you are foremost among those who dwell in the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*).
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should train in this manner; training in this manner is what is called training in the perfection of wisdom.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this manner, is this called truly training in the prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this manner, it is called truly training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, in what dharma do they train?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not train in any dharma."
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because all phenomena do not exist in the manner that foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp them to exist.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If that is so, how do all phenomena exist?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It exists in such a way that it is non-existent.
If one cannot thoroughly comprehend this dharma of non-existence, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Foolish ordinary beings, regarding the non-existent nature of all dharmas, through the predominant power of ignorance and craving, conceptually construct and cling to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Consequently, they neither know nor see the non-existent nature of all dharmas, yet they conceptually differentiate these dharmas. Because of this conceptual differentiation, they give rise to clinging; because of this clinging, they conceptually differentiate the non-existent nature of dharmas. Thus, they neither see nor know dharmas."

Because they neither see nor know all phenomena, they differentiate between the past, future, and present; due to this differentiation, they become attached to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because of attachment to name-and-form, they differentiate and cling to non-existent phenomena; and because of differentiating and clinging to non-existent phenomena, they neither know nor see the path of reality as it is, and are unable to escape the cycle of birth and death within the three realms. They do not believe in the Dharma of the Truths and do not awaken to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); for these reasons, they fall among the ranks of the foolish.
"Therefore, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no attachment whatsoever to the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, do they not seek to train in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not even seek to learn the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Nevertheless, when bodhisattvas train in this way, although there is nothing to be learned, it is called truly learning the knowledge of all modes, for they are able to swiftly accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
suppose someone were to come and ask this question:”
"If a phantom were to study the knowledge of all modes, would it also be able to accomplish that knowledge of all modes?
If I were asked this question, how should I answer?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?"
"Is illusion different from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Subhūti replied: "Illusion is not different from form;
form is not different from illusion. Illusion is itself form, and form is itself illusion. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Based on the five aggregates of clinging, does one give rise to perceptions and designations, and establish through conventional expression the provisional name 'bodhisattva mahāsattva'?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and cultivate the study of the perfection of wisdom do so entirely like a phantom person cultivating the study.”
Why is this? Because a phantom person is precisely the five aggregates of clinging. Why is that so?
"I have taught that the five aggregates, the six sense faculties such as the eye, and so forth, are all like magical illusions and are not at all substantially real.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is newly training in the Great Vehicle hears such a teaching, will his mind not become startled, terrified, or disheartened?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle associates with evil friends and hears such a teaching, his mind will become terrified and he will give rise to despondency.”
"If one draws near to virtuous friends, even upon hearing this teaching, one will not be startled or terrified, nor will one feel discouraged or retreat.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called a 'bad friend' for a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those who are evil friends to bodhisattvas are those who teach bodhisattvas to feel revulsion toward the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), to abandon the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) and grasp at the signs of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), to cause them to study worldly scriptures that involve grasping at signs, to cause them to study the sūtras and dharmas associated with the śrāvakas, and furthermore, to cause them to associate with and practice the activities of Māra. These are called the evil friends of bodhisattvas."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is called a bodhisattva’s spiritual friend?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The spiritual friends of bodhisattvas are those who instruct bodhisattvas to diligently cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, and even explain to them the deeds of Māra and the faults of Māra, causing them to recognize these through skillful means and abandon them; these are called the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends for a newly initiated bodhisattva adorned with great vows."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"One who trains in all dharmas without attachment or obstruction, awakens to all dharmas without attachment or obstruction, and seeks to realize bodhi is therefore called a Bodhisattva.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason, furthermore, is he called a Mahāsattva?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because these bodhisattvas shall become the leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings, they are further named Mahāsattvas.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to explain the meaning of 'mahāsattva'; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Speak as you intend."
Śāriputra said:

"By means of the skillful means of bodhisattvas, they proclaim the essential points of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to sever the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a person, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, and views of annihilationism and eternalism; it is by virtue of this meaning that they are called 'mahāsattvas'."
At that time, Subhūti also addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I now wish to expound upon the meaning of ‘mahāsattva’; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Speak as you wish. Subhūti replied:
"Because bodhisattvas have generated the mind of awakening, the unequaled mind, and a mind that cannot be led away by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they do not even cling to such a mind."
Why is this? Because the mind of omniscience is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms; one should not give rise to attachment toward it.
It is by virtue of this principle that one is called a Mahāsattva.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason and by what causal conditions does one not even cling to such a mind?
Subhūti replied:
"Since these various minds lack the nature of mind, one should not cling to them.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra also addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to speak on the meaning of 'Mahāsattva'; I only pray that you will grant me leave to do so!"
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
“Speak as you wish.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

"Because all bodhisattvas don the armor of great vows for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, because they set out upon the Great Vehicle, and because they ride upon the Great Vehicle, they are called mahāsattvas."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has spoken of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas donning the great armor of vows, to what extent can it be said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have donned the great armor of vows?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas form this thought:
'I should deliver immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.'"
Although these things are performed, there is no dharma nor any sentient being that attains nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because such is the natural state of the true nature of all dharmas.
Suppose, for example, a magician or his apprentice were to conjure a great crowd at a crossroads who then began to harm one another. What do you think?
Is there, in this case, any actual phenomenon of harming?
Subhūti replied:
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is likewise for all bodhisattva mahāsattvas; although they manifest the deliverance of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings by causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, there is no dharma and no sentient being that attains nirvana.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such matters, is not startled, not terrified, and does not feel any retreat or dejection, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the armor of the great vow.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it should be known that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who do not don the armor of the great vow are, in fact, the ones who have donned the armor of the great vow."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

Why is this? Because the knowledge of all-knowledge is neither created nor fashioned, and all sentient beings are likewise neither created nor fashioned; yet, for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas don the armor of great vows.

Why is this? Form is neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
"Why is this? Because form, up to and including consciousness, cannot be apprehended.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, from form up to consciousness, there is neither defilement nor purification. Why is this?
Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither bound nor liberated."
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Subhūti:
"Venerable sir, do you say that form is neither bound nor liberated? And do you say that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither bound nor liberated?"
Subhūti replied: “So it is! So it is!”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"What kind of form do you say is neither bound nor liberated?
What kind of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do you also say is neither bound nor liberated?"
Subhūti replied:

"It is said that for a person who is like an illusion, form is neither bound nor liberated; it is also said that for such a person, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither bound nor liberated."

Why is this? Because form, and so on up to consciousness, are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated; because they are detached, they are neither bound nor liberated; because they are quiescent, they are neither bound nor liberated; because they are without arising or ceasing, they are neither bound nor liberated. This is called a bodhisattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle and donning the armor of the great vow.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having heard this teaching, received it with joy and faith, and remained silent.
Then, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out upon the Great Vehicle, what is this Great Vehicle?”
How does a bodhisattva set out upon the Great Vehicle?
From where does such a Great Vehicle emerge, and where does it abide?
Furthermore, who is it that mounts this Great Vehicle and departs?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"That which is called 'the Great Vehicle' is a synonym for the immeasurable and the innumerable, because it is accomplished through the convergence of boundless merits."

What is meant by a bodhisattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle? It refers to those bodhisattvas who diligently cultivate the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and are thus able to progress from one stage (bhūmi) to the next; this is called a bodhisattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle.

As for where this Mahāyāna emerges from and where it abides: it is said that this Mahāyāna emerges from within the three realms and abides within the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); yet, because it employs non-duality as its skillful means, there is neither emergence nor abiding.
Who, moreover, is it that departs by mounting this Great Vehicle?
There is absolutely no one who departs by mounting this Great Vehicle. Why is this so?
“The one who rides and that which is ridden—these two dharmas are both non-existent. Within that which is non-existent, who could ride what dharma to be called a ‘rider’?
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Such a Great Vehicle universally surpasses all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras; such a Great Vehicle is equal to space.”

Just as space is universally able to contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, so too is the Mahāyāna universally able to contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.
Furthermore, just as space has no coming, no going, and no abiding that can be perceived, so too is the Mahāyāna: it has no coming, no going, and no abiding that can be perceived.

Furthermore, just as space cannot be apprehended in its prior, posterior, or middle limits, so too is the Mahāyāna; since its prior, posterior, and middle limits are all unapprehendable and it is equal throughout the three periods of time, it is called the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, you previously instructed the Venerable Subhūti to proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; why is it that you now speak of the Mahāyāna?"
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In my exposition of the Great Vehicle, have I perhaps contravened what has been taught regarding the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What you have said regarding the Great Vehicle is entirely in accord with the perfection of wisdom and does not deviate from it.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not apprehend a bodhisattva in the past, the future, or the present.

Because form (*rūpa*) is infinite, the bodhisattva is also infinite; because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are infinite, the bodhisattva is also infinite.
Whether as form or apart from form, the bodhisattva does not exist and cannot be apprehended.”

Even feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the departure from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the Bodhisattva likewise does not exist and cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!

Regarding all these dharmas, throughout every mode, in every place, and at every time, I have sought the bodhisattvas and found nothing at all; they are ultimately unobtainable. How then can I proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
That which is called a 'bodhisattva' exists only as a provisional designation and possesses no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Just as it is said that 'self' and so forth are ultimately unarisen, existing only as provisional designations and possessing no intrinsic nature, so too are all phenomena ultimately unarisen, existing only as provisional designations and possessing no intrinsic nature."
In this context, what is form that is ultimately unarisen?
If it is ultimately unarisen, it is not called form.
What are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are ultimately unarisen?
If there is ultimate non-arising, then they are not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
World-Honored One!
Form is unattainable as a bodhisattva; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise unattainable as a bodhisattva; even this unattainability is itself unattainable.
Regarding all such dharmas, throughout all modes, in all places, and at all times, I seek these bodhisattvas and they are entirely unfindable; what dharma, then, should I teach?
"What dharmas are cultivated?
In what place and at what time are what dharmas realized?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas exists only as a provisional name and possesses no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Just as it is said that "self" and so forth are ultimately unarisen, existing only as provisional names and possessing no intrinsic nature, so too are all phenomena: they exist only as provisional names and possess no intrinsic nature.
What is this form that is neither graspable nor subject to arising?
What are these sensations, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses that are neither graspable nor subject to arising?

Since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is neither graspable nor subject to arising, and since a phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature is also not subject to arising, and even this non-arising phenomenon is not subject to arising—how could I, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* which is ultimately non-arising, instruct a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is ultimately non-arising?
"Bhagavān!
Apart from the dharma of non-arising, no dharma can be apprehended, nor is there any bodhisattva who can practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Bhagavān!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing these words, is neither startled nor terrified, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and contemplates all phenomena, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at form.
Why is this so? Because the non-arising of form is not form, and the non-ceasing of form is also not form; since there is neither arising nor ceasing, there is neither duality nor distinction.
To speak of form is, in itself, to enter the category of non-dual dharmas.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and contemplates all phenomena, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.

Why is this? Because the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; the non-ceasing of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Since they are neither arising nor ceasing, they are without duality and without distinction.
"If one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they enter into the category of non-dual dharmas.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"According to my understanding of the meaning of what you have said, bodhisattvas are ultimately unborn. If this is so, for what reason do bodhisattvas undergo hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful practices and endure the great suffering of immeasurable births and deaths in order to liberate immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings?"
Subhūti replied:

"It is not that I do not acknowledge within those non-arising dharmas that there are bodhisattvas who, for the sake of liberating immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, practice hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities and undergo the great suffering of immeasurable births and deaths; yet, although these bodhisattvas perform these deeds, they harbor no conception of them as 'painful austerities' therein."

Why is this? Śāriputra, if one perceives ascetic practices as being painful, one cannot benefit infinite sentient beings. Therefore, a bodhisattva perceives all ascetic practices as pleasant practices, perceives difficult practices as easy practices, and perceives all sentient beings as their own parents or as themselves; for the sake of liberating them, they resolve upon bodhicitta, and by means of this, they are able to bring about great benefit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:

"Just as my own self-nature cannot be found when sought through all modes, in all places, and at all times among all phenomena, so too it is with all internal and external phenomena; they are entirely non-existent and unobtainable."

If one dwells in this perception, one will not perceive any difficulty in performing arduous practices; by means of this, one is able to cultivate hundreds of thousands of arduous practices for the sake of infinite sentient beings, thereby bringing great benefit to the class of sentient beings.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“Are these bodhisattvas truly without arising?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! All bodhisattvas are indeed without arising."
Śāriputra asked:
"Is it only the bodhisattva who is truly non-arisen, or is omniscience also truly non-arisen?
Subhūti replied:
"This omniscience is also truly without arising.
Śāriputra asked:
"Is it only omniscience that is truly without arising, or are all classes of ordinary beings also truly without arising?"
Subhūti replied,
"Even all ordinary beings are truly without birth.
Śāriputra said:
"If all bodhisattvas are truly non-arisen, then the dharmas of bodhisattvas should also be non-arisen;
if omniscience is truly non-arisen, then the dharmas of omniscience should also be non-arisen;
if the class of ordinary beings is truly non-arisen, then the dharmas of the class of ordinary beings should also be non-arisen."
"If that is so, when a bodhisattva attains omniscience, they should be able to realize non-arising through dharmas that are themselves non-arising.
Subhūti replied, "In my view,
I do not admit that there is any attainment or realization within dharmas that are non-arising."
"Why is this? Because within the dharma of non-arising, there is neither realization nor attainment.
Śāriputra said:
"Do you assert that a dharma that arises realizes a dharma that arises, or do you assert that a dharma that does not arise realizes a dharma that does not arise?
Subhūti replied, "In my view,
I do not assert that a dharma that arises realizes a dharma that arises, nor do I assert that a dharma that does not arise realizes a dharma that does not arise."
Śāriputra asked:

"Is it that one who has realized the dharma of non-arising is permitted to realize the dharma of arising, or is it that one who has realized the dharma of non-arising is permitted to realize the dharma of arising?
Subhūti replied:

"I do not intend to allow that one who realizes the dharma of non-arising should realize the dharma of arising, nor do I allow that one who realizes the dharma of non-arising should realize the dharma of arising.
Śāriputra said: "If this is so, then there should be neither attainment nor realization."
Subhūti replied,
“Although there is attainment and realization, they do not exist as real entities.
Śāriputra said:
"Do you assert that an unarisen dharma arises, or do you assert that an already-arisen dharma arises?
Subhūti replied, "In my view,
I do not assert that an unarisen dharma arises, nor do I assert that an already-arisen dharma arises."
Śāriputra asked:
"Do you assert that arising arises, or do you assert that non-arising arises?
Subhūti replied:
"I do not intend to allow for the arising of what has already arisen, nor do I allow for the arising of what has not yet arisen.
Śāriputra said: "Virtuous one, regarding the dharma of non-arising you have spoken of, do you delight in explaining the characteristics of non-arising?"
Subhūti replied,
“Regarding the dharmas of non-arising that have been taught, I likewise do not delight in discoursing upon the characteristics of non-arising.
Śāriputra said:
"Regarding the dharmas that are unarisen, one gives rise to the expression 'unarisen. Is this expression 'unarisen' itself also unarisen? Subhūti replied:

"Regarding the dharmas that are unarisen, one gives rise to the expression 'unarisen'; both these dharmas and this expression are, in meaning, unarisen, yet they are spoken of as having the characteristic of being unarisen in accordance with worldly convention."
At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Among those who preach the Dharma, you are the foremost; none can equal you except for the Blessed One, the World-Honored One."
"Why is this? Because he is able to provide answers to whatever various Dharma-gates one may inquire about or challenge him with.
Subhūti replied:

“Those disciples of the Buddhas who are without dependence or attachment toward any phenomena naturally possess the capacity to respond to every inquiry and interrogation with sovereign fearlessness.”
"Why is this? Because all dharmas have no basis.
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!
If bodhisattvas are able to answer questions in such a manner, by the power of which *pāramitā* is this accomplished?”
Subhūti replied:
"This is accomplished through the power of the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is that? Because..."
It is said that all phenomena have no basis of reliance, because it is through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that one realizes all phenomena have no basis of reliance. Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such words, does not become confused or distressed, nor harbor any doubt or uncertainty, it should be known that this bodhisattva is able to abide in such a dwelling, never abandoning it, and is also constantly not separated from the mental engagement of great compassion.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If all bodhisattvas were to abide in such an abiding and never abandon it, and were likewise never to be separated from such mental attention, then all sentient beings would be bodhisattvas."

Why is this so? Because all sentient beings likewise never abandon this dwelling and this mental attention, and because the nature of wisdom and great compassion is equal, there would then be no distinction between bodhisattvas and sentient beings.
Subhūti replied:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Although this may seem to refute me, it actually establishes my meaning.
Why is this? O Śāriputra!
Because all sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention likewise lack intrinsic nature;
because all sentient beings are by nature remote, one should know that the nature of this dwelling and this mental attention is also remote;
because all sentient beings lack cognition, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention likewise lack cognition.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, these bodhisattvas never abandon such a dwelling and this mental attention, nor do they differ from all sentient beings.

If bodhisattvas can know in this way without any obstruction, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); it is my intention that all bodhisattvas should employ this mental attention to practice the profound perfection of wisdom.

Chapter 5: The Chapter on Śakra, Lord of Devas, Part Two. At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, arrived together with forty thousand devaputras; the Four World-Protecting Kings arrived together with twenty thousand devaputras; Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā World, arrived together with ten thousand Brahmā hosts; and furthermore, five thousand devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens arrived together. The light from the bodies of these various deva hosts, which was the fruit of their own karma, all vanished in the presence of the Buddha’s majestic radiance.
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
"There are now immeasurable devaputras who wish to hear the Venerable One proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā. We pray that the Venerable One, out of compassion, will explain for them:
how should a bodhisattva abide in the Prajñāpāramitā?"
At that time, Subhūti addressed Śakra, saying:
"Empowered by the Buddha's might, I shall proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly of devas, as it is in which all bodhisattvas should abide."
"You gods, all of you who have not yet resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, should now do so.
Those who have already entered the fixed course of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can no longer resolve upon the mind of great bodhi."
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because for them, saṃsāra has limits and obstructions.
If among them there are those who can give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
I likewise rejoice in it.
Why is this, Kausika?
"Those who are superior persons should seek the superior Dharma; I shall never obstruct another's pursuit of excellent and wholesome qualities.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
