You have now skillfully encouraged all bodhisattvas.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since I have recognized this kindness, how could I fail to repay it!
That is to say, the Buddhas of the past and their disciples taught the various essential dharmas to the bodhisattvas, providing skillful means for them to enter the pāramitās."
At that time, the Tathāgata also trained therein; he has now realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and turned the wondrous wheel of Dharma to benefit us.

Therefore, I should now follow the Buddha’s teaching, receiving and protecting these bodhisattvas so that they may swiftly realize unexcelled enlightenment and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma for the benefit and happiness of all. This is what is called repaying his debt of gratitude.
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra:
"All you devas, you should listen attentively; I shall explain to you the characteristics of how the bodhisattvas should abide within the profound perfection of wisdom."

“Kauśika! The assembly of bodhisattvas, adorned with great vows and set out upon the Mahāyāna, should dwell in the perfection of wisdom by means of the characteristic of emptiness; they should not dwell in form, nor should they dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they should not dwell in the fruit of stream-entry, nor should they dwell in the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.”
One should not dwell on the thought that "this is form," nor should one dwell on the thought that "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

One should not dwell on the thought that "this is the fruit of stream-entry," nor should one dwell on the thoughts that "this is the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
One should not dwell on whether form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, empty or non-empty.

One should not dwell upon the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, for all these are manifested as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), are true fields of merit, and are worthy of receiving offerings;
one should not dwell upon the fruit of stream-entry as being "one who returns at most seven times before necessarily entering nirvāṇa";
nor should one dwell upon the fruit of once-returning as being "one who, though not yet reaching the ultimate, will certainly exhaust all suffering by returning once more to this world."
One should not dwell in the fruit of the Non-returner, thinking: "Having gone there to attain parinirvāṇa, I shall not return again. One should not dwell in the fruit of Arhatship, thinking:
"In this very life, I shall certainly enter nirvana without remainder. One should not dwell in the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood, thinking:

"Transcending the stage of Śrāvaka yet not reaching the stage of Buddhahood, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. One should not dwell in Buddhahood, [thinking]: "Manifested by the unconditioned, I am a true field of merit who should receive offerings; transcending the stages of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, I bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder; even if the entire realm of sentient beings were to be exhausted, I would likewise enter the realm of nirvana without remainder."
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
"If that is so, how should a bodhisattva abide?
Then, Subhūti, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, said to him:
“What do you think?
In what does the mind of the Tathāgata abide?
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

“The mind of the Tathāgata abides nowhere; because it abides nowhere, he is called the Tathāgata. This means that he does not abide in the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), nor does he abide in the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), yet it is not that he does not abide.”
Subhūti replied: "The Bodhisattva is likewise;

just as all Tathāgatas have no mental abiding in any phenomena, nor yet do they not abide, so too should Bodhisattvas, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, abide in and train in the profound perfection of wisdom."
At that time, there were among the assembly certain sons of gods who thought to themselves:

"Although the words and incantations of the yakṣas and others, with all their various distinctions, are indeed obscure, we are still able to understand them; yet although the venerable Subhūti has displayed the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through various expressions, we are ultimately unable to comprehend it."
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, addressed them, saying:
"In this matter, I have neither spoken nor shown anything; you likewise have heard nothing—what, then, is there to be understood?"
At that time, the sons of the gods again had this thought:
"The Venerable Subhūti wishes to make this meaning easy to understand, yet it becomes increasingly profound and subtle, difficult to fathom."
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing what those devaputras were thinking, spoke to them again:

"All those who wish to realize or abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; or who wish to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha—must rely upon this patience in order to realize and abide therein."
At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"Venerable Subhūti, for what kind of sentient beings does he now wish to preach what Dharma?
The venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed them, saying:
"I now wish to preach the illusory Dharma for sentient beings who are like illusions, because they neither hear, nor understand, nor realize what is preached.
At that time, the sons of the gods again had this thought:

"Is it that the listeners of the Dharma and the Dharma itself are like illusions, or are other sentient beings, such as those who have attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), also all like illusions?"
Subhūti, knowing what was in their minds, addressed them, saying:

"Other sentient beings—whether those in the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; or those with the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha—all these, too, are like an illusion."
Then, the sons of the gods asked Subhūti:
"Is even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas also like an illusion?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"Even nirvāṇa is likewise like an illusion.
At that time, the sons of the gods asked Subhūti,
"Can it be that even nirvāṇa is likewise like an illusion?"
Subhūti replied:
"Even if there were another dharma superior to nirvāṇa, it would likewise be like an illusion, let alone nirvāṇa! Why is this? Because..."
O sons of the gods!
Illusion, sentient beings, all phenomena, and even nirvāṇa are non-dual and without distinction, for they are all ungraspable and inexpressible.
At that time, Śāriputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākāśyapa, and others asked Ānanda:
"The Prajñāpāramitā you have described is so profound; who is able to believe and accept it?"
Ānanda replied:

"There are bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogression and are able to believe and accept this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught. Furthermore, there are immeasurable individuals endowed with right view and arhats whose aspirations are fulfilled, who are likewise able to believe and accept this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught."
At that time, Subhūti spoke as follows:
"This profound *prajñāpāramitā* thus described cannot be believed or accepted. Why is this so?
"Because herein there is no dharma that can be manifested or shown, even one who has faith and acceptance cannot be found.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"The Venerable Subhūti is raining down the great rain of Dharma; I should manifest and scatter exquisite *mañjūṣaka* flowers as an offering."
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested a subtle and wondrous flower and scattered it over Subhūti.
At that time, Subhūti thought to himself:
"The flowers now scattered have never before been seen in the realms of the devas."
"These flowers are so subtle and wondrous that they certainly could not have been produced by water or land plants; they must have been emanated from the minds of the devas.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing what Subhūti was thinking, said to him:
"These scattered flowers were indeed not produced by water or land plants, nor were they emanated from the minds of the devas, because these scattered flowers possess the nature of non-arising."
The Venerable Subhūti said to Śakra:
"These flowers are unarisen; therefore, they lack the nature of flowers.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"Venerable Subhūti’s awakened wisdom is profound and vast; he does not subvert conventional designations while expounding the ultimate meaning.
Having reflected thus, he addressed Subhūti, saying: "It is so! It is so!"
"So it is! It is truly as your venerable teaching states.
Among all dharmas, the assembly of bodhisattvas should study in accordance with what the Venerable One has taught."
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
All bodhisattvas, among all dharmas, should train in accordance with what I have taught. Kausika!"
When the assembly of bodhisattvas trains in this manner in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to my teaching,
they do not train for the sake of the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor for the sake of the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat,
nor do they train for the sake of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; if they do not train by relying on these stages, then—
One studies the all-knowledge of all Buddhas; if one studies the all-knowledge of all Buddhas, then one studies the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas;

if one studies the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, then one does not study the increase or decrease of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. If one does not study form, feeling, perception, mental formations...
If one does not study that consciousness has increase and decrease, then one does not study that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have grasping and abandoning.

If one does not study that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have grasping and abandoning, then one does not study that all phenomena are subject to being grasped or to being destroyed. If one does not study all phenomena...
If there were anything to be grasped or anything to be destroyed, then one would not train in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) as being something to be grasped or destroyed.
When the bodhisattvas train in this manner, it is called training truly in the knowledge of all modes, and they will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If there is nothing to be grasped or destroyed regarding the omniscience of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) for those bodhisattvas who do not train in it, then when these bodhisattvas train in this way, is it called truly training in the omniscience of all-knowledge, and are they able to swiftly realize the omniscience of all-knowledge?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"Because taking non-apprehension as the means.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"Where should one seek the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in which Bodhisattvas train?"
Śāriputra said:
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* in which a bodhisattva trains should be sought within what Subhūti has spoken.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Subhūti:
“By whose spiritual power and support does Śāriputra speak thus?
Subhūti replied,
“It is by the spiritual power and support of the Tathāgata that Śāriputra speaks thus.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"By whose spiritual power and support is the Venerable One able to teach this profound perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:
“It is by relying on the Tathāgata’s spiritual power that I am able to speak this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kausika! As for what you asked—‘Where should one seek the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in which a bodhisattva trains?’—”
"Kauśika! The profound *prajñāpāramitā* in which a bodhisattva trains should not be sought within form (*rūpa*), nor should it be sought apart from form;

it should not be sought within feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor should it be sought apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? Form is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is there a perfection of wisdom that exists apart from form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the perfection of wisdom, nor is there a perfection of wisdom that exists apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
“The profound perfection of wisdom is a great perfection; it is an immeasurable perfection; it is a boundless perfection.”
Subhūti replied: "So it is! So it is!"
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because form is limitless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also limitless; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also limitless.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Because the objects of focus are infinite, you should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also infinite. Kauśika!"
How is it that because the object of focus (*ālambana*) is boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless?

It is said that because the prior, middle, and subsequent limits of all phenomena (*dharma*) cannot be apprehended, they are called "boundless. Since phenomena are boundless, their objects of focus are boundless; for this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also said to be boundless.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Because all dharmas are boundless, you should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also boundless. Kauśika!"
How is it that because all phenomena (*dharma*) are limitless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also limitless?
It is because a limit of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.

Why is this so? Because form, up to and including consciousness, cannot be apprehended in their prior, middle, or final limits; and because, by virtue of this, the prior, middle, and final limits of the *prajñāpāramitā* also cannot be apprehended, it is said to be "boundless."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Because sentient beings are infinite, you should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also infinite. Kauśika!"
Why is it that because sentient beings are limitless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also limitless?
Kauśika! It is not that the number of categories of sentient beings is exceedingly great; rather, it is said to be limitless because their limit cannot be calculated.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
"For what purpose do you speak thus?
Subhūti replied:
"I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?
Of what dharma is the term 'sentient being' a metaphorical designation?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"The term 'sentient being' is not a designation for a dharma; it is comprised of a provisional, adventitious name, a name without a real entity, and a name without an objective referent."
Subhūti again addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"What do you think?
Within this, is there any truly existent sentient being that can be pointed out?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No,
Venerable Sir!"
Subhūti replied: "Kauśika,
because no real sentient beings can be pointed out, they are said to be infinite."
What do you think?

Suppose a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to pass through as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, speaking with boundless voices the infinite names of sentient beings; in this regard, would there be any truly existent sentient being who undergoes birth or cessation?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No,
Venerable Sir!"
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings are pure by nature.
Subhūti replied:
"For this reason it is said:
because sentient beings are limitless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also limitless.
Their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is profound, for both are limitless."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 556; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 557.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Five: The Stūpa. Part Three: The Stūpa Chapter. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas of the Desire Realm; Mahābrahmā and the other devas of the Form Realm; as well as the various ṛṣis and immortals, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. Simultaneously, three times they cried out in a loud voice: "How marvelous! How marvelous!"
How marvelous!
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound and subtle.

The Tathāgata has appeared in the world and, through the power of his supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), empowered Subhūti and others to proclaim and reveal it. If bodhisattvas do not depart from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), we shall honor and make offerings to them as we would to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devas and others, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"If bodhisattvas do not depart from the perfection of wisdom, you gods and others should all make offerings to them as you would to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
You gods should know this!"

In the past, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I saw Dīpaṃkara Buddha at the crossroads of the capital city of Padmarāja. I offered him five stalks of flowers, spread my hair to cover the mud, and heard the essential points of the True Dharma; all this was never apart from the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, that Tathāgata bestowed upon me this prophecy:
"In a future age, after incalculable eons have passed, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śāntamati, who will proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā and bring great benefit to all sentient beings."
At that time, the various devas all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!
Such is the great majestic power of this Prajñāpāramitā that it enables all bodhisattvas to swiftly attract and gather all-knowledge."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the various devas and the fourfold assembly had gathered like clouds to serve as witnesses, immediately turned his attention to Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and said: “Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters are able to listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently study, and reflect upon the Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere heart, or further transcribe it for others and explain it to them, then Māra and his retinue, as well as humans and non-humans, shall never be able to find any flaw in them; neither calamities nor epidemics shall be able to harm them.

If there are sons of the gods who have already resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but have not yet well heard, received, upheld, read, or recited the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should all come to where this son or daughter of good family is, and with a sincere heart listen to, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, so that it may become thoroughly mastered and they may in turn explain it to others.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and contemplate according to the principle the Prajñāpāramitā—or even write it out for others or explain it to them—then whether they are in an empty house, a wilderness, a perilous path, or a place of danger, the devas and benevolent spirits will constantly come to protect them, ensuring they are free from fear and alarm."
At that time, the Four Great Kings, Śakra, Lord of Devas, Brahmā, and others, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha together, saying:

"If any sons or daughters of good family can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and contemplate according to principle this Prajñāpāramitā, or further transcribe it for others and explain it, we and our retinues will constantly follow and protect them, ensuring that no calamities or afflictions shall invade or distress them."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous! O Sugata!
These sons and daughters of good family who serve the Perfection of Wisdom will acquire such merits pertaining to the present life."
"Bhagavān!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family embraces the Prajñāpāramitā, they then fully embrace the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said. Furthermore, Kauśika,

if any sons or daughters of good family can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and contemplate according to principle this Prajñāpāramitā— or even write it down for others or explain it to them— you should listen attentively and pay close heed to the merit they shall obtain!
"I shall explain it for you.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied: "Indeed!"
"Please speak!
We wish to hear it.
The Buddha said:

“Kauśika! If there are various evil non-Buddhist brahmins, or various evil Māras or their retinues, or other violent and arrogant individuals who wish to perform various harmful acts, as soon as they give rise to such thoughts, they will encounter calamities and misfortunes of their own accord; they shall gradually be extinguished and fail to achieve their desires.”
Why is this? Kausika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family are able to hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon the Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere heart, or further transcribe and explain it for others; by the very nature of things (dharmatā), they cause those who harbor evil intentions to encounter calamities and fail to achieve their desires.
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family who honor and serve the Prajñāpāramitā obtain such meritorious benefits as these.”

Suppose there were a wondrous medicine called Makī; by the power of this medicine, it can neutralize all poisons, and wherever this wondrous medicine is located, various venomous insects cannot approach it.

There was a large venomous snake that, hungry, went about seeking food; encountering a living being, it wished to sting and devour it. That creature, terrified of death, fled toward a potent medicinal herb. Upon smelling the scent of the medicine, the snake immediately retreated and ran away.
Why is this? Kauśika!
Such a wondrous medicine possesses great majestic power; it can benefit life and body, and it can subdue and eliminate all poisons.

One should know that the Prajñāpāramitā possesses great majestic power in this very same way. If good sons and good daughters, with a sincere heart, listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, or correctly contemplate it, or even write it out or explain it for others, then any evil persons who wish to cause them harm will surely be utterly extinguished and rendered powerless, for the majestic spiritual power of the Prajñā can destroy them.

“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family are constantly protected by the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the other hosts of devas, and all the ṛṣis, who prevent any calamities or afflictions from invading them. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas also constantly guard and keep them in mind; whatever they seek in accordance with the Dharma shall be fulfilled without exception. Their speech is majestic and solemn, and all who hear it respectfully accept it. They speak with due deliberation, and their words are not confused or frivolous. They steadfastly serve virtuous friends and deeply understand how to repay their kindness. Their minds are never obscured by stinginess, envy, anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, flattery, deception, or hypocrisy.”
Why is this? Kausika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family, through the power of their prajñā, have disciplined their body and mind, causing them to remain far removed from the latent tendencies (anuśaya), the outbursts (paryavasthāna), and the fetters (saṃyojana) such as greed, hatred, and delusion.

These sons and daughters of good family, endowed with mindfulness, clear comprehension, and the [four immeasurables] of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, constantly maintain this thought:

"I should not allow myself to be moved by the power of stinginess and greed, violation of precepts, anger and resentment, laziness, distraction, or delusion. If I were to follow them, my practice of generosity, pure morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and sublime wisdom would not be accomplished; I would not even attain a purified form-body, let alone attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!"
"Therefore, I should not allow myself to be turned by their power.
By means of this reflection, these sons and daughters of good family always maintain right mindfulness, and no evil afflictions can obscure their minds.

“Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon the Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth—or even write it down for others or explain it to them—they will obtain such meritorious benefits as these.”
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is truly rare; it is able to discipline the bodhisattva, causing them to abandon arrogance and to dedicate [their merit] toward the attainment of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna)."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:

"In what way is the Prajñāpāramitā so exceedingly rare, being able to discipline a bodhisattva so as to cause them to abandon arrogance and turn toward the sought-after knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

“If bodhisattvas do not rely on the perfection of wisdom, because they lack skillful means, although they cultivate various virtues, they give rise to a haughty mind and are unable to turn toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes.

If bodhisattvas are able to rely on the perfection of wisdom, because they possess skillful means, the virtues they cultivate can subdue their haughty minds and be dedicated toward the sought-after knowledge of all modes.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Kausika! If sons and daughters of good family can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā, they shall not be afflicted by any calamities or misfortunes."

If, while in the midst of military conflict and battle arrays, one recites this Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, maintaining compassion and protective mindfulness toward all sentient beings, one will not be harmed or killed by blades or weapons; all opposing enemies will give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness, and even if they harbor evil intentions, they will naturally retreat and be defeated.
It is impossible that these sons and daughters of good family should lose their lives or have their bodies destroyed when wounded by swords or arrows on the battlefield. Why is this?

Kauśika! This Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, it is the unsurpassed mantra. If one can diligently study and practice it, one will not be harmed by oneself, nor harmed by others, nor harmed by both; one will swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

By this, one attains the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), observes the distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings, and accordingly turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma for them, enabling them to practice as taught and thereby attain great benefit.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters write down this Prajñāpāramitā and place it in a pure location to offer worship and respect, or if they diligently uphold, recite, and read it, then humans and non-humans alike shall never be able to find any fault in them, except for the retribution of evil karma from past lives that must be experienced."
Kauśika! For example, if a person or even an animal were to enter the precincts of the Bodhi tree or merely reach its vicinity, neither humans nor non-humans would be able to harm them.
Why is this? Kausika!

All Buddhas of the three periods of time have sat upon this very spot and attained great bodhi, bestowing fearlessness, freedom from dread, absence of enmity, and non-harm upon all sentient beings, so that their bodies and minds abide in peace and happiness.
One should know that it is likewise with wherever the Prajñāpāramitā resides: all devas, nāgas, asuras, and others constantly come to protect it.
One should know that this place is a true caitya; all sentient beings should pay homage to it, and they should never for a moment cease their respectful offerings, veneration, and praise.
Why is this? Kauśika! It is because these sentient beings take it as their refuge.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If good sons and good daughters write down this Prajñāpāramitā, and with various adornments offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to it, further making offerings of various exquisite flower garlands and even lamps;”

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, erect a stūpa adorned with the seven precious gems, place the Buddha’s śarīra within a casket made of jewels and enshrine it therein, and then offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise, further making offerings of various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps and illumination.
"Of these two resulting merits, which is greater?
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
What do you think?
By what path did the Tathāgata train and thereby attain the knowledge of all modes, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment he realized, and the body upon which it rests?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"They all attain it by training and studying in reliance upon the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

“Kauśika! It is not merely by attaining the body endowed with the marks and signs that one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; rather, it is by realizing the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) that one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

Kauśika! The omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) attained by the Tathāgata arises necessarily with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its cause; the Buddha’s body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana-kāya*) serves merely as its basis. If one does not rely upon the Buddha’s body of marks and signs, there would be no means for it to arise. Therefore, while the perfection of wisdom is the direct cause that gives rise to omniscient wisdom, one further cultivates and accumulates the Buddha’s body of marks and signs in order to bring this wisdom into manifestation and maintain its continuity.
For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, the devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, non-humans, and others shall offer worship and reverence to my śarīras.

“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters write down this Prajñāpāramitā, uphold, read, and recite it with various adornments, and further honor, revere, respect, and praise it with offerings of various sublime flower garlands up to lamps, they are thereby making offerings to the knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), to the Buddha’s body endowed with the marks and signs of excellence upon which that knowledge relies, and to the Buddha’s relics after his parinirvāṇa.”
Why is this so? Kauśika!
It is because the knowledge of all modes, as well as the body endowed with the marks and signs and the śarīra relics, all have the perfection of wisdom as their root.
For this reason, Kauśika,

the mass of merit obtained from writing down this Prajñāpāramitā and honoring, revering, and making various offerings to it surpasses the merit obtained from erecting stūpas with the seven precious gems to enshrine the relics of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Kauśika!
To make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā is to make offerings to the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), to the Buddha’s body of marks and signs (lakṣaṇavyañjana), and to the śarīra relics.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The people of Jambudvīpa do not write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, revere, or make offerings to this Prajñāpāramitā; is it that they do not know the merit and benefits spoken of in this way?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?"
Within Jambudvīpa, how many people have attained the verified confidence in the Buddha, the verified confidence in the Dharma, and the verified confidence in the Saṅgha?
How many people have attained the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship?
"How many people have resolved their minds to definitely proceed toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?
How many people have resolved their minds to definitely proceed toward unsurpassed enlightenment?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:

“In Jambudvīpa, there are few people who achieve the three forms of verified clarity; even fewer attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; even fewer resolve their minds to definitely proceed toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and even fewer resolve their minds to definitely proceed toward unsurpassed enlightenment.”
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika, it is so!
It is thus!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said. Kausika!"

Within Jambudvīpa, there are very few people who resolve their minds and are certain to proceed toward unsurpassed enlightenment; among those, few, having already resolved their minds, diligently practice and train in the conduct leading to enlightenment;
among those, few, while diligently practicing the conduct of enlightenment, receive and accept this profound Prajñāpāramitā with deep conviction;
and among those, few, having received it with deep faith, actually practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having practiced even a small portion therein, they gradually abide in the stage of non-retrogression;
having abided in this stage for even a short duration, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Kauśika! Only those bodhisattvas who have already attained abiding on the stage of non-retrogression and seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are able, with a profound mind, to believe in and accept the Prajñāpāramitā, and to receive, uphold, read, recite, reverently worship, copy, and explain it.”

Kauśika! Among the immeasurable and boundless classes of sentient beings who have resolved their minds upon bodhicitta, perhaps only one, two, or three may attain the stage of non-retrogression as a bodhisattva; for the most part, they regress and remain at the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, you should know that if sons of good family and others who have resolved upon bodhicitta and practice the bodhisattva path wish to abide in the stage of non-retrogression and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without hindrance, they should write down, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, honor, revere, and explain to others this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Kauśika! These bodhisattvas should form this thought:
"When the Tathāgata formerly dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently practiced and studied this Prajñāpāramitā; we, too, should diligently practice and study it."
"In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom is my great teacher; by training in accordance with it, my aspirations shall be fulfilled. Kausika!
Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all bodhisattvas should always rely upon and diligently train in the profound Perfection of Wisdom.

“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha’s śarīras, erect stūpas made of the seven excellent jewels, adorned with various rare and wonderful treasures, and further offer various celestial flower garlands up to lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them throughout their entire lives;”
"What do you think?
Would these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this cause and condition?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write down this Prajñāpāramitā, uphold, read, and recite it adorned with various jewels, and furthermore offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it.
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Kauśika! Let this one matter be set aside."

If good sons or good daughters, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha’s śarīras, were to erect stūpas made of the seven exquisite jewels, adorned with various rare and wonderful treasures, filling an entire Jambudvīpa, or the four continents, or a small thousand-world system, or a medium thousand-world system, or even a trichiliocosm; and if they were to offer all kinds of celestial flower garlands up to lamps and lights, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them throughout their entire lives.
"What do you think?
Would these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this cause and condition?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write down this *prajñāpāramitā*, uphold, read, and recite it adorned with various jewels, and further offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it—the mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
Kauśika! Let us set aside this matter for a moment.

Suppose all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were simultaneously to obtain human bodies; and suppose each one of them, for the sake of making offerings to the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha, were to erect after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels, adorned with various rare and wonderful ornaments, such that each individual stūpa filled the entire trichiliocosm. Furthermore, suppose they were to take various celestial flower garlands, up to and including lamps and lights, and throughout their entire lives, offer, revere, respect, and praise them.
"What do you think?
Would those sentient beings, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write down this Perfection of Wisdom, uphold it, read and recite it adorned with various jewels, and furthermore offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it—then the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Sugata!

If sons or daughters of good family offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that they are thereby offering worship, honor, respect, and praise to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
“World-Honored One!
Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

Suppose that all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions were to simultaneously attain human bodies; and suppose that each of these individuals, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha’s *śarīra*, were to erect a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels, adorned with various rare and wonderful treasures, after the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa.”

In this way, each [offering] fills as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; furthermore, they hold various kinds of celestial, exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and lights, and for one kalpa or more than one kalpa, they make offerings, show reverence, respect, and praise.

Although the mass of merit obtained by these sentient beings through such causes and conditions is indeed immeasurable, there are yet other sons of good family who write down this Prajñāpāramitā, adorn it with various jewels, and uphold, recite, and chant it; furthermore, they offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it. The merit they obtain is far greater than the former, being immeasurable and incalculable.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said,
Kauśika! The merit and roots of goodness of those sons and daughters of good family who make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā are immeasurable, innumerable, incalculable, and inconceivable."

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and because the omniscient wisdom of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas can give birth to the *śarīras* (relics) of the Buddhas.
Therefore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to write down the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, read and recite it adorned with various jewels, and furthermore offers various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it—the merit they obtain is a hundred times superior, a thousand times superior, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold superior to the merit previously created by those stūpas and their offerings.

Chapter 4: Divine Spells, Part Five, Section Four: Divine Spells. At that time, forty thousand sons of gods within the assembly raised their voices in unison and addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"O Great Sage!
Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should constantly listen to it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and offer it worship, respect, honor, and praise.

Why is this? If one can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this profound Prajñāpāramitā, then all unwholesome dharmas will diminish and wholesome dharmas will increase.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
"You should, with a sincere mind, listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? If the asuras and their evil factions should give rise to such a thought:
"We shall wage war against the Trāyastriṃśa gods."
At that time, you all should each, with utmost sincerity, recite and contemplate this profound Prajñāpāramitā, making offerings to it, honoring it, respecting it, and praising it.
At that time, the evil intentions arising from the asuras and their factions naturally subsided and vanished.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If this is so, then the profound Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and a mantra equal to the unequaled."
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said. Why is this? Kausika!

All Buddhas of the three periods of time have, by relying upon this profound Great Dharani King of Prajñāpāramitā, realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and have expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

Kauśika! Relying upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there appear in the world the ten paths of wholesome action, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
Kauśika! By relying on this great king of dhāraṇīs, the profound Prajñāpāramitā, bodhisattvas appear in the world;

and by relying on bodhisattvas, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas are able to appear in the world.

“Kauśika! If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not appear in the world, there will still be bodhisattvas who, through the predominant power of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* previously heard, will skillfully establish for all sentient beings the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, and so forth, causing them to diligently practice and study them.”

Kauśika! For example, during the night, because the light of the full moon shines and touches them, the stars, medicinal herbs, and other such things all flourish according to their respective powers. In the same way, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already passed into parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma has vanished, before another appears, all the wholesome conduct and right practice in the world depend entirely upon the appearance of a bodhisattva.

All the skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) possessed by Bodhisattvas are accomplished by relying upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā); therefore, the perfection of wisdom is the root of all these sublime and virtuous dharmas.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons and daughters of good family can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā, they shall obtain various benefits in the present life; that is to say, poisons, water, fire, weapons, calamities, and epidemics shall all be unable to harm them."

If one encounters official litigation or is oppressed by enemies and bandits, and recites the profound Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, then upon reaching their presence, those individuals will ultimately not inflict punishment or harm; they may seek out one's faults, but none shall be found.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the majestic power and influence of the profound Prajñāpāramitā cause all phenomena to be thus.

Kauśika! If these sons and daughters of good family wish to go before kings, princes, ministers, and the like, and recite the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere mind, they will certainly be greeted with joy by those kings and others, who will offer them sustenance, respect, honor, and praise.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* constantly brings forth various acts of compassion and mercy toward sentient beings, for this reason, those who seek their faults cannot find any by means of any of their various expedients.
At that time, a great multitude of non-Buddhist brahmins, desiring to challenge the Buddha, approached the place where he was.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw them, he thought to himself:
"Now these many non-Buddhist brahmins are coming to this Dharma assembly seeking to find fault with the Buddha; could this not be an obstacle created by Prajñā?"
"I shall recite the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as I received it from the Buddha, so that those followers of heterodox paths may return by the way they came.

Having thought this, he then recited the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Thereupon, the many non-Buddhist brahmins paid their respects from afar, circumambulated the World-Honored One to the right, and departed by the way they had come.
At that time, having seen this, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"For what reason has he just come and now departed?
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, addressed Śāriputra:
“Those non-Buddhists came seeking my faults, but because Śakra, Lord of the Devas, recited and contemplated the Prajñāpāramitā, they were made to depart.
Śāriputra! ”
I do not see even the slightest trace of white dharma in those non-Buddhists; they have come to me with nothing but malicious intent, seeking to find fault with me. Śāriputra!

I do not see any among the sentient beings of all the worlds—whether gods, Māras, or followers of external paths—who, when the Prajñā is being taught, could harbor a malevolent mind and come seeking an opportunity to cause harm, for the power of the Prajñā is indestructible.
At that time, Māra the Evil One secretly thought to himself:
"Now the Buddha is surrounded by his fourfold assembly in reverent attendance, and the devas of the desire and form realms have all gathered to hear him proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā."

Within this assembly there must be various great bodhisattvas who have personally received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha; they shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, emptying my domain. I shall go there to destroy their vision.
Having formed this thought, he manifested four armies and, displaying fierce and sharp valor, approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw them and thought:
"Is it not the Evil Māra who has manifested these things, desiring to come and disturb the Buddha and create obstacles for the Prajñāpāramitā?"
Why is this? Such an array of fourfold armies, so magnificently adorned and exquisite, is beyond the reach of any other royal hosts; it must surely be a magical creation of Māra the Evil One.

For a long night, Māra has been watching for a weakness in the Buddha and seeking to destroy the wholesome roots cultivated by sentient beings; I shall now recite the profound Prajñāpāramitā as received from the Buddha, so that this evil Māra may be sent back on his way.

At that time, having formed this thought, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, recited the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Thereupon, the evil Māra gradually retreated and departed, compelled by the majestic power of the great dhāraṇī-king, the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

At that time, immeasurable devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven simultaneously manifested celestial *divyagandhapuṣpa* (flowers of divine sound) and, leaping into the air, scattered them over the Buddha. Joining their palms in reverence, they addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"May this Prajñāpāramitā long abide among the people of Jambudvīpa, and may the Prajñāpāramitā continue to circulate among the people of Jambudvīpa."
"You should know that in such a place, the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha shall never perish; it will benefit the world, causing it to obtain supreme benefit and peace.
At that time, those devas each further manifested celestial *manojñā-puṣpa* (wondrous-sound flowers) and scattered them over the Buddha, again addressing the Buddha:
"If sentient beings practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, all evil Māras and their retinues, though seeking their flaws, will be unable to find an opportunity."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If sentient beings merely hear the name of the merit of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that such sentient beings have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, have formed great vows in the presence of those Buddhas, and have accumulated much merit to be able to accomplish this; it does not come from meager roots of goodness. How much more so for those who can hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, and reflect according to the truth, and furthermore transcribe, explain, and provide offerings, respect, honor, and praise for it on behalf of sentient beings!”

Why is this so? Those who wish to seek the omniscient wisdom of all Buddhas should seek it within the principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, just as sentient beings who wish to seek a great treasure must diligently seek it through skillful means within the great ocean.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said:
all the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) attained by the Buddhas is accomplished in reliance upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason does the Tathāgata not praise the perfections from generosity up to meditative concentration, but praise only the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Because this perfection of wisdom serves as the sovereign and the guide for the preceding five perfections, I praise it exclusively.”
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
What do you think?

If one practices giving, up to and including wisdom, without dedicating it toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), can this be called truly practicing the perfection of giving, up to and including the perfection of wisdom?"
Ānanda replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What do you think?
If one were apart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), would it be possible to truly dedicate [merit] toward omniscience (sarvajñājñāna)?"
Ānanda replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"For this reason, I say that the perfection of wisdom can act as the sovereign and the guide for the first five perfections; therefore, I praise it specifically."
“Ānanda, you should know this!

For example, when seeds are scattered upon the great earth, they grow through the convergence of various conditions. You should understand that the great earth serves as the basis and the support for the growth of those seeds.”

Thus, because this perfection of wisdom and the omniscience toward which it is dedicated serve as the basis and the support for the perfections such as generosity, enabling them to grow and flourish, I say that the perfection of wisdom is the sovereign and the guide for the first five perfections; therefore, I praise it preeminently.
"Ānanda, you should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also able to encompass all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*); therefore, it is praised and taught with particular emphasis.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Now, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has not yet finished explaining the meritorious benefits of this profound Prajñāpāramitā. Why is that?
The merit and benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā* that I have received from the Blessed One are exceedingly profound, vast, and of limitless measure.

Sons of good family who, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle, and furthermore transcribe it for others, explain it, or make offerings to it with various exquisite flower garlands and even lamps—the merit they obtain shall likewise be limitless.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

"I do not say that this profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses only the merits and benefits previously described; for the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is endowed with boundless merits and benefits, such that they could never be fully expounded."

I do not say that those sons of noble family who listen to this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere mind, or even offer it worship, possess only the merits previously described; for the merit they obtain is boundless.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We devas shall constantly follow and protect these sons and daughters of good family, ensuring that they are not harmed by any humans or non-humans through various adverse conditions.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
"If good sons and good daughters, etc., receive, uphold, read, and recite the profound Prajñāpāramitā, and extensively proclaim, explain, and reveal it to others."
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras gathered together for the sake of hearing the Dharma; with joy and exultation, they reverently received this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

By their celestial power, these devaputras cause the Dharma-preacher to increase in eloquence and proclaim the teaching inexhaustibly; they cause those who do not delight in speaking to delight in speaking, and they restore those whose body and mind are exhausted to health and vigor.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family who uphold, recite, and extensively explain and reveal this profound Prajñāpāramitā to others shall obtain such benefits in this very life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters, among the fourfold assembly, proclaim this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds will be free from fear and they shall not be overcome by any polemical challenges."

Why is this? Because they are protected by this great king of mantras, the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, those who abide in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) do not perceive at all a challenger, an object of challenge, or that which is spoken; nor do they perceive anyone who can seek out faults in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they perceive any deficiency in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family who proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to the assembly shall obtain such benefits in this present life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, with a sincere mind, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth, and furthermore extensively transcribe and explain it for others, these good sons and good daughters will not have their minds sink, nor will they feel regret; they will have no fear and no dread."
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family do not perceive any dharma that could cause them to sink, to feel regret, or to be terrified; they have no attachment toward any dharmas.
Kauśika! Because these sons and daughters of good family listen to the *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere mind, and even explain it, they obtain such benefits in this present life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If any sons or daughters of good family are able to listen to,
receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon the Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, they likewise..."
If they further transcribe it for others, explain it, and offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands,
up to lamps and lights as an act of worship, these sons and daughters of good family will constantly serve their parents,
teachers, elders, relatives and friends, kings, ministers, and all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
They are revered and beloved by [the assembly], and are likewise protected and mindful of by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions;
furthermore, they are guarded by the devas, Māras, Brahmās, humans, and non-humans of the world.
All calamities and misfortunes shall naturally be extinguished, and all heterodox arguments and dissenting views...
They cannot be overcome. Kauśika!
Because these sons and daughters of good family listen to the *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere mind and even make offerings to it, they obtain such benefits in this present life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā, adorn it in various ways, and place it in a pure location, making offerings to it, honoring, respecting, and praising it."

At that time, all those from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Vast Results within this trichiliocosm, as well as in the infinite worlds of the ten directions—who had already resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta—would constantly come to this place to behold and pay homage, recite and chant, make offerings, show reverence, respect, and praise, and then circumambulate to the right, prostrate, join their palms, and depart.

The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens also constantly come here to behold and pay homage, to read and recite, and to offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise; they circumambulate him to the right, prostrate, join their palms, and depart.

Nāgas and yakṣas of great majesty and power, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, also constantly come here to behold and pay homage, to recite and chant, to make offerings, show respect, honor, and praise, and then circumambulate to the right, prostrate, join their palms, and depart.
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family should form this thought:

‘Now, all the devas, nāgas, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, from this trichiliocosm and the infinite worlds of the ten directions, constantly come here to behold and pay homage to, read and recite, and to offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to this profound Prajñāpāramitā that I have transcribed, circumambulating it to the right, prostrating, and joining their palms before departing; by this, I shall have already provided them with the gift of Dharma.’”
Having formed this thought, they will rejoice and leap for joy, causing the merit they have obtained to increase twofold. Kausika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family are constantly followed and protected by the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others of the boundless realms, humans and non-humans alike cannot harm them where they dwell—except in cases where the causes of fixed evil karma from past lives are due to ripen in the present, or where heavy evil karma is transformed so that it is experienced lightly in the present life.
“Kauśika! By the great majestic power of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, these sons and daughters of good family obtain such benefits in the present life.”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“By what signs can it be known that these sons and daughters of good family have this trichiliocosm and the other infinite worlds of the ten directions—with their devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth—come to that place to behold and pay homage to, read and recite, and to offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to the profound Prajñāpāramitā they have written and upheld, circumambulating them with palms joined in joy and mindfulness?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

"If these sons and daughters of good family see a wondrous radiance at the place where such profound *prajñāpāramitā* resides, or if they smell a rare and fragrant incense wafting from that place, or again hear subtle and pleasant sounds, they should know that at that time, devas, nāgas, and others of great supernormal power and blazing majesty have come to that place to behold and pay homage to, read and recite, and to offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to this written and upheld profound *prajñāpāramitā*, circumambulating it with palms joined in joy and mindfulness."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family cultivate pure and fresh conduct to adorn their dwelling and worship the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere heart, you should know that at that time, devas, nāgas, and others of great supernormal power and blazing majesty will come to that place. They will observe and pay homage to, read and recite, and make offerings to, revere, respect, honor, and praise the profound *prajñāpāramitā* written and upheld there; they will join their palms, circumambulate it to the right, and joyfully protect and keep it in mind."

Kauśika! Whichever gods, nāgas, and others endowed with such great supernormal powers and blazing majesty may come to that place, all the malevolent spirits and heterodox deities therein will be struck with terror and disperse, none daring to remain.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, these sons and daughters of good family will develop a vast and expansive mind of pure resolve; the wholesome karma they cultivate will become doubly increased and clarified, and all their endeavors will be free from obstacles.
For this reason, Kauśika, wherever this profound Prajñāpāramitā may be located,

one should thoroughly clear away all filth and impurities, sweep and scrub the area, apply fragrant plaster, sprinkle scented water, arrange a precious throne to enshrine it, and make offerings by burning incense and scattering flowers.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If these sons and daughters of good family can thus make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they will certainly attain a body and mind free from weariness, a body and mind at peace and happy, a body and mind that are pliant and supple, and a body and mind that are light and agile."

With the mind bound to the *prajñāpāramitā*, when sleeping at night, one has no evil dreams but only auspicious ones; that is to say, one sees the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, his body of true golden color adorned with the marks and signs, emitting great radiance that universally illumines all things, surrounded by reverently attending śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and while situated among the assembly, one hears the Buddha expounding for them the meaning of the six *pāramitās* beginning with generosity, as well as other dharmas associated with roots of goodness.

Or, within a dream, one may see a Bodhi tree, vast in height and breadth and adorned with various jewels; a great Bodhisattva approaches the foot of the tree, sits cross-legged, realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turns the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
Or, in dreams, they may see immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas debating and resolving various meanings of the Dharma;

or, in dreams, they may see immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas practicing the six perfections, maturing sentient beings, purifying buddha-fields, and dedicating their merits to encompassing all-knowledge.

Or, within a dream, they may see in each of the ten directions immeasurable nayutas of buddhas, and they also hear their voices, saying: "In such-and-such a world, such-and-such a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, is preaching such a Dharma."

Or, in a dream, one may see that in each of the worlds of the ten directions there are immeasurable nayutas of Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa; after each of those Buddhas has passed into parinirvāṇa, there are donors who, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddhas' śarīras, erect immeasurable great stūpas made of the seven exquisite jewels. Furthermore, at each of these stūpas, they offer immeasurable, most excellent flower garlands, up to lamps and lights, for immeasurable kalpas, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them.
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family who see such auspicious dream-omens will experience peace and happiness in body and mind, whether they are asleep or awake.”

The various devas augment his vital energy, causing him to perceive for himself that his body has become light and agile. Due to these causes and conditions, he does not harbor much craving for food and drink, medicine, clothing, or bedding; his mind remains detached toward the four types of offerings. This is just like a yogācāra who has entered a sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*): because his body and mind are nourished by the power of that concentration, even when he encounters exquisite food after emerging from meditation, his mind remains detached; so it is in this case as well.
Why is this so, Kauśika?

It is because these sons and daughters of good family are protected and sustained by the compassion of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others throughout this trichiliocosm and the infinite worlds of the ten directions; thus, through the subtle and vital essence that secretly drenches their bodies and minds, their resolve becomes courageous and their physical strength becomes full and flourishing.

“Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family wish to attain such benefits in this present life, they should constantly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the truth, and extensively proclaim and reveal it to sentient beings.”

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, although unable to hear, receive, uphold, recite, diligently study, or reflect upon the Prajñāpāramitā in accordance with the truth, nor able to extensively proclaim and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings, nevertheless writes down this profound Prajñāpāramitā and adorns it with various jewels; and furthermore, holding immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, up to lamps and lights, they offer them with worship, reverence, respect, and praise—because they act so that the True Dharma may long abide in the world and benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings without perishing—they too shall obtain the aforementioned benefits.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 557;
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 558.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five: On the Relics (Śarīra). Section Five of Chapter Five: On the Relics. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose this Jambudvīpa were filled with the relics of the Buddha as one portion, and the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā were written down as another portion; between these two portions, which would you take?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"In my mind, I would rather take up the profound and wondrous Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Because—"

It is not that I lack faith, acceptance, worship, or reverence for the *śarīra* relics of the Buddhas; rather, it is because the bodies of the Buddhas and their *śarīra* relics are all produced from this profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and are all perfumed and cultivated by the merit and majestic power of this profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that they are thus worshipped and revered by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!

Just as when I am seated upon the throne of Śakra, Lord of Devas, in the Sudharma Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, preaching the True Dharma for the assembly of devas, there are immeasurable sons of gods who come to my presence to listen to what I say, making offerings and paying respect, and then depart after circumambulating me to the right.”

If I am not present at that Dharma seat, the sons of the gods will also come to that place; although they do not see me as they did when I was there, making offerings and paying respect, they will all say:

"This is the seat where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, preached the Dharma for the sake of the devas. We should all pay homage and respect to it just as we did when the Lord of the Devas was here, and then circumambulate it to the right before departing."

The *śarīra* of the Buddha is likewise so: because it is produced by the profound and wondrous *prajñāpāramitā* as its cause and serves as the basis for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), it is honored and revered by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
Therefore, I say that between these two portions, my inclination would rather be toward the profound and wondrous *prajñāpāramitā*.
"World-Honored One!

Suppose one portion were filled with the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha, and another portion were the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the written *prajñāpāramitā*; between these two portions, my inclination would rather be toward the profound and wondrous *prajñāpāramitā*."

Why is this? It is not that I lack faith, acceptance, offering, or reverence toward the *śarīra* relics of the Buddhas; rather, it is because the bodies of the Buddhas and their *śarīra* relics are all born from the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and are all cultivated by the power and majesty of the merit of the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, they are honored and revered by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!

It is like a debtor who, fearing his creditor, immediately seeks the protection and service of a king; by relying on the king’s power, he escapes that fear, yet instead becomes fearful of making offerings to the creditor.”
Why is this so? Because that person relies upon the power of the king and is sustained by the king’s majesty.

The king is a metaphor for the *prajñāpāramitā*, while the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are a metaphor for those who rely on the king; for it is by relying upon the *prajñāpāramitā* that they receive the offerings and respect of the world.

Since the omniscient wisdom attained by all Buddhas is likewise accomplished by relying upon the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), I would rather take up this profound and sublime perfection of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!

It is like a priceless great divine jewel that possesses immeasurable kinds of supreme and wondrous majestic power; wherever this divine jewel resides, humans, non-humans, and others cannot cause harm.”

Suppose there is a man or a woman who, being possessed by a spirit, suffers physical and mental distress; if one were to show this divine jewel to them, the spirit would immediately depart by the power of the jewel.
Whether there be fevers caused by wind, phlegm, or a combination of two or all three, if this divine bead is tied to the body, none of these ailments will fail to be cured.

This jewel can provide illumination in the darkness; it cools when it is hot and warms when it is cold. In whatever region this divine jewel is present, the seasons remain harmonious, being neither too cold nor too hot.
If this divine jewel is present in a locality, poisonous creatures such as snakes and scorpions will not dare to remain there.
Should a man or a woman be struck by poison such that the pain is unbearable, if they are made to see this divine jewel, the poison will be immediately extinguished by the power of the jewel.

If any sentient beings suffer from leprosy, malignant sores, swellings, blisters, eye diseases such as vertigo and cataracts, or diseases of the ears, nose, tongue, throat, body, or various limbs and joints, all these ailments shall be healed by wearing this divine pearl.

If there are ponds, pools, springs, or wells whose water is turbid and foul, or which is about to run dry, when this jewel is cast into them, the water immediately becomes full, fragrant, pure, and clear, endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.

If one wraps this divine jewel in garments of various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, green, or variegated patterns—and casts it into water, the water will take on those various colors according to the hues of the cloth.

Thus, this priceless great jewel, the divine pearl, possesses boundless majesty and virtue that cannot be fully described; even when placed within a chest or casket, it causes that vessel to be fully endowed with boundless majesty and virtue.
"Even if an empty box or casket once contained jewels, that vessel will still be held in high esteem by all people.
At that time, Ānanda asked Śakra:
"Is such a divine jewel possessed only by the devas, or do humans also have it?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"This jewel exists both among humans and in the heavens. If it is among humans, its form is small and heavy; if it is in the heavens, its form is large and light.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the jewel among humans are incomplete, whereas those in the heavens are perfectly complete."
"The divine jewel of the heavens possesses such majestic power and excellence that it exceeds all that humans possess by immeasurable multiples.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The profound and wondrous Prajñāpāramitā is likewise so. It is the source of all virtues and is capable of extinguishing immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas. Wherever it resides, it extinguishes the physical and mental suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings, and neither humans nor non-humans can cause them harm."
The Tathāgata’s attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and his other immeasurable and boundless qualities are all due to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Because the Buddha’s relics (śarīra) have been perfumed by these various qualities and serve as the vessel that supports them, they are worthy of receiving the offerings and veneration of all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, I say that between these two portions, my inclination would be to take the profound and wondrous Prajñāpāramitā.
"World-Honored One!

Suppose one portion were filled with the relics of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions, and another portion consisted of the written profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā; between these two portions, my inclination would still be to take the profound and wondrous Prajñāpāramitā."

Why is this? It is not that I lack faith, acceptance, worship, or reverence for the *śarīra* relics of the Buddhas; rather, it is because the bodies of the Buddhas and their *śarīra* relics are all born from the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and are all cultivated by the power and majesty of the merit of the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that they are thus worshipped and revered by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

This profound and wondrous Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). The knowledge of all modes attained by the Tathāgata can, in turn, give birth to the Buddha-body and the śarīra. Therefore, to make offerings to such Prajñāpāramitā is to make offerings to the knowledge of all modes and the śarīra of all Buddhas of the three periods of time."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If good sons and good daughters and others wish to constantly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions, they should practice and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
