At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said, Kauśika!
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, the Tathāgata honors and reveres it.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Such is the perfection of wisdom, the great unsurpassed perfection; all Tathāgatas rely upon this perfection of wisdom to know the distinctions in the mental activities of all sentient beings."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said,
Kauśika! For this reason,

the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom for a long night in order to know, as they truly are, the distinctions in the mental activities of all classes of sentient beings.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do all bodhisattvas only practice the perfection of wisdom, or should they also practice the other five perfections?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

"The assembly of bodhisattvas should practice the six pāramitās in their entirety; however, when practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration while contemplating all phenomena, they must take the perfection of wisdom as their foremost guide."
Kauśika! Just as all the trees in Jambudvīpa—though their branches, trunks, flowers, leaves, and fruits differ in various shapes and kinds—their shadows are entirely without distinction.

Although these six perfections each have their own distinct characteristics, through the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, they are embraced and dedicated toward omniscience; thus, no differentiation between their various marks can be apprehended at all.
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* accomplishes vast, perfect, immeasurable, and boundless merit. If there is one who writes down and upholds such *prajñāpāramitā*, adorning it with various jewels, and further offers various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, even lamps and so forth, to worship, revere, respect, praise, and protect it without forsaking it."
Furthermore, suppose there is one who writes out this Prajñāpāramitā, adorns it with various jewels, and bestows it upon others so that they may receive, uphold, read, and recite it.
Between these two accumulations of merit, which is greater?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.

Suppose there are sentient beings who, having requested from others the relics of the Buddha, place them in a precious casket and set it in a pure location; they further take various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and lights, to make offerings, pay homage, respect, praise, and protect them without abandoning them."
Furthermore, suppose there is another person who receives from others a portion of the Buddha’s *śarīra* relics and distributes them to others so that they may make offerings to them.
What do you think?
Between these two accumulations of merit, which is superior?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, of these two accumulations of merit, the latter is superior.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
It is just as you have said.”

Kauśika! Between the merit of one who writes down and upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and offers it worship themselves, and the merit of one who transfers it to another so that they may uphold, read, and recite it—the latter accumulation of merit is greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can, according to reality, analyze and explain the profound meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā for others, the mass of merit they obtain will be hundreds of thousands of times greater than that of one who gives [material gifts] to others; such a Dharma-preacher should be revered as one would revere a Buddha."
6. Chapter on the Scriptures, Part Five: Chapter on the Scriptures, Part Six. "Furthermore, Kausika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action; and if they were to continue in this manner, even teaching all sentient beings throughout as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action."
"What do you think?
By this cause and condition, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Sugata! The Buddha said, “Kauśika!”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write down and uphold this *prajñāpāramitā*, and then bestow it upon others—adorned with various jewels—for them to read and recite, the mass of merit they would obtain would be far greater than the former.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, causing them all to dwell securely in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers—and so on successively until they have universally instructed all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges, causing them all to dwell securely in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."
"What do you think?
By this cause and condition, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If a son or daughter of good family were to write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā, and then offer it to others adorned with various jewels for them to read and recite, the mass of merit obtained would be far greater than the former.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son or daughter of good family were to write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā, adorning it with various jewels and constantly reading and reciting it themselves, it would not be as meritorious as someone who writes down and upholds this Prajñāpāramitā, adorns it with various jewels, and gives it to others for them to read and recite."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son or daughter of good family were to write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā, and having adorned it with various jewels, give it to others for their recitation, this would not be as meritorious as someone who, regarding this profound Prajñāpāramitā, thoroughly understands its meaning and purport and explains it to others."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what kind of sentient beings should one explain the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! If there are sons or daughters of good family who do not understand the profound meaning and intent of the Prajñāpāramitā, you should explain it to them.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet upon hearing others proclaim a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds will become confused and deluded, causing them to fall away from the Middle Way.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called 'semblance prajñāpāramitā'?
The Buddha said:

“Kauśika! In future ages there will be certain bhikṣus who are foolish and deluded; though they wish to proclaim the true Prajñāpāramitā, they will instead perversely expound a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.”
How does a bhikṣu perversely proclaim a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*?
It is when that bhikṣu says to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta:
"Form is called impermanent because it is subject to disintegration; it is called impermanent because it is not eternally present."

He said: "Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are subject to disintegration, they are called impermanent; because they are not permanent and do not exist [eternally], they are called impermanent.
He further spoke thus:
“If one seeks in such a manner, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Kausika! This is called the perverted teaching of a counterfeit perfection of wisdom.

Kauśika! One should not contemplate the impermanence of form by means of its disintegration; one should not contemplate the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness by means of their disintegration. Rather, one should contemplate form through to consciousness as impermanent by means of their lack of permanence.
For this reason, Kauśika,

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding this profound Prajñāpāramitā, well understands its meaning and purport and explains it to others, their merit will be exceedingly great.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, causing them all to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and if they were to continue in this manner until they have universally instructed all sentient beings in as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, causing them all to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would those sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write down and uphold this *prajñāpāramitā*, and having adorned it with various jewels, give it to others for reading and recitation, and instruct and admonish those beings, saying:
"You should diligently practice and study the Buddha-dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*; you will certainly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former.
Why is this? Kausika!
All the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, all flow forth from this very perfection of wisdom.

This means that they realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and transform immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, enabling them to attain the stages from stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the limitlessness of pratyekabuddhahood.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to each resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and suppose this were to extend successively until every single sentient being in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in each of the ten directions had likewise resolved upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who write down and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, and having adorned it with various jewels, bestow it upon others so that they may read and recite it.
What do you think?
"Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:
"Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write down and uphold this *prajñāpāramitā*, and having adorned it with various jewels, were to bestow it upon someone who has already become non-retrogressive from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening so that they may diligently practice and study it, the mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family would be far greater than the former.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because such a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and swiftly brings it to fulfillment, causing the profound perfection of wisdom to be widely practiced and disseminated.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to each resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and suppose this were to extend progressively until every single sentient being in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in each of the ten directions had likewise resolved upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

There may be sons of good family or daughters of good family who write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā, adorn it with various jewels, bestow it so that others may read and recite it, and further explain its subtle and ingenious words and meanings.
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write down and uphold this *prajñāpāramitā*, and then bestow it upon one who has already become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment so that they may read and recite it, and furthermore explain its subtle words and meanings, the mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family would be far greater than the former.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and suppose this were to extend successively until all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in each of the ten directions had likewise attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who write down and uphold this *prajñāpāramitā*, and having adorned it with various jewels, bestow it upon others so that they may read and recite it.
What do you think?
"Would these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this cause and condition?
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, replied:
"Very much!"
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!"
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! Among those bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, there is one bodhisattva who speaks as follows:”
"I now rejoice in swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to rescue sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth and death.

If sons or daughters of good family, for the sake of accomplishing that goal, write down and uphold this *prajñāpāramitā*, and adorn it with various jewels to offer so that it may be read and recited, the mass of merit obtained by those sons or daughters of good family will be far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and suppose this were to extend successively until all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in each of the ten directions had likewise attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write down and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, adorn it with various jewels, bestow it so that it may be read and recited, and further explain its subtle and skillful words and meanings.
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
Among those bodhisattvas who had already attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one bodhisattva spoke as follows:
"I now rejoice in swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in order to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth and death."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of accomplishing that matter, write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā, adorn it with various jewels, bestow it upon others so they may read and recite it, and further explain its subtle and skillful words and meanings, the mass of merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
World-Honored One!"

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should increasingly and earnestly instruct and admonish them with the perfection of wisdom; and one should honor and provide for them with excellent food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other requisites, ensuring they lack for nothing.

If good sons or good daughters are able to provide such gifts of Dharma and gifts of material wealth to receive and support those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, these good sons and good daughters will, by virtue of these causes and conditions, obtain immeasurable merit.

Why is this? Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of such gifts of Dharma and gifts of material wealth, receive sustenance and offerings, and thereby swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti praised Śakra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
They are well able to embrace, encourage, and assist all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
“Kauśika! You have now performed that which a noble disciple of the Buddha ought to do. Why is this?

Kauśika! All Tathāgatas and their noble disciples, desiring to bring benefit to all sentient beings, naturally embrace, encourage, and assist bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Why is this? All the supreme accomplishments of the world—whether of the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas—arise solely through the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Why is this? Kauśika!

If there were no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who had resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), then there would be no bodhisattva mahāsattvas capable of training in the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas did not practice and train in the six perfections, then there would be no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas capable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

if there were no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then there would be no excellence in the world such as that of the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

Therefore, for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s noble disciples ought, by the very nature of the Dharma, to embrace, encourage, and support the assembly of bodhisattvas, causing them to train in the six perfections so that they may swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
Chapter Seven: Dedication, Part Five. At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed Subhūti, saying:

“The meritorious deeds associated with a bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy and dedication are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honorable, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most superior, and the unsurpassed among all other sentient beings’ meritorious deeds consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation.”
At that time, Subhūti asked the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"If the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication generated by bodhisattvas universally takes as its object immeasurable and innumerable worlds,
and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have already entered parinirvāṇa in each and every one of those immeasurable and innumerable worlds..."
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, continuing through the successive stages until entry into parinirvāṇa,
and even until the Dharma is completely extinguished— in this interval, all the roots of virtue associated with the six perfections,
as well as the various meritorious actions of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation performed by the disciples, and their training— [all these are dedicated].

The untainted roots of goodness of one beyond training; the Buddha’s aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of meditative concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
great loving-kindness and great compassion for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, as well as other immeasurable and boundless qualities of a Buddha;
the essential points of the Dharma; and training in accordance with the essential points of the Dharma.
Regarding all roots of goodness— whether those planted by sentient beings after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the World-Honored One—
one gathers and weighs them together, and manifests a mind of sympathetic joy that is most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime.

Furthermore, with these various meritorious deeds accompanied by such sympathetic joy, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, saying:
"May this root of virtue, together with all classes of sentient beings, bring forth unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"What do you think?

Regarding those bodhisattvas who, based on such matters, give rise to such modes of activity and a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication—can such objects of focus be found as they are grasped by those bodhisattvas?"
Maitreya Bodhisattva replied to Subhūti:

"Those bodhisattvas, taking such things as their object, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication characterized by such mental aspects; yet, in reality, no such objects can be found as they are grasped as signs by those bodhisattvas."
The Venerable Subhūti said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

"If those objective bases do not exist as they are apprehended as signs by those bodhisattvas, would not all those rejoicings and dedications of merit by the bodhisattvas constitute perversions of perception, mind, and view?"

Why is this so? It is because there are those who cling to non-existent things, perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the selfless as self, and the impure as pure; from this, they give rise to perversions of perception, thought, and view.
Just as the objective referent (ālambana-vastu) is in fact non-existent, so too should be enlightenment (bodhi) and the mind.
If that were so, there would be no distinction between them at all; what, then, in this case, would be the objective referent?
What is the mind of sympathetic joy? What is bodhi?
And what is dedication?
"How does a bodhisattva, taking such matters as an object, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Bodhisattva Maitreya replied to Subhūti:
"Such giving rise to sympathetic joy and dedication should not be spoken of in the presence of a newly trained bodhisattva who has recently set out in the Mahāyāna."
Why is this? Because upon hearing such rejoicing and dedication, all their faith, delight, and respectful mind will utterly perish.

This method of rejoicing and dedication should be explained and revealed for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive, or who have made offerings to immeasurable buddhas in the past, have long since made great vows, have planted many roots of goodness, and are sustained by many virtuous friends.
Why is this? Because upon hearing such rejoicing and dedication, they are not startled, not terrified, do not retreat, and do not sink in despair.
"The assembly of bodhisattvas should dedicate all these meritorious deeds accompanied by such rejoicing toward the attainment of the omniscient wisdom they seek."
At that time, one should form this thought:

"The mind that is employed for sympathetic joy and dedication—this mind is subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and transformation; likewise, the objects of focus and all these roots of goodness are also like the mind, subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and transformation."
In this regard, what is the mind that is employed?
Furthermore, by means of what objects of focus and what roots of goodness does one speak of sympathetic joy and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
This mind, with respect to the nature of mind, should not have rejoicing or dedication, because two minds cannot arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, the mind itself cannot rejoice or dedicate, because it is the very nature of mind; therefore, both the mind that rejoices and dedicates and the object of that rejoicing and dedication are unattainable.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
"When the assembly of bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna hear such matters, will their minds not become startled, terrified, discouraged, or despondent?"
How does a bodhisattva give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the objects of focus?
How does he take up those meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti spoke these words concerning the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

“The assembly of bodhisattvas universally takes as their object all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions—those who have severed the paths of existence and cut off the way of conceptual proliferation; who have extinguished all clouds and mists and crushed all thorns; who have laid down all heavy burdens and attained their own welfare; who have exhausted all fetters of existence and are liberated through right knowledge; who have reached the supreme ultimate of mastery over the mind and entered the realm of nirvana without remainder—from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, continuing through the successive stages until their entry into parinirvāṇa, and even until the eventual disappearance of the Dharma. Within this interval, they collect and weigh all the merits and the roots of goodness planted by those disciples, and they manifest before them a heart of sympathetic joy that is most honored, most excellent, most supreme, and most sublime.”
Furthermore, they take these various meritorious deeds associated with sympathetic joy and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
How is it that these bodhisattvas do not fall into perversions of perception, thought, or view?
The Bodhisattva Maitreya said to Subhūti:

“If bodhisattvas have no perception of a mind or of mental equality regarding the various dharmas such as the mind of sympathetic joy and the dedication [of merit] that they themselves have generated, they do not fall into the perversions of perception, mind, and view.

If bodhisattvas do have a perception of a mind or of mental equality regarding the various dharmas such as the mind of sympathetic joy and the dedication that they themselves have generated, they then fall into the perversions of perception, mind, and view.”

Furthermore, with such a mind, bodhisattvas rejoice in the roots of virtue and the merits of the Buddha’s disciples; they correctly know that this mind of rejoicing is subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and transformation, and thus it is not the agent of rejoicing. They correctly know that those dharmas [of the disciples] are likewise in their nature, and thus they are not the objects of rejoicing.

Moreover, they correctly realize that the nature of the mind that performs the dedication is also thus—it is not the agent of dedication—and they correctly understand that the nature of the dharmas to which there is dedication is also thus—they are not the objects of dedication.

If there are those who can rely upon this aforementioned rejoicing and dedication—which is correct and not erroneous—all bodhisattvas should likewise initiate such rejoicing and dedication toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, all Bodhisattvas universally take as their object the merits of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present; the roots of goodness of all disciples; the roots of goodness of ordinary beings; the roots of goodness of those in the animal realm who have heard the true Dharma; and the roots of goodness of others—devas, nāgas, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans—who have heard the true Dharma and resolved upon bodhicitta. Having gathered and weighed all such things together, they manifest a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) that is most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime. Having thus rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At such a time, if one correctly understands that all phenomena associated with rejoicing and dedication are exhausted, ceased, detached from, and transformed, and that the nature of all those phenomena of rejoicing and dedication is likewise so, then even while knowing this, one is able to rejoice and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, at that time, if one correctly understands that there is no dharma whatsoever that can be rejoiced in or dedicated toward any dharma, yet despite knowing this, is able to rejoice and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, one will not fall into the perversions of perception, mind, or view.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas do not give rise to attachment toward the mind that rejoices and dedicates, nor toward the dharmas that are rejoiced in and dedicated; this is called the unsurpassed dedication through sympathetic joy.

If bodhisattvas, regarding the phenomena of rejoicing and dedication, give rise to the perception of phenomena as "phenomena of rejoicing and dedication," and regarding the phenomena that are the objects of rejoicing and dedication, give rise to the perception of phenomena as "phenomena that are the objects of rejoicing and dedication," yet still perform the rejoicing and dedication toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they then fall into the perversions of perception, mind, and view; all such rejoicing and dedication they have performed is erroneous.
“A bodhisattva should know how to distance themselves through skillful means.

If a bodhisattva, regarding the various meritorious deeds they perform, understands as it truly is that they are distant from and quiescent; and regarding the mind that rejoices in and dedicates these merits, also understands as it truly is that it is distant from and quiescent—having understood this as it truly is—they practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, remaining without attachment to any phenomena, and giving rise to rejoicing and dedication toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thus, they do not fall into the perversions of perception, thought, or view.”

If bodhisattvas, regarding the various meritorious deeds they perform, do not know them as they truly are in their detachment from tranquility, and likewise cannot know the mind that rejoices in and dedicates these merits as being detached from tranquility, yet instead grasp at the signs of all phenomena while rejoicing and dedicating toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they will fall into the perversions of perception, mind, and view.

"If Bodhisattvas wish to correctly initiate sympathetic joy and dedicate the roots of merit and virtue of the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have already entered parinirvāṇa, as well as their disciples, they should form this thought:
'Just as the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples have all already entered parinirvāṇa and their intrinsic nature does not exist, so too are their roots of merit and virtue.'"
"The nature and characteristics of my arousal of sympathetic joy and dedication, as well as that to which they are dedicated—unsurpassed enlightenment—are likewise entirely unapprehendable.

Having known this according to reality, one arouses sympathetic joy toward all roots of goodness and dedicates them to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; thus, one is able to avoid giving rise to distortions of perception, mind, or view.
Because one does not grasp at signs, this is what the Buddha has permitted and is called "right sympathetic joy and dedication to enlightenment."

If bodhisattvas, employing the grasping of signs as their means, practice the profound perfection of wisdom and, regarding the merit and roots of goodness of Buddhas and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, grasp at signs while rejoicing and dedicating them toward enlightenment, this is not a skillful rejoicing or dedication.

If bodhisattvas, taking non-apprehension of signs as their skillful means, practice the profound perfection of wisdom and, regarding the merit and roots of goodness of the Buddhas and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, rejoice in them while remaining free from signs and dedicate the merit toward enlightenment, this is called "skillful rejoicing and dedication."
The Bodhisattva Maitreya asked Subhūti:

"How is it that a bodhisattva, without grasping at signs regarding the merits and roots of goodness of the Buddha and his disciples, is nevertheless able to rejoice in them and dedicate them toward enlightenment?"
Subhūti replied:

"It should be known that the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the bodhisattva’s training in the *prajñāpāramitā* accomplishes its task even without grasping at signs; yet, apart from the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no way to correctly give rise to rejoicing (*anumodanā*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to accomplish their task should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Bodhisattva Maitreya said to Subhūti:
"Do not speak thus. Why is that?

Within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the meritorious roots of virtue of the Buddhas and their disciples are entirely unapprehendable; likewise, the rejoicing that arises and the dedication toward enlightenment are also unapprehendable.
"In this regard, a bodhisattva should reflect as follows:

'The nature of the merit and roots of goodness of the past Tathāgatas and their disciples has already ceased; the nature of the minds of sympathetic joy and dedication they have generated, as well as the nature of great enlightenment itself, are all quiescent. "

If I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding that, thereby giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would not permit it. Why is this so?

To grasp at signs and make conceptual distinctions regarding the disciples of Buddhas who have already entered parinirvāṇa, and then to rejoice and dedicate [merit], is called having great attainment. This is because the past has already ceased and is non-existent; likewise, the disciples of Buddhas of the future and the present have not yet arrived and do not abide, and are thus unobtainable. If they are unobtainable, they are not objects for grasping at signs. If one grasps at their signs and gives rise to rejoicing and dedication toward Bodhi, one falls into perversion.

"Therefore, when a bodhisattva wishes to correctly generate sympathetic joy and dedicate toward enlightenment the merits and roots of goodness of the Tathāgatas and their disciples, they should not, within that process, give rise to conceptualizations of grasping at signs based on the notion of 'something to be attained' while generating sympathetic joy and dedicating."

If, within that [practice], one gives rise to conceptualization based on grasping at signs and the notion of something to be attained, while rejoicing and dedicating [merit], the Buddha does not say that such a person possesses great benefit. Why is this?
Such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is called "mixed with poison" because it is characterized by false conceptualization and discrimination.

It is like food that possesses excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, yet is mixed with poison; a person of shallow understanding greedily takes and eats it, which, though pleasing at first, results in great suffering later.

In this way, a certain class of individuals, having failed to properly uphold, fail to properly examine, and fail to properly penetrate the profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, says to those of the Mahāyāna lineage:
"Come!..."

"Good son! Regarding the five aggregates, beginning with morality, of the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time, as well as their other immeasurable and boundless merits; the roots of goodness planted by the disciples of the Buddha; the roots of goodness planted by those sentient beings for whom the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has bestowed the prediction of *samyak-saṃbodhi*—whether as Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas; and the roots of goodness planted by devas, humans, asuras, and others—all such things, taken together and weighed, you should now rejoice in them and dedicate them toward enlightenment."

“Such rejoicing and dedication as have been described are based on the method of apprehending something to be attained; they are like worldly food mixed with poison. A person of the Bodhisattva lineage should not train according to what has been said therein.”
"Therefore, Venerable One,

you should explain how the sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should rejoice in and dedicate the roots of goodness and merits of the Buddhas and their disciples of the three times and ten directions so that it may be called 'free from poison'?"
Subhūti replied:
"If bodhisattvas wish to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication without slandering the Buddha, they should form this thought:

'Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have realized the roots of virtue and merit in accordance with reality—possessing such a nature, such characteristics, and such a dharma that they may be rejoiced in.'"

I too should now likewise rejoice; just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have realized according to reality, so should these various meritorious actions be dedicated toward enlightenment;
I too should now likewise dedicate them.

"If one performs such rejoicing and dedication in this manner, then one does not slander the Buddha, is not defiled by the various poisons, is free from all faults, and properly accords with the Buddha's teaching."

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should perform such sympathetic rejoicing and dedication as follows: just as the aggregate of ethical discipline and so forth do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time, so too should sympathetic rejoicing and dedication be performed."

Why is this? Because those dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), they do not fall within the three realms nor are they subsumed under the three periods of time; rejoicing and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) are likewise so.
If one can thus rejoice and dedicate [merit], it will not be mixed with various poisons and shall not be lost or destroyed;
if one does not rejoice and dedicate in this manner, know that it is a perverted rejoicing and dedication.
If bodhisattvas form this thought:

"Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have realized all qualities and so forth according to reality, there exists such a dharma by which one may generate unerring sympathetic joy and dedication."
"I should now likewise, relying upon such a Dharma, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication.
This is what is meant by correctly giving rise to sympathetic joy and dedication.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!
You are now able to perform the great work of a Buddha for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were each to attain the mundane and supramundane meritorious qualities characterized by signs, such as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers."

This non-erroneous rejoicing and dedication undertaken by this bodhisattva is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all those merits.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to each give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and each were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, employing the method of 'attainment' (upalambha), and constantly and uninterruptedly offer superior garments, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other articles of comfort to as many sentient beings as there are in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, honoring and making offerings to them."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would these bodhisattvas acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
If this mass of merit were to have a physical form, even the worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, would not be able to contain it.”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

If one bodhisattva, being sustained by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, generates the merit of unerring rejoicing and dedication, that merit is a hundred times superior, a thousand times superior, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold superior to the mass of conditioned merit of the former bodhisattva."

At that time, the four great heavenly kings, each accompanied by twenty thousand sons of gods as their retinue, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Because this non-erroneous rejoicing and dedication undertaken by these bodhisattvas is embraced by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, its power and majesty are vastly greater—hundreds of thousands of times more so—than the aforementioned giving that involves apprehension of objects.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, up to the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, each accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand devaputras, all holding various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered perfumes, garments, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, and many wonderful, rare treasures, played celestial music as an offering to the Buddha. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms, and said:

“Because this non-erroneous sympathetic joy and dedication generated by these bodhisattvas is embraced by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, its power and majesty are vastly greater—hundreds of thousands of times more so—than the aforementioned giving performed with the apprehension of a self.”

At that time, the Great Brahma King, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas from as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and spoke with one voice:
“How rare! How extraordinary!”
“World-Honored One!

Because this non-erroneous sympathetic joy and dedication generated by these bodhisattvas is embraced by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, its power and majesty are vast and great, exceeding by many hundreds of thousands of times the aforementioned giving that involves apprehension.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, including those of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, saying:
"Let us set aside for a moment the case of all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm who have each resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Suppose that in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, all sentient beings were to each generate the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and suppose that each of them, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were to employ the method of "attainment" to constantly and uninterruptedly offer superior garments, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other articles of pleasure, respectfully making offerings to as many sentient beings as there are in those Ganges-sand worlds.

If there is a bodhisattva who universally takes as their object the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the three periods of time, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; and the roots of goodness possessed by all disciples; and the wholesome dharmas practiced by other sentient beings—if they collect and weigh all such things together and, in their presence, initiate meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy that are most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime.
Furthermore, one takes these various meritorious deeds accompanied by such sympathetic joy and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The merit obtained from such sympathetic joy and dedication far surpasses the previously mentioned mass of conditioned merit; it is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has taught regarding the performance of various meritorious deeds accompanied by rejoicing—those which are most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most sublime—manifestly brought forth before one.”
“What is meant by the most honored, most excellent, most supreme, and most sublime meritorious action accompanied by sympathetic joy?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If bodhisattvas do not grasp, do not reject, do not dwell upon, and do not apprehend the phenomena of the three periods of time; knowing that there is no phenomenon that has arisen, is arising, or will arise, and knowing that there is no phenomenon that has ceased, is ceasing, or will cease; and thus, in accordance with the true nature of phenomena, give rise to sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—this is called the most honored, most excellent, most supreme, and most sublime meritorious action accompanied by sympathetic joy.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas wish to generate unerring sympathetic joy and dedicate the roots of virtue associated with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—along with right liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation—of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples throughout the three periods of time, they should form this thought:
'Just as true liberation is, so too are the roots of virtue associated with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.'"

Just as with true liberation, so too are the roots of goodness associated with the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
just as with true liberation, so too is all resolute conviction;
just as with true liberation, so too is sympathetic joy and dedication.
Just as true liberation is, so too are all past dharmas that have already ceased;
just as true liberation is, so too are all future dharmas that have not yet arisen;
just as true liberation is, so too are all present dharmas currently evolving.
As is true liberation, so too were the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples in the immeasurable and incalculable worlds of the past;
as is true liberation, so too will the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples in the immeasurable and incalculable worlds of the future;
as is true liberation, so too are the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples in the immeasurable and incalculable worlds of the present.
Such is the *tathatā* and *dharmatā* of all phenomena: it has no leaning toward nor turning away from, no bondage nor liberation, no defilement nor purity.

I rejoice in these roots of merit and qualities with manifest presence, employing as my means the absence of shifting, the absence of loss or destruction, signlessness, and non-attainment, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is called the most honored, the most supreme, the highest, and the most wondrous rejoicing and dedication.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
compared to the merit obtained from such unerring rejoicing and dedication,
suppose all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions were to each generate the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Suppose one were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
employing the method of "attaining something," and constantly and uninterruptedly offer superior and exquisite clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine,
and other articles of comfort to all sentient beings throughout worlds in each of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the merit obtained thereby—
The merit of giving, as well as the roots of virtue associated with pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
cultivated by all sentient beings throughout Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each remaining for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
by means of the conceptualization of "attainment"— [are surpassed by] a hundredfold...
"It is twice as superior, a thousand times as superior, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold more superior. —
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 558.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 559.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight: Hell, Part Five. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Such non-perverted rejoicing and dedication are all accomplished through the power of the perfection of wisdom.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is able to provide illumination and should be honored by all; it cannot be defiled by any worldly dharmas. It can remove cataracts and darkness, and can produce radiance; it can bestow benefit and peace, and act as a leader. It serves as pure eyes for those who are blind, and acts as a bright lamp and torch for those traveling through the dark. It leads those who have lost their way into the correct path, and reveals the nature of all dharmas as being omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). It demonstrates that all dharmas are neither extinguished nor born. It is the mother of all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, capable of enabling all Buddhas to fully turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects. For those without refuge or protection, it provides refuge and protection; it can eliminate all the suffering and affliction of birth and death, and reveal that the naturelessness of all dharmas is itself their true nature.”
“World-Honored One!
How should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dwell in profound prajñāpāramitā as they would dwell in the presence of the Buddha; they should honor and serve prajñāpāramitā as they would honor and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.”
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, thought to himself:
"For what cause and for what reason does Śāriputra now ask the Buddha about this matter?
Having reflected thus, he asked Śāriputra:
“For what reason do you ask this? Śāriputra replied to Śakra:

“Because the former Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught that by being embraced by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the various meritorious deeds arising from sympathetic joy and dedication quickly enable one to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*). This is superior to the roots of goodness associated with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom practiced by bodhisattvas who grasp at attainments; for this reason, I now ask such a question.”

“Kauśika! Suppose there were a multitude of those born blind, numbering a hundred or a thousand, who lacked one with pure vision to skillfully guide them; they would not even be able to enter the right path when near it, let alone reach the great city of abundance and joy from afar!”

In this way, these five perfections are like a multitude of those born blind; if they lack the guidance of the pure eye of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they cannot even set out upon the correct path of a bodhisattva, let alone enter the city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Kauśika! The five pāramitās, such as generosity and the rest, are designated as "possessing eyes" only by means of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, it is through being embraced by the prajñāpāramitā that they are designated as "reaching the other shore."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If bodhisattvas do not bring forth form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and do not perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, this is precisely what is called bringing forth the perfection of wisdom."
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If bodhisattvas bring forth the perfection of wisdom, for the sake of accomplishing what dharma?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If bodhisattvas bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they accomplish nothing at all regarding any phenomena. Because there is nothing accomplished, it is named the perfection of wisdom."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Can this Prajñāpāramitā not bring about the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! Even this prajñāpāramitā cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Why is that?
“Kauśika! Because it cannot be accomplished through anything that is acquired, anything that is conceptualized by name, or anything that is constructed.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If that is so, how does the *Prajñāpāramitā* speak of the accomplishment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
"In this way, because this perfection of wisdom does not accomplish anything regarding the omniscience it brings forth, it is said to be 'accomplished.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!"
World-Honored One!

Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world not for the sake of the arising and ceasing of all phenomena, nor for the sake of the formation and destruction of all phenomena, yet it performs beneficial deeds for the world.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If bodhisattvas give rise to such a conception, they will then abandon and distance themselves from the profound perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
Furthermore, there are causes and conditions for abandoning and distancing oneself from the *prajñāpāramitā*, namely, giving rise to this notion:
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is empty and non-existent."
They will then abandon and distance themselves from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this?
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva is neither empty nor existent, and is free from all conceptual discrimination.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For the purpose of manifesting what dharma does the Buddha teach the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I say that the perfection of wisdom does not manifest form, nor does it manifest feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it does not manifest the fruit of stream-entry, nor does it manifest the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The profound perfection of wisdom is itself the vast perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“For what reason do you say that the profound perfection of wisdom is itself the vast perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:

“The profound perfection of wisdom does not make form great, nor does it make it small; it does not cause it to accumulate, nor does it cause it to disperse. It likewise does not make feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness great, nor does it make them small; it does not cause them to accumulate, nor does it cause them to disperse.”
One does not regard the ten powers of a Buddha as strong or weak, nor does one regard omniscience as vast or narrow.
If bodhisattvas give rise to such conceptions, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because such conceptualizations are not the natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* were to give rise to such conceptualizations:
"To think, 'I shall deliver so many sentient beings and lead them into the realm of nirvana without remainder'—this is called having great objective attainment;
that which involves objective attainment cannot accomplish anything."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Because sentient beings are without arising, one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also without arising.

Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, are detached, are inconceivable, are without destruction, and are without cognition, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* likewise lacks intrinsic nature, and so on, up to being without cognition.
“World-Honored One!
Because the power of sentient beings is accumulated, one should know that the power of the Tathāgata is likewise accumulated.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there are bodhisattvas who are able to give rise to faith and understanding toward this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, being without doubt, without confusion, and without delusion—whence have these bodhisattvas passed away to be reborn here?”
"How long has he accumulated such practice that he is able to realize and comprehend the profound meaning of the Dharma?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
These bodhisattvas have passed away from the assemblies of various Buddhas in other realms where they served them, and have come to be born here.

Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas have already drawn near to many Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and have previously inquired into the profound meanings of the Dharma herein; having practiced and accumulated hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities throughout immeasurable and incalculable great kalpas, they have come to be born in this land by the power of their great vows.
Upon seeing or hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they give rise to great joy and think:
"I am now seeing the Buddha; I am hearing what the Buddha has spoken."
"For this reason, one should respectfully believe and accept it.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Can this profound Prajñāpāramitā be seen or heard?"
The Buddha said, “No.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“If there are bodhisattvas who are able to diligently train in this profound perfection of wisdom, for how long have these bodhisattvas accumulated their practice?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This should be analyzed.

There are bodhisattvas who, from the very first moment they resolve upon awakening, encounter true spiritual friends who skillfully guide and sustain them; these are able to practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and give rise to faith and understanding toward the profound gateways of the Dharma.

There are some bodhisattvas who, although they have encountered many hundreds of thousands of buddhas and diligently practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya) in their presence, are unable to study the profound *prajñāpāramitā* because they take "attainment" as their expedient means; upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they fail to give rise to faith and understanding, and immediately depart.

Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas, having heard the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* from past buddhas, abandoned the assembly out of a lack of faith and reverence; now, hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, they again abandon it out of a lack of faith and reverence.

Regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are neither physically nor mentally in harmony with it; because they lack such harmony, they perform and increase karma that leads to the attainment of poor wisdom (*duṣprajñā*). Due to this karma, upon hearing the profound perfection of wisdom, they revile, slander, and abandon it.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if any bodhisattvas revile, disparage, or abandon the profound perfection of wisdom, you should know that they are reviling, disparaging, and abandoning omniscience. If they revile, disparage, or abandon omniscience, they are reviling, disparaging, and abandoning the Buddhas of the three times.”

Due to these causes and conditions, they commit and increase the sin of harming the True Dharma; because of this sin, they undergo various heavy sufferings for a long duration. Since the sins they have committed are extremely grave, they fall into the great hells for many hundreds of thousands of years, wandering back and forth between this world and other realms, undergoing various heavy sufferings without finding liberation. When the kalpas of fire, water, or wind arise in this world, they are transferred to the great hells of other realms; when the kalpas of fire, water, or wind arise in other realms, they are transferred to the great hells of this world. Thus they cycle through countless kalpas, enduring the most unbearable sufferings of the great hells.

The force of their karmic offenses for harming the Dharma is somewhat diminished; emerging from hell, they fall into the realm of animals, where they transmigrate through this world and other realms as before, undergoing various intense sufferings for many eons.

The force of their karmic offenses for harming the Dharma gradually thins; they escape the realm of animals and fall instead into the realm of hungry ghosts, wandering through saṃsāra in this world and other directions, undergoing various heavy sufferings for immeasurable eons.

As the residual force of that karma of harming the Dharma was about to be exhausted, he escaped the realm of hungry ghosts and was reborn among human beings. However, he experienced all the sufferings of the human condition, such as poverty, low status, dullness and folly, illness, and ugliness; he did not even hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, let alone being able to diligently cultivate various wholesome karmas!
"Because they have harmed the True Dharma through various evil deeds, they undergo such complete fruits of suffering as these.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are the karma of harming the True Dharma and the five actions of immediate retribution similar to one another in their nature as evil deeds?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Do not say that this karma is like the five deeds of immediate retribution. Why is that?

Although the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya-karma) induce heavy suffering, they cannot be compared to the disparagement of the True Dharma. This refers to those who, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, disparage and reject it, saying:
"This *prajñāpāramitā* is not the true word of the Buddha; it should not be practiced or studied; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the instruction of the Great Teacher."
"By reason of this cause and condition, their transgression is exceedingly grave; it cannot even be compared to the five deeds of immediate retribution. Śāriputra!

These people who harm the Dharma slander the True Dharma themselves and incite others to slander it; they destroy their own bodies and cause others to destroy theirs; they drink poison themselves and make others drink it; they lose for themselves the blissful fruits of rebirth in heaven and liberation and cause others to lose them; they consign their own bodies to the fires of hell and cause others to do so; they sink into the sea of suffering themselves and cause others to drown; and not believing or understanding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* themselves, they teach others not to believe or understand it, leading them into delusion and perversion."
Śāriputra! Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, I do not even wish for those who would harm the True Dharma to hear its name, much less for me to explain it to them!
Śāriputra! I do not even permit those who harm the true Dharma to be looked upon by sons of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle, let alone to dwell together with them!
Śāriputra! I do not even permit those who harm the True Dharma to wear the kāṣāya robe, much less accept offerings! Why is this?
Śāriputra! Those who harm the True Dharma fall into the category of darkness; they are like stinking, putrid excrement, like filthy snails and slugs, and like lepers—truly loathsome and detestable.
"Those who place their trust in the words of those who harm the Dharma shall likewise undergo the great suffering previously described.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"For what reason do you not state the dimensions of the bodies in the evil destinies that those who harm the True Dharma will receive in the future?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"Stop! There is no need to describe the dimensions of those bodies in their destinies; lest those who harm the Dharma, upon hearing this, become terrified and their minds suddenly fall into sorrow as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, and their bodies gradually wither away like cut-off seedlings."
"If they were to hear this, they would vomit hot blood, lose their lives, or suffer near-death agony; therefore, I do not speak of the dimensions of their bodies.
At that time, Śāriputra again requested, saying:
"I only pray that you will explain it for them as a final admonition!"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"I have previously stated that those who undergo suffering for many kalpas shall serve as a great warning and admonition for future generations."

When noble sons and others like them hear what I have previously said regarding the retribution for harming the True Dharma, they would rather sacrifice their bodies and lives than ever slander the Dharma, lest they suffer for a long time in the future.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All wise sons of good family should skillfully guard their actions of body, speech, and mind."
“Could it not be that, due to the evil karma of their speech, they suffer for a long time among those in the evil destinies and among humans?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

"So it is! So it is! Within my true Dharma and Vinaya, there will be certain foolish renunciants who, though they claim me as their Great Teacher, will slander and oppose the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught."

Subhūti, you should know this: if one slanders the profound *prajñā*, one slanders unsurpassed enlightenment; if one slanders unsurpassed enlightenment, one slanders the Buddhas of the three periods of time; if one slanders the Buddhas of the three periods of time, one slanders the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*); if one slanders the knowledge of all modes, one slanders the Dharma; if one slanders the Dharma, one slanders the Saṅgha; if one slanders the Saṅgha, one then creates immeasurable karmic offenses; and if one creates immeasurable karmic offenses, one then takes upon oneself boundless retributive suffering.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By how many causes and conditions do those foolish people slander and reject the profound *prajñā*?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is due to two causes and conditions.
First, they are instigated and deluded by malevolent māras."
"Second, they are unable to have faith or understanding in the profound Dharma. Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are four causes and conditions by which one slanders and rejects the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
First, being enticed and deceived by evil friends;
second, being unable to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas;
third, harboring malice and delighting in seeking out the faults of others.
Fourth, out of jealousy, they praise themselves and disparage others.
Due to such causes and conditions, those deluded persons slander and reject the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, thereby generating boundless and extremely grave evil karma.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Those foolish persons who do not apply themselves with diligent effort will find it truly difficult to believe in and understand the profound Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the Buddha.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is this Prajñāpāramitā so profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Form is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because form has non-existence as its intrinsic nature.”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness all have the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Form is neither bound nor liberated in its prior, subsequent, or middle limits. Why is this?
Because form—its prior, posterior, and middle limits—all have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—across their prior, posterior, and middle limits—are neither bound nor liberated.
"Why is this? Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness all have 'lack of intrinsic nature' as their intrinsic nature throughout the past, future, and present limits.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If one does not apply oneself with diligence, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is extremely difficult to believe and understand.
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is so.]”
"So it is! So it is! Why is this so?"
The purity of form is the purity of the fruit; because form is pure, the fruit is also pure.
The purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the purity of the fruit; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the fruit is also pure.

Furthermore, Subhūti! The purity of form is the purity of all-knowledge; because all-knowledge is pure, form is also pure. This purity of form and this purity of all-knowledge have from the very beginning been non-dual, undifferentiated, uninterrupted, and indestructible.

The purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the purity of all-knowledge; because all-knowledge is pure, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also pure. This purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and this purity of all-knowledge have from the very beginning been non-dual, undifferentiated, uninterrupted, and indestructible.
Chapter 5, Part 9: Purity. Chapter 9: Purity. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Such purity is most profound.”
The Buddha said, “So it is!
Because it is utterly pure.”
Śāriputra said: “Such purity is great radiance.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because it is utterly pure. Śāriputra said:
"In this way, there is purity, yet no attainment and no clear realization.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it is utterly pure.
Śāriputra said: "Such purity is without arising."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because it is utterly pure.”
Śāriputra said:
"Such purity does not arise within the three realms.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because it is utterly pure. Śāriputra said:
"Thus it is pure, without cognition and without understanding.
The Buddha said: "So it is!"
“Because it is utterly pure.
Śāriputra said, “Such purity is without cognition of form; it is also without cognition of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because it is utterly pure."
Śāriputra said:
"Because the profound perfection of wisdom is utterly pure, it neither diminishes nor augments omniscience.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because it is utterly pure. Śāriputra said:
“Because the profound perfection of wisdom is utterly pure, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to any phenomena.
The Buddha said, “So it is!”
“Because it is utterly pure.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Because I am pure, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also pure.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because it is ultimately pure.”
Subhūti spoke again:
“Because I am pure, the fruit is also pure.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because it is ultimately pure.
Subhūti spoke again:
"Because I am pure, all-knowledge is also pure.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it is ultimately pure.
Subhūti spoke again:
"Because I am pure, there is neither attainment nor realization."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because it is ultimately pure.”
Subhūti spoke again:
“Because the self is infinite, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also infinite.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because it is ultimately pure.
Subhūti spoke again:
"If bodhisattvas can awaken in this way, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Subhūti spoke again:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom is neither this shore, nor the other shore, nor that which is between.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because it is ultimately pure."
Subhūti spoke again:
"If bodhisattvas give rise to such a conceptualization, they abandon and distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent, Subhūti!”
"These bodhisattvas are attached to names and attached to signs.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous!"
“World-Honored One!
You have skillfully revealed and analyzed for the Bodhisattva how one ultimately clings to signs within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“What is the attachment to signs that a bodhisattva may give rise to regarding the profound perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied,
“If a bodhisattva regards form as empty, this is called attachment.”
To say that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty is called attachment;

to regard the phenomena of the three periods of time as being the phenomena of the three periods of time is called attachment; and to say that immeasurable merit arises when Bodhisattvas first resolve their minds [on enlightenment] is called attachment.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"For what reason is even this called 'attachment'?
Subhūti replied:
"Because of grasping at the existence of mind—meaning that one grasps this mind as being able to correctly dedicate itself toward unsurpassed enlightenment—it is called 'attachment.
Kausika! The intrinsic nature of the mind is empty and cannot be dedicated."

If bodhisattvas wish to instruct others in the path to great enlightenment, they should demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and gladden them in accordance with the true nature of reality (dharmatā). In doing so, they neither harm themselves nor harm others; this is what all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have equally authorized, as it is free from all conceptual proliferation and attachment.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have skillfully explained for the sake of the bodhisattvas the conceptualization of attachment to signs, enabling the bodhisattvas to recognize and distance themselves from it.
Furthermore, there are other subtle attachments which I shall now explain to you; you should listen attentively!"
Subhūti replied, "So be it!
I pray that you will speak."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle take up signs in the presence of the Buddhas and recollect them according to those signs they have taken up, all such acts are called attachment.

If they give rise to deep sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) of the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time, and having given rise to such sympathetic joy, dedicate it toward enlightenment (*bodhi*) together with all sentient beings, this also is called attachment."

The true nature of all phenomena is not subsumed within the three periods of time; it cannot be grasped as a sign, nor can it be taken as an object of focus. Furthermore, because there is no matter of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, it cannot be dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“The true nature of all phenomena is most profound.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because its intrinsic nature is detached.
Subhūti spoke again:
"One should pay homage to this Prajñāpāramitā in such a manner.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without action and without cognition.
Subhūti spoke again:
"Is it that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is without creation and without cognition?"
The Buddha said:
"In this way, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is solely one; it is non-dual, uncreated, and unconditioned, beyond cognition and beyond discrimination."
"If bodhisattvas can understand in this way, they will be able to remain far removed from all attachments.
Subhūti spoke again:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to realize."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because there is no knower.”
Subhūti spoke again:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom is inconceivable.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! It cannot be comprehended by the mind or by mental objects.
Subhūti spoke again:
