“Thus, this perfection of wisdom is without any creative agency.
The Buddha said, “So it is!”
"Because no agent can be apprehended.
Subhūti spoke again:
"How should a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva does not practice with respect to form, nor likewise practices with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they do not practice with respect to the emptiness of form, nor likewise practice with respect to the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."

If one does not practice the characteristic of the non-perfection of form, nor likewise practices the characteristic of the non-perfection of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? Because form that is not fulfilled is not form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are not fulfilled are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. To practice in such a manner is to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!
You are able to speak of non-attachment within attachment."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If one does not practice with a sign of non-attachment toward form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will not give rise to attachment toward form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; nor will they give rise to attachment toward the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the unobstructed awakening that transcends all attachments is called sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Thus it is, Subhūti!
“If bodhisattvas wish to transcend all attachments, they should practice the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
“It is marvelous!”
“World-Honored One!
Whether this profound nature of phenomena is spoken of or not, there is neither increase nor decrease.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So it is! So it is! Just as with space, even if all Buddhas were to exhaust their lifespans in either praising or disparaging it, that space would neither increase nor decrease; the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise: whether it is spoken or not spoken, it neither increases nor decreases."

For example, when a phantom person is praised or reviled, they feel neither joy nor sorrow, and neither increase nor decrease; the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise: whether it is explained or not, it remains no different from its original state.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“It is a most difficult task for the assembly of bodhisattvas to practice the profound perfection of wisdom; for whether this profound perfection of wisdom is cultivated or not cultivated, there is neither increase nor decrease, neither progress nor regression.”
When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do so as if cultivating empty space, wherein nothing at all exists.
This assembly of bodhisattvas—us sentient beings alike—should pay homage to, revere, and praise them. Why is this so?
The assembly of bodhisattvas don the armor of merit to deliver sentient beings, like those wishing to engage in battle with space who don impenetrable armor;
the assembly of bodhisattvas don the armor of merit to deliver sentient beings, like a strong man wishing to uproot space and place it upon a high and exalted site.

The assembly of bodhisattvas, for the sake of all sentient beings who are like space, seeking to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, are called "Greatly Courageous" and have attained the perfection of great diligence.
At that time, a bhikṣu had this thought:
"One should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, for herein there is no arising or ceasing of any phenomena whatsoever."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Subhūti:
"How should a bodhisattva who wishes to study the profound perfection of wisdom train?"
Subhūti replied,
“A bodhisattva who wishes to train in the profound perfection of wisdom should train with diligent application as if in space.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha:
“If sentient beings are able to train in the perfection of wisdom, how are they to be protected?
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra:
“Do you perceive any dharma that can be protected?”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied: "No,
Venerable Sir!"
Subhūti replied:
"If bodhisattvas practice in accordance with what is taught in the Great Prajñāpāramitā, they are thereby protected.
If they depart from the Prajñāpāramitā, humans and non-humans alike will find an opportunity to harm them."

“Kauśika! If one wishes to protect those bodhisattvas who practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is no different from someone exerting diligent effort to protect empty space; their labor would be in vain and entirely without benefit.”
“Kauśika! Is it possible to guard or protect an echo and such things?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:
"No, Venerable Sir! Subhūti replied.
"Likewise, those who wish to protect bodhisattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom will also find their efforts entirely in vain, yielding no benefit whatsoever."

“Kauśika! When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, although they know that all phenomena are like echoes and the like, they neither perceive nor manifest such a state of abiding; this is the practice of *prajñāpāramitā*.

At that time, through the majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One, the Four Great Heavenly Kings of this trichiliocosm, as well as Śakra Devendra, Mahābrahmā, and all the hosts of devas, came to where the Buddha was; they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, in each of the worlds of the ten directions, they saw a thousand Buddhas proclaiming the *Prajñāpāramitā*; their names, characteristics, and appearances were all identical to those here. The leading members of the assembly of bhikṣus who requested the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* were all named Subhūti, and the leading members of the assembly of devas who questioned and debated the *Prajñāpāramitā* were all named Śakra.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Subhūti, saying:
"When the Bodhisattva Maitreya realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he shall likewise proclaim this Prajñāpāramitā by this very name in this very place."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When the Bodhisattva Maitreya realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, by what name will he proclaim the Perfection of Wisdom right here?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When the Bodhisattva Maitreya realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, he will not speak of the emptiness of form, nor will he speak of the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he will not speak of the bondage or liberation of form, nor will he speak of the bondage or liberation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The profound perfection of wisdom is the most pure.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because form is pure, the profound perfection of wisdom is most pure;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the profound perfection of wisdom is most pure;
because space is pure, the profound perfection of wisdom is most pure.”
Because form is unstained, the profound perfection of wisdom is most pure;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unstained, the profound perfection of wisdom is most pure;
because space is unstained, the profound perfection of wisdom is most pure.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If sentient beings uphold, read, and recite this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they shall never meet with untimely death, nor shall they suffer from untimely illness or untimely calamities; they will always be reverently surrounded, followed, and protected by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas."

If sons or daughters of good family, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the dark and light fortnights, recite and expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā* wherever they may be, they shall obtain boundless merit and benefits.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Subhūti, you should know that when this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being taught, heard, and so forth, there will be many obstacles."
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is a great treasure that has many enemies and thieves; it is without attachment and without grasping toward any phenomena (*dharma*).
Why is this? Because all phenomena are entirely non-existent and unattainable.
Subhūti, you should know this!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended in any phenomenon, it is neither that which defiles nor that which is defiled. Why is this?

Because non-dharmas cannot defile non-dharmas, and because there is no defilement, it is called the "stainless perfection" (*vimala-pāramitā*). Since this *prajñāpāramitā* is undefiled, all other dharmas are likewise undefiled.
If one does not even conceptualize in this way, that is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, you should know that because the profound perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual, regarding all phenomena there is neither seeing nor not-seeing, neither grasping nor abandoning.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras dwelling in the midst of the sky leaped for joy and, congratulating one another, cried out with a single voice:
"We now behold in Jambudvīpa the Buddha’s second turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma!"
At that time, the Blessed One said to Subhūti:
"Such a wheel of Dharma is neither the first turning nor the second, because the profound perfection of wisdom has no turning back."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the vast *pāramitā*.

It is without bondage or attachment toward any phenomena (*dharma*). Although one realizes awakening (*bodhi*), there is nothing realized; although one turns the wheel of Dharma, there is nothing turned. There is no phenomenon that can be shown, no phenomenon that can be revealed, no phenomenon that can be obtained, no phenomenon that can be turned, and no phenomenon that can be returned. This is because all phenomena are ultimately neither born nor extinguished; since they are neither born nor extinguished, there is neither turning nor returning."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Subhūti, saying: "So it is! So it is!"

Why is this? Because within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-cessation, and lack of intrinsic nature, neither turning forward nor returning can be apprehended.

If one can proclaim and reveal it in this way, it is called the pure and excellent proclamation of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Within this, there is no speaker and no recipient; there is no one who realizes and attains *nirvāṇa*, nor is there anyone who teaches the Dharma to serve as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Since the field of merit does not exist, the nature of merit is also empty. Because neither representation nor names can be apprehended, it is therefore called the "vast *pāramitā*."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The profound perfection of wisdom is the boundless perfection, because it is like the great void which has no limits;
it is the perfectly equal perfection, because the nature of all phenomena is equal."
This is the perfection of detachment, because all phenomena are ultimately empty;
this is the perfection of being difficult to subdue, because all phenomena are unapprehendable;
this is the perfection of tracelessness, because all phenomena lack name and essence.
This is the perfection of non-action, because all phenomena have no coming or going;
this is the perfection of non-seizure, because all phenomena cannot be grasped;
this is the perfection of inexhaustibility, because all phenomena cannot be exhausted.
This is the perfection of non-arising, because all phenomena cannot arise;
this is the perfection of non-action, because no agent can be found;
this is the perfection of non-cognition, because no cognizer can be found.
This is the non-reverting perfection, because birth and death are unapprehendable;
this is the stainless perfection, because afflictions are purified;
this is the undefiled perfection, because a basis for defilement is unapprehendable.
This is the indestructible perfection, because it is free from a prior limit;
this is the illusion-like perfection, because all phenomena are unarisen;
this is the dream-like perfection, because of the equality of all mental consciousnesses.
This is the perfection of non-proliferation, because it awakens to the equality of all proliferations;
this is the perfection of non-mentation, because all mentational phenomena are ultimately non-existent;
this is the perfection of immovability, because it abides in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
This is the perfection of detachment from defilement, because all phenomena are not false;
this is the perfection of non-action, because there is no conceptual differentiation regarding all phenomena;
this is the perfection of tranquility, because the characteristics of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
This is the perfection of being without afflictions, because it is free from faults;
this is the perfection of being without sentient beings, because the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of sentient beings cannot be apprehended;
this is the perfection of being uninterrupted, because all phenomena lack any origination.
This is the perfection of non-duality, because it is without attachment to any phenomena;
this is the perfection of non-appropriation, because it is without discrimination regarding the stages of the two vehicles;
this is the perfection of non-discrimination, because it realizes the equality of all discriminations.
This is the immeasurable *pāramitā*, because of the immeasurability of phenomena;
this is the non-arising *pāramitā*, because of being free from the self and phenomena;
this is the space-like *pāramitā*, because there is no obstruction regarding any phenomena.
This is the perfection of non-arising, because all phenomena are unarisen;
this is the perfection of impermanence, because all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature;
this is called the perfection of suffering, because it is the equality of the nature of affliction.
This is the perfection of selflessness, because there is no attachment to any phenomena;
this is called the perfection of emptiness, because all phenomena are unapprehendable;
this is the perfection of signlessness, because all phenomena are free from all signs.
This is the perfection of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-pāramitā*), because all phenomena are unestablished;
this is called the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), because all phenomena are indestructible;
this is the perfection of the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, because they transcend all calculation and number.
This is the perfection of fearlessness, because the mind is without timidity;
this is the perfection of suchness, because all phenomena are not false;
this is the perfection of spontaneity, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said. Chapter Ten:
The Inconceivable (Acintya), Part Five, Section One of Chapter Ten: The Inconceivable. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, had this thought:

"If one merely hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that they have already made offerings to the Buddhas and have given forth great vows; how much more so for those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain it to others, and practice according to its teachings!"

It should be known that such a person has, in the past, approached and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and heard the Prajñāpāramitā. Having heard it, they have upheld, recited, read, transcribed, explained it to others, and practiced according to the teachings; or they were able to question and answer regarding this sutra. By the power of their former merit, they have now accomplished these matters.

If sentient beings have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and their merit is purely refined, then upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds will not be startled, terrified, or afraid.
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the thoughts in the mind of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are bodhisattvas who are able to give rise to faith and understanding toward this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that such persons are like great bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive."

Why is this? Because the principle of this *prajñāpāramitā* is extremely profound and exceedingly difficult to believe and understand. If one has not practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a long time in previous lives, nor questioned and received it before the Buddhas, nor planted many roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas, how could one possibly believe and understand it upon hearing it only briefly?

If there are those who, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, revile and reject it, one should know that such persons have already reviled and rejected the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their previous lives.
Why is this? Because such foolish persons have few roots of virtue, they do not give rise to pure faith in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;

and because they have never questioned the Buddha or his disciples regarding its profound meaning, upon hearing the exposition of the profound significance of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they slander and reject it.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Śāriputra:

"The principle of this Prajñāpāramitā is so profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand that it is not at all surprising if those who have not long been devoted to the practice of the profound Prajñāpāramitā do not give rise to faith and understanding upon hearing its profound meaning."
"If a person pays homage to the profound perfection of wisdom, they pay homage to the knowledge of all modes.
Śāriputra said, "So it is!"
So it is! It is just as you have said. Why is this?

Kauśika! The Tathāgata’s attainment of the knowledge of all modes arises entirely from the perfection of wisdom; furthermore, the profound perfection of wisdom exists by virtue of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.
Kauśika! All bodhisattvas should practice in this way, should dwell in this way, and should train in this way in the profound perfection of wisdom.
Then Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How do the bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom such that they are said to ‘abide’ in the profound perfection of wisdom and are said to ‘train’ in the profound perfection of wisdom?”
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Kauśika, you have relied upon the Buddha’s power to be able to ask the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning. Kauśika,

when the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they do not dwell in form, nor dwell in the thought ‘this is form,’ this is called training in form.”

If one does not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor dwells in the thought "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," this is training in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Furthermore, Kauśika, when the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if they do not study form (*rūpa*), nor study that "this is form," they do not abide in form;

if they do not study feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), nor study that "these are feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," they do not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Kauśika! This is called a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, it is also called abiding in the profound perfection of wisdom, and it is also called training in the profound perfection of wisdom.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Such is the Prajñāpāramitā—most profound, difficult to fathom, difficult to grasp, and without limit.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said, Śāriputra!

When bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they do not abide in the profound nature of form, nor abide in the thought that "this is the profound nature of form," this is what it means to train in the profound nature of form.

If one does not dwell in the profound nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor dwells in the thought "this is the profound nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," this is the training in the profound nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if they do not study the profound nature of form (*rūpa*), nor study that "this is the profound nature of form," this is called not abiding in the profound nature of form;

if they do not study the profound nature of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor study that "this is the profound nature of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness," this is called not abiding in the profound nature of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Since this Prajñāpāramitā is thus most profound, difficult to fathom, and difficult to grasp, and being without limit, it is difficult to believe and understand; it should therefore be taught only to those bodhisattvas who have reached the stage of non-retrogression, for they have no doubt, no confusion, and no delusion regarding it.”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"If one were to explain this to bodhisattvas who have not yet received their prediction, what fault would there be?
Śāriputra replied:

“Hearing this, they may become terrified or give rise to slander; due to these causes and conditions, they will undergo great suffering for a long time and find it difficult to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:

“Is there any bodhisattva who, though not yet having received a prediction, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, does not become terrified, does not give rise to slander, and instead possesses deep faith and understanding?”
Śāriputra said: "There are!

These bodhisattvas have long since resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and have long cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Although they have not yet received the prediction of great enlightenment, after no more than one or two buddhas, they will certainly receive the prediction of great enlightenment."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said, Śāriputra!

If bodhisattvas who have not yet received a prophecy of enlightenment hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and their minds are not startled or terrified, but instead give rise to deep faith and understanding, it should be known that they have long since resolved upon great bodhicitta, planted many roots of merit, and served many virtuous friends."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I now wish to offer a brief illustration; I only pray that you will grant me leave to speak.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Speak as you wish.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle see themselves in their dreams sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one should know that such persons are close to realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If there are those who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not feel fear or alarm and instead give rise to deep faith and understanding, it should be known that such persons have long since resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) and their roots of goodness are matured;
they have either already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of great enlightenment, or are close to receiving it, and will swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person traveling through a vast wilderness, passing through dangerous paths for a hundred *yojana*s, or two, or three, even up to five hundred. Seeing the preliminary signs of cities and royal capitals—such as herdsmen, groves, and fields—and having seen these signs, he would think:
‘The cities and royal capitals are not far from here.’”
Having formed this thought, his body and mind become serene; he fears neither wild beasts, evil bandits, nor hunger and thirst.

Thus, when a bodhisattva hears the *prajñāpāramitā* and gains deep-seated faith and reverence, one should know that before long they will receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and fall away from the fear of falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because they have already attained the prior signs of having seen, heard, honored, and with faith accepted the profound Prajñāpāramitā, which is the precursor to unsurpassed bodhi.
“World-Honored One! [he asked.]
For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to behold the great ocean; traveling toward it gradually over a long period of time, he sees no mountains or forests and thinks to himself:
"Judging by these signs, the great ocean is not far away."
"Why is this? Because near the great ocean, the ground must gradually slope downward and be devoid of mountains and forests.
At that time, although that person had not yet seen the sea, seeing these signs of its proximity, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, gains deep-seated faith and reverence, you should know that they will before long receive the prediction of enlightenment and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Why is this? Because they have already attained the vision and hearing of the supreme precursor signs of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and unsurpassed *bodhi*.
"World-Honored One!"
For example, in the springtime, when the flowers and fruits of trees have already shed their old leaves and their branches and twigs are lush and moist, all who see them think:
"It will not be long before new flowers, fruits, and leaves emerge."
"Why is this? Because the preliminary signs of new flowers, fruits, and leaves have appeared upon these trees.

In the same way, one should know that when a bodhisattva hears the Prajñāpāramitā and develops deep faith and reverence, they will before long receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
At that time, there were among the assembly certain sons of the gods who, having seen this, rejoiced and thought to themselves:

"In the past, when bodhisattvas attained these marks, they soon thereafter received the prediction of great enlightenment; now this bodhisattva has also attained these marks, and he too shall soon receive the prediction of great enlightenment."

“World-Honored One! It is like a woman who has been pregnant for some time; her body grows increasingly heavy and she becomes restless in her movements. Her appetite for food and drink diminishes, as does her need for sleep. She takes no pleasure in much speech and grows weary of her usual activities. Because she suffers from pain, all her tasks suddenly cease. When another woman observes these signs, she immediately knows that this woman will give birth before long.”

When a bodhisattva hears this Prajñāpāramitā and develops deep faith and reverence, it should be known that they will before long receive the prediction of enlightenment, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have now skillfully explained the parables of the bodhisattvas;
all of this is through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.

Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Tripiṭaka, by Imperial Decree.
Part Five, Chapter Ten: The Inconceivable, Section Two. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!
You are most skillfully able to entrust [the teachings] to the bodhisattvas and most skillfully able to protect and mind them."
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”

It is so! Why is this? Because the assembly of bodhisattvas, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to many beings throughout the long night, and out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to cause gods and humans to attain great purpose, benefit, peace, and happiness, and thus proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound perfection of wisdom, how should they cultivate this profound perfection of wisdom so that it is swiftly brought to fulfillment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If bodhisattvas, relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, practice the perfection of wisdom without seeing an increase in form and without seeing a decrease in form; without seeing an increase in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and without seeing a decrease in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and without seeing this as a dharma or seeing it as a non-dharma—these bodhisattvas cultivate the perfection of wisdom and will swiftly attain its fulfillment.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"That which the Tathāgata has spoken is inconceivable.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! Form is also inconceivable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also inconceivable."

If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not give rise to the thought of inconceivability regarding form while practicing the perfection of wisdom; nor do they give rise to the thought of inconceivability regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness while practicing the perfection of wisdom. These bodhisattvas, by thus cultivating the perfection of wisdom, will swiftly attain its fulfillment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The meaning and purport of this Prajñāpāramitā are so profound; who is able to believe and understand it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If bodhisattvas have long cultivated sublime practices, they will be able to give rise to faith and understanding in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way can the assembly of bodhisattvas be said to have long cultivated sublime practices?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not discriminate the ten powers of a Tathāgata, they do not discriminate the four fearlessnesses, they do not discriminate the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and they do not discriminate all-knowledge."

Why is this? The ten powers of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, and even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they are inconceivable; form (*rūpa*) is inconceivable, and feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also inconceivable; indeed, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inconceivable.

If bodhisattvas practice in this manner, they have no place of practice at all; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and these bodhisattvas may then be called those who have long cultivated sublime conduct.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This profound Prajñāpāramitā is a mass of jewels and a mass of purity, like the pure void free from clouds, smoke, and the like."
"How marvelous!
The meaning and purpose of the Prajñāpāramitā are exceedingly profound and beset by many obstacles; yet now, as it is extensively taught, no obstacles shall arise.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! By the spiritual power of the Buddha, no obstacles shall arise."
Therefore, sons of good family of the Mahāyāna who wish to write down, uphold, read, recite, or explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, must ensure that they fully master it within one year.
"Why is this? Because this great jewel of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* encounters many obstacles.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
The evil Māra constantly seeks to create obstacles for this great jewel of the divine pearl, the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Although all Māras constantly seek to obstruct the Prajñāpāramitā in order to prevent Bodhisattvas from accomplishing their tasks, their wishes shall not be fulfilled."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By whose spiritual power was that evil Māra unable to create obstacles for this profound Prajñā?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“This is the spiritual power of the Buddha, and it is also the spiritual power of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Śāriputra!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas collectively protect and keep in mind those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom, ensuring that no evil Māras can obstruct them.

Why is this? Śāriputra, if bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is the natural law that they are all protected and sustained by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions. If they are protected and sustained by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, it is the natural law that the māras and their followers cannot obstruct them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are sons of good family with pure faith who, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, engage in writing it down, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, practicing it, contemplating it, and explaining it without hindrance, they should form this thought:

"That I am now writing down, receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, practicing, contemplating, and explaining the *prajñāpāramitā* is entirely due to the spiritual power and protective mindfulness of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, which enables its accomplishment."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle write down, receive, uphold, recite, study, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is all due to the spiritual power, compassion, and protective mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions, which causes all such supreme wholesome deeds to be unable to be obstructed by any evil Māras.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the worlds in the ten directions will all collectively recognize them, rejoice in them, and protect them with mindfulness."

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the worlds in the ten directions, constantly behold [this] with their Buddha-eyes, collectively observing with compassion and providing protective mindfulness, so that whatever they cultivate shall be accomplished without fail.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle write down, receive and uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will always be seen, known, and protected by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, with their Buddha-eyes throughout all worlds in the ten directions. Thus, no evil Māras shall be able to harass them, and all the wholesome deeds they perform shall be swiftly accomplished.

If sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle are able to write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and expound this Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that they are already close to unsurpassed enlightenment, and the retinues of Māra will be unable to obstruct them.

If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle can write down this *prajñāpāramitā*, and having adorned it in various ways, receive, uphold, read, recite, and make offerings to it with reverence, they will always be protected and remembered by all Buddhas; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they will obtain great benefit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā will, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, spread to the south and gradually flourish there; subsequently, it will spread from the south to the north and gradually flourish there as well."

The unsurpassed true Dharma of the Vinaya that is not attained by a Buddha does not possess the characteristic of extinction; rather, the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Vinaya attained by the Tathāgata is precisely this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Good sons and others who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle shall copy, receive and uphold, read and recite, cultivate and practice, contemplate, expound, and reverently make offerings to such sutras as these.
"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will constantly behold and protect them with their Buddha-eyes, praising and extolling them so that they shall have no sorrow or suffering.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā will, in a future time and at a later stage, be widely disseminated in the northeast."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
Śāriputra!

In the future time, in the final period, those sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who dwell in the northeast, upon hearing this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*, if they are able to believe in it with joy, write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice it, contemplate it, explain it, and respectfully make offerings to it, you should know that these persons have long since generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and have long practiced the conduct of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“In that northeastern direction, during a later time and a later age, how many sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle will there be who, upon hearing this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*, will be able to give rise to faith and joy, and to write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice and cultivate it, contemplate it, explain it, and respectfully make offerings to it?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"In the future, during the final period in the northeast, although there will be immeasurable sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, they will rarely hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and even rarer will be those who, with deep faith and joy, write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and make offerings to it.

Although there will be immeasurable sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and, having heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, will with deep faith and joy write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and make offerings to it, those who cultivate and contemplate it even to a small degree will be rare; and those who can explain and reveal its profound meaning for the sake of others will be exceedingly difficult to find."

“Śāriputra! If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, upon hearing this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, do not sink in heart, are not startled, and are not terrified, but instead give rise to deep faith and delight, and copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and explain it—then you should know that these persons have already personally approached, made offerings to, and venerated immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as various Bodhisattvas, and have inquired about the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*.”

These sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle will certainly fulfill all the bodhisattva practices, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

I constantly teach the Dharma associated with omniscience for those sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle; these persons, upon changing their bodies, will always be able to cultivate and accumulate the various practices of a bodhisattva, swiftly proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings, causing them to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

These sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle possess such stability of body and mind that even the evil Māras and their retinues cannot destroy their aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, let alone others who delight in practicing evil!

Śāriputra! When sons of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds attain vast, pure joy and bliss, and they are also able to establish immeasurable sentient beings in the wholesome dharmas associated with unsurpassed enlightenment.
“Śāriputra! These sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle have now made a great vow before me:
‘We shall certainly establish immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;’”

They cultivate the bodhisattva practices, manifesting them, exhorting others, inspiring them, and gladdening them, so that beings may attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and even receive the prediction of non-retrogression.
"I feel deep sympathetic joy toward such individuals.
Why is this? Śāriputra!"

I observe that the person’s aspiration is in accord with their words; in the future, they will certainly be able to establish immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and by demonstrating, exhorting, encouraging, and gladdening them in the practice of the bodhisattva path, lead them to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and even receive the prediction of non-retrogression.
These sons of noble family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise made such vows in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas of the past.
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past also deeply rejoiced in those vows, because they perceived that their minds and words were certainly in accord.

These sons of noble family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, possessing vast faith and understanding and practicing vast conduct, aspire to be born in the Buddha-fields of other directions where Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently reside and proclaim the profound Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Having heard this profound Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*, he is further able to establish countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings within that buddha-field, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening;

he causes them to practice the bodhisattva deeds, providing demonstrations, exhortations, encouragement, and inspiration, so that they attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”

Regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, as well as the distinctions in the mental activities of all sentient beings, there is nothing that the Buddha and bodhisattvas do not realize or comprehend.
"Bhagavān!

If there are bodhisattvas who, with a sincere heart, listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this *prajñāpāramitā*, and if these bodhisattvas continue to seek the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with tireless diligence in future lives—will there be times when they attain this *prajñāpāramitā* and times when they do not?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"These bodhisattvas constantly seek the profound *prajñāpāramitā* without ceasing; they obtain it at all times, and there is no time when they do not obtain it. Or, even without seeking, they obtain it spontaneously, because all Buddhas and bodhisattvas always protect and keep them in mind."
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If these bodhisattvas obtain at all times, without ever failing to find them, the sūtras associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, will they likewise be able to constantly obtain the sūtras associated with the six *pāramitās*?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“If bodhisattvas always courageously seek out the sūtras associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* with faith, disregarding even their own bodies and lives, it is impossible that they should at times fail to obtain other sūtras.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden all sentient beings, causing them to receive, uphold, read, and recite the sūtras associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* as well as other sūtras; they themselves also diligently practice and study therein. By the power of this merit, in whatever place they are born, it is by the very nature of things that they always encounter the sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the sūtras associated with the other six *pāramitās*, never being separated from them.
Chapter Eleven: The Deeds of Māra, Part Five. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Regarding what was said about the various demonic obstacles that arise when sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle cultivate wholesome dharmas: what is meant by "demonic obstacles for a bodhisattva"?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to expound the essential points of the Dharma but eloquence only arises after a long time, the bodhisattva should know this to be a demonic obstacle."
If, while expounding the essentials of the Dharma, eloquence suddenly ceases, the bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra;
if, while expounding the essentials of the Dharma, eloquence becomes excessive, the bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra;
if, before what one wishes to say is exhausted, one stops abruptly, the bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra.
If, while expounding the essential teachings, the words and phrases become confused and disordered, the bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra;
if, while expounding the essential teachings, the words and phrases are interrupted, the bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra;

or if, at the time of expounding the Dharma, various adverse events arise that prevent what one intends to say from being fulfilled according to one's original intention, the bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattvas are transcribing or otherwise engaging with sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if they yawn or stretch repeatedly; or if they mock one another, or treat each other with contempt; or if their bodies and minds are restless and agitated; or if they lose mindfulness and become distracted; or if the phrasing is inverted; or if they are confused regarding the meaning; or if they fail to find the flavor [of the teaching] and give rise to weariness and abandonment; or if sudden calamities arise; or if they fall into mutual discord and contention—by means of such matters, their work will not be accomplished. A bodhisattva should know that these are the deeds of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattvas hear the teaching of sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom, they may think:
'I have not received a prophecy regarding this; what is the use of listening? "
Or they might think:
"Our names are not mentioned here; what is the use of listening?
Or they might think:
"In this teaching, our birthplaces—cities, towns, and villages—are not mentioned; what use is there in listening to it?

Due to such causes and conditions, their minds become impure, and they rise from their seats and depart in disillusionment and abandonment, without any sense of attachment or longing. A Bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Subhūti, you should know this:

if any bodhisattvas, upon hearing the teaching of a sūtra associated with the perfection of wisdom, have impure minds and abandon it in weariness, then according to the measure of those steps they take while harboring such impure and weary minds, they shall diminish their merit by that many aeons and incur the transgression of obstructing enlightenment for that many aeons."

Having undergone those punishments, one must again exert diligent vigor for that same duration to cultivate the bodhisattva practices before being able to restore their original state; therefore, this is called a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas abandon the sūtras associated with the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that lead to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and instead study other sūtras that do not lead to the knowledge of all modes but conform to the two vehicles, abandoning the root to grasp at branches and leaves—bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra."

Why is this? Because the sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to the mundane and supramundane, preeminent merits of a bodhisattva, and by means of these, they can induce the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

If one studies the sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one studies the mundane and supramundane, preeminent qualities of a bodhisattva, and will swiftly be able to bring forth the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna).
Subhūti, you should know this:

just as a foolish, starving dog abandons its primary food and instead seeks it from a servant, so too will there be bodhisattvas in the future who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study the sūtras associated with the two vehicles.
These belong to the class of the deluded; they abandon the root to seek the branches and will ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a person who, wishing to observe the size, proportions, and superior or inferior qualities of a fragrant elephant's body, were to obtain it yet fail to observe it, instead seeking its tracks. You should know that such a person is exceedingly foolish."

In this way, there will be bodhisattvas in the future who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; such deluded types abandon the root to pursue the branches, and will ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a person who, for the sake of precious jewels, set out for the great ocean; yet having reached the seashore, instead of entering the great ocean, he looked back at a cow's footprint and thought to himself:
'How could the depth and breadth of the water in the great ocean possibly equal this?'"
"In this place there must also be various precious jewels.
Know that such people are utterly foolish.

Likewise, in the future, there will be certain bodhisattvas who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; these are of a foolish nature who discard the root to seek the branches, and they shall ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose there were a master carpenter or his apprentice who, wishing to construct a great palace equal in scale to the magnificent palace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, were to see that palace and instead take the palaces of the sun and moon as their model. You should know that such a person is utterly foolish."

In this way, there will be bodhisattvas in the future who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; being of a foolish nature, they abandon the Great and seek the Small, and shall ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if someone who wishes to see a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), having seen him but not recognizing him, leaves him and goes elsewhere; there they see a minor king and, observing his physical appearance, thinks:
'How could the physical appearance and majestic power of a wheel-turning sage king possibly surpass this? "
"You should know that such persons are utterly deluded.

Likewise, there will be bodhisattvas in the future who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; being of this deluded class, they abandon the superior for the inferior and will ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose there were a hungry person who, having obtained food of a hundred flavors, would discard it to seek out and eat sixty-day-old grain porridge; you should know that such a person is exceedingly foolish."

In this way, there will be bodhisattvas in the future who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; being of a foolish nature, they abandon the superior for the inferior and will ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is as if there were a poor man who, having obtained a priceless jewel, cast it away and instead took up a glass trinket; you should know that such a person is utterly foolish."

In this way, there will be bodhisattvas in the future who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; being of a foolish nature, they discard the superior for the inferior and will ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When there are bodhisattvas who, while correctly writing down, receiving, upholding, reciting, contemplating, and practicing the profound sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom, suddenly find themselves overcome by manifold eloquence and take pleasure in expounding various distinct dharma-gates, such that they are unable to bring their writing and other practices to completion—bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Can this profound *prajñāpāramitā* be written down?
The World-Honored One replied:
"No, Subhūti! If sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, while copying the sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom, should form such a thought:
"If I were to write down the *prajñāpāramitā* in letters, these very letters would be the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Or, if one clings to the idea that the *prajñāpāramitā* exists by depending on letters, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
At that time, one should admonish that bodhisattva, saying:

"You should not now cling to the notion that there are written characters capable of transcribing the Prajñāpāramitā. To hold such a view is the work of Māra; if you abandon this clinging, you will abandon the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattvas write down, receive and uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate,
and expound the sūtras associated with the profound perfection of wisdom, they may think of their native lands or cities."
One may think of a village, a royal capital, a region, or teachers and friends;
or one may think of parents, wife and children, kinsmen, companions, or kings and ministers; or one may think of thieves, various wicked birds and beasts, evil people, or malevolent spirits;
or one may think of assemblies, music, games, requiting kindness, or seeking vengeance.
Whether they think of food, clothing, bedding, or other material possessions;
or think of composing literary verses, treatises, or commentaries; or think of the seasons, cold and heat, or abundance and scarcity;
or think of matters such as elephants, horses, water, or fire; or think of various other tasks to be performed—the Bodhisattva should know that all of these...
This is the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattvas are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, or explaining sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they may obtain great fame, profit, honor, and offerings; if they, on account of these conditions, neglect their spiritual practice, the bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattvas are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding the sūtras associated with the profound perfection of wisdom, Māra employs skillful means to provide them with various worldly treatises or sūtras associated with the two vehicles, giving them to the bodhisattva and saying:
'These scriptures contain a profound and subtle meaning; you should diligently study them and abandon the sūtras you have been practicing.'"
If this bodhisattva, through skillful means, should not accept or become attached [to them], they will be unable to lead to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If this bodhisattva accepts and becomes attached to the books and scriptures bestowed by an evil Māra, thereby abandoning the sūtras they have practiced, the bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma delights in hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, while the one who preaches the Dharma is attached to pleasure and indolence and does not wish to preach it—or conversely—if the two are incompatible and fail to achieve both preaching and receiving, the bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the listener possesses the power of mindfulness and wisdom and delights in hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the teacher of the Dharma wishes to go elsewhere and is unable to teach it—or conversely—if the two are not in harmony and thus fail to engage in teaching and receiving, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma cherishes fame and profit, while the one who listens to the Dharma is unwilling to practice generosity—or if it is the reverse—and thus the two are not in harmony, failing to achieve both preaching and receiving, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the listener has a mind of faith and joy, desiring to hear the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the speaker of the Dharma has not mastered it through study and recitation and is thus unable to explain it; or suppose the speaker has mastered it through study and recitation and delights in explaining it to others, yet the listener harbors doubts because they have not mastered it and does not wish to listen and receive it. When these two do not harmonize and fail to achieve both speaking and listening, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who can preach the Dharma delights in preaching the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, while the one who can listen to the Dharma has no desire to hear or receive it—or conversely—if the two are not in harmony and thus fail to achieve both preaching and listening, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When those who are able to hear the Dharma take pleasure in hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet those who are able to teach the Dharma are physically heavy and exhausted, overcome by sleep so that they cannot teach it; or when the opposite occurs and the two are not in harmony, such that neither teaching nor hearing is achieved—Bodhisattvas should know this to be the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattvas are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding the sūtras associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if someone comes and speaks of the various sufferings of the three evil destinies to urge them to abandon bodhicitta, or if someone comes and speaks of the various pleasures of the human and celestial realms—all of which are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—to urge them to enter parinirvāṇa."
When they say, "Because of these matters such as copying [the scriptures], one cannot reach completion," and harbor grief and distress in their hearts,
a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma delights in gathering a following and takes pleasure in attending to the affairs of others while neglecting his own duty, whereas the one who listens to the Dharma has no worldly entanglements and devotes himself exclusively to his own practice while neglecting the affairs of others—or if it is the reverse of these conditions, such that the two are not in harmony and fail to achieve the preaching and listening—the Bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma delights in noisy commotion while the one who listens to the Dharma does not delight in noisy commotion—or vice versa—and the two are thus not in harmony, such that preaching and listening cannot be accomplished, a bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who can preach the Dharma wishes to go to another region where life and limb are in danger, while the one who can listen to the Dharma fears for their life and does not wish to go with them—or vice versa—and thus the two are not in harmony, failing to achieve both preaching and listening, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a Dharma-preacher wishes to go to another land that is infested with many bandits, plagued by epidemics, and suffering from famine and thirst, while a Dharma-listener, fearing such hardships, is unwilling to go with him; or conversely, the two are at odds and do not harmonize, so that they fail to preach and listen. A bodhisattva should know this to be the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to travel to another region, but the road he must traverse passes through a wilderness that is perilous and obstructed, abounding in threats from bandits, outcasts (caṇḍāla), fierce beasts, hunters, venomous snakes, and other such terrors."
The one who wishes to hear the Dharma desires to follow him, but the one who preaches the Dharma uses skillful means to test him, saying:
"For what reason do you now follow me for no purpose, wishing to go to such perilous and difficult places?"
"You should reflect well upon this and not harbor regrets later.
The one capable of hearing the Dharma, having heard these words, thinks to himself:
"The teacher likely does not wish for me to follow him; even if I were to go along with him by force, why would I necessarily hear the Dharma?"
For this reason, one does not follow them; thus, the two do not harmonize, and one fails to obtain the opportunity for teaching and listening. A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When a Dharma teacher has many donors who follow him constantly, and a listener comes to request that he preach the *prajñāpāramitā*, or requests that he copy, uphold, recite, or practice it according to the teaching, the teacher may have many obstacles and lack the leisure to provide instruction. Consequently, the listener gives rise to feelings of resentment; even if the teacher later provides instruction, the listener does not accept it. Because the two are thus in disharmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, nor do they receive, copy, uphold, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are various Māras who assume diverse forms and approach the bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy him, so that he may not write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others the sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom."
Therefore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle engage in such acts as writing out the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should know that whatever obstacles arise are all the deeds of Māra.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason do evil Māras assume various forms and go to the place of a bodhisattva to employ skillful means to destroy them, so that they may not transcribe, or even expound, the sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: “The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*). From the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes, the Buddha’s teachings are produced; from the Buddha’s teachings, the sublime wisdom of sentient beings is produced; and through the sublime wisdom of sentient beings, the severance of boundless afflictions is realized. For those who have severed their afflictions, no evil Māras can find an opportunity.”
Because those evil Māras could find no opportunity, they were filled with great sorrow and suffering as if an arrow had pierced their hearts, thinking:
"May I not be deprived of this profound sphere of the Prajñāpāramitā."

For this reason, Māra the Evil One assumes various forms and approaches the bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy them, so that they may not copy, nor even expound, the sūtras associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what manner do evil Māras assume various forms and approach Bodhisattvas to skillfully destroy them?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Various Māras assume various forms and approach the Bodhisattva, employing skillful means to destroy his resolve and cause him to despise and reject the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, saying:
‘The formless sūtras you study and recite are not the true *prajñāpāramitā*; the sūtras with signs that I study and recite are the true *prajñāpāramitā*.’”

When these words were spoken, there were bodhisattvas who had not yet received their prediction who then conceived doubts and hesitations regarding the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because of these doubts and hesitations, they came to feel revulsion and weariness toward the *prajñāpāramitā*; because of this revulsion and weariness, they ultimately failed to transcribe it, and so forth, up to failing to explain it. Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are various evil Māras who assume diverse forms and approach a bodhisattva, saying to them:

'When bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they only realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka, or perhaps they may realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they certainly cannot realize the fruit of Buddhahood. For what reason do you labor in vain upon this?'"
“A Bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
Chapter Twelve: Suchness, Part Five. Chapter Twelve: Suchness. “Furthermore, Subhūti!”
When copying and performing other such acts regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, many demonic obstacles (*mārakarman*) will arise to create hindrances.

A bodhisattva should recognize them; having recognized them, they should apply themselves with diligence, maintaining right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*), and employ skillful means to remain far removed from them.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being written down and so forth, there will be many obstacles. It is like a priceless great jewel, a divine pearl, which is difficult to obtain and easily beset by many enemies and thieves."

This principle of the *prajñāpāramitā* is profoundly deep and endowed with supreme merit; yet when the assembly of bodhisattvas transcribes it and so forth, many evil māras create obstacles, such that although they have the desire [to practice], they are unable to achieve success.

Why is this? There are those who are foolish and possessed by Māra, who create obstacles for newly initiated sons of good family practicing the Mahāyāna when they are transcribing and so forth the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

There are those who are deluded and deficient in merit and wisdom, who lack faith and delight in the vast Dharma; such newly initiated sons of good family practicing the Mahāyāna will create obstacles when others are transcribing and so forth this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

In future ages, there will be those who are ignorant and deficient in merit and wisdom; they will not themselves have faith or delight in the Prajñāpāramitā, and when seeing others transcribing it or performing similar acts, they will create obstacles for them by the power of Māra. You should know that such individuals will incur boundless transgressions and will wander through saṃsāra for many kalpas, undergoing all manner of intense sufferings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there are no demonic activities when bodhisattvas engage in such acts as transcribing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that these are all due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power."

Why is this? Although the retinues of Māra exert themselves with skillful means, desiring to obstruct the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise exert themselves with skillful means to protect, mindfully sustain, and embrace it, ensuring that no obstacles arise to its transcription and other such activities.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a woman who had many sons—perhaps five, ten, or even a hundred thousand—and her mother fell ill. Each of the sons diligently sought out medicine and treatment, all thinking to themselves:

'How can we cause our mother’s illness to be cured? How can we ensure she is free from obstacles, that her life and reputation do not perish, that she remains long in peace and comfort so that no painful sensations arise, and that all exquisite articles of enjoyment come to our mother?'"
"Why is this? To give birth to and raise us, and to show us the ways of the world, our mothers have undergone immense hardship.

Having formed this thought, they vied with one another to employ skillful means to seek peaceful conditions to protect their mothers' bodies, ensuring they were not touched by mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, wind, rain, humans, non-humans, or other unpleasant things. They diligently applied themselves to grooming and care so that their mothers would be free from all illnesses, their six sense faculties pure, and devoid of all sorrow and suffering.
Furthermore, with various kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of enjoyment, they made offerings and paid respect, saying:
"Our mother, out of compassion, gave birth to us and instructed us in all worldly affairs; how could we fail to repay our mother's kindness?"
"In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, constantly protects and mindfully attends to the Prajñāpāramitā through various skillful means."

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, expound, or transcribe [this teaching], the Tathāgata will likewise employ various skillful means to diligently protect and mind them, ensuring they suffer no harm or affliction.

Furthermore, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in other worlds throughout the ten directions—who out of compassion seek to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings—likewise employ various skillful means to protect and mindfully attend to this Prajñāpāramitā, ensuring that no evil Māras can destroy it, so that it may long endure for the benefit and happiness of the entire world.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it can correctly manifest the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and it can demonstrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world; furthermore, the knowledge of all modes also arises from it.

"Subhūti, you should know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom, have diligently practiced and studied it to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is able to correctly manifest the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), and it is able to reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way does the perfection of wisdom reveal the true nature of all phenomena in the world?
What dharma, as taught by the Buddha, is called 'the world'?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The Buddha has taught that the five aggregates are called the world.

Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate that the five aggregates, such as form, possess no characteristic of transformation or decay, it is said that *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.”

Why is this so? Because the five aggregates, such as form and the rest, lack intrinsic nature, they are called empty, signless, and wishless; that is the true dharma-realm. Since phenomena such as emptiness cannot undergo transformation or decay, it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the true reality of all worldly phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to universally realize and know the various distinctions in the mental activities designated for immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings; therefore, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, realize and know as they truly are that all immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings possess no nature of distraction because of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) regarding their distracted minds;
and they possess no nature of contraction because of the exhaustion and detachment regarding their contracted minds."
All minds characterized by greed, by their suchness, are not minds characterized by greed;
all minds characterized by hatred, by their suchness, are not minds characterized by hatred;
all minds characterized by delusion, by their suchness, are not minds characterized by delusion.
In all minds free from attachment, there is nothing within that freedom;
in all minds free from aversion, there is nothing within that freedom;
in all minds free from delusion, there is nothing within that freedom.
All expansive minds neither increase nor decrease, nor are they detached; because they are already detached, they lack the nature of an expansive mind.
All great minds neither come nor go, nor do they abide anywhere; they lack the nature of a great mind.
All immeasurable minds are without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without differentiation; having no point of reliance, like the great void, they are not immeasurable minds.
All minds that are invisible are not "invisible minds" because no characteristics can be apprehended therein and because they are free from various objective realms;
all minds that are imperceptible are not "imperceptible minds" because they do not fall within the range of the three eyes and because they lack the nature of mind.
For these reasons, it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the *prajñāpāramitā* to realize, as they truly are, the emergence and submergence of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings—that is, they know, as they truly are, the emergence and submergence of the minds and mental factors of those classes of sentient beings, all of which arise based upon form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."
This refers to the minds and mental factors of sentient beings;

or those who, based on form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, maintain that after the Tathāgata’s death he exists, or does not exist, or both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist—and that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish and false;

or those who, based on form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, maintain that the self and the world are either eternal, or non-eternal, or both eternal and non-eternal, or neither eternal nor non-eternal—and that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish and false.

Some, relying on form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, cling to the self and the world as being either finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite, asserting: "This alone is the truth; all else is foolish and false.
