Others, relying on form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, cling to the idea that the life-principle is identical to the body or that it is distinct from the body, asserting: "This alone is the truth; all else is foolish and false."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the emergence and submergence of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as it truly is, the emergence and disappearance of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings; that is to say, they know, as it truly is, that all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are identical to suchness (tathatā), being non-dual and without distinction."
"Subhūti, you should know this:
the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the five aggregates; the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of the world;
the suchness of the world is the suchness of all phenomena; and the suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry."
The suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning;
the suchness of the fruit of once-returning is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning; the suchness of the fruit of non-returning is the suchness of the fruit of arhatship;
the suchness of the fruit of arhatship is the suchness of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; the suchness of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha...
That is the suchness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the suchness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
the suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. All...
The suchness of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is the very suchness of all sentient beings.
Subhūti, you should know that suchnesses like these are not separate from one another; they are neither one nor different, inexhaustible, non-dual, without division, and cannot be differentiated.
“Subhūti, you should know that all Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize the ultimate suchness of all phenomena, and thereby attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

For this reason, it is said that the profound perfection of wisdom can give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; she is the mother of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and she is able to reveal to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas the true reality of the world.

Subhūti, you should know that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā to realize, as they truly are, the suchness of all phenomena, their non-illusory nature, and their unchanging nature. Because they have realized the characteristic of suchness as it truly is, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The suchness, the non-falsity, and the non-alteration realized by the profound perfection of wisdom are exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize."

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by means of this suchness of all phenomena, their non-falsity, and their unchanging nature, proclaim, reveal, analyze, and manifest all the practices of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas.
Who is able to believe and understand suchness, the nature of non-falsity, and the nature of immutability?

Only irreversible bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, great arhats whose vows are fulfilled, and sons of good family who possess right view can, upon hearing the Buddha speak of this profound suchness, the nature of non-falsity, and the nature of immutability, give rise to faith and understanding.
“The Tathāgata, for their sake, reveals and distinguishes [these] based on the characteristics of the suchness (tathatā) realized by himself.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “It is so!”
It is so! Why is this? Because true thusness (*tathatā*) is inexhaustible, it is profoundly deep;

only the Tathāgata has realized perfect awakening to the profound characteristics of inexhaustible true thusness, and he proclaims and reveals it for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to give rise to faith and understanding.
"Subhūti, you should know this: because form is inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because form is profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between form and suchness.

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and suchness."

"Subhūti, you should know this: because the eye-base is inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because the eye-base is profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the eye-base and suchness.

Because the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases and suchness."

"Subhūti, you should know this: because the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is inexhaustible, suchness (*tathatā*) is inexhaustible; because the sphere of form is profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the sphere of form and suchness.

Because the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena and suchness."

“Subhūti, you should know this: because the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is inexhaustible, suchness (*tathatā*) is inexhaustible; because the eye-element is profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the eye-element and suchness.

Because the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements (*śrotra-ghrāṇa-jihvā-kāya-manodhātu*) are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements and suchness.”

“Subhūti, you should know this: because the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is inexhaustible, suchness (*tathatā*) is inexhaustible; because the realm of form is profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the realm of form and suchness.

Because the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena are profound, suchness is profound; because there is no distinction between the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena and suchness.”

"Subhūti, you should know this: because the eye-consciousness element is inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because the eye-consciousness element is profound, suchness is profound; because the eye-consciousness element and suchness are without distinction.

Because the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements are profound, suchness is profound; because the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements and suchness are without distinction."

“Subhūti, you should know that because all phenomena are inexhaustible, suchness is inexhaustible; because all phenomena are profound, suchness is profound; and because all phenomena are indistinguishable from suchness, suchness is therefore extremely difficult to believe and understand.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 560; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 561.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Thirteen: On the Profound Characteristics. Section Five: Chapter Thirteen, "On the Profound Characteristics. At that time, there were ten thousand devaputras from the desire realm, with Śakra, Lord of Devas, as their leader; furthermore, there were twenty thousand devaputras from the Brahma world, with Mahābrahmā, King of Devas, as their leader.
They all went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha in unison:
"World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of these various profound dharmas that you have taught?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying:

"The various profound dharmas that I have proclaimed take emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-cessation, non-reliance, and the absence of intrinsic nature as their characteristics."
Then the assembly of devas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Dharma taught by the Buddha has no basis of reliance; it is, for example, like space, which cannot be pointed out or demonstrated.”
The profound characteristics of phenomena taught by the Tathāgata cannot be established nor can they be subverted by the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras. Why is this?
Since the world—including gods, humans, asuras, and others—is entirely characterized by marks, those who possess marks are unable to establish or destroy the markless within the realm of marks.

The profound characteristics of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata do not fall within the category of form, nor do they fall within the categories of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; furthermore, they do not fall within the category of humans or non-humans, for humans and non-humans alike cannot create or destroy them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"Suppose someone were to come and ask this question:
'Who created space, and who can destroy it?'"
"Do you consider that person to have asked the correct question?
The assembly of devas replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Space has no substance, is unconditioned, and is without marks; how could one ask whether it undergoes arising and ceasing?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

O celestial hosts, you should know that the profound nature of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) which I proclaim is likewise thus: it cannot be established, nor can it be destroyed; whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the Dharma remains eternally as it is.
"The Buddha has awakened to these characteristics as they truly are; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the assembly of devas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The various characteristics awakened to by the Tathāgata are exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to awaken to."
Because the Tathāgata has realized such characteristics as these, his wisdom regarding all phenomena is free from obstruction.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas abide in such characteristics, analyzing and revealing the profound Prajñāpāramitā; they gather the characteristics of all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings and provide skillful instruction, so that they may attain unobstructed wisdom regarding the Prajñāpāramitā.

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the constant sphere of practice for all Tathāgatas; by practicing therein, the Buddha realizes *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and analytically reveals it to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
O celestial hosts,
you should know that the Tathāgata has awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena as being, in reality, signless.
"For this reason, I say that the unimpeded wisdom attained by all Buddhas is unsurpassed.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Subhūti, saying:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of all Buddhas; it can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world. Therefore, all Buddhas abide in accordance with this Dharma. They honor, revere, respect, praise, embrace, and protect the Dharma upon which they rely and abide—this Dharma is precisely the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
There are no Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, honoring, revering, respecting, praising, upholding, and protecting it. Why is this so?
The profound perfection of wisdom can give birth to all Buddhas, serves as the locus of reliance for all Buddhas, and reveals the true reality of all phenomena in the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are knowers of gratitude and are capable of repaying that gratitude.
If someone were to ask: "
"Who is it that knows gratitude and is able to repay kindness?
One should answer correctly:
"The Buddha is the one who knows gratitude and is able to repay kindness."
"Why is this? Because among all those in the world who recognize kindness and repay it, none surpass the Buddha.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha recognize kindness and repay kindness?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas mount this very vehicle and travel this very path to arrive at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having attained enlightenment, they at all times make offerings to, revere, respect, praise, embrace, and protect this vehicle and this path without ceasing for even a moment. One should know that this vehicle and this path are none other than the profound Prajñāpāramitā.”
This is called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s knowing of kindness and repaying kindness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are no Tathāgatas, Arhats,
or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to realize that all phenomena lack real activity, because there is no agent who acts."

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, without exception, rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to awaken to the fact that all phenomena are not established as real entities, because no physical form or substance can be apprehended.
Subhūti, you should know this:

because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon this very profound Prajñāpāramitā, realize that all phenomena are devoid of activity and lack anything to be accomplished, and because they have at all times—without interruption—honored, revered, respected, praised, sustained, and protected it, they are therefore said to truly know gratitude and repay their debt of gratitude.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are no Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to turn the wheel of wisdom regarding all phenomena as being without action, without accomplishment, and without arising; moreover, they are able to know the causes and conditions for this non-turning. Therefore, you should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and can also reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The Tathāgata has always taught that the nature of all phenomena is without arising, without origination, without cognition, and without vision. How can it be said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and can also reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
As you have said, the nature of all phenomena is without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision.
In what way is the nature of phenomena without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision?
Because all phenomena are empty, non-existent, without basis, and without attachment, for these reasons they are unarisen, unoriginated, unknowable, and invisible.
"Subhūti, you should know this!
Although the profound perfection of wisdom can give birth to Buddhas and manifest the characteristics of the world, there is nothing that is born, nor is there anything that is manifested."

Subhūti, you should know that because this profound perfection of wisdom does not perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, it is called that which reveals the characteristics of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In what way does the perfection of wisdom, by not perceiving form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, demonstrate the characteristics of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because this prajñāpāramitā does not give rise to consciousness by taking form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as its object, it is called 'not seeing' form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Because of this non-seeing, it is said to demonstrate the characteristics of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."
By virtue of this meaning, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.

Furthermore, Subhūti, because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty, detached, pure, and tranquil in relation to the world, it is called "that which reveals the true reality of the world"; for there is nothing in the world that does not have emptiness, detachment, purity, and tranquility as its true reality.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for a great purpose; it appears in the world for an inconceivable purpose, for an immeasurable purpose, for an incalculable purpose, and for an unequaled purpose.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said, Subhūti!
In what way does the profound perfection of wisdom appear in the world for the sake of a great task?"

It is because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas take as their primary task the rescue and liberation of all sentient beings without ever abandoning them for even a moment; it is for this purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
“Subhūti, how is it that the profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of inconceivable matters, immeasurable matters, incalculable matters, and matters equal to the unequaled?”

It is said that the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and omniscient nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are all inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; it is for this purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it only the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and all-knowledge nature of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled;
or are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even all phenomena—likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is not only that the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and all-knowledge nature of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled;
rather, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—even all phenomena—are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.”
Why is this? Because within the true nature of all phenomena, both mind and mental factors are unfindable.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"
Because all forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, cannot be designated, they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
Why is this? Because these dharmas lack intrinsic nature, are unapprehendable, and are empty of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because all forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, are unapprehendable, they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are immeasurable, non-existent, and empty of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as all phenomena, are without limit, they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions are all forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, without limit?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Can space be measured by the mind or mental factors?"
Subhūti replied,
"No, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as all phenomena, are likewise so; because their intrinsic nature is empty, the mind and its mental factors cannot measure them."

For this reason, because all forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses, as well as all phenomena, are limitless, they are all inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

Subhūti, you should know that because all phenomena are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, so too are all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and all-knowledge dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
"Subhūti, you should know that all these dharmas are inconceivable, because conceptualization has ceased;
they are immeasurable, because measurement has ceased."
It is immeasurable because all measure has ceased;
it is peerless because all that is equal or unequal has ceased.
Subhūti, you should know this!
Thus, all these dharmas are inconceivable, because they transcend conception;
they are immeasurable, because they transcend measurement;
they are innumerable, because they transcend number.
"Unequaled, because it transcends all that is equal.
Subhūti, you should know that 'inconceivable,' 'immeasurable,' 'incalculable,' and 'unequaled' are merely designations; they possess no reality whatsoever."
"Subhūti, you should know that that which is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled is entirely non-existent, just like space."

For this reason, all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

Because śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the worldlings—including devas, humans, and asuras—are all utterly unable to conceive of, weigh, measure, or calculate these dharmas as being equal to anything else.

When the Tathāgata taught this inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus and twenty bhikṣuṇīs in the assembly attained liberation of mind through the permanent exhaustion of all outflows.
Furthermore, sixty thousand upāsakas and thirty thousand upāsikās, regarding all phenomena, became free from dust and removed from defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye.

Additionally, twenty bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); the World-Honored One prophesied that they would become Buddhas within the Bhadrakalpa to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Does this profound perfection of wisdom truly constitute a great matter for appearing in the world?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! This profound perfection of wisdom has indeed appeared in the world for a truly great purpose."

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is fully capable of accomplishing the stage of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), wherein both the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha are included.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

just as a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration, possessing majestic power and sovereignty over all, entrusts all affairs of state to his ministers and remains seated with folded hands in non-action, enjoying peace and happiness.”

The Tathāgata is likewise; as the Great Dharma King, possessing sovereign majesty and power, he subdues all beings and entrusts all the teachings of the Buddhas, whether those of the Pratyekabuddhas or the Śrāvakas, entirely to the profound Prajñāpāramitā, so that they may be universally accomplished.
Therefore, Subhūti,
this profound perfection of wisdom truly emerges in the world as a great matter.
Subhūti, you should know this!

The profound perfection of wisdom does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping at or adhering to form, nor even to consciousness; it does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping at or adhering to the fruit of stream-entry, nor even to the knowledge of all modes.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way does the perfection of wisdom also not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or clinging to the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Do you see any fruit of arhatship that can be grasped or clung to?
Subhūti replied, "No, indeed!"
“World-Honored One!
I do not see any fruit of arhatship that could be grasped or clung to therein.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Excellent, Excellent, Subhūti!”
I also do not perceive any dharma of a Tathāgata within which one could grasp or become attached.
Therefore, Subhūti,
this profound perfection of wisdom does not appear in the world for the sake of grasping or becoming attached to the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, the devaputras from the desire realm and the Brahma world together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound; it is difficult to see, difficult to realize, and extremely difficult to believe and understand."
Only those sentient beings who have, in the past, made great vows before immeasurable Buddhas and cultivated various roots of virtue are able to believe and understand this.

Even if all the sentient beings in the three-thousandfold world system were to become followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and so forth, and were to practice their respective stages for an eon or more, it would not equal the merit obtained by someone who, for a single day, endures, delights in, contemplates, weighs, and examines this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; the latter’s merit is infinitely superior to that of the former.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.

O Devaputra, you should know that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will swiftly attain *nirvāṇa*. This is superior to what was previously described regarding those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and others, even if they practice the conduct of their own stage for an eon or more than an eon—how much more so for those who possess patience and delight!"

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the sons of the gods rejoiced and leaped for joy; they prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata, circumambulated him three times to the right, and took their leave to return to their palaces. Not long after they had departed from the assembly, they suddenly vanished and returned to their respective original palaces within their own realms, where they exhorted the devas to cultivate sublime practices.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are bodhisattvas who can give rise to profound faith and understanding in the *prajñāpāramitā*, from where did they pass away to come to be born here in this world?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, can give rise to faith and understanding, without doubt or weariness; if they delight in seeing and hearing it, and in recollecting and contemplating its profound meaning and intent; if they always delight in following those who can expound the Dharma—just as a calf follows its mother without ever leaving her for even a moment—and until they have attained a thorough mastery of the ultimate meaning and intent corresponding to this profound *prajñāpāramitā* so that they may explain it to others, they never depart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the Dharma-preacher for even a single moment; such bodhisattvas have passed away from among humans and been reborn here, and it is by virtue of their past superior causes that they are able to accomplish these things."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there perhaps a bodhisattva who, having accomplished such sublime merit and having served and made offerings to Buddhas in other directions, passes away from that place and is reborn here?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are bodhisattvas who, having accomplished such sublime merits and having served and made offerings to Buddhas in other directions, pass away from those places and are reborn here in this world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattvas who have accomplished such sublime merits; in previous lives, they already served and made offerings to Maitreya Bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven, heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and inquired about its most profound meanings and purports. Having passed away from that place, they have come to be born here in this world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattvas who, although they heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, were unable to inquire about its profound meaning and intent. Consequently, having now been born among humans, when they hear the *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they fall into doubt and confusion, and it is difficult for them to attain awakening."
Why is this? Those who do not understand the provisional meaning have many doubts in their minds, are bewildered and distressed, and are difficult to instruct.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are some bodhisattvas who, although they heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives and once inquired into its meaning and intent for a period ranging from one day to five days, did not practice with diligence according to the teaching.

Having now been born among humans, although they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* for only a short time, their minds are firm and indestructible; yet, if they are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* and the Dharma teacher who inquires into its profound meaning, they will immediately fall away and lose it.

Why is this so? Although these bodhisattvas heard the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives and were even able to inquire about its profound meaning, they did not practice with diligence according to the teachings. Consequently, in this present life, regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, at times they delight in hearing it and at times they do not; at times their resolve is firm and at times they regress. Their minds are light and fickle, advancing and retreating without constancy, like *tūla-cotton* tossed and turned by the wind.

Thus, a bodhisattva who has newly begun training in the Mahāyāna may possess faith, yet it is neither firm nor pure; unable to maintain faith, joy, and practice toward the profound *prajñāpāramitā* over a long period, they may fall into the level of one of the two vehicles.
Chapter 14: The Parable of the Ship, Part Five "Furthermore, Subhūti, it is like a caravan of merchants traveling upon the great ocean whose ship suddenly breaks apart.

Among them, if those individuals are able to take hold of wooden vessels, floats, planks, or even a corpse as something to rely upon, you should know that such people will ultimately not drown; they will reach the safe shore on the other side of the great ocean, arriving without injury or harm and experiencing all manner of happiness."

It is the same for the assembly of bodhisattvas: if they possess faith in the Great Vehicle, patience, delight, and aspiration; if they possess diligence, resolute conviction, heedfulness, and superior intention; if they possess equanimity, reverence, and a pure mind; and if they do not abandon the yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, further being able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as their support, you should know that such individuals will never fall back midway into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a man or a woman who, taking a well-fired jar, went to a river, a pond, a well, a spring, or a canal to fetch water; you should know that this jar would never break or dissolve.
Why is this? Because this jar is well-fired, capable of holding water, and extremely sturdy. It is the same with the assembly of bodhisattvas:

if they possess faith in the Mahāyāna, patience, joy, and aspiration; if they possess diligence, resolute conviction, heedfulness, and superior intention; if they possess equanimity, reverence, and a pure mind; and if they do not abandon the yoke of supreme, perfect enlightenment while being able to embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that such individuals will never fall back midway into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but will certainly realize supreme, perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is like a merchant who possesses skillful wisdom; having first thoroughly repaired his ship by the seashore, he then lowers it into the water to ensure there are no leaks. Only after that does he load his goods upon it and set sail. You should know that such a ship will certainly not be wrecked or sink, and both the people and their cargo will reach their destination in safety."

It is the same for the assembly of bodhisattvas: if they possess faith in the Mahāyāna, patience, joy, and aspiration; if they possess diligence, superior resolve, heedfulness, and a superior intention; if they possess equanimity, reverence, and a pure mind; and if they do not cast off the yoke of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment while further being able to embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that such individuals will never regress midway to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, decrepit and worn out by age, further afflicted by various ailments—namely, disorders of wind, bile, phlegm, or a combination of these three. This aged and sick person wishes to rise from his bed and go elsewhere, yet he is unable to do so himself."
Two strong men each supported one of his armpits, slowly assisting him to rise and said to him:
"Do not be discouraged; go wherever you wish. Now we two shall never abandon you; you will surely reach your destination in safety and without harm."

The assembly of bodhisattvas is also like this: if they possess faith in the Mahāyāna, patience, delight, and aspiration; if they possess diligence, resolute conviction, and heedfulness; if they possess superior intention, equanimity, reverence, and a pure mind; and if they do not abandon the yoke of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment while further being able to embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that such individuals will never regress midway to enter the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but will certainly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"That which is contrary to the above is called the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Chapter Fifteen: On the Tathāgata, Part One of the Fifth Section. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should a newly initiated bodhisattva train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A newly initiated bodhisattva who wishes to study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should first draw near to and serve virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Those who can proclaim the profound perfection of wisdom and provide instruction and guidance to bodhisattvas are called virtuous friends.”
That is to say, he speaks these words: "Come,
noble son!"
You should diligently cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
When you practice diligently, you should do so with the skillful means of non-apprehension, dedicating [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When you dedicate [merit], do not grasp at awakening on account of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? The nature of the knowledge of all modes is not something to be grasped.
"O son of good family!
Do not give rise to craving or attachment for the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

If one can thus instruct and advise a newly initiated bodhisattva, causing them to gradually enter the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that such a person is a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to the bodhisattva.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is a most difficult matter for these bodhisattvas to resolve to attain awakening and set out toward awakening.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So it is! So it is! The bodhisattvas perform what is exceedingly difficult; that is to say, for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all the world, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, making this solemn vow: "

"For the sake of rescuing and delivering all the world, for the sake of acting as a dwelling for all the world, for the sake of acting as a refuge for all the world, for the sake of acting as an island for all the world, for the sake of showing the ultimate path to all the world, for the sake of acting as a guide for all the world, and for the sake of acting as a destination for all the world, I shall exert diligent vigor to advance toward great enlightenment."
"Subhūti! How do the bodhisattvas, having vowed to rescue and deliver all the world, exert diligent vigor and advance toward great enlightenment?

It is because the bodhisattvas see that the world is submerged in the suffering of birth and death and is unable to escape it; they therefore exert diligent vigor and advance toward great enlightenment in order to extract them from that suffering by preaching the essentials of the True Dharma."
"Subhūti!
How do the bodhisattvas, for the sake of acting as a dwelling place for all the world, exert diligent effort and advance toward great enlightenment?
It is that the bodhisattvas, wishing to proclaim to the world that all phenomena are fundamentally non-composite, exert diligent effort and advance toward great enlightenment."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“In what way does a bodhisattva wish to explain to the world that all phenomena are non-composite?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! Bodhisattvas who wish to proclaim to the world that the five aggregates and all phenomena are entirely non-composite, neither bound nor liberated, neither arising nor ceasing, are thereby able to provide shelter and protection for all beings, just like a house.”
“Subhūti! How do the bodhisattvas, for the sake of providing a refuge for all the world, exert diligent effort and advance toward great enlightenment?

It is by desiring to liberate the world from all birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, and suffering that the bodhisattvas exert diligent effort and advance toward great enlightenment, skillfully employing means to preach the essentials of the True Dharma.”
“Subhūti! How do the bodhisattvas, for the sake of acting as an island for all the world, exert diligent effort toward great awakening?

It is that when bodhisattvas proceed toward great awakening, they desire to proclaim to the world that the prior and posterior limits of the five aggregates of clinging are severed; because these are severed, all phenomena are severed. This total severance is itself the subtle and wondrous nirvāṇa of cessation, and it is also the nature of reality, free from inversion.”
For example, in small seas, great oceans, rivers, or ponds, high ground that can be inhabited is called an island; nirvāṇa is likewise, for it is a place of peace and security. "Subhūti!
How is it that the assembly of bodhisattvas exerts diligent effort toward great enlightenment in order to demonstrate to the world the ultimate path?

It is because when bodhisattvas proceed toward great enlightenment, they desire to teach the world that form (*rūpa*) is ultimately not called "form," and that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise so; for the ultimate nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not form and the other aggregates.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the ultimate dharmatā of dharmas such as form is not called ‘form’ and so forth, then all bodhisattvas must have already attained bodhi, for within the ultimate nature there is no conceptual differentiation.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

In the ultimate nature, there is no conceptual differentiation whatsoever; yet for bodhisattvas, this is an exceedingly difficult task. Although they are able to contemplate all phenomena in this way, they neither realize [nirvana] prematurely nor do they sink into despondency, thinking:
"Having attained manifest perfect enlightenment regarding these phenomena, I shall proclaim and reveal them to all the world, so that they may know the characteristics of such an ultimate path."
"Subhūti! How do the bodhisattvas, in order to act as guides for all the world, exert diligent effort toward great enlightenment?

It is that when bodhisattvas advance toward great enlightenment, they desire to explain to the world that the intrinsic nature of form is without arising and without cessation; and it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
I wish to explain for the sake of the world that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena— from the fruit of stream-entry up to unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment— is neither produced nor extinguished. "Subhūti, how do the bodhisattvas serve as a destination for the world?"
What is the diligent exertion for proceeding toward great enlightenment?

It refers to when bodhisattvas, proceeding toward great enlightenment, desire to proclaim and reveal to the world that form has space as its destination, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and all phenomena likewise have space as their destination;

and they desire to proclaim and reveal to the world that form has no destination and is equal to space, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and all phenomena likewise have no destination and are equal to space.
Just as the great void has no coming and no going, no activity and no abiding, no birth and no cessation, so too are all phenomena; they are all like space, without any discrimination.
Why is this? Because all forms are empty, they neither come nor go; because feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and all phenomena are likewise empty, they too neither come nor go.

Why is this so? Because all phenomena have as their destination emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-activity, non-creation, non-arising, lack of intrinsic nature, being like a dream, being like an illusion, selflessness, boundlessness, tranquility, nirvāṇa, non-appropriation, non-rejection, no coming, no going, and ultimate quiescence; one cannot transcend that destination.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Who is able to believe and understand such a profound Dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there are bodhisattvas who have long cultivated the great practice, who have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, who have made vast vows in the presence of those Buddhas, whose planted roots of goodness have all reached maturity, and who have been sustained and protected by immeasurable spiritual friends, they will be able to give rise to faith and understanding toward this profound Dharma."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what is the nature of these bodhisattvas constituted?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"These bodhisattvas have the nature of being disciplined and detached; by virtue of this nature, they are able to know and understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When these bodhisattvas are able to know and comprehend this profound prajñāpāramitā, where will they go?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"These bodhisattvas are proceeding toward all-knowledge.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If bodhisattvas, having realized this destination, are able to serve as a refuge for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings," the Buddha told Subhūti, "It is so! It is so!"
"It is so! If bodhisattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are able to serve as a place of refuge for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"These bodhisattvas are able to perform what is difficult; that is to say, they don such firm armor, desiring to deliver immeasurable and boundless sentient beings and lead them into nirvāṇa, yet no such category of sentient beings can be apprehended at all."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the armor donned by these bodhisattvas does not belong to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it does not belong to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, the knowledge of all modes, or any phenomena whatsoever."
"Why is this? Because all phenomena are without any point of attachment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not abide in the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Based on what meaning do you speak thus?"
Subhūti replied:
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without any abiding or attachment.

If one cultivates the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is nothing at all among all phenomena that is cultivated, nor is there any cultivator. At the time of cultivation, the place of cultivation, and that by which one cultivates—all these are unapprehendable."
"Bhagavān!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no fixed dharma; if one cultivates emptiness, cultivates all dharmas, cultivates the boundless, and cultivates non-appropriation, this is the cultivation of *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
one should observe a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom."

This means that if bodhisattvas do not crave or cling to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not grasp at the words or instructions of others as being the ultimate truth, and do not act merely out of faith in others; but rather, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, do not sink, do not despair, and are without doubt, regret, or confusion; and they joyfully delight in hearing it, receiving it with deep faith—such bodhisattvas are certainly non-retrogressive. Because these bodhisattvas have already heard the meaning and intent of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, their minds are now without alarm and so forth when they hear it now.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If bodhisattvas, upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, have no fear or the like in their hearts, how do these bodhisattvas contemplate this profound perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“These bodhisattvas should observe the perfection of wisdom with a mind that accords with omniscience.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“How does one, in accordance with the mind of omniscience, contemplate the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If bodhisattvas, in accordance with space, contemplate the perfection of wisdom, this is what it means to contemplate the perfection of wisdom in accordance with the mind of omniscience.”
Why is this? Because all-knowledge is immeasurable and boundless;

that which is immeasurable and boundless is neither form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It is without attainment, without clear realization, without wisdom, and without cognition. It is without arising and without cessation, without cultivation and without action. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it has no direction, no domain, and no place of abiding—it can only be described as immeasurable and boundless.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Because space is immeasurable and boundless, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is also immeasurable and boundless. Because all-knowledge is immeasurable and boundless, there is no one who can realize it; it cannot be realized by form (*rūpa*), nor even by consciousness (*vijñāna*); it cannot be realized by the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), nor even by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
Why is this? Form through to consciousness is itself all-knowledge; they are non-dual and without distinction.
The perfection of generosity through to the perfection of wisdom is itself all-knowledge; they are non-dual and without distinction.
At that time, the devaputras from the desire realm and the Brahma-world went together to where the Buddha was and addressed him in unison, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
When I contemplate this matter, I recall that upon first attaining Buddhahood, I sat in meditative seclusion and was reluctant to preach the Dharma, thinking to myself:
"My Dharma is exceedingly profound; it is not something that the world can suddenly believe and accept."

"The Dharma that I have realized is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā; this Dharma is profoundly deep. It is neither the subject that realizes nor the object that is realized; there is no place of realization and no time of realization, and even the act of realizing it by means of these cannot be apprehended."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!
Because space is profound, this Dharma is profound; because the self is profound, this Dharma is profound; because the nature of all phenomena has neither coming nor going, this Dharma is profound."
At that time, the sons of the gods again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is extremely difficult for all the world to believe and understand;
the Dharma taught by the Buddha involves neither grasping nor abandoning, whereas sentient beings in the world act out of grasping and abandoning.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha is subtle and profound; it accords with all phenomena, is without obstruction, and is equal to space."
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is ultimately unarisen, because all phenomena that arise are unattainable;
the Dharma taught by the Buddha has no location whatsoever, because all locations are unattainable.
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! So it is!”
"So it is! Then the sons of the gods addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Venerable Subhūti is a true son of the Buddha; he is born after the manner of the Tathāgata, for everything he says is entirely in accord with emptiness."
At that time, Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"You say that I am born after the Tathāgata; in what way, Subhūti, am I born after the Tathāgata?"
This is because they arise in accordance with the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata, and because all phenomena that arise are unattainable.

The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes; its original nature is non-arising. Subhūti’s *tathatā* likewise neither comes nor goes; its original nature is non-arising. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti arises in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is the suchness of all phenomena; the suchness of all phenomena is the Tathāgata’s suchness. This suchness has no nature of suchness, nor does it have a nature of non-suchness. Subhūti’s suchness is likewise so; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s true suchness is without change, without discrimination, and pervades all places; Subhūti’s true suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s true suchness has permanence as its characteristic, yet it abides nowhere; Subhūti’s true suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is without obstruction; the suchness of all phenomena is likewise without obstruction; and the suchness of Subhūti is also thus. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness and the suchness of all phenomena are one single suchness; they are non-dual, undifferentiated, uncreated, and unconditioned. Such suchness is eternally the characteristic of suchness; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of suchness. Therefore, suchness is non-dual and undifferentiated. Subhūti’s suchness is likewise so; for this reason, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is without recollection and without conceptualization in all places; the suchness of all phenomena is likewise without recollection and without conceptualization in all places; and the suchness of Subhūti is also thus. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata.

The suchness of the Tathāgata is without distinction and cannot be apprehended; the suchness of all phenomena is likewise without distinction and cannot be apprehended; the suchness of Subhūti is also thus. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the likeness of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is not separate from the suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of all phenomena is not separate from the Tathāgata’s suchness. The Tathāgata’s suchness is eternally the characteristic of suchness; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of suchness. Subhūti’s suchness is likewise so; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
Although it is said that he is born in accordance with [the Tathāgata], there is nothing with which he is born in accordance, because Subhūti’s suchness is not different from the Buddha’s.

The suchness of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes; likewise, the suchness of all dharmas now neither comes nor goes, and the suchness of Subhūti now is also thus. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata conforms to the suchness of the past, and the suchness of the past conforms to the suchness of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata conforms to the suchness of the future, and the suchness of the future conforms to the suchness of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata conforms to the suchness of the present, and the suchness of the present conforms to the suchness of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata conforms to the suchness of the three times, and the suchness of the three times conforms to the suchness of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of the three times are non-dual and without distinction; the suchness of all phenomena and the suchness of Subhūti are likewise non-dual and without distinction. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.
The suchness of a bodhisattva is the suchness of a Buddha; because of this suchness, when the assembly of bodhisattvas attains awakening, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
When the Tathāgata realized this suchness, the three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways.
Because I have engendered deep faith and understanding in the suchness of all these phenomena, I say that Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

However, I, Subhūti, do not follow after the Tathāgata by way of form, nor even by way of consciousness; I do not follow after the Tathāgata by way of the fruit of stream-entry, nor even by way of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; I do not follow after the Tathāgata by way of omniscience; rather, I follow after the Tathāgata solely by way of suchness.”
"Son of Heaven, you should know this!

However, I, Subhūti, do not arise following form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor do I arise following the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. Therefore, I, Subhūti, arise following the Tathāgata."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Such is the profound and subtle nature of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."
"Thus is the Tathāgata’s profound and subtle nature.
When this description of the Tathāgata’s marks was being spoken, three thousand bhikṣus, having forever exhausted all outflows, attained liberation of mind and became arhats;
five hundred bhikṣuṇīs were freed from dust and defilement, and the pure Dharma-eye arose within them.
Five thousand devas and humans attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
sixty bodhisattvas, with all outflows forever exhausted, attained liberation of mind.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“Among this assembly, there are sixty bodhisattvas who, in the past, have personally approached and made offerings to five hundred buddhas. Although they have cultivated generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they did not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means; instead, they gave rise to divergent conceptions and practiced divergent conduct. Therefore, although they have now heard the Great Dharma, they have exhausted all outflows and attained liberation of mind.”

Śāriputra! Although the assembly of bodhisattvas possesses the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the bodhisattva path, if they do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they will realize the limit of reality and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
“Śāriputra! It is as if there were a bird whose body was vast, measuring one hundred yojanas or even five hundred, yet its wings and feathers were either not yet fully formed or had already decayed.”
Suppose this bird, having descended from that Trāyastriṃśa Heaven toward Jambudvīpa, were suddenly to think midway:
"I shall now return to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
"What do you think?
Would this bird be able to return to the Heaven of the Thirty-three?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Suppose this bird were to form this aspiration midway:
'Upon reaching Jambudvīpa, may my body be without injury and without suffering.
What do you think?"
"Can this bird's wish be fulfilled?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Bhagavān!
When this bird reaches this Jambudvīpa, its body will certainly suffer injury and pain; it will either be near death or meet its end."
"Why is this? Because this bird's body is large, and it has fallen from a great distance; furthermore, its wings and feathers have not yet developed, or they are withered and decayed.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Similarly, there are sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who, although they have resolved upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and have already passed through as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, diligently practicing generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and also cultivating the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—if they do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they will realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.”

Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattvas recollect the aggregates of morality up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of all Buddhas of the three times, their minds grasp at signs. They do not know the true merits of these five aggregates as they really are; merely hearing empty sounds, they grasp at signs, become attached to them, and dedicate [their merit] toward Bodhi, thereby falling into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because it is the natural law that these bodhisattvas lack the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if bodhisattvas are devoid of skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), then even though they possess immeasurable stores of merit, they may or may not attain awakening.”
"Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain awakening must certainly not remain far removed from the perfection of wisdom and skillful means.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "It is so!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 561.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 562.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

The Fifteenth Chapter on the Tathāgata, Part Two of the Fifth Division. At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the Brahma world, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha together, saying:

“This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand; likewise, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also most profound and extremely difficult to believe and attain.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, unsurpassed enlightenment is not difficult to attain through faith."
Why is this? Because all dharmas are ultimately empty; within emptiness, there is no dharma that can be used to believe in or realize other dharmas. Why is that?
Since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, if one were to teach such a phenomenon for the sake of permanently severing such phenomena, that teaching itself is also empty.

For this reason, regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, both the subject who realizes it and the object realized, as well as the knower and the known, are all empty and quiescent. Therefore, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is not difficult to believe and understand, nor is it difficult to realize; because all phenomena are without exception empty, by believing and knowing them thus, one attains realization.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because one who can believe in and realize unsurpassed enlightenment cannot be apprehended; because unsurpassed enlightenment is not substantially existent; and because there is no accumulation [of it], it is said to be difficult to believe in and attain."
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Because all phenomena are ultimately empty, unsurpassed enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe in and attain."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and are all like space.
For example, space does not form such a thought:
"I shall attain supreme enlightenment with faith.
All phenomena are likewise; therefore, supreme perfect enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain with faith.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If the Buddha’s bodhi were not difficult to believe and attain, then there should not be such a multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and yet subsequently regress; therefore, the Buddha’s bodhi is extremely difficult to believe and attain.
Subhūti replied, "What do you think?
Does form regress from awakening?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness regress from awakening? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Subhūti!
Is there any dharma apart from form that regresses from awakening?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! Apart from feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that regresses from awakening?"
Śāriputra said, “No, Subhūti!”
“Does the suchness of form regress from awakening?
Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Subhūti!
Does the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever regress from awakening?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! Apart from the suchness of form, is there any dharma that regresses from awakening?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Is there any dharma apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness that can regress from enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Subhūti! Does suchness ever regress from awakening?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! Is there any turning back from awakening apart from suchness?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"If all phenomena, by virtue of their truth and their abiding nature, are entirely non-existent and unapprehendable, what phenomenon could be said to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “According to what you have said, there is truly no dharma, nor is there any sentient being who can be said to regress from awakening.

If that is so, for what reason did the Buddha speak of three types of those dwelling in the bodhisattva vehicle? One should speak of only one, and one should not establish three distinct vehicles; there should be only the single vehicle of perfect enlightenment.”
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"One should ask Subhūti whether he admits that there is a single vehicle of the bodhisattvas;
only then may one challenge him by saying that there should be no establishment of distinctions between three vehicles, but rather only a single vehicle of perfectly complete awakening."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Is it admitted that there is such a thing as the bodhisattva vehicle?
Subhūti replied:
"Is there, within suchness, any three kinds of bodhisattvas or three vehicles?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Is there, within true suchness, even one who belongs to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas or the vehicle of the buddhas?
Śāriputra said:
"No, Subhūti! Is there any dharma whatsoever that can be seen within suchness which could be called 'one bodhisattva' or 'one vehicle'?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"If all phenomena, by virtue of their truth and their stability, are utterly non-existent and cannot be apprehended, then the three vehicles of the bodhisattva are likewise so; how can one be censured for asserting that there is one [vehicle] or that there are three?"

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing it taught that suchness has no differentiated characteristics, are not startled, not terrified, and do not sink into despondency, these bodhisattvas will swiftly realize awakening and will certainly never regress.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is well that you are now able to skillfully expound the essential Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
What you have spoken is sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha; all Tathāgatas rejoice in your teaching.

If bodhisattvas develop deep faith and understanding regarding the non-differentiated nature of the suchness of all phenomena, and upon hearing the teaching of the suchness of these phenomena, they are neither startled, nor terrified, nor do they sink into despondency, then these bodhisattvas will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will certainly never regress.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, will they certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"These bodhisattvas will certainly not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas and so forth.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If bodhisattvas wish to realize awakening, in what manner should they abide?"
"How should one train?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattvas wish to realize awakening, they should abide in equanimity toward all sentient beings; that is to say, they should give rise toward those beings to a mind of equality, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of equanimity, a mind free from differentiation, a humble mind, a mind of benefit, a mind of happiness, a mind free from anger and vexation, and a mind like that of parents. Furthermore, they should speak to them with such a mind."
"Subhūti, you should know that if bodhisattvas wish to realize awakening, they should abide in this way and train in this way.
Chapter 16: Non-Retrogression, Part Five. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what conduct, characteristics, and marks shall we recognize this non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If all bodhisattvas can know, as it truly is, the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas—though they are spoken of as being distinct—yet within the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, there is no alteration and no differentiation; they are all non-dual and indivisible.”
Although these bodhisattvas truly awaken to and enter into the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, they do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding that suchness;
although they hear that suchness and all phenomena are non-dual and indistinguishable, they harbor no doubt or obstruction;
and although they hear of the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena, they remain without attachment toward them.

These bodhisattvas never utter speech frivolously; whatever they say is always drawn from what is meaningful and beneficial. They never observe the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others, but rather preach the Dharma with impartial compassion.
If bodhisattvas accomplish such practices, characteristics, and signs, they are certain never again to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

These bodhisattvas do not regard the appearance, speech, or claims of non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brahmins, thinking that they truly know and truly see the Dharma, or that they could establish a gateway to the Dharma of right view; such a thing is impossible. They never pay homage to the celestial deities of non-Buddhists, nor do they make offerings to them in pursuit of superior merit.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

These bodhisattvas do not fall into the evil destinies, nor do they receive a female body, nor are they born into lowly lineages—except as a skillful means for the sake of liberating those sentient beings, wherein they manifest birth among them to provide for them through such inclusion."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

These bodhisattvas always delight in practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, and they are also able to skillfully encourage others to practice them; even in their dreams, they do not commit any transgression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All the various sūtras that these bodhisattvas receive, uphold, contemplate, read, and recite until they have mastered them thoroughly are entirely for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings."
He constantly reflects:
"By proclaiming and revealing this Dharma to all sentient beings, I shall cause all their aspirations regarding the Dharma to be fulfilled.

Furthermore, he takes these roots of goodness from such giving of the Dharma and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward the attainment of the omniscient wisdom (sarvajñājñāna) that he seeks.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Regarding these profound Dharma-gates spoken by the Buddha, these bodhisattvas do not give rise to doubt or hesitation, nor do they become bewildered; they receive them with joy and faith.
Whatever they speak is for the benefit of others; they speak with moderation and their words are gentle."
In sleep and rest, afflictions are slight and do not arise; in coming and going, entering and exiting, the mind is never deluded or mistaken.
At all times one dwells securely in right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*);

one's deportment in advancing and retreating is likewise so. Wherever one travels, one must observe the ground; with steady composure and focused attention, one walks while looking straight ahead. In movement and speech, one is always free from abruptness or violence.
All bedding and clothing they use are always fragrant and clean, free from any foul odors or impurities; they are also devoid of filth, grease, lice, nits, and other such insects.
They constantly delight in tranquility and are forever free from illness, with no eighty thousand families of worms within their bodies.
Why is this so? Because these bodhisattvas’ roots of goodness are superior and transcend the world; as their roots of goodness gradually increase, so too do their body and mind become purified.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is the mind of this bodhisattva pure?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As these roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas gradually increase, so too do all forms of flattery, crookedness, and deceit never again arise within their minds."

By virtue of these causes and conditions, all afflictions and other unwholesome states are forever extinguished; one also transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, swiftly proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. From this, one should know that the mind is eternally pure.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! These bodhisattvas do not value gain and offerings, nor do they pursue fame and reputation; their minds are free from envy and stinginess, and their bodies are without fault. When they hear the most profound Dharma, their minds are not confused or mistaken; their wisdom is deep and firm, and they respectfully accept it with faith. Whatever they hear, they are able to integrate it into the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Even all the worldly activities they perform are integrated into the *dharmatā* through skillful means based on the *prajñāpāramitā*; they do not perceive even a single thing that transcends the *dharmatā*. Should there be anything that does not accord with the *dharmatā*, they are still able to use skillful means to integrate it into the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, whereby they do not perceive anything that transcends the *dharmatā*."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose an evil Māra were to manifest before these bodhisattvas and conjure up eight great hells; within each hell, he conjures up immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, all of whom are being scorched by intersecting, fierce flames. He then says to the bodhisattva:
'These bodhisattvas have all received the prediction of non-retrogression, yet they have fallen into such great hells and constantly undergo such fierce and intense suffering.'"
"Since you have all received the prediction of non-retrogression, you shall likewise undergo such great suffering as this.

Therefore, you should quickly abandon the mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); by doing so, you may escape this suffering and be reborn among the gods or among humans, where you will enjoy wealth, nobility, sovereignty, and every pleasure."
At that time, when the bodhisattvas saw and heard this matter, their minds remained unmoved and they were neither startled nor suspicious; they thought only this:

"If there are bodhisattvas who have already received the prediction of non-retrogression from enlightenment, it is absolutely impossible that they would again fall into the evil destinies and undergo various sufferings like foolish ordinary beings."
"What we have now seen and heard must surely be the work and speech of an evil Māra; none of it is real.
Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose an evil Māra were to assume the form of a śramaṇa and come to where these bodhisattvas are, speaking these words:

"All those profound sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom that you have previously heard, received, upheld, read, and recited are all false teachings; you should quickly abandon them and not consider them to be true."
If you are able to swiftly abandon these, I shall teach you the truly pure Buddha-dharma, enabling you to quickly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
What you have previously heard is not the true word of the Buddha; it is a deceptive compilation by poets. What I am teaching is the true word of the Buddha.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
if bodhisattvas, upon hearing such words, experience agitation, fear, or doubt, it should be known that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression.

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such words, do not experience fear or doubt, but abide in accordance with the nature of phenomena—which is unconditioned, signless, and unborn—it should be known that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression. Whatever these bodhisattvas undertake, they do not rely on the words of others, nor do they waver by following the instructions of others."
