Just as an Arhat, in all that he does, does not rely on the words of others but directly realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without confusion or doubt, such that no Māras can shake him; so too is it with a Bodhisattva who has reached the stage of non-retrogression: no Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, followers of external paths, or any Māras can destroy his resolve or cause him to fall back from his pursuit of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose an evil Māra were to come to where these bodhisattvas dwell, falsely appearing as a friend and saying to them:
'The practices you are engaged in are the dharmas of saṃsāra; they are not the practice of awakening.'"

"You all should now cultivate the path that exhausts suffering, so as to quickly end all sufferings and attain parinirvāṇa. You should even feel weary of and abandon this present body of suffering; how much more so should you do so regarding pleasant sensations and the body of suffering in the future!"
"You should examine yourself and abandon what you previously believed.
When those bodhisattvas heard these words, their minds were not startled or doubtful; they thought only this:
"One who speaks thus must certainly be an evil Māra."
Then, that evil Māra spoke again to the Bodhisattva:
“Do you wish to hear of the bodhisattvas’ fruitless practices?

This refers to those bodhisattvas who, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, make offerings to the Buddhas with immeasurable kinds of supreme and exquisite requisites; who further cultivate immeasurable kinds of difficult ascetic practices (brahmacarya) in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and who attend upon and serve as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, inquiring about the immeasurable and boundless path that a bodhisattva should cultivate and how one should abide therein.”
"How should one practice?
How should one train?

Thus, the Bodhisattvas of the path were questioned by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who explained it to them in successive order. Those Bodhisattvas dwelt according to the teaching, practiced according to the teaching, and trained according to the teaching; yet even after the passage of immeasurable eons, they were still unable to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they sought—how much less so could you now possibly attain it!
At that time, although the Bodhisattva heard these words, his mind remained unmoved and he felt no doubt.
Then, that evil Māra again manifested at that spot the forms of immeasurable bhikṣus and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"All these bhikṣus, in the past, practiced immeasurable kinds of difficult ascetic disciplines for countless kalpas, yet they were unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi; they have now all regressed and abide in the fruit of arhatship. How can you possibly realize bodhi?"
When those bodhisattvas have seen and heard this, they immediately think:

"This must certainly be the evil Māra creating such disturbances to trouble us; it is certain that there are no bodhisattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom who, upon reaching the stage of fulfillment, fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and instead regress to abide in the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
He further thought to himself:

"If bodhisattvas practice the path to enlightenment as taught by the Buddha and yet do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such a thing is simply impossible. One should know that what I have now seen and heard is surely the work and the speech of a wicked Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose an evil Māra, assuming the form of a bhikṣu, should come to where these bodhisattvas are and speak as follows: 'The knowledge of all modes is equal to space;

its nature is the absence of intrinsic nature, being empty of self-characteristic from the very beginning. All phenomena are likewise entirely non-existent. Within this, there is no dharma that can be called the 'realizer,' nor is there any dharma that can be called the 'object realized. The place of realization, the time of realization, and that by which one realizes—all these are unapprehendable.'"

Since all phenomena are equal to space, having non-existence as their nature and being empty of intrinsic characteristics from the very beginning, for what reason do you undergo such toil and hardship in vain, seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"All that you have previously heard regarding the multitude of bodhisattvas who should seek unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is all the teaching of Māra, not the true word of the Buddha.
You should abandon the mind of great enlightenment; do not pointlessly undergo hardships for others' sake."
When these bodhisattvas hear those words, they are able to know them as they truly are:
"This is the work of Māra, who wishes to cause my great bodhicitta to regress and fail; I should now further strengthen my mind and must not believe or accept what Māra says."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If these bodhisattvas wish to discipline their minds and enter the four dhyānas, they can enter them at will and dwell therein with mastery; yet, in order to deliver sentient beings, they return to birth in the desire realm. Although born in the desire realm, they are not defiled by desire, nor do they ever fall away from the dhyānas they have cultivated."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas do not prize fame nor cling to renown; they harbor no ill will or resentment toward sentient beings, but always desire to bring them benefit and happiness.
Whether coming or going, entering or exiting, they possess no distracted mind, and in all their movements and postures, they constantly abide in right mindfulness."
For the sake of sentient beings, although they dwell in a household, they do not give rise to greedy attachment therein;
although they manifest the enjoyment of desires, they are constantly weary of and terrified by them, like one traversing a perilous path whose mind is ever-stricken with alarm;
although they have food to eat, they remain anxious and uneasy, thinking only of when they might emerge from this dangerous ordeal.
Although they manifest the enjoyment of various kinds of precious wealth, they do not give rise to craving or attachment toward them;
they do not sustain themselves through wrong livelihood or unrighteous means, preferring death over harming others.
Why is this? These bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;

they are the most honored among humans, the virtuous sages among humans, the dragon-elephants among humans, the lotuses among humans, the charioteers among humans, and the heroic and valiant among humans. Having originally sought to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, they now dwell in the household life as a skillful means to provide abundant aid; how could they harm others for the sake of their own livelihood?
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas are sustained by the power of skillful means (upāyakauśalya) within the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, Subhūti!

These bodhisattvas are constantly followed and guarded on their left and right by the Vajradhara yakṣa lords, who secretly protect them so that they cannot be harmed in body or mind by the power of any humans, non-humans, or malevolent spirits.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, these bodhisattvas, until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, remain serene in body and mind and are never deranged or confused. They possess the marks of a great man with all faculties fully perfected; their mental conduct is harmonious and virtuous, and they constantly cultivate a pure livelihood. They do not practice illusionist arts, divination, prognostication of good or bad fortune, incantations, exorcisms of spirits, or the compounding of medicinal decoctions. They do not entice or deceive lowly men, nor do they curry favor with the noble and powerful. They do not treat sages and worthies with contempt, nor do they form intimate attachments to men or women. For the sake of fame or profit, they do not praise themselves or disparage others. They do not look about with lustful intent or engage in frivolous laughter. Their precepts and views are pure, and their will and nature are sincere and honest.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Although these bodhisattvas have attained skill in the various worldly arts and crafts, they do not become attached to them, because they realize that all phenomena are unapprehendable and because all such things are comprised within frivolous speech and wrong livelihood.

Although they are also well-versed in the secular treatises of non-Buddhist outsiders, they do not take pleasure in or become attached to them, because they realize that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness."
Furthermore, the principles and phenomena taught in the secular treatises of non-Buddhists often involve exaggeration or omission; therefore, they do not accord with the path of a bodhisattva.
"Moreover, Subhūti!..."
These bodhisattvas also possess other practices, characteristics, and signs, which I shall now analyze and explain for you. That is to say,
when those bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they realize the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmas*) and take no pleasure in observing or discussing various matters,
such as affairs of state, affairs of bandits, military affairs, battles, or cities.

Regarding matters such as towns, villages, elephants, horses, carriages, clothing, food and drink, bedding, flowers and incense, the beauty or ugliness of men and women, gardens, groves, ponds, lakes, mountains, and seas, he does not delight in observing or discussing them;
nor does he delight in observing the affairs of various spirits, such as yakṣas and rākṣasas. He does not delight in observing these things.
He does not delight in observing or discussing matters such as streets, marketplaces, towers, and merchants;
he does not delight in observing or discussing matters such as singing, dancing, music, actors, and jesting;
nor does he delight in observing or discussing matters such as continents, islands, boats, rafts, bridges, and precious jewels. He does not delight in observing [any such things].
He does not delight in observing or discussing matters such as the movements of the stars, cold and heat, wind and rain, or auspicious and inauspicious events;
he does not delight in observing or discussing various doctrines that are contradictory, nor in verses and the like;
he does not delight in observing or discussing matters associated with ordinary beings, pratyekabuddhas, or śrāvakas; rather, he delights only in observing and discussing the *pāramitās*.

Regarding matters associated with the *pāramitās*, these bodhisattvas never depart from the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they ever depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*). They do not delight in discord but rejoice in harmony and the settling of disputes; they always aspire to the True Dharma and do not love what is contrary to the Dharma; they constantly yearn for virtuous friends and do not take pleasure in evil friends; they delight in uttering words of the Dharma and avoid words contrary to the Dharma; they rejoice in seeing the Tathāgatas and take joy in the community of renunciants.

Wherever in the lands of the ten directions there are Buddha-Bhagavāns proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma, they vow to be reborn there to attend upon, make offerings to, and hear the True Dharma.

These bodhisattvas mostly pass away from the heavens of the desire realm and the form realm to be born in the human realm of Jambudvīpa, specifically in the central lands. They are skilled in the arts, incantations, scriptures, geography, astronomy, and the meanings of all dharmas; or they are born in great kingdoms and great cities of the borderlands, bringing great benefit to sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas never doubt for themselves: 'Am I regressing, or am I non-regressing?
Nor do they give rise to doubt regarding the dharmas of their own stage, wondering: 'Do they exist, or do they not exist?'"

They are well able to discern all demonic activities; just as a stream-enterer never gives rise to doubt regarding the dharmas of their own stage, even if an evil Māra employs various forms of delusion and confusion, they cannot be shaken.

Just as when one has committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), that immediate state of mind constantly follows them until the end of life, cannot be abandoned, and cannot be suppressed even if other states of mind arise; so too it is with these bodhisattvas: the non-retrogressive mind constantly follows them, and as they abide on the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression, neither the gods, humans, nor asuras of the world can shake or destroy the dharmas they have attained.

They are well able to recognize all demonic activities; they are always free from doubt regarding the Dharma they have realized; even when born in other worlds, they do not give rise to thoughts associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor do they doubt that they will realize unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment in a future life.
"Not abiding in their own stage, they do not follow other conditions, and no one can destroy them regarding the dharmas of their own stage. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattvas have accomplished unshakable and non-retrogressive wisdom; all adverse conditions cannot tilt or move them, for their minds are as firm and solid as a diamond."
Suppose a wicked Māra, assuming the form of a Buddha, were to come to that person's place and say:
"You should now seek the fruit of Arhatship; exhaust all outflows forever and enter parinirvāṇa."
"You are not yet fit to receive the prediction of great enlightenment, nor have you yet realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

You do not yet possess the practices, characteristics, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression; therefore, the Tathāgata should not grant you the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
When those bodhisattvas hear those words, their minds remain unshaken and do not retreat; they are neither startled nor terrified, but think only this:
"This must be an evil Māra or a member of Māra’s retinue who has manifested as a Buddha-image and come to me to speak these words; if it were the true Buddha speaking, there would be no difference."
When a bodhisattva hears those words, they should be able to observe and reflect in this way:

"This must certainly be Māra, who has transformed himself into the likeness of a Buddha, in order to lead me away from the profound Prajñāpāramitā and cause me to abandon unsurpassed bodhi; therefore, I should not follow what he says."
At that time, Māra was struck with terror and immediately vanished.
These bodhisattvas were firmly established in the stage of non-retrogression; long ago, the Buddhas of the past had already bestowed upon them the prophecy of great enlightenment.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas possess the practices, characteristics, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression, they are able to recognize the activities of evil Māras, causing them to vanish and never appear again.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas protect and uphold the true Dharma, not sparing even their own bodies or lives, let alone other treasures, friends, or kinsmen!"
To protect the True Dharma with courageous diligence, one should constantly reflect:
"This True Dharma is the pure Dharmakāya of all Buddhas, which all Tathāgatas revere and make offerings to."
"I now protect and uphold such True Dharma; this is precisely to protect and uphold the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas.
He further reflects:
"Such True Dharma belongs universally to the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time, and I too am included among the number of future Buddhas."
The Buddha has already bestowed upon me the prophecy of great enlightenment; the true Dharma of all Buddhas is now my own possession, and I shall now protect my own true Dharma.
When I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I too shall proclaim this Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

These bodhisattvas, seeing such benefit and purpose, uphold and protect the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; they do not begrudge their own bodies, lives, relatives, or precious wealth, remaining ever free from weariness until the attainment of Bodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, have no confusion and no doubt; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, never forgetting it.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"These bodhisattvas, upon merely hearing the Buddha’s words, are without confusion or doubt and never forget them; they are likewise able to do so when hearing the true Dharma spoken by bodhisattvas and śrāvakas."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"These bodhisattvas universally hear the speech, sounds, characters, and meanings of all sentient beings; they are able to penetrate them all, remaining without confusion, without doubt, and never forgetting."

Why is this so? Because these bodhisattvas have attained the endurance of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and have thoroughly mastered the true nature of all phenomena; thus, upon hearing them, they accord with the teachings like water flowing through the ears, remaining free from doubt or confusion. Furthermore, because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, they are always able to remember them and never forget.
“Subhūti, you should know that these are the practices, tokens, and signs of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Chapter 17: On the Conduct of Desire (Rāgacarita-varga), Part Five, Section One. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed,
World-Honored One!
These bodhisattvas have accomplished such a great accumulation of merit.”

"Blessed One, you are able to explain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges the practices, characteristics, and signs of non-retrogression; we pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will further proclaim the points of meaning associated with the profound Prajñāpāramitā, so that all bodhisattvas may dwell therein, cultivate the practices for awakening, and swiftly attain perfection!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
That you are now able to ask such a question—
listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you.

Subhūti, you should know that the thematic domains associated with the profound perfection of wisdom are designated by the terms: emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, effortlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-existence, tranquility, detachment, and nirvāṇa.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it only this dharma that is called the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, or are all dharmas likewise named the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All other dharmas may also be called the locus of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this so?"
It means that all form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also called "profound. "Subhūti,
why are form through to consciousness also called profound?"
It is because True Suchness is profound that form, and so on up to consciousness, are also called profound.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Where there is no form, it is called the profundity of form; and so on, in detail, until: where there is no consciousness, it is called the profundity of consciousness.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous,
World-Honored One!”
"By means of subtle and wondrous skillful methods, he dispels the five aggregates and reveals nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so! It is so!"
"So it is! If bodhisattvas are able to carefully and thoroughly examine the points of meaning associated with this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should form this thought:
'I should now abide as taught by this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; I should now train as explained in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.'"

If these bodhisattvas, by means of such thorough and discerning observation based on the meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practice with diligence for even a single day, the mass of merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless.

"Suppose a person of greedy temperament who is also prone to discursive thought makes an appointment with a beautiful woman; if she is obstructed and fails to meet him at the appointed time, this person's lustful mind becomes intensely inflamed and flows forth."
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Where does that person's desirous mind turn?"
“World-Honored One!
This person’s mind turns toward a woman with desire, thinking:
‘When will she come so that we may meet and enjoy ourselves here in pleasure and sport?’”
“Sudhana! What do you think?
How many thoughts of desire arise in that person during a day and night?”
“World-Honored One!
This person has many thoughts of desire day and night.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva, relying on the meaning associated with the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), should examine it with careful discernment and practice with diligence for even a single day, the number of kalpas of cyclic existence they transcend would equal the quantity of desire-thoughts arising in a person of greedy temperament over the course of a single day and night."

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattvas, in accordance with the points of meaning associated with this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, examine them with discernment and practice with diligence, they are able to liberate themselves from all faults that obstruct unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, those bodhisattvas who rely on the points of meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and examine them with discernment, practicing with diligence and without weariness, will swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva, relying on the meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, examines it with discernment and practices with diligent application for even a single day and night, the merit they obtain will surpass the merit of all other bodhisattvas who, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, practice the giving of alms apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—it is immeasurable and boundless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva, relying on the meaning associated with the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), examines it with discernment and practices with diligence for even a single day and night, the merit they obtain surpasses the merit of all bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound perfection of wisdom, practice the giving of various offerings to stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the merit they obtain by diligently practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for even a single day and night surpasses the immeasurable and boundless merit obtained by other bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, diligently practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for even a single day and night, the merit they obtain by bestowing the sublime Dharma upon sentient beings surpasses the merit obtained by bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, bestow the sublime Dharma upon sentient beings for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—[the former merit is] immeasurable and boundless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas abide according to what is taught in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and other roots of goodness for even a single day and night, the merit they obtain will surpass the merit obtained by those bodhisattvas who, apart from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and other roots of goodness for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—indeed, it is immeasurable and boundless."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for even a single day and night practices various kinds of material giving and the giving of Dharma, dwelling in a secluded place with focused mindfulness and reflection, the merit obtained from dedicating those previously practiced various meritorious deeds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment surpasses the merit obtained by all other bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practice various kinds of material giving and the giving of Dharma, dwell in secluded places with focused mindfulness and reflection, and dedicate their previously practiced various meritorious deeds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, even for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for even a single day and night, and—universally taking as their object the roots of virtue and merit of the Buddhas and their disciples of the three times—unites, weighs, and rejoices in them before them, and dedicates that merit toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the merit obtained will surpass that of all other bodhisattvas who, apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, dwell for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, universally taking as their object the roots of virtue and merit of the Buddhas and their disciples of the three times, uniting, weighing, and rejoicing in them before them, and dedicating that merit toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; [the former] is immeasurable and boundless."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata has often said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and are not at all substantially real.”
"For what reason do these bodhisattvas obtain immeasurable and boundless merit?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"These bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and also constantly observe that the wholesome deeds they perform are empty, non-existent, false, and unreal. To the extent that they observe these performed wholesome deeds as empty, non-existent, false, and unreal, to that same extent they are able not to be separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. To the extent that they are not separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, to that same extent the merit they obtain is immeasurable and boundless."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the distinction between the meanings of 'immeasurable' (apramāṇa) and 'boundless' (ananta)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"To say 'immeasurable' means that within this state, all measure has forever ceased;
to say 'boundless' means that at this point, numbers cannot be exhausted.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is there any cause and condition by which form, and so on up to consciousness, are also immeasurable and boundless?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There is indeed a cause and condition by which form, and so on up to consciousness, are immeasurable and boundless.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions are form through to consciousness immeasurable and boundless?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because form up to consciousness are all empty by nature, they are immeasurable and boundless.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it only form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are empty, or are all phenomena entirely empty?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I say that there are no dharmas that are not empty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the designation for 'immeasurable and boundless'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"'Immeasurable and boundless' is a designation for emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it only that which is immeasurable and boundless that is empty, signless, and wishless, or is there further meaning beyond this?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Have I not taught that there is no dharma-gate whatsoever that is not empty?"
Subhūti replied,
“The Tathāgata has always taught that there is no dharma-gate whatsoever that is not empty.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Emptiness is inexhaustible; emptiness is immeasurable; emptiness is boundless; emptiness is the ultimate meaning.
Therefore, Subhūti, although all dharma-gates have various distinctions in their verbal expressions, they do not differ in their meaning."

“Subhūti, you should know that the principle of the emptiness of all phenomena is ultimately ineffable; yet, through the skillful means of the Tathāgata, it is described as inexhaustible, or as immeasurable, or as boundless, or as empty, or as signless, or as wishless, or as unconditioned, or as non-arising, or as non-ceasing, or as non-existent, or as quiescent, or as free from defilement, or as nirvāṇa.”
"All such immeasurable Dharma gates as these are in truth without difference in meaning; they are all the skillful means through which the Tathāgata has expounded them.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!"
"Bhagavān!
The true nature of all phenomena, through skillful means, is ineffable, yet it is expediently revealed for the sake of sentient beings.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the true nature of all phenomena is ineffable."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, and there is nothing that can be proclaimed as 'ultimately empty.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Is there any increase or decrease in the ineffable meaning?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, there likewise should be no increase or decrease."

If these six perfections are likewise without increase or decrease, how can a bodhisattva, by means of perfections that neither increase nor decrease, seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and be able to draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"If bodhisattvas increase or decrease the six perfections, they will be unable to draw near to unsurpassed enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!"

It is so! The meaning of the perfections is ineffable and is neither increased nor diminished; yet, when Bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, they do not form the thought:
"These six perfections are subject to increase or decrease."
They maintain only this thought:
"There are merely names and concepts, which are called 'generosity' up to and including 'perfection of wisdom.

These bodhisattvas, practicing generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom, take these six types of mental engagements as their practice; together with the minds and roots of virtue arising therefrom, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Just as the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is subtle, wondrous, and profound, one should generate dedication; through the superior power of this skillful means of dedication, one is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'unsurpassed perfect enlightenment'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The suchness of all phenomena is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, you should know this:
because the suchness of all phenomena neither increases nor decreases, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas likewise neither increases nor decreases.”
If bodhisattvas frequently abide in such mental attention associated with thusness, they will draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Although the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, one does not lose the mental attention directed toward true suchness;
although the pāramitās neither increase nor decrease, one does not lose the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that is sought.
If bodhisattvas abide in such mental engagement with true thusness and practice the six perfections, they draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do these bodhisattvas approach awakening through the arising of the initial thought, or do they approach awakening through the arising of the final thought?"
If the initial thought arises and can approach bodhi, at the time the initial thought arises, the subsequent thought has not yet arisen; thus, there is no sense of conjunction.
If the subsequent thought arises and can approach bodhi, at the time the subsequent thought arises, the preceding thought has already ceased; thus, there is no sense of conjunction.
In this way, when one examines and analyzes preceding and succeeding moments of mind and mental factors, there is no sense of their combination; how, then, can roots of goodness be accumulated?
If roots of goodness cannot be accumulated, how can a bodhisattva draw near to enlightenment?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When a lamp is lit, is it the initial flame that burns the wick, or is it the final flame that burns the wick?"

Subhūti replied, “As I understand it, it is not by the first flame that the wick is burned, yet it is not apart from the first flame; nor is it by the last flame that the wick is burned, yet it is not apart from the last flame.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is the wick burned?"
Subhūti replied,
“In the world it is clearly seen that the wick has indeed been burned.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The Bodhisattva is also like this: it is not by the arising of the initial mind that one can approach enlightenment, yet one does not depart from the initial mind; it is not by the arising of the final mind that one can approach enlightenment, yet one does not depart from the final mind. Rather, through the skillful means of practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Bodhisattvas cause all roots of goodness to grow and reach fulfillment, thereby enabling them to approach enlightenment.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This principle of dependent origination is profound; it is not by means of the arising of preceding and succeeding moments of mind that one can approach enlightenment, nor is it apart from the arising of preceding and succeeding moments of mind that one can approach enlightenment, yet it is through these that bodhisattvas are able to approach enlightenment."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Once the mind has ceased, can it arise again?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
This mind has already ceased and cannot arise again.
"What do you think?
If a mind has already arisen, does it have the nature of cessation?"
"So it is, World-Honored One!
If a mind has already arisen, it necessarily possesses the nature of cessation."
“What do you think?
Is a mind subject to cessation not destined to cease? “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!
A mind subject to cessation is certain to cease.
“What do you think?”
"Can a mind that is not subject to cessation be produced? "No,
World-Honored One!"
"A mind that is not subject to cessation has no sense of being produced. "What do you think?
Can a mind that is not subject to production be ceased?"
"No, World-Honored One!
A mind that is an unarisen dharma has no meaning of cessation."
“What do you think?
Regarding phenomena that are without arising and ceasing, can the mind arise and cease? “No, sir!”
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, the mind has no meaning of arising or ceasing.
“What do you think?”
"If a dharma has already ceased, can it cease again? "No,
World-Honored One!"
"If a phenomenon has already ceased, it cannot cease again.
"What do you think? If a phenomenon has already arisen, can it arise again?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If a dharma has already arisen, it cannot arise again."
“What do you think?
Does the true nature of all phenomena have arising and ceasing?
“No, [World-Honored One].”
“World-Honored One!
The true nature of all dharmas is without arising and without cessation.
“What do you think?”
“Does the mind abide as the suchness of the mind? “It is so,
World-Honored One!”
"Just as the suchness of the mind, so does the mind abide. "What do you think?
If the mind abides as suchness, does that mind abide eternally as the nature of suchness and the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi)?"
"No, World-Honored One!
This mind is not like true thusness or the limit of reality; its nature is not eternally abiding."
"What do you think?
Is the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena extremely profound? "It is so!"
“World-Honored One!
The suchness of all dharmas is exceedingly profound. “What do you think?”
"Is suchness itself the mind? "No,
World-Honored One!"
"What do you think?
Is there a mind apart from *tathatā* (suchness)? "No, indeed!"
“World-Honored One!
What do you think? Is this very mind itself suchness?”
"No, World-Honored One! What do you think?"
"Is there suchness apart from the mind? "No,
World-Honored One!"
“What do you think? Is it possible for suchness to see suchness? “No, it is not.”
“World-Honored One!
What do you think? Do you perceive any real, true suchness?”
"No, World-Honored One! What do you think?"
"If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, are they practicing the profound perfection of wisdom? "It is so,
World-Honored One!"
"If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 562 (and 566).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Part Five, Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on the Temperament of Greed, Part Two. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, where do they practice?
Subhūti replied,
"If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, there is no place at all where they practice."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas that manifest do not undergo transformation.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, what kind of ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) do they practice?
Subhūti replied,
"If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the ultimate truth."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When bodhisattvas practice the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), do they grasp at signs within that ultimate truth?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do these bodhisattvas, while not apprehending signs within the ultimate truth, nevertheless practice by means of signs?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do these bodhisattvas, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), not practice by way of signs in order to destroy signs?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do these bodhisattvas, regarding the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), not destroy signs while yet eliminating signs?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If these bodhisattvas do not dismantle or dispel the marks of ultimate reality, how can they eliminate the perception of grasping at marks?
Subhūti replied:
"These bodhisattvas do not form such thoughts as:
'I am now destroying signs, dispelling signs, and severing perceptions; yet I have not yet trained in the path that severs perceptions.'"

If bodhisattvas who practice with diligence the path of the perception of cessation were not yet endowed with the Buddha-dharmas, they would fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; however, these bodhisattvas possess skillful means such that, although they deeply understand the faults of signs and the perception of grasping at signs, they do not eliminate them, but rather swiftly sever this perception and realize the signless.
"Why is this? Because all the Buddha-dharmas have not yet been perfected.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva practices the three doors of liberation while dreaming, does it bring any increase to the profound perfection of wisdom?
If practicing the three doors of liberation during the waking state brings an increase to the profound perfection of wisdom, then practicing them while dreaming should likewise bring an increase!"
"Why is this? Because the Buddha has taught that there is no distinction between dreaming and waking.
Subhūti replied:

"If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* while awake, they are said to be 'dwelling securely in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*'; likewise, when these bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their dreams, they are also said to be 'dwelling securely in the three doors of liberation within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.'"
"It is likewise with the ability to increase [the roots of virtue] through the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, for there is no difference in meaning between dreaming and waking.
Śāriputra asked,
"Is there an increase in the karma created within a dream?"

Since the Buddha taught that all phenomena are unreal, like dreams, the various karmas performed within a dream should not result in any increase [of merit or demerit]; it is only upon waking, through recollection and conceptual discrimination, that an increase occurs.
Subhūti replied:

"If sentient beings were to take the life of another in a dream, and upon waking, they were to engage in conceptualization and discrimination, thinking with self-congratulation, 'I have killed,' would the karma they have created not increase?"
Śāriputra said:

"If there were no objective referent, neither volition nor karma could arise; it is only when there is an objective referent that volition and karma originate. With respect to what, then, do the volitions and karma in a dream arise?"
Subhūti replied: “So it is! So it is!”
Whether in a dream or while awake, volitional action does not arise without an object of perception; it is only when there is an object of perception that volitional action arises.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
It is because cognitive wisdom functions with respect to the various signs of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that defilement or purification arises therefrom;
if there were no such signs of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, cognitive wisdom would not function, and neither defilement nor purification would exist.
"From this it is known that whether in a dream or while awake, mental karma arises only when there is an object of perception; if there is no object of perception, mental karma does not arise.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"The Buddha has taught that all objects of perception are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); how then can it be said that mental karma arises when there is an object of perception, and that it does not arise when there is no object of perception?"
Subhūti replied:

"Although all volitional actions and their objective referents are devoid of intrinsic nature, because one’s own mind grasps signs and engages in conceptual differentiation, it is conventionally designated that there are objective referents from which volitional actions arise; yet these referents do not exist apart from the mind."
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva practices giving while dreaming, and having given, dedicates it toward unexcelled enlightenment, does that bodhisattva truly dedicate the gift toward unexcelled Buddha-enlightenment?"
Subhūti replied, “The Bodhisattva Maitreya has long ago received the prophecy of great enlightenment; you should question him, for he will certainly answer.”
Then, Śāriputra, having been addressed by Subhūti as he had spoken, respectfully questioned the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya said to Śāriputra:
"Who is this so-called 'Bodhisattva Maitreya' who claims to be able to answer the Venerable One's question?"
Is it form? Is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Or is it the emptiness of form?
Is it because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty?
Furthermore, form is not the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and thus cannot answer the Venerable’s question;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and thus cannot answer the Venerable’s question either.
The emptiness of form is not the Bodhisattva Maitreya, nor can it answer the Venerable One's question;
the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not the Bodhisattva Maitreya, nor can it answer the Venerable One's question.

I do not perceive any dharma that can be named "Maitreya Bodhisattva," nor do I perceive any dharma that is able to answer, any dharma that is answered, the place of answering, the time of answering, or even that by which one answers. All these I likewise do not perceive.

I do not perceive any dharma that can bestow a prediction, nor any dharma that is predicted; I likewise do not perceive the place of prediction, the time of prediction, or that by which the prediction is made. Why is this?
"Śāriputra! Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and because upon ultimate investigation they cannot be apprehended.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Maitreya, saying:
“Virtuous one, is the Dharma you have taught exactly as it was realized?
Maitreya replied,
“The Dharma I have taught is not exactly as it was realized.”
"Why is this? Because the Dharma realized by me is ineffable.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
“Maitreya Bodhisattva possesses profound awakening-wisdom; having practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a long night, he is able to speak thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Śāriputra’s mind, immediately addressed him, saying:
“What do you think?”
"By means of this Dharma you have become an Arhat; do you perceive this Dharma as something that can be expressed?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) realized therein is likewise ineffable.”
These bodhisattvas, through their skillful means, do not form such thoughts as:
"By means of this dharma, I have already received a prediction regarding great enlightenment, I am now receiving a prediction, or I shall receive a prediction."
They do not form this thought:
"By means of this dharma, I shall realize awakening.

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). They have no fear regarding the attainment of awakening because they know with certainty that they shall realize it. These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, are not startled, terrified, or submerged when hearing the most profound teachings.
"These bodhisattvas have no fear even when in wildernesses inhabited by fierce beasts. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattvas, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, are able to relinquish all that they possess, both internal and external, and constantly maintain this thought:"
"May these various beasts of prey devour my body; I shall give it to them so that they may be fully satisfied.
By this root of virtue, may I swiftly bring the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) to fulfillment and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that, when I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there shall be no animals or hungry ghosts whatsoever in my buddha-field.
"Furthermore, these bodhisattvas have no fear even when in wilderness regions infested with wicked bandits. Why is this?

Because these bodhisattvas, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, are able to relinquish all internal and external possessions and cultivate various virtues; they have no regard or stinginess for their bodies, lives, or wealth, and constantly maintain this thought:"
"If sentient beings should come in competition to plunder my various requisites, or if they should even take my life on that account, I shall not give rise to anger or resentment toward them."

By this cause and condition, may my perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) be swiftly fulfilled, and may I quickly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that, when I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, there shall be no harm from calamities or hostile thieves within my buddha-field; for because my buddha-field is utterly pure, there shall likewise be no other evils.
“If these bodhisattvas find themselves in a wilderness devoid of water, they shall have no fear, and they will think:
‘I shall proclaim the unsurpassed, sublime Dharma to sever the disease of craving in all sentient beings.’”

Even if my life were to end through this thirst, I shall certainly not abandon the mental engagement of great compassion toward all sentient beings, but shall instead bestow the water of the sublime Dharma.
How extraordinary!
How meager their merit!
"These sentient beings dwell in such a world devoid of water.
I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that when I realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, there shall be no such parched wilderness lacking water within my buddha-field.

I shall employ skillful means to exhort all sentient beings to cultivate superior meritorious deeds, ensuring that wherever they may be, they are fully provided with the eight qualities of auspicious water."
“Furthermore, these bodhisattvas have no fear even when dwelling in lands of famine, and they think to themselves:

‘I shall diligently purify a buddha-field; when I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there shall be no such famines as these in my buddha-field. All sentient beings shall be endowed with happiness, and whatever they require shall arrive immediately upon their thought, just as everything desired is obtained in the heavens.’”

I shall arouse firm and fierce diligence so that the Dharma-wishes of all sentient beings may be fulfilled, and that at all times and in all places, all sentient beings may lack nothing in terms of any kind of requisite conditions.
"If bodhisattvas are free from such fear, they will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
These bodhisattvas likewise have no fear when encountering epidemics."
Why is this? These bodhisattvas constantly and critically contemplate:
"There is no dharma called 'sickness,' nor is there one who is sick; all things are empty and should not be feared."

I shall thus diligently cultivate correct practice so that, when I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all sentient beings within my buddha-field will be free from the three types of illness; they will energetically cultivate sublime and virtuous dharmas, never becoming weary or negligent, as the Buddha has taught.
“If these bodhisattvas contemplate awakening, even though it may take a long time to attain, they will have no fear. Why is this?

Although the number of kalpas in the past limit is immeasurable, it is formed through the accumulation of recollection and discrimination within the span of a single thought-moment; one should know that the number of kalpas in the future is likewise so. Therefore, a bodhisattva should not conceive the notion of vast duration therein and give rise to fear.”
Why is this? Because the duration of kalpas in both the past and future limits is, in all cases, associated with a single moment of mind (*citta-ksana*).

Thus, a bodhisattva who is able to contemplate fearful matters with careful discernment and does not give rise to fear will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Chapter 18: Sisters, Part Five, Chapter Eighteen on Sisters. At that time, a goddess within the assembly rose from her seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared her right shoulder while her right knee touched the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I too have no fear in this matter; I vow that when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I shall likewise preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Having spoken these words, he took exquisite golden flowers and, with reverent sincerity, scattered them over the Tathāgata.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, these golden flowers leaped up into the void and remained suspended there in profusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his face issued forth a golden radiance that illuminated the ten directions and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, having seen and heard this, Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile? The manifestation of a smile by all Buddhas is never without cause or condition.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In a future age, this goddess shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; the kalpa shall be named Star-Parable, and the Buddha’s name shall be Golden Flower."

Ānanda, you should know that this goddess has now received her final female body; once she has cast off this body, she will receive a male body and shall never again be female for as long as the future endures.

After passing away from here, she will be reborn in the eastern realm of Akṣobhya Buddha, where she will diligently practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya). In that world, this girl shall be named Suvarṇapuṣpā.
After passing away from the world of Akṣobhya Buddha, she will again be reborn in other buddha-fields; wherever she is born, she will never be separated from a Buddha.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, from one palace to another, enjoys pleasures and delights until the end of his life without ever setting foot upon the ground;

so too is this woman: from one buddha-field to another, wherever she is born, she never remains apart from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, until she attains bodhi, constantly practicing the holy life.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought to himself:
"When this sister becomes a Buddha, her assembly of bodhisattvas should also be like this present assembly."
The Buddha, knowing his thought, addressed Ānanda, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have thought.

When the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim this very profound Prajñāpāramitā to a great assembly; the number of bodhisattvas in that assembly will be just like the number of bodhisattvas in my present assembly.
As for his śrāvaka disciples, their number is difficult to know, and can only be described in general terms as immeasurable and incalculable.
"In that Buddha-world, there are none of the following: fierce beasts, wicked bandits, hunger, thirst, disease, or any other afflictions and fears.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, under which Buddha did this sister first resolve her mind upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, planting various roots of goodness and dedicating them toward her vow?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, this girl first gave rise to the great resolve; she also scattered golden flowers over that Buddha and dedicated the merit toward her aspiration, whereby she has now encountered me."
Ānanda, you should know that in the past,
at the place of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I scattered five stalks of flowers over that Buddha, dedicating them and making a vow.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, knowing that my faculties were mature, bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śāntamati (The Able One of Tranquility), your world shall be named Sahā, and your kalpa shall be called Bhadra.

When the goddess heard the Buddha bestow upon me this prediction of great Bodhi, she was filled with joy and exultation. She immediately scattered golden flowers over that Buddha and made this dedication and vow:

"In a future age, when I have attained Buddhahood through this Bodhisattva, may I likewise receive a face-to-face prediction of great Bodhi from him, just as the present Buddha has bestowed it upon me."
"Therefore, I now bestow this prediction upon him.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Now these sisters have long cultivated the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*); through their dedication and aspiration, they have now attained maturity.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is so! It is so!"
"It is so! It is as you have said.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom enter the meditative absorption on emptiness?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom contemplates the emptiness of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and while making this contemplation does not allow the mind to become distracted—if the mind is not distracted, one sees phenomena as they truly are; yet, although seeing phenomena as they truly are, one does not realize them.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that a bodhisattva, though seeing dharmas as empty, does not realize [this emptiness]?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When these bodhisattvas contemplate the emptiness of phenomena, they first form this thought:
'I should contemplate that all characteristics of phenomena are empty, yet I should not realize [this emptiness] therein.'"
"I contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena for the sake of training, not for the sake of realization; now is the time for training, not the time for realization.
These bodhisattvas have not yet entered the state of meditative absorption; they are gathering their minds upon objects, which is not the time for entering absorption.
At that time, although the bodhisattvas do not fall away from the factors conducive to enlightenment, they do not yet exhaust their outflows. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattvas have accomplished vast roots of wisdom and goodness, and are able to reflect upon themselves with discernment:
"Regarding the dharma of emptiness, at this time I should study it but not realize it.

I should embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena, and bring all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) to fulfillment; I should not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) at this time, lest I fall into the stage of the two vehicles and fail to attain bodhi."

"Suppose, for example, there were a person who was brave, robust, and majestic; whose resolve was firm and whose appearance was dignified; who possessed all sixty-four arts without exception; who had mastered every other craft to its ultimate limit; who was endowed with many supreme virtues of ethical discipline (*śīla*); who was wise, eloquent, and skilled at responding to others; who was compassionate, righteous, and possessed great power; and who, because he could accomplish all his undertakings as virtuous deeds, achieved much benefit with little effort—therefore, everyone would respect and love him."

Due to certain causes and conditions, he set out for another region with his parents, wife, children, and kinsmen; on the way, they passed through a perilous wilderness filled with many predatory beasts and hostile bandits, so that all his kinsmen, both great and small, were filled with alarm.
That man, relying on his many skills and arts, was fierce and courageous, with a mind at ease; he comforted his parents, wife, children, and kinsmen, saying:
"Do not have any anxiety or fear; I shall certainly ensure that you suffer no distress."
He swiftly crossed the wilderness and reached a place of safety.
At that time, the man manifested various kinds of courageous and sharp weapons; when he encountered his enemies, they saw them and naturally retreated and dispersed.

Therefore, that hero, amidst the wilderness, has no intention of harming him from wild beasts or hostile bandits; through skillful means, he leads his retinue swiftly across the wilderness to a place of peace and security.

The assembly of bodhisattvas is also like this: out of compassion for all sentient beings suffering in saṃsāra, they maintain their mindfulness while dwelling securely in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they embrace the supreme roots of goodness of the *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful means, and as permitted by the Buddha, they dedicate all merits toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Although they fully cultivate emptiness, they do not realize it [as a final cessation], for with a profound heart they take pity on all sentient beings, desiring to bestow peace and happiness upon them.

These bodhisattvas transcend the category of afflictions, as well as the category of Māra and the stages of the two vehicles; though they abide in the concentration of emptiness, they do not exhaust their outflows, and though they are well-practiced in emptiness, they do not realize it as a final cessation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwells in the concentration of emptiness; though he does not cling to signs, he does not realize signlessness.

Just as a bird with strong wings soars through the void, flying freely for a long time without falling, and though it sports in dependence upon the sky, it does not dwell in the sky nor is it obstructed by the sky—so too it is with the assembly of Bodhisattvas: although they train in the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not dwell in emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; until the Buddha-dharma is fully perfected, they never rely on those states to exhaust all outflows forever.

“Suppose there were a strong man, well-versed in the art of archery, who, wishing to display his skill, shot an arrow upward into the air. To prevent the arrow from falling to the ground, he would shoot a subsequent arrow into the notch of the preceding one; continuing this succession for a long time, each arrow supported the next so that none fell. If he wished for them to fall, he would simply cease shooting further arrows, and at that moment all the arrows would suddenly drop. These Bodhisattvas are just like this: practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and embracing sublime skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway as long as their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) have not yet reached full maturity. When their roots of goodness have reached full maturity, they then realize the limit of reality and attain great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).”

"Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they should employ skillful means in this very way: they should carefully and precisely observe the profound nature of phenomena, yet should not realize [nirvana] so long as the qualities of a Buddha have not reached ultimate fulfillment."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!
These bodhisattvas are able to perform what is difficult: though they study the profound Dharma, they do not realize it as a direct attainment."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

These bodhisattvas vow not to abandon any sentient being and are thus able to accomplish this task: namely, that these bodhisattvas, having generated the vast mind for the sake of liberating sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, repeatedly induce the three gates of liberation, yet do not realize the limit of reality midway.

Why is this? Because those whom one wishes to deliver and liberate should not be abandoned; because they are sustained by skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); and therefore, one should not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas, at the point of profound depth, wish to examine with thorough discernment by means of the perfection of wisdom—that is, the sphere traversed by the three doors of liberation, namely the meditative stabilizations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
"These bodhisattvas should think: 'Sentient beings, throughout the long night, give rise to the notion of a sentient being;
clinging to the existence of something to be attained, they are drawn into various wrong views and wander through birth and death, suffering without end.'"

In order to sever those wrong and evil views, I should seek unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and preach the profound Dharma of emptiness for all sentient beings, so that they may abandon their attachments and emerge from the suffering of birth and death.
"Therefore, although they study the gate of liberation that is emptiness, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) midway.

By means of this skillful means arising from such a thought, these bodhisattvas, while not realizing the limit of reality midway, do not fall away from the four sublime meditative concentrations of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are embraced by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their pure qualities (*śukladharma*) increase manifold, their faculties gradually become sharper, and their powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path further increase.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas should form this thought:
'Sentient beings have for a long night wandered among various signs, giving rise to manifold attachments; because of this, they transmigrate and undergo suffering without end.'"

In order to sever their attachment to signs, I should seek unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and preach the signless Dharma to all sentient beings, so that they may sever their attachment to signs and emerge from the suffering of birth and death; for this reason, I frequently enter the samādhi of signlessness.

"Because these bodhisattvas have previously perfected skillful means and the mindfulness they have generated, although they repeatedly enter the meditative absorption of signlessness, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim;
and although they do not realize the limit of reality in the interim, they do not fall away from the four immeasurable concentrations."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are sustained by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their pure dharmas increase manifold, their faculties gradually become sharper, and their powers, factors of enlightenment, and branches of the path further increase.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas should form this thought:

'Sentient beings, throughout the long night, constantly give rise in their minds to the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of self, and the perception of purity; from these they produce inverted attachments, causing them to revolve in birth and death and undergo endless suffering.'"

In order to sever those four inversions, I should seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and preach the non-inverted Dharma for all sentient beings; that is to say, I shall teach that saṃsāra is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity, whereas only nirvāṇa is subtle, tranquil, and endowed with various kinds of true merits. By means of this, I frequently enter the concentration of wishlessness (apraṇihita-samādhi).

Because these bodhisattvas have previously perfected skillful means and cultivated mindfulness, although they repeatedly enter the concentration of wishlessness, they do not realize the limit of reality midway until all the Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected;
and while they do not realize the limit of reality midway, they do not fall back from the four immeasurable concentrations.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are sustained by the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their pure dharmas increase manifold, their faculties gradually become sharper, and their powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path further increase.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! These bodhisattvas should form this thought: 'Sentient beings have for a long night already practiced with apprehension and now likewise practice with apprehension;

they have already practiced with signs and now likewise practice with signs; they have already practiced with perversions and now likewise practice with perversions; they have already practiced with the notion of combination and now likewise practice with the notion of combination; they have already practiced with false imagination and now likewise practice with false imagination; they have already practiced with wrong views and now likewise practice with wrong views; because of this, they transmigrate and undergo suffering without end.'"

In order to sever such faults as these, I should seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and preach the profound Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, so that those faults may be forever eliminated, they no longer transmigrate through the suffering of birth and death, and they may swiftly realize the eternal, blissful, true, and pure nirvana.

Because these bodhisattvas, out of deep compassion for all sentient beings, have accomplished sublime skillful means and are sustained by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they constantly delight in contemplating the profound nature of phenomena—namely, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, effortlessness, non-arising, non-ceasing, absence of intrinsic nature, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
When these bodhisattvas have accomplished such sublime wisdom and vision, it is impossible for them to fall into signless and unconditioned dharmas or to dwell within the triple world.

It is impossible that these bodhisattvas, having accomplished such sublime qualities, would abandon all sentient beings to enter parinirvāṇa, rather than realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to benefit sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If bodhisattvas wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should inquire of other bodhisattvas:
'How does a bodhisattva cultivate all the factors conducive to enlightenment?'"

By giving rise to what kind of mind can a bodhisattva train in emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-cessation, and the reality-limit of the absence of intrinsic nature, yet refrain from realizing them while practicing the perfection of wisdom?
"If other bodhisattvas receive this question, they should answer thus:

'The assembly of bodhisattvas should merely contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and so forth, rather than demonstrating them; they should instead keep in mind not abandoning all sentient beings and embrace superior skillful means.'"
"You should know that those bodhisattvas have not yet received from the Buddhas the prophecy of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?

Because those bodhisattvas are unable to reveal, analyze, or clarify the unique characteristics of the bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression; they do not know, as it truly is, the practices, marks, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression when questioned by others, nor can they provide an answer."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is there any cause or condition by which one may know that bodhisattvas are non-retrogressive?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are also causes and conditions by which one knows that various bodhisattvas are non-retrogressive. That is to say, there are bodhisattvas who, whether they have heard or not heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are able to answer as they truly are the questions previously asked, and are able to practice the conduct of bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression as it truly is; by these causes and conditions, one knows that those bodhisattvas are non-retrogressive."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions is it that while many bodhisattvas practice the conduct of awakening, few are able to provide a response that accords with reality?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Although many bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path, few bodhisattvas receive such a prediction of the subtle wisdom of the stage of non-retrogression; those who do receive such a prediction are all able to answer correctly regarding this matter."

"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas possess roots of goodness that are sharp and keen, and wisdom that is profound and vast; thus, neither the gods, humans, nor asuras of the world can destroy their great mind of awakening."
19. Chapter on Dreaming Practice, Part Five, Chapter Nineteen: Dreaming Practice.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas do not become attached even in their dreams to the three realms or the levels of the two vehicles, nor do they praise them; and although they contemplate all phenomena as being like what is seen in a dream, they are able to refrain from realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), this is the mark of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva sees the Buddha in a dream, surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of hundreds of thousands who are preaching the Dharma for them, or if they see themselves in such a situation, this is a mark of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva sees the Buddha in a dream—endowed with all the marks and signs, with a constant light extending one fathom illuminating all around, leaping into the air with immeasurable hosts, manifesting great supernormal powers, and preaching the essentials of the True Dharma; or if they see themselves creating emanations who go to boundless Buddha-fields in other directions to perform the works of Buddhas; or if they see their own self performing such deeds—these are the signs of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva sees in a dream mad bandits destroying a village or city, or sees a fire breaking out and burning down a settlement, or sees wild beasts coming to harm his body, or sees enemies seeking to cut off his head, or sees his parents on the verge of death, or sees himself beset by manifold sufferings—though he sees such terrifying things, he is neither startled nor afraid, nor does he feel any distress.
Having awakened from the dream, he is able to reflect correctly:"

"The three realms are not real; they are all like things seen in a dream. When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall preach to sentient beings that the dharmas of the three realms are entirely false and illusory, just like dream-objects."
These are the marks of bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if bodhisattvas, even in their dreams, see sentient beings in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, they then form this thought:
"I shall diligently cultivate the bodhisattva practices and swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In my buddha-field, there shall not even exist the names of the evil destinies of the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts."
Upon awakening from the dream, he likewise thinks this.

Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattvas attain buddhahood, their lands will be pure and will certainly be devoid of the evil realms, even the very names of which shall not exist; such are the marks of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva, while dreaming, sees sentient beings in the hells and other realms being burned by fire, or sees cities, towns, and villages being consumed by flames, they should then make this aspiration:
'If I have already received the prediction of non-retrogression, may these great fires be transformed into coolness.'"
"If, when this bodhisattva makes such a vow, the fire seen in a dream is immediately extinguished, one should know that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression;
if, when this bodhisattva makes such a vow, the fire seen in a dream is not immediately extinguished, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression."
"When awake, they see fires burning various cities and towns; the fires may be extinguished according to their wish, or they may not be extinguished—likewise.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If, when awake, bodhisattvas see fires burning various cities and towns, they then form this thought:"
“If I truly possess the marks of non-retrogression, may this great fire be suddenly extinguished and transformed into coolness.

Having thought this, he spoke these words; yet the fire was not suddenly extinguished. Instead, it burned for one *li* and then skipped over another *li*, burning again for one *li*; or it would burn one house and skip over another house, burning yet another house. In this manner, proceeding by turns, the fire finally went out. One should know that these bodhisattvas have likewise already received the prediction of non-retrogression; however, those who were burned suffered the lingering karmic retribution of slandering the Dharma, or it manifested the future suffering of those who slander the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva sees a man or a woman who has been possessed by a non-human spirit, suffering various afflictions and unable to escape them, they should think:
