'If the Tathāgatas know that my intention is pure, know that I have received the prediction of non-retrogression, and know that I have already transcended the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—may they look upon me and observe the thoughts in my mind! "

If I am truly able to cultivate the bodhisattva practices and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to rescue sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, may this man or this woman not be troubled or harassed by non-human spirits; upon my word, they shall immediately depart.
When these bodhisattvas speak these words, if that non-human being does not depart, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression;
if that non-human being immediately departs, one should know that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who have not yet actually received the prediction of non-retrogression. Seeing a man or a woman currently possessed by a non-human spirit, suffering various afflictions and unable to escape them, they immediately utter a solemn declaration with ease:
'If I have already received the prediction of non-retrogression, let this man or this woman not be disturbed or tormented by the non-human spirit; following my word, it shall depart at once.'"
At that time, the evil Māra, in order to deceive and delude him, immediately coerced and drove away the non-human beings. Why was this?
Because the power of the evil Māra surpassed that of those non-human beings; therefore, having received Māra’s command, the non-human beings immediately departed.
At that time, the bodhisattva thought to himself:
"That non-human has now departed because of my own majestic power. Why is this so?"
"The non-human beings have released this man or woman because they followed my vow; it was not for any other reason.

Since these bodhisattvas do not recognize that this is the work of Māra, they think it is due to their own power. They look down upon other bodhisattvas and give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Although they exert themselves with diligence, they ultimately fail to attain unexcelled enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) and fall to the level of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). They are repeatedly deceived and deluded by Māra; therefore, a bodhisattva should skillfully recognize the deeds of all evil Māras and cultivate all wholesome actions.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who have not yet actually received the prediction of non-retrogression; being devoid of the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they remain susceptible to the delusions of Māra."
This means that there may be an evil Māra who, for the sake of deception and delusion, employs skillful means to manifest various forms and approaches the bodhisattva, speaking these words:
"Do you know this yourself?"
The Buddhas of the past have already bestowed upon you the prediction of great enlightenment.
I fully know the names and distinctions of you, your retinue, and even those down to the seventh generation of your kin.

"You were born in such-and-such a direction, such-and-such a country, such-and-such a city, such-and-such a town, and such-and-such a village; you were born under such-and-such a lunar mansion on such-and-such a year, such-and-such a month, such-and-such a day, and at such-and-such a time."
If an evil Māra sees that a bodhisattva is by nature gentle and has dull faculties, he will falsely declare:
"In your previous lives, the nature of your faculties was already like this."
If he sees that a bodhisattva is by nature firm and strong, with keen and sharp faculties, he then falsely predicts:
"In a previous life, you were also like this.
If he sees that a bodhisattva is fully endowed with various dhūta virtues and other superior practices, he then falsely predicts:
"You, too, in a former life, possessed such merits as these; you should congratulate yourself and not disparage yourself.

At that time, having heard this evil Māra recount his past and present names and other merits, that bodhisattva leaped for joy and gave rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), looking down upon, despising, and reviling all other bodhisattvas.
The Māra, having understood this, spoke to him again:
"You have certainly accomplished sublime merit; the Buddha has already bestowed upon you the prophecy of Great Bodhi, and extraordinary auspicious signs have now appeared before you."
At that time, the evil Māra, for the sake of causing disturbance, again conjured various forms and approached the Bodhisattva, speaking words of feigned affection:
"You have now already perfected the virtues of non-retrogression; you should regard yourself with respect and not hastily honor others."
At that time, having heard those words, this bodhisattva’s mind of overweening pride became even more firm, causing all-knowledge to recede further and further away.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain awakening should skillfully recognize these various deeds of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattvas who do not correctly understand the true nature of names, but upon merely hearing them, they give rise to false attachments.
That is to say, an evil Māra may employ skillful means to manifest various forms and come to tell them:..."
"The practices and vows you have cultivated are already fulfilled; before long, you shall realize unsurpassed bodhi.
When you attain Buddhahood, you shall obtain such supreme merits and this noble name."
That is to say, that evil Māra knows this bodhisattva’s long-standing thought and aspiration:
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall obtain such a noble name.
According to that thought and aspiration, he then prophesies it for him.
At that time, this bodhisattva, being devoid of skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom, hears the Mara’s prophecy and thinks to himself:
"This person is truly extraordinary!"

Please prophesy for me the noble name I shall attain upon becoming a Buddha, so that it may correspond with my long-standing aspirations; by this, I shall know for certain that I will surely become a Buddha, and that my name shall surpass those of others.

"In whatever way Māra pronounces that name, in that very way his pride increases further; he comes to despise other bodhisattvas of genuine virtue, and by this means he becomes increasingly distant from unsurpassed enlightenment, destined to fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."

Among these bodhisattvas, some may, with this very body, draw near to virtuous friends and sincerely repent their transgressions; though they may continue to wander through birth and death for a long time, they will eventually realize unsurpassed bodhi.

If, however, with this very body they do not encounter virtuous friends and sincerely repent, they will certainly wander through birth and death for a long time, remaining deluded and inverted; even if they later apply themselves with diligence to cultivating various wholesome deeds, they will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Thus, the transgression of arrogance and looking down upon other bodhisattvas is countless times greater than the four grave offenses or the five deeds of immediate retribution.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should skillfully recognize such subtle demonic activities as the recording of false names and titles, and should not be arrogant or look down upon other bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattvas who dwell in mountains or wildernesses practicing the conduct of seclusion. At that time, an evil Māra comes to their place and, paying them homage and offering praise, speaks as follows:
'O Great Being!'"
"One who is able to cultivate the practice of true seclusion is praised by the noble ones and protected by all the devas and nāgas.
Subhūti, you should know this!
"I do not praise this practice of seclusion as being ultimate reality. Subhūti said:
"If this practice of seclusion is not ultimate reality, what else could it be?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattvas—whether dwelling in cities or in mountain wilds—remain free from the mental engagements of afflictions and the two vehicles while practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, this is called the bodhisattva’s true practice of seclusion."
This practice of seclusion is praised and authorized by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; Bodhisattvas should train in it so that they may swiftly realize bodhi.
Subhūti, you should know this!

Though praised by Māra for constantly dwelling in mountain wilds in meditative seclusion and contemplation, if one still harbors the mental engagements of the two vehicles mixed with afflictions and remains separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one will be unable to perfect the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

There are some bodhisattvas who, though they delight in practicing the dharmas of seclusion praised by Māra, look down upon other bodhisattvas who dwell constantly in villages and cities while practicing genuine seclusion.

"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas, having distanced themselves from the perfection of wisdom, may dwell for a long time in deep mountains and wildernesses practicing the conduct of seclusion; yet, because they do not understand the dharma of true seclusion, their pride increases, and they develop a deep attachment to the levels of the two vehicles. Consequently, they will ultimately never attain unsurpassed enlightenment. This is neither praised nor permitted by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, nor is it a practice that a bodhisattva should engage in."

"Subhūti, you should know that the truly pure and secluded dharmas which I praise for the assembly of bodhisattvas are not at all accomplished by them; furthermore, within those practices of true purity and seclusion, they do not perceive even a semblance of such conduct."

Then various evil Māras, in order to deceive and delude him, cause him to give rise to arrogance and to look down upon other Bodhisattvas; they come into the air and earnestly praise and exhort him, saying:
"This is the true dharma of pure and secluded practice."
"Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattvas dwell in mountains and forests, their minds are distracted and tumultuous, and they are unable to cultivate the practice of true seclusion.
There are other bodhisattvas who, though dwelling in villages and cities, have tranquil minds and are always able to cultivate the practice of true seclusion."
"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas treat those bodhisattvas who constantly train in the practice of true seclusion with contempt and derision, as if they were outcasts;
yet they offer worship and respect to those bodhisattvas who are unable to cultivate true seclusion, as if they were the World-Honored Buddhas."
“Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas,
being far removed from the perfection of wisdom, give rise to various forms of conceptualization and attachment, thinking to themselves:
‘Because my practice and training constitute true seclusion, non-human beings have come to me to praise and protect me.’”
"Those who dwell in cities have their bodies and minds agitated; who would then protect, mindfully attend to, praise, or respect them?
Thus, these bodhisattvas are full of arrogance, and their afflictions and evil karma increase day and night.

Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas are *caṇḍālas* among the assembly of bodhisattvas; they defile the community of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and are great thieves among gods and humans, deceiving and deluding gods, humans, asuras, and others.
Although their bodies are clothed in the dharma-robes of śramaṇas, their minds constantly harbor the intentions and inclinations of hateful thieves.
Those who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle should not associate with, make offerings to, or show respect toward such people. Why is this?
These individuals harbor overweening pride; though they appear outwardly to be bodhisattvas, they are inwardly full of afflictions and their evil karma is intensely flourishing.
Therefore, Subhūti,

if bodhisattvas truly do not abandon the knowledge of all modes, seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and act for the universal benefit, happiness, and welfare of all sentient beings, they should not associate with such evil persons.

“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattvas should always be diligent in cultivating true practice; they should feel weary of and detached from birth and death, and not be attached to the three realms. Toward those wicked, murderous Cāṇḍālas, they should constantly give rise to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and should think:

‘I must not give rise to the faults that those evil persons give rise to; even if I should momentarily lose mindfulness and such faults arise as they do, I shall immediately recognize them and swiftly eliminate them.’”

Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should skillfully recognize the deeds of Māra; they should diligently apply themselves to distance themselves from and eliminate such faults as those arising for that bodhisattva, and strive earnestly to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If bodhisattvas train in this manner, they are skillfully aware of the works of Māra.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 563 (Fascicle 564).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Order.
Chapter 20: Superior Intention, Part Five. Chapter Twenty: Superior Intention. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If bodhisattvas, with a superior intention, desire to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should always draw near to, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise true and pure spiritual friends.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by a ‘virtuous friend’ of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All Buddhas are called good friends of bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, if anyone can proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, instructing and guiding the assembly of bodhisattvas so that they may gain entry into this profound dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, such a person is also called a good friend of bodhisattvas."
One should know that the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are also called the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends.

In this way, these six perfections serve as teachers and guides for all bodhisattvas; they are a lamp and a torch, a light and an illumination; they are a shelter and a protection, a refuge and a destination; they are an island and a landing place; they are a father and a mother.
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have accomplished their meritorious activities by relying upon the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). Why is this so?
In this way, these six perfections are universally able to encompass all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, Subhūti,
if bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should train in the six perfections.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas wish to train in the six perfections, they should, with a sincere mind, hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this profound sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom; they should examine its meaning and resolve their doubts."
Why is this so? Because this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā serves as the sovereign, the guide, and the nurturing mother for the six pāramitās.
Subhūti, you should know this:

if bodhisattvas wish to act without following the instructions of others, wish to abide on the stage of not following the instructions of others, wish to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, and wish to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, they should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the characteristics of the profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The profound perfection of wisdom has non-obstruction as its characteristic.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is there any cause or condition by which other dharmas, besides the profound perfection of wisdom, may also possess this characteristic of non-obstruction?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"By reason of certain causes and conditions, while the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of non-obstruction, it may also be said that all other phenomena likewise exist."
"Why is this? Because all phenomena are none other than the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is empty and detached.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If all phenomena are empty and detached, how can sentient beings be defiled or purified? Why is this so?

It cannot be said that empty and detached phenomena are subject to defilement or purification; emptiness and detachment cannot realize bodhi; nor is there any other distinct phenomenon to be found apart from emptiness and detachment. How am I to understand such a meaning?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do sentient beings, throughout the long night, possess the notion of a self and grasp at a self?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Are the 'self' and 'what belongs to the self' grasped by sentient beings empty and remote?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is it not the case that sentient beings wander through birth and death due to 'I' and 'mine'?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is in this way that sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death, and the designations of 'defilement' and 'purification' are established.
Because sentient beings falsely cling to a self and what belongs to a self, one speaks of defilement; yet, within that very state, there is no one who is defiled."
Because sentient beings do not falsely cling to a self or what belongs to a self, it is said that there is purity; yet within that, there is no one who is pure.
Therefore, Subhūti!

Although all phenomena are empty and detached, sentient beings can nonetheless be designated as having defilement or purity; if bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, it is called practicing the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous,
World-Honored One!”
Although all phenomena are empty and detached, sentient beings still possess defilement and purification.

If Bodhisattvas can practice in this manner, they do not course in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; neither the gods, humans, nor asuras of the world can subdue them. They universally surpass all that is practiced by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, reaching the state where there is no further excellence. By means of these mental engagements associated with the perfection of wisdom, these Bodhisattvas dwell day and night in skillful means, proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?

Suppose all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously, without one preceding another, obtain human bodies, give rise to the mind of enlightenment, and practice giving for the duration of their lives, dedicating this giving toward enlightenment. Would they, by reason of these causes and conditions, acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied,
“It would be very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, for as little as one day, abides in a mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, the merit they obtain is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable."

Why is this? Because as such a bodhisattva dwells thus in accordance with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through corresponding mental engagement (*manasikāra*), to that same extent they become worthy of being a field of merit for all sentient beings. Consequently, no sentient beings can surpass the loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arising from this bodhisattva, except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

"In this way, the bodhisattva possesses sublime and wondrous wisdom; through that sublime and wondrous wisdom, seeing all sentient beings undergoing great suffering and torment as if being executed, he gives rise to great compassion."

Furthermore, with the divine eye, he sees sentient beings who have committed deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and fallen into states of no leisure (*akṣaṇa*) to undergo various sufferings and afflictions; or those who are shrouded by the net of views and fail to attain the right path. Having seen this, he gives rise to compassion and great revulsion and fear, and universally directing his attention toward the entire world of sentient beings, he engages in a mental orientation (*manasikāra*) associated with great loving-kindness and compassion, thinking:
"I shall act as a great guide for all sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from all suffering."
Although they form this thought, they do not abide in this perception, nor do they abide in any other perception; this is called the Great Wisdom Light of a Bodhisattva.

By abiding in this state, they are able to serve as a field of merit for all the world; although they have not yet realized the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they are already non-retrogressive regarding enlightenment and are worthy of receiving all offerings from donors.
"In this way, a bodhisattva who is well-established in the perfection of wisdom is able both to ultimately repay the kindness of their benefactors and to draw near to the knowledge of all modes."

Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes not to receive the faithful offerings of the world in vain; who wishes to show sentient beings the path of true purity; who wishes to bring great benefit to sentient beings; who wishes to act as a great illumination for the world; who wishes to liberate sentient beings from the prison of birth and death; and who wishes to bestow upon sentient beings the pure eye of Dharma, should always abide in a mental engagement associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
By means of this mental attention, all speech is in accord with the principle of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and no other mental attentions can arise for even a moment.
Why is this so? It is because such a bodhisattva maintains a continuous flow of mental attention associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

For example, suppose there were a person who had never before possessed a maṇi-jewel, and later happened to obtain one; he would rejoice and celebrate within himself. Yet, having lost it again due to some circumstance, he would experience great distress and sorrow, constantly harboring lamentation and never ceasing to think of it, wondering what plan he might devise to recover that jewel.
Because of this associated mental attention (*manasikāra*), that person never for a moment abandons his focus on this precious jewel.

In the same way, a bodhisattva should always abide in the associated mental attention of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; if one does not abide in such mental attention, then one loses the mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all dharmas and all mental attentions (*manasikāra*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how is it that a bodhisattva does not depart from the mental attention associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If bodhisattvas know that all phenomena and all mental attentions are devoid of intrinsic nature, these bodhisattvas do not depart from the omniscience of the knowledge of all aspects."
"Why is this? Because the profound *prajñā*, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), and all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are by their very nature empty, neither increasing nor decreasing.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"If the intrinsic nature of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is eternally empty, without increase or decrease, how can a bodhisattva increase their *prajñāpāramitā* and thereby draw near to enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they know that all phenomena neither increase nor decrease, and thus there is no increase or decrease even within the profound perfection of wisdom."
If bodhisattvas can understand in this way, hearing that all phenomena neither increase nor decrease, they will not be startled, terrified, or despondent.

These bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to its ultimate limit, abide securely on the stage of non-retrogression, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
is it that the perfection of wisdom itself is able to practice the perfection of wisdom?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, it is not so.
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it possible, apart from the perfection of wisdom, to find any dharma that can practice the perfection of wisdom?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is it that which is empty of the perfection of wisdom that is able to practice the perfection of wisdom? “It is not so.”
“Subhūti!
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended as empty or existent, apart from the perfection of wisdom, which is able to practice the perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, [it is not so].
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Can that which is itself emptiness practice the perfection of wisdom?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is it possible to practice the perfection of wisdom by means of attaining any dharma apart from emptiness? “It is not so.”
"Subhūti!
"World-Honored One!
Is it that emptiness itself can practice emptiness?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, [it is not so].
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Can one who has abandoned the apprehension of phenomena as either empty or existent practice emptiness?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is it that the Prajñāpāramitā itself is able to practice emptiness? “It is not so.”
"Subhūti!
"World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma to be found apart from the perfection of wisdom that is able to practice emptiness?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, it is not so.
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are able to practice the perfection of wisdom and practice emptiness? "No, it is not so."
"Subhūti!
"World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma apart from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that can practice the perfection of wisdom or practice emptiness?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, it is not so.
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“Is it that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness themselves are empty, such that one can practice the perfection of wisdom and practice emptiness? “No, it is not so.”
“Excellent, Subhūti!
“World-Honored One!
Is it by being detached from form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—that is, through their emptiness—that one can practice the perfection of wisdom and practice emptiness?”
"No, Subhūti! At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If that is so, by what dharma can a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom and practice emptiness?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think?”
"Do you see any dharma that is able to practice the perfection of wisdom or to practice emptiness?
Subhūti replied, "No, indeed!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
“What do you think?”
"Do you perceive a *prajñāpāramitā* and do you perceive emptiness as being the sphere of activity for these bodhisattvas?
Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
“What do you think?”
"Can that dharma which you do not see be apprehended?
Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think?”
"Is there any dharma that cannot be apprehended which yet arises? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The true reality of all dharmas—which you do not see and which you do not apprehend—is precisely the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas."

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such patience, they become worthy of receiving the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is also called the path of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness.

If bodhisattvas diligently practice this path, it is impossible that they should not attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening—the wisdom of great knowledge, the sublime wisdom, the self-arisen wisdom, the wisdom of all-knowledge, and the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does a bodhisattva receive the prediction of enlightenment regarding the Buddha’s bodhi by means of the non-arising of all phenomena? "It is not so!"
“Subhūti!
‘World-Honored One!
If that is so, how does a bodhisattva receive the prediction of enlightenment?’”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do you perceive any dharma that receives the prediction of enlightenment from a Buddha?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

I do not perceive any dharma that is capable of receiving the prediction regarding the Buddha's enlightenment; nor do I perceive any dharma that is able to realize the Buddha's enlightenment. Furthermore, I do not perceive the time of realization, the place of realization, that by which one realizes, or the dharma that is realized.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because all dharmas are unattainable, one should not think or say that ‘this is the realization’ or ‘this is the realized’ regarding the Buddha’s bodhi.”
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize; because it is ultimately detached, sentient beings with meager roots of virtue are unable to write it down, hear it, receive and uphold it, or read and recite such a profound Prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said, Kauśika!

Even if all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa were to fully accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action, such a mass of merit would not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part of the merit obtained by one who writes down, hears, receives, upholds, reads, and recites this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra."
At that time, a bhikṣu said to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"Is there anyone who, by writing down, hearing, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Prajñāpāramitā, attains merit superior to yours?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

"Those classes of sentient beings surpass even me when they first resolve their minds [upon awakening], let alone when they write down, hear, receive and uphold, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon the Perfection of Wisdom according to the principle!"
“Bhikṣus, you should know that those sentient beings are indeed bodhisattvas.
The mass of merit obtained by such bodhisattvas universally surpasses that of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.”

The mass of merit obtained by such a bodhisattva also surpasses that of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas; it also surpasses the merit of a bodhisattva who, being devoid of skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom, practices the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, as well as other virtues.
"O Bhikṣus, you should know this!

If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) as it has been taught, these bodhisattvas will universally surpass all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—and all the gods, humans, and asuras of the world should make offerings to them."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas are able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* exactly as it is taught, following it to its ultimate conclusion.

These bodhisattvas are able to perpetuate the lineage of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*) so that it is never interrupted; they are never separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they are never separated from the sublime seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); and they are always able to rescue and deliver sentient beings who are mired in the mud of birth and death.
When these bodhisattvas train in this manner, they constantly train in the dharmas that bodhisattvas ought to learn, and do not train in the dharmas that those of the two vehicles ought to learn.
The devas and other celestial beings constantly follow and protect them; the Four Great Heavenly Kings come to their abodes to make offerings and pay respect, all saying:
"Excellent!"
O Mahāsattva!

You should diligently apply yourself with vigor to study the dharmas that all bodhisattvas ought to learn; you shall swiftly sit upon the sublime seat of awakening and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Just as the four bowls formerly offered by the Heavenly King, I too shall offer them.
O Bhikṣus, you should know that even we, the Lord of Devas, go to those Bodhisattvas to make offerings and pay them respect; how much more so other celestial deities!
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

When these bodhisattvas train in this way, all Tathāgatas, as well as bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and others, will constantly follow and protect them. By virtue of this cause and condition, they shall not be harmed by worldly dangers or calamities, nor by physical or mental distress; furthermore, no diseases whatsoever shall arise.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know that these bodhisattvas obtain such benefits in the present life, and their merits in future lives will be immeasurable and boundless.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought to himself:
"Is it through his own eloquence that Śakra, Lord of Devas, has thus praised the merits of this bodhisattva, or is it through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power?
Then, Śakra, Lord of Devas, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and knowing the thoughts in Ānanda’s mind, addressed him, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"This is not my own eloquence; it is entirely through the majestic spiritual power and empowerment of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "So it is!"
"So it is! Today Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has been able to speak thus by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Ānanda, you should know this!"
When a bodhisattva contemplates and trains in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the evil Māras of the trichiliocosm give rise to doubt and fear, and they all think:

"Will these bodhisattvas realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway and fall into the stage of the two vehicles, or will they proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and turn the wonderful wheel of Dharma, thereby emptying my realm?"
"Furthermore, Ānanda! When a bodhisattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they apply themselves with diligence day and night, never abandoning it."
At that time, Māra’s retinue felt as if arrows had pierced their hearts; they were terrified, trembling, and filled with such anxiety and dread that they could no longer remain in their places.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), exerting themselves day and night until reaching its ultimate consummation."

At that time, Māra’s retinue came to his location and manifested various terrifying sights, wishing to cause the Bodhisattva’s body and mind to be struck with alarm, so that he might momentarily retreat from Great Enlightenment; this would have sufficed for their purpose.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is not the case that all bodhisattvas who practice and study the *prajñāpāramitā* are disturbed and distracted by Māra.

However, if there are bodhisattvas who, having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, lacked faith and understanding and instead reviled and slandered it, then those bodhisattvas, while practicing and studying the *prajñāpāramitā*, will indeed be disturbed and distracted by Māra."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, harbor doubts and hesitations as to whether it exists or does not exist, then those bodhisattvas who practice and study the *prajñāpāramitā* will be disturbed and distracted by Māra, the Evil One."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If bodhisattvas distance themselves from virtuous friends and are influenced by evil friends, they will not hear the profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because they do not hear it, they neither know nor see it; how then could they practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
When these bodhisattvas practice and study the perfection of wisdom, they will be disturbed and distracted by Māra.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
if bodhisattvas embrace false teachings, at that time Māra will think to himself:

"Thinking, 'Now this bodhisattva is my companion; he will cause immeasurable people to abandon the true Dharma and fulfill my wishes,' these bodhisattvas who are training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are then disturbed and distracted by Māra, the Evil One."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If, when various bodhisattvas hear the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they say to other bodhisattvas:
'This principle of the *prajñāpāramitā* is so profound, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand; what is the use of writing it down, receiving and upholding it, or reciting it? "
"I am still unable to reach its source or its bottom, much less others of meager merit and shallow wisdom!
Thus, these bodhisattvas who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* are disturbed and distracted by Māra, the Evil One.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If any bodhisattvas look down upon other bodhisattvas, saying:
'I am able to abide in the practice of true seclusion, whereas you all possess none of it.'"
At that time, Māra the Evil One was filled with joy and exultation; for these bodhisattvas who were training in the perfection of wisdom would thereby be disturbed and distracted by him.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

When a bodhisattva, relying on his own name, lineage, and the merits of the dhūta practices he performs, looks down upon other bodhisattvas who are cultivating superior wholesome dharmas; who constantly praises himself and disparages others; and who, lacking the conduct, marks, and signs of non-retrogression, claims to possess them, thereby giving rise to afflictions and karma."
At that time, Māra the Evil One was greatly delighted and thought to himself:
"Now this bodhisattva will ensure that my realm, lands, and palaces are not empty, thereby increasing the populations of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of hungry ghosts."

At that time, Māra, the Evil One, aided him with his supernatural power, causing his authority and eloquence to increase even further. Consequently, many people believed and accepted his words; because of this, they were exhorted and incited to share his evil views. Having shared those evil views, they followed his false teachings; having followed those false teachings, their afflictions flared up intensely.

Because their minds are inverted, the three types of karma they initiate are all capable of producing undesirable fruits; by these causes and conditions, they increase the realms of evil destinies and cause the palaces of Māra to become ever more filled. Consequently, the evil Māras rejoice and leap for joy, and whatever they do is accomplished with sovereign ease. Thus, when these bodhisattvas practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are immediately disturbed and distracted by the evil Māras.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva mutually disparages, quarrels with, and slanders those who seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, at that time Māra the Evil One thinks to himself:
'Although this bodhisattva is far from awakening, he is not extremely far; although he is near the evil destinies, he is not very near.'"
"If at any time a bodhisattva and other sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle revile, quarrel with, or slander one another, at that time Māra the Evil One thinks:
'These two bodhisattvas are very far from awakening and very close to the evil destinies.'"

Having formed this thought, they will leap for joy and exultation, increasing their own power and causing the two factions to fight and quarrel without ceasing. They will cause immeasurable and boundless other sentient beings to develop a deep-seated aversion toward the Mahāyāna; thus, when these bodhisattvas practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be disturbed and distracted by Māra, the Evil One.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If bodhisattvas who have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression from enlightenment harbor harmful intentions toward those bodhisattvas who have received the prediction of non-retrogression—engaging in strife, contempt, abuse, or slander—then for as many moments as they give rise to such thoughts of non-benefit, they shall retrogress for that many eons from their previously cultivated sublime practices; for that long they shall remain far removed from virtuous friends, and for that long they shall again undergo the bonds of birth and death."

If one does not abandon the great bodhicitta, and continues for that many eons to don the armor of the great vow and diligently cultivate sublime practices without interruption, only then will one replenish those merits.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Regarding the karmic suffering of birth and death resulting from the evil thoughts generated by these bodhisattvas, must they necessarily wander through saṃsāra for such a duration, or can they also attain liberation in the interim?"

Regarding these superior practices from which these bodhisattvas have regressed: must they necessarily exert diligent effort for that many eons without interruption before they can restore them, or is there a possibility of restoring them in the interim?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"For the sake of bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas, I have taught that there exists a dharma for the restoration of virtue and the expiation of transgressions.
Ānanda, you should know this!"
If Bodhisattvas, after committing such offenses, lack a sense of shame and remorse, harbor malice without relinquishing it, and are unable to confess and repent according to the Dharma,
I say that for such individuals, there is no possibility of emerging from the suffering of those offenses or restoring their virtue in the interim.

"If, after committing such a transgression, a bodhisattva gives rise to a sense of deep shame and remorse, does not remain bound by evil, and is immediately able to confess and repent according to the Dharma, thinking thus:
'I have now obtained this human body so difficult to find; how could I allow myself to again give rise to such faults and evils as to lose this great benefit of goodness?'"
"I ought to benefit all sentient beings; why then do I instead cause them harm?
I ought to revere all sentient beings as a servant serves his master; why then do I instead give rise to arrogance, insult, and contempt toward them?"
I ought to endure all the beatings and verbal abuse of sentient beings; how could I allow myself to retaliate against them with violent or wicked deeds and words?
I ought to reconcile all sentient beings so that they may respect and love one another; how could I allow myself to again give rise to harsh speech and engage in conflict with them?
I ought to endure the long-term treading upon me by all sentient beings, like a road or a bridge; how could I permit myself to respond to them with contempt or insult?

I seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in order to uproot the great suffering of birth and death for sentient beings and enable them to attain ultimate peace and bliss in nirvana; how could I possibly wish to inflict further suffering upon them?
From this day forth until the end of the future, I shall be like one who is foolish, mute, deaf, and blind, making no conceptual discriminations toward any sentient beings.

Even if one were to sever their head, feet, arms, gouge out their eyes, cut off their ears, slice off their nose, cut out their tongue, or saw apart every limb and member of their body, they would never give rise to malice toward those sentient beings.

If I were to give rise to evil thoughts, I would immediately fall away from and destroy the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment I have resolved to attain; I would obstruct the omniscience I seek and be unable to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to sentient beings.

"Ānanda, you should know that for these bodhisattvas, I say there is an intermediate stage where they undergo the suffering of transgressing precepts and then restore their virtue; it is not necessary for them to pass through such a number of kalpas, for Māra cannot disturb them, and they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Bodhisattvas should not engage in discourse with those who seek the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; even if they do engage in discourse, they should not dwell together with them. Even if they dwell together, they should not debate or resolve doctrinal points with them. Lest, because of this, they give rise to a mind of anger or produce coarse and evil speech, thereby obstructing unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and destroying the boundless dharmas of bodhisattva practice."

If bodhisattvas dwell together with sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle and look upon one another, they should honor and serve them as they would a Great Teacher, further forming this thought:

"They are our true, pure, and virtuous friends; we are aboard the same ship, heading toward the same destination, traveling the same path, and engaged in the same activity. Our time of study, our points of training, and the dharmas to be learned—whatever is studied through these—are in every way identical."
He further reflects:
"If that bodhisattva dwells in distracted attention, I shall not train in accordance with him therein;
if that bodhisattva is free from distracted attention, I shall always train in accordance with him therein."
“If bodhisattvas train in this way, they will swiftly realize the omniscient wisdom (sarvajñajñāna) that they seek.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If bodhisattvas train for the sake of exhaustion, train for the sake of non-arising, train for the sake of detachment, and train for the sake of cessation, is this training in omniscient wisdom?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
“When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they are not training in the knowledge of all aspects.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason, when a bodhisattva trains in this way, does he not train in the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?"
Because the Buddha has realized the ultimate perfection of suchness, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; can such suchness be said to be exhausted, or even to cease?
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"Why is this? Because True Suchness is without marks; it cannot be fully described, even unto its cessation.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Therefore, when a bodhisattva trains in this manner, they do not train for the sake of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If bodhisattvas train not for the sake of exhaustion, nor even for the sake of cessation, then when training in this way, they are training in the knowledge of all modes; they are also training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and they are also training in the Buddha-ground, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the boundless qualities of a Buddha."

Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattvas train in this manner, they reach the ultimate perfection of all training; neither the celestial Māras nor the followers of external paths can subdue them. They extinguish all evils and bring all virtues to full completion. Only a few sentient beings are able to train in this way; therefore, if a bodhisattva wishes to be counted among the very few sentient beings [who have attained such excellence], they should diligently cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
22. Chapter on the Roots (Mūla-varga), Part Five, Section One:

“Furthermore, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas thus train in the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, they do not give rise to a mind accompanied by roots [of affliction], nor do they give rise to a mind accompanied by stinginess, immorality, anger, laziness, distraction, wrong view, or doubt.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If bodhisattvas thus train in the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, they are able to encompass all perfections."
Just as the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) can fully encompass the sixty-two views, so too does the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) encompass all the perfections (pāramitās).

For example, just as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is able to sustain all the other faculties such that when the life-faculty ceases, the other faculties also cease accordingly, so too does the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) sustain all the perfections; if one loses the perfection of wisdom, then one loses all the perfections.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can sustain all supreme wholesome dharmas and can extinguish all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
Therefore, Subhūti,
if bodhisattvas wish to encompass all the pāramitās, they should train in the prajñāpāramitā.
If bodhisattvas are able to train in the prajñāpāramitā, they are the most honored and most supreme among all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
what do you think?
Are the sentient beings in this trichiliocosm many?"
Subhūti replied: “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
“The sentient beings within Jambudvīpa are already numerous; how much more so those in the trichiliocosm!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Suppose that all sentient beings in the great trichiliocosm were to become bodhisattvas, and each one were to provide every kind of supreme and exquisite article of comfort to all sentient beings for as long as they lived.”
"What do you think?
By this cause and condition, would these bodhisattvas acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If there is a bodhisattva who practices and studies the perfection of wisdom for even as long as a finger-snap, their merit will surpass that [of the former] immeasurably and boundlessly. Why is this? "

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses great purpose and function, for it is able to encompass unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

wish to be the foremost among all sentient beings; wish to universally benefit all sentient beings; wish to be a refuge for all sentient beings; wish to realize all the Buddha-dharmas in their entirety; wish to traverse the spheres traversed by all Buddhas; wish to sport in the places where Buddhas sport; wish to let out the great lion’s roar of all Buddhas; and wish, with a single voice, to proclaim the true Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm so that all may universally obtain great benefit—they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti, you should know this:
I have never seen any bodhisattvas who, while training in the perfection of wisdom, failed to attain the superior merits and benefits of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva practices and trains in the profound perfection of wisdom, can they also attain the merits and roots of virtue of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The merits and roots of goodness of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, these bodhisattvas are also able to attain them, yet their minds do not take delight in dwelling therein.
Through superior wisdom and vision, they observe without error, transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and reveal them to others so that all may realize them."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they become a truly pure field of merit for all the world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—surpassing the fields of merit of all worldly śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they are swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes, never abandoning the profound perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva is able to practice the perfection of wisdom, it should be known that they have already attained non-retrogression regarding all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), have distanced themselves from the levels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and are drawing near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
if bodhisattvas should form such a thought as, 'This is the perfection of wisdom;
by means of the perfection of wisdom, I shall be able to bring forth the knowledge of all modes.'"
These bodhisattvas do not practice the perfection of wisdom, nor do they know or see the perfection of wisdom.
If these bodhisattvas do not form this thought:
"This is the perfection of wisdom; by means of the perfection of wisdom, I shall be able to bring forth the knowledge of all modes."
"These bodhisattvas are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and they are also able to know and see the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If bodhisattvas do not see the perfection of wisdom, do not hear, perceive, or know the perfection of wisdom, and furthermore do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding those phenomena that are unseen, unheard, unperceived, and unknown—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, thought to himself:
"If bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom already surpass all classes of sentient beings, how much more so when they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!"

If sentient beings, upon hearing the name of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), give rise to deep faith and understanding, they will already obtain the excellent benefits of human existence and the most supreme lifespan in the world; how much more so for those who resolve their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or who are able to hear this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)!
"These sentient beings will be revered and loved by the world, and they shall be able to discipline all sentient beings.
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested the *sūkṣmasvara* flower and scattered it as an offering over the Tathāgata and the various Bodhisattvas.
Having scattered the flowers, they made this aspiration:

"If there are bodhisattvas who seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, by the roots of goodness and merit born from my [act], may their Buddha-dharma swiftly reach fulfillment; may all the dharmas of omniscience and untainted dharmas they seek likewise swiftly reach fulfillment."
Having made this vow, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who have already resolved upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, I shall never give rise to even a single thought of a contrary intention to cause them to retreat from their great bodhicitta;

I shall never give rise to even a single thought of a contrary intention to cause those bodhisattvas to grow weary of great enlightenment and to retreat to abide in the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
I shall never give rise to even a single thought of a contrary mind that would cause these bodhisattvas to fall away from their mental engagement associated with great compassion.

If these bodhisattvas have already resolved upon the Great Mind, I vow that their resolve may increase and advance further. Having seen the various sufferings within birth and death, I vow that these bodhisattvas will, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—give rise to various firm and great vows:
"Since I have already crossed over myself, I shall also diligently strive to cross over those who have not yet crossed over;..."
Since I have liberated myself, I shall also diligently strive to liberate those not yet liberated;
since I have established myself in peace, I shall also diligently strive to establish those not yet at peace;
since I have personally realized ultimate *nirvāṇa*, I shall also diligently strive to cause those who have not yet realized it to likewise attain the realization of ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who, with a profound mind, rejoice in the merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved for awakening, how much merit do they obtain?

If they, with a profound mind, rejoice in the merit of a bodhisattva who has long since resolved and cultivated various sublime practices, in the merit of a bodhisattva on the stage of non-retrogression, and in the merit of a bodhisattva bound to only one more birth, how much merit do they obtain?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:

"The weight of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, may be known; yet the merit produced by the minds of these sentient beings accompanied by sympathetic joy cannot be measured. Even the weight of a trichiliocosm may be known; yet the merit produced by the minds of these sentient beings accompanied by sympathetic joy cannot be measured."
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are sentient beings who do not give rise to sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue of all bodhisattvas—from their first generation of the mind until their attainment of buddhahood—or if they neither hear of nor know of those merits of sympathetic joy, you should know that they are all possessed by Māra, infatuated by Māra, and partisans of Māra; having passed away from the celestial realm of Māra, they have been reborn here."

Why is this? If bodhisattvas resolve upon bodhicitta and cultivate the bodhisattva practices, attaining the stage of non-retrogression up to the ultimate state, anyone who is able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward them will certainly be able to destroy the retinues of all Māras and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If sentient beings, with deep-seated reverence and love for the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, desire in every place of rebirth to constantly see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and meet the Saṅgha, they should deeply rejoice in the meritorious roots and virtues of all bodhisattvas and dedicate them toward enlightenment without giving rise to attachment.
"If one can act in this way, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings and destroying the hosts of Māra.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "It is so! It is so!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said, Kauśika!"

If sentient beings, with a profound mind, rejoice in the merits and roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas and dedicate them toward enlightenment, they will swiftly fulfill all bodhisattva practices and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings who, with a profound mind, rejoice in the merits and roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas and dedicate them toward enlightenment, these sentient beings possess great power; they are always able to serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and they skillfully understand the meaning and intent of the profound sūtras.

In whatever place they are born, they will be honored and provided for by all the world; they shall not see unpleasant sights, hear unpleasant sounds, smell unpleasant odors, taste unpleasant flavors, experience unpleasant tactile sensations, contemplate unwholesome dharmas, or fall into evil destinies; instead, being born among humans and devas, they will constantly enjoy supreme bliss.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because these sentient beings are able to rejoice with a profound mind in the immeasurable merits of the bodhisattvas and dedicate them toward awakening; their roots of goodness increase, enabling them to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), thereby benefiting immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings and establishing them in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
For this reason, Kauśika,

sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should, with sympathetic joy, dedicate all the merits and roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas toward enlightenment, for the benefit and happiness of infinite sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the mind is like an illusion, how can a bodhisattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do you perceive a mind that is like an illusion?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do you perceive an illusion?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?

If you do not perceive an illusion, nor perceive a mind that is like an illusion, and if in that place there is neither illusion nor a mind like an illusion, do you see any such mind that can attain awakening?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
In a state that is free from illusion and free from an illusory mind, do you perceive any such dharma that can attain bodhi?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
I do not perceive any dharma that is either identical to or distinct from the mind; what dharma, then, could I say exists or does not exist?
Since all dharmas are ultimately detached, it is impossible to designate them as being either existent or non-existent.

If a phenomenon cannot be established as having existence or non-existence, then it cannot be said that one can attain bodhi; for it is not by means of a non-existent phenomenon that bodhi is attained.

For this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also ultimately detached (*atyantavivikta*); it should not be cultivated through negation, nor should anything be brought forth from it, for unsurpassed bodhi is also ultimately detached.
How can it be said that the assembly of bodhisattvas, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, can realize awakening?

Therefore, should it not be said that *prajñāpāramitā* can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, because one cannot obtain that which is apart from phenomena, nor is there anything apart from phenomena?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! The profound perfection of wisdom and unsurpassed enlightenment are both ultimately detached.

Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately detached, one attains ultimately detached unsurpassed enlightenment; if the profound *prajñāpāramitā* were not ultimately detached, it would not be *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, Subhūti!

It is not that one attains great enlightenment without relying on the profound perfection of wisdom; although one cannot attain the state free from phenomena by means of phenomena, one does attain enlightenment without failing to rely on the profound perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should diligently practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 564 (Fascicle 56).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Fifth Division, Chapter Twenty-two on Roots and Stumps, Part Two. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"These bodhisattvas practice the profound meaning.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!"
"So it is! These bodhisattvas practice the profound meaning.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

These bodhisattvas are able to perform what is difficult: namely, although the meaning of their practice is exceedingly profound, they do not realize the dharmas of the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the deeds performed by these bodhisattvas are not difficult; one should not say that they are able to perform a difficult task.”

Why is this? Because the profound meaning realized by these bodhisattvas is unapprehendable, and the *prajñāpāramitā* that realizes it is likewise unapprehendable; furthermore, the realization itself, the one who realizes, the place of realization, and the time of realization are all unapprehendable.
If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such words, do not sink in spirit nor feel regret, and are neither startled nor terrified, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

When these bodhisattvas practice in this manner, they do not perceive any signs, nor do they perceive that "I am practicing the perfection of wisdom. Yet they draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and remain far removed from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, these bodhisattvas do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding such matters.
"For example, space does not form the thought:
'I am far from or near to that thing. Why is this so? "
Because space is motionless and without discrimination, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. It does not form such thoughts as:
"The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are far from me; unsurpassed *bodhi* is near to me."
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without conceptual differentiation regarding all phenomena.
"For example, an illusory person does not form such a thought:"
"The illusionist and the illusory object are near to me; the bystanders are far from me.
Why is this? Because that which is conjured by illusion is devoid of discrimination.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise; it does not form such a thought as:
"The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are far from me, while unsurpassed bodhi is near to me."
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without conceptual differentiation regarding all phenomena (*dharma*).
One should know that the analogies of reflections, images, and so forth are likewise so.
"For example, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has neither attachment nor aversion toward any phenomena. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata has forever severed all conceptualizations of attachment, aversion, and the like."
The profound perfection of wisdom is likewise thus: it has neither attachment nor aversion toward any phenomena.
Why is this? Because in the profound perfection of wisdom, all conceptual discriminations have been forever severed.

"Just as a transformation created by a Tathāgata performs various activities yet remains free from conceptual discrimination, so too is the profound Prajñāpāramitā: although it accomplishes all its tasks, it is free from conceptual discrimination."

"Just as a skilled craftsman constructs various mechanical devices such as men and women, and although these mechanisms possess movement, they lack discrimination; so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*: although it performs all manner of deeds that ought to be done, it is devoid of discrimination."
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, are they practicing a firm dharma, or are they practicing a non-firm dharma?"
Subhūti replied,
“If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the non-solid dharma and do not practice the solid dharma.”
At that time, immeasurable sons of the gods from the desire realm had this thought:

"If bodhisattvas are able to resolve upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, even while practicing the profound meaning of the perfection of wisdom, they are able not to realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
"For this reason, it is most rare; they are able to perform what is difficult to do, and all the world should pay them homage.
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, addressed them, saying:

"If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom and yet do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), nor fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is not particularly rare, nor is it a difficult feat."

If bodhisattvas, knowing that all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately non-existent and unapprehendable, yet give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, don the armor of diligence, and vow to deliver immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder—this is truly most rare and constitutes a deed of great difficulty.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Although bodhisattvas realize that all phenomena and all sentient beings are ungraspable, they nevertheless resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and don the armor of diligence, desiring to discipline and subdue the multitudes of sentient beings;
it is as if one who desires to discipline space dons a firm armor and battles against space.”
Why is this? O sons of the gods!

Because space is detached, sentient beings are also detached; because sentient beings are detached, the armor is also detached; because sentient beings are detached, beneficial activities are also detached; because sentient beings are detached, the five aggregates are also detached; and because sentient beings are detached, all phenomena are also detached.
"If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such words, do not sink in spirit nor feel regret, and are neither startled nor terrified, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom."
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Subhūti, saying:
"By what causes and conditions do these bodhisattvas, upon hearing such words, have minds that do not sink, nor feel regret, nor are they startled or terrified?"
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
it is because all dharmas are utterly remote and non-existent.”

Why is this? Because regarding all phenomena, these bodhisattvas—whether it be the act of sinking and so forth, that which is sunk and so forth, the locus of sinking and so forth, the time of sinking and so forth, or the one who sinks and so forth—all such instances of sinking and so forth are non-apprehendable, because all phenomena are unapprehendable.
If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such matters, do not sink in spirit nor feel regret, and are neither startled nor terrified, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"When Bodhisattvas practice in this manner, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, Mahābrahmā, the Sovereign of the World, and others all pay them homage together.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If Bodhisattvas are able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they are not only constantly paid homage by Śakra, the Lord of Devas, Mahābrahmā, the Sovereign of the World, and others."

These bodhisattvas are also honored by the prostrations of all those beyond the Heaven of Utmost Purity of Radiance—whether they be gods of the Heaven of Universal Purity, the Heaven of Vast Results, or the Pure Abodes—as well as by other devas, nāgas, asuras, and so forth; they are likewise protected and remembered by all the buddhas and bodhisattvas throughout the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions.

Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas are constantly remembered and protected by all buddhas, the assemblies of bodhisattvas, and the devas, nāgas, asuras, and others; their roots of merit and virtue increase from moment to moment, and they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas have already established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression.

Even if all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River were to become Māras, and each of those hosts of Māras were further to transform themselves into as many evil Māras— each of whom possessed immeasurable and innumerable supernormal powers— even if all these evil Māras exhausted their supernatural might, they would be unable to obstruct these bodhisattvas or cause them to fail in practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor could they cause them to regress from awakening.
“Subhūti, you should know that if bodhisattvas accomplish two dharmas, no evil Māras can obstruct them. What are these two?
First, they contemplate the emptiness of all dharmas.”
Second, not abandoning any sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas accomplish two dharmas, all evil Māras will be unable to create obstacles. What are these two?
First, they are able to practice everything exactly as it has been taught.
Second, they are constantly protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.
Subhūti, you should know this!
If bodhisattvas accomplish these two kinds of superior dharmas, the devas and other celestial beings will constantly come to pay homage, draw near to offer worship, inquire, and exhort them, saying:
"Excellent!..."

"O Mahāsattva! You are able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means through correct conduct; you will swiftly be able to abide in the ground of wisdom of all Buddhas. To all sentient beings who are without a protector, you can become their protector; to those without a savior, you can become their savior; to those without a dwelling, you can become their dwelling; to those without a refuge, you can become their refuge; to those without an island, you can become their island; to those without a place of resort, you can become their place of resort; to those without a shelter, you can become their shelter; and for those in darkness, you can provide illumination; for those who are deaf or blind, you can provide ears and eyes."
Why is this? Son of good family!

If one can abide securely in the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and no evil Māras will be able to obstruct or hinder them.
“Subhūti, you should know this!

If bodhisattvas are able to dwell well in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, then the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the great assemblies throughout the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, will spontaneously rejoice and proclaim their names, clans, physical marks, and merits—just as I now, amidst this great assembly, spontaneously rejoice and proclaim the names, clans, physical marks, and merits of the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu and other bodhisattvas who currently dwell in the presence of Akṣobhya Buddha, purifying their Brahma-conduct and abiding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Do all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, within the midst of the assembly, spontaneously rejoice in and proclaim the names, lineages, physical characteristics, and meritorious qualities of all bodhisattvas?”
The Buddha said, “No!

If bodhisattvas have attained non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and practice the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, those bodhisattvas will be spontaneously and joyfully praised by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the midst of the great assembly for their names, clans, physical characteristics, and meritorious qualities.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it possible that there are bodhisattvas who have not yet attained non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet are nonetheless favored by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who, amidst the great assembly, spontaneously and joyfully proclaims, extols, and praises their names, clans, physical marks, and meritorious qualities?"
The Buddha said:
"There are indeed such cases!

That is to say, although certain bodhisattvas have not yet attained non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom through skillful means; these bodhisattvas likewise receive the spontaneous joy, praise, and commendation of their names, clans, physical marks, and virtues from the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas amidst the great assembly."

Suppose there is a bodhisattva who, following the example of Akṣobhya Buddha when he was practicing as a bodhisattva, trains in what he practiced, abides in what he performed, and cultivates the perfection of wisdom through skillful means.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who train in accordance with what the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu and others have practiced, and who dwell in accordance with what they have performed, practicing the perfection of wisdom through skillful means.

Although these bodhisattvas have not yet attained non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are nonetheless graced by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who, amidst the great assembly, spontaneously rejoices in and extols their names, clans, physical characteristics, and virtues.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom; although they have deep faith and understanding in the non-arising nature of all phenomena, they have not yet realized the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Although they have deep faith and understanding in the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena, they have not yet attained mastery in the stage of a bodhisattva’s non-retrogression."
Although they abide in the nature of quiescence of all phenomena, they have not yet entered the stage of non-retrogression.

These bodhisattvas are likewise blessed by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who, amidst the great assembly, spontaneously expresses joy and extols their names, clans, physical characteristics, and virtues.
