“Subhūti, you should know that if bodhisattvas are spontaneously and joyfully praised by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the midst of the great assembly—by their names, clans, physical marks, and virtues—these bodhisattvas have transcended the stages of the two vehicles and are close to great enlightenment; they have either already received the prediction of non-retrogression, or they are near to receiving the prediction of non-retrogression.”
Chapter 23: Entrustment, Part Five, Chapter Twenty-three on Entrustment.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if bodhisattvas, upon hearing the exposition of the meaning and purport of the *prajñāpāramitā*, develop deep faith and understanding, being without confusion, without doubt, without delusion, and without despondency, but merely think:
'The principle taught by the Buddha is necessarily and certainly not erroneous.'"

"These bodhisattvas will certainly, in the presence of Akṣobhya Buddha and the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, hear the *prajñāpāramitā* extensively; they will be able to give rise to faith and understanding regarding its profound meaning and intent. Having attained such faith and understanding, they will diligently cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and shall abide on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). Abiding in this stage, they will swiftly realize awakening (*bodhi*)."

Subhūti, you should know that if bodhisattvas merely hear this perfection of wisdom, they will still obtain boundless meritorious benefits; how much more so for those who have profound faith and understanding, and practice according to what has been taught!
"These bodhisattvas draw near to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), abide in suchness (tathatā), swiftly realize awakening, and proclaim the essential points of the Dharma.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since no dharma apart from suchness can be found, what dharma do you speak of as drawing near to all-knowledge and abiding in suchness?"
"Who realizes enlightenment?
Who expounds the essential points of the Dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So it is! So it is! Since phenomena are utterly unattainable apart from *tathatā*, what phenomenon could one speak of that approaches omniscience, abides in *tathatā*, swiftly realizes *bodhi*, and proclaims the essentials of the Dharma?"
"Since even the self-nature of suchness cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any other dharma capable of performing an action!
It is only in accordance with worldly convention that I speak thus.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, the principle of the *prajñāpāramitā* is profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand.

If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, although they know that all phenomena are ungraspable, they nevertheless seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and desire to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; this is a most difficult task."

When the assembly of bodhisattvas heard these words, their minds did not sink, they were without confusion, without doubt, without delusion, and without distress; such matters as these are truly rare.
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra:
"As you have said, 'When the assembly of bodhisattvas hears such words, their minds do not sink, they have no confusion, no doubt, no delusion, and no distress—such matters are truly rare. "

"Kauśika! When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate that all phenomena are empty and utterly non-existent; who could sink, who could drown, who could be deluded, who could doubt, who could be confused, or who could be distressed?"
Therefore, this matter is not at all rare.

However, because sentient beings are deluded and inverted, unable to penetrate the fact that all phenomena are empty, it is not at all difficult to seek awakening and desire to proclaim the skillful means for them.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

"Venerable Subhūti, everything you say is without exception based upon emptiness; therefore, your words are always free from obstruction, just as when an arrow is shot upward into the sky, it meets no resistance whether it is near or far."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does what I and the Venerable Subhūti have spoken accord with the Tathāgata’s true words and the words of the Dharma? Is it a correct exposition that conforms to the Dharma within the Dharma?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Everything you and Subhūti have said accords with the Tathāgata’s words of truth and his words of Dharma; it conforms to the Dharma and follows the Dharma, and is all a correct exposition."
Why is this? Kauśika!
All the eloquence possessed by the Venerable Subhūti is established without exception in reliance upon emptiness.

Why is this? Because the Venerable Subhūti perceives that all phenomena are ultimately empty; he does not even apprehend the perfection of wisdom, much less one who can practice the perfection of wisdom!
One cannot even attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, much less one who can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
One cannot even attain the knowledge of all modes, much less one who can realize the knowledge of all modes!
If one cannot even attain suchness, how much less can one attain that which realizes suchness and becomes a Tathāgata!
If one cannot even attain the nature of non-arising, how much less can one attain that which realizes the nature of non-arising!
If one cannot even attain the state of a bodhisattva, how much less can one attain that which realizes the Buddha's bodhi!
If one cannot even attain the ten powers or the four fearlessnesses, how much less can one attain that which accomplishes the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses!
"One does not even attain the Dharma, much less one who can preach the Dharma! Kausika,

the abiding in detachment and the abiding in non-apprehension of all dharmas by the Venerable Subhūti does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a *upaniṣad* (fractional) part of the subtle abiding in the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in which the bodhisattvas abide."

Kauśika! This subtle dwelling and practice of the Prajñāpāramitā in which these bodhisattvas abide—excluding the dwelling of the Tathāgata—is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most superior, and the unsurpassed among the dwellings of all other bodhisattvas, as well as those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, Kauśika!

If any bodhisattvas wish to be the foremost, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, and the unsurpassed among the entire assembly of sentient beings, they should dwell in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

At that time, immeasurable and innumerable devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven among the assembly, having heard the Dharma with joy, each took celestial *sūkṣmasvaragandha* flowers and scattered them over the World-Honored One and the various bodhisattvas.
Six hundred bhikṣus rose together from their seats, knelt with their right knees upon the ground, and joined their palms toward the Buddha.
Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, each of them had exquisite *sūkṣmasvara* flowers spontaneously fill the palms of their hands.
The assembly of bhikṣus leaped for joy and, each scattering these flowers upon the Buddha, made this vow together once they had finished:

"By the power of these supreme roots of goodness, may we always abide securely in the subtle and profound practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.

According to the constant law of the Buddhas, he emitted various rays of light from his face—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, green, gold, silver, and crystal—which shone obliquely upon boundless Buddha-lands, reaching upward to the Brahma-world and downward penetrating to the wind-circle. They then gradually returned, circled the Buddha three times to the right, and entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and said:
"World-Honored One,
for what cause and by what condition do you manifest this smile?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:

"In a future age known as the Nakṣatra-kalpa, all these bhikṣus shall become Buddhas, all bearing the same name Puṣpasaṃpuṣṭa and being endowed with the ten titles. The number of their śrāvaka saṃghas shall all be equal, and the lifespan of each Buddha shall likewise be twenty thousand kalpas. Wherever they dwell, five-colored flowers shall rain down; for this reason, I smile."
If bodhisattvas wish to dwell securely in the most excellent dwelling, they should dwell in the perfection of wisdom;
if bodhisattvas wish to dwell securely in the dwelling of the Tathāgata, they should dwell in the perfection of wisdom.
Ānanda, you should know this:

if bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom with diligence until its ultimate fulfillment, these bodhisattvas have either passed away from among humans and been reborn here again, or they have passed away from the Tuṣita heaven and come to be born in the human realm.
Why is this? Because the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* is easily accomplished in these two places, and not elsewhere.
Ānanda, you should know this!

The Tathāgata clearly perceives that if bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom with diligence, being regardless of body, life, or wealth, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If any bodhisattvas hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and gladden those sons of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle, these bodhisattvas have previously planted roots of merit under immeasurable Buddhas of the past; they are not merely those of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without being startled or terrified, upholding, reciting, maintaining mindfulness of, and reflecting upon it—thoroughly penetrating and practicing in accordance with its phenomena, meanings, phrasing, and intent—then these bodhisattvas are directly beholding us, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing the exposition of the profound meaning of this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*, give rise to deep faith and understanding, do not slander it, and cannot be deterred or destroyed, these bodhisattvas have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, have planted many roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas, and have also been taken into the care of immeasurable virtuous friends."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If sentient beings are able to plant various roots of goodness within the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the supreme field of merit—then although they will certainly attain either the fruit of a śrāvaka, the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, or the fruit of a Tathāgata, they must nevertheless master the profound meaning and intent of the Prajñāpāramitā without obstruction, and practice the various bodhisattva deeds with diligence until they are perfectly fulfilled, in order to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā to you; you should correctly receive, uphold, recite, and master it, so that it is not lost or forgotten."
Ānanda, you should know this:
except for this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*, if one should forget any other teachings I have spoken that they have received and upheld, their transgression is still light.
If one does not properly uphold this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, even to the extent of forgetting a single phrase, the transgression is extremely grave.
Ānanda, you should know that if one can properly receive and uphold even a single verse from this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā without forgetting it, the merit obtained will be immeasurable.
If one does not properly uphold this profound sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, and forgets even a single verse, the heavy sin incurred will be equal in measure to the aforementioned merit.

Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā to you with earnest care. You should correctly receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and reflect upon it according to the principle; you should explain it extensively to others, analyzing and elucidating it so that those who uphold it may thoroughly understand its words, meanings, and underlying intent.

Why is this? If bodhisattvas take up, read, recite, master, and reflect upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle, and extensively explain it to others, analyzing and elucidating it so that it is easily understood, these bodhisattvas are thereby upholding the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and proclaiming and elucidating it extensively for the sake of sentient beings.
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if there are sentient beings who give rise to a fervent and pure mind, and who, being present before me, wish to offer various kinds of sublime and excellent offerings with reverence and without weariness, they should listen to the *Prajñāpāramitā* with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and contemplate it according to the principle. They should also extensively analyze and explain it for the sake of sentient beings, or else write it down, adorn it in various ways, and offer it with reverence, never abandoning it for even a moment.”
Ānanda, you should know this!

If any bodhisattvas offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are thereby offering worship, honor, respect, and praise to me and to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time in the present.
Ānanda, you should know this:

if any bodhisattvas, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, give rise to a heart of earnest purity, reverence, and love, they thereby give rise to a heart of earnest purity, reverence, and love toward the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Ānanda! If you love me and do not forsake me, you should likewise love and not forsake this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, ensuring that not even a single phrase is forgotten or lost.

“Ānanda! Even if I were to spend an eon, or even as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, I could not exhaustively describe the causes and conditions for entrusting this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā.”

To state the essentials: just as I am your great teacher, you should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise your great teacher; just as the Buddhas of the three periods are the unsurpassed great teachers for gods, humans, and asuras, you should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise the unsurpassed great teacher for the world’s gods, humans, and asuras.
Since you—gods, humans, asuras, and others—hold me in reverence, you should likewise hold the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in reverence.
Therefore, Ānanda!
I entrust to you this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā through immeasurable skillful means; you should receive and uphold it so that it is not forgotten or lost.

I now hold this profound Prajñāpāramitā and entrust it to you before this great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, and others; you should receive and uphold it correctly, ensuring that it is not lost or forgotten.
Ānanda! I now tell you this in truth:

any sons of good family who possess pure faith, and who do not wish to abandon the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha jewels, nor the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Buddhas of the three times, must certainly not abandon the profound Prajñāpāramitā. This is what is called our instruction and teaching for all disciples.
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if there are those who delight in hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, and who receive, uphold, read, recite, master it thoroughly, contemplate it according to the principle, transcribe it, and explain it, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Why is this? Because the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas arises in dependence upon the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Ānanda!
If bodhisattvas wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should diligently apply themselves with vigor to cultivate the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it enables bodhisattvas to swiftly realize awakening.
"Ānanda, you should know this!"

If Bodhisattvas, at a time when the Dharma is about to perish, protect and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, they thereby protect and uphold the omniscience of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and they also protect and uphold the unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
“Ānanda, you should know this!
If bodhisattvas diligently train in the six perfections, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Ānanda!”
I further entrust these six perfections to you; you should receive and uphold them correctly, never allowing them to be forgotten or lost.
Why is this? These six perfections are the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Ānanda, you should know that the essential teachings spoken by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, all flow forth from this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the six pāramitās.

The Buddhas and their disciples of the ten directions and the three periods of time all rely upon this inexhaustible treasury of Dharma to practice with diligent effort; they have realized, are realizing, and will realize unsurpassed bodhi, and they have entered, are entering, and will enter nirvana without remainder.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose you were to teach the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, and by means of this Dharma, every sentient being in the trichiliocosm were to attain the fruit of Arhatship; even so, you would not yet have performed the duty of a disciple for me, and I would not be particularly pleased with your service."

If you can expound even a single verse of the profound Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* for those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle, that shall be called performing the duty of a disciple for me; I shall feel deep sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) in this matter.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were simultaneously to realize the fruit of arhatship; the various meritorious actions consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation that they would thereby accomplish—[would their merit be great?]"
"What do you think? Would that not be much?
Ānanda replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is a śrāvaka who can expound for a bodhisattva the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, even for a single day and night, or down to the duration of a finger-snap, the mass of merit obtained by that śrāvaka will be far greater than the former."
Why is this? Because the mass of merit obtained by these śrāvakas surpasses all the roots of goodness of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of śrāvakas, teaches the Dharma of the śrāvakas, and by means of this Dharma all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were to realize the fruit of arhatship; [this would not equal the merit of another bodhisattva’s practice].
"What do you think?
Is the mass of merit obtained by such a bodhisattva great or not?
Ānanda replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of sentient beings, proclaims the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom for even a single day and night, or even for as little as the snap of a finger, the mass of merit obtained by such a bodhisattva is far greater than the former."

Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses all gifts of Dharma associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all the roots of goodness belonging to those two vehicles.
Ānanda, you should know that if bodhisattvas accomplish such mindfulness of these roots of goodness, it is impossible for them to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Chapter 24: Seeing Akṣobhya Buddha, Part Five, Section Two. At that time, the Tathāgata was surrounded by the fourfold assembly as he praised and expounded the Prajñāpāramitā. Having entrusted it to Ānanda to uphold, he further manifested supernormal powers within the great assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, causing everyone to see the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, surrounded by a great multitude of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas. He saw him preaching the True Dharma to an assembly as vast and unshakeable as the great ocean, and he beheld the marks of the pure adornments of that land.

The assembly of śrāvakas were all arhats; their outflows were exhausted and they were free from further afflictions. They had attained true mastery, with minds well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated. Like well-trained thoroughbred horses and like great dragons, they had done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished. Having laid down the heavy burdens and attained their own benefit, they had exhausted the fetters of existence and were liberated through right knowledge, reaching the sovereignty of mind and the supreme culmination.

That assembly of bodhisattvas was entirely composed of those renowned to all, who had attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, and who had accomplished immeasurable, inconceivable, and unfathomable, subtle and wondrous merits.

The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, causing this assembly of the fourfold community, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, no longer to see that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, nor his śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and the rest of the great assembly, nor the marks of the pure adornments of that buddha-field.
The assembly of that Buddha and his adorned pure land are all beyond the range of visual perception for those in this land.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has withdrawn his supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*), and thus there is no causal condition for seeing such distant objects.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Do you see again the land and the assembly of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya?”
Ānanda said, "I no longer see that matter, for it is not within the range of this eye.
Then, the Buddha again addressed Ānanda:

"Just as the assembly and the land of that Tathāgata are not within the range of the visual faculty of this land, you should know that all phenomena are likewise not within the range of the visual faculty or other sense organs."
Ānanda, you should know this!
A dharma does not act upon a dharma; a dharma does not see a dharma; a dharma does not know a dharma; a dharma does not realize a dharma.
Ānanda, you should know this!
The nature of all phenomena cannot be practiced, cannot be seen, cannot be known, cannot be realized; it is without movement and without activity.
Why is this? It is because all phenomena are devoid of functional activity; both the grasper and the grasped are like space, for their nature is utterly remote.
It is because all phenomena are inconceivable; both the conceiving subject and the object of conception are like illusory beings, for their nature is utterly remote.
Because all phenomena are without agent or recipient, being as insubstantial as shadows and reflections.

Ānanda, you should know that if bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are said to be practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), remaining without attachment to the characteristics of any phenomena.
If bodhisattvas are able to train in this way, they are said to be training in the perfection of wisdom, without grasping at or rejecting any phenomena.
Ānanda, you should know this!
If bodhisattvas wish to attain all the pāramitās, swiftly bringing them to full completion and reaching the ultimate further shore of all phenomena, they should study the prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this? Because such training is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all trainings; it brings benefit, welfare, and peace to the entire world.

Ānanda, you should know that if bodhisattvas train in this way, they act as a refuge for those who are without refuge; this training in the perfection of wisdom is permitted and praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Ānanda, you should know that after the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have trained in this training and established themselves therein, they are able to take up the trichiliocosm with their right hand or even the toe of their right foot, casting it away to another direction or returning it to its original place, while the sentient beings within it remain unaware, unperceiving, uninjured, and undisturbed.
Why is this so? Because the merit and majestic power of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are inconceivable.

All Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as all bodhisattvas, having studied this *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the dharmas of the past, future, present, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, Ānanda, I declare that among all trainings,
the training in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the supreme, and the unsurpassed.
“Ānanda, you should know this:
those who wish to grasp the measure or the limit of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are like foolish people who wish to grasp the measure and the limit of space.”
Why is this? Because the merit of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable and boundless.
Ānanda, you should know this!

I never say that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has a measure or limit, such as those possessed by the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and syllables (*vyañjanakāya*). Why is this?

Because the collections of names, phrases, and syllables are phenomena that possess measure, whereas the meritorious benefits of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are not phenomena that possess measure. The collections of names and so forth cannot measure the meritorious benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can the meritorious benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā* be measured by them.
The Venerable Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason and by what causes is the profound *prajñāpāramitā* described as immeasurable?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Because the nature of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is inexhaustible and its nature is detached, it is said to be immeasurable.

Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas of the three times study the *prajñāpāramitā*, and having reached ultimate perfection, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) and proclaim and reveal it to all sentient beings; yet this *prajñāpāramitā* never diminishes or comes to an end.”
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is as inexhaustible as space; therefore, those who wish to exhaust the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would be wishing to exhaust the limits of space.
"Therefore, Ānanda!
The profound perfection of wisdom is called inexhaustible; because it is inexhaustible, it is called immeasurable.
At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"This matter is profound; I shall question the Buddha about it.
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata declare the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to be inexhaustible?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because the profound perfection of wisdom is like space, it is inexhaustible.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All bodhisattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are all inexhaustible; they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that ignorance through to old age and death are all inexhaustible.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
Subhūti, you should know this!
The assembly of bodhisattvas observes the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in this way, remaining far removed from the two extremes.

Observing the twelve links of dependent origination as being neither with a center nor with an end is the sublime contemplation unique to these bodhisattvas; that is to say, only by sitting firmly upon the seat of sublime enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) can one thus observe the twelve links of dependent origination according to reality. Because its principle is as profound as space and inexhaustible, they are then able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Subhūti, you should know that if bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a mode of activity as inexhaustible as space, and contemplate dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as it truly is, they will not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Subhūti, you should know that if any among the assembly of bodhisattvas should regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is all because they do not rely on such skillful means of mental attention, and thus do not know as they truly are how the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound perfection of wisdom— how they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom through inexhaustible modes of conduct, and how they should correctly contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.”

Subhūti, you should know that if any among the assembly of bodhisattvas should regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is entirely because they have distanced themselves from the skillful means that give rise to the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, you should know that all those bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening do so entirely by relying on the skillful means that induce the perfection of wisdom.

By relying on such skillful means, these bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom and observe the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are, through the mode of activity that is inexhaustible like space. When observing the dharma of dependent origination in this way, they do not perceive any phenomenon arising without a cause, nor do they perceive any phenomenon with an eternally abiding nature or characteristics, nor do they perceive any phenomenon involving an agent or an experiencer.

These bodhisattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, observe the twelve links of dependent origination in accordance with reality through the mode of practice that is as inexhaustible as space; they thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom and are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

when a bodhisattva contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are and thereby brings forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), at that time the bodhisattva does not perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; he does not perceive this buddha-field, nor does he perceive that buddha-field; nor does he perceive any dharma capable of perceiving these various buddha-fields.”

When bodhisattvas are able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, at that time Māra the Evil One experiences extreme distress as if pierced by a poisoned arrow; just as a person suffers physical and mental agony when their parents suddenly pass away, so too does Māra.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it that a single evil Māra, upon seeing a bodhisattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, experiences extreme distress as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, or is it that all the evil Māras throughout the entire trichiliocosm experience the same?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If all the evil Māras throughout the trichiliocosm were to see bodhisattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, they would experience extreme distress as if pierced by poisoned arrows, each unable to remain at ease in their own seats."

Why is this? Because if bodhisattvas abide in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the gods, humans, asuras, and others of the world cannot find any fault in them, nor can they disturb, cause them to regress, or destroy them.
Therefore, Subhūti,
if bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should diligently abide in the profound perfection of wisdom.

If bodhisattvas are able to diligently abide in the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will then be able to cultivate and fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

If bodhisattvas are able to correctly practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be able to fully cultivate and perfect the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of all *pāramitās*, and they will be able to truly recognize and distance themselves from all arising demonic activities (*mārakarman*).
"Therefore, Subhūti,
if bodhisattvas wish to correctly embrace skillful means, they should correctly practice the profound perfection of wisdom."

When a bodhisattva practices and brings forth the profound perfection of wisdom, at that time all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in immeasurable and boundless worlds, together protect and mindfully attend to them.
These bodhisattvas should form this thought:
"Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise give birth to all-knowledge from the perfection of wisdom."
Having formed this thought, one should further reflect:
"Just as the dharmas that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas ought to realize, I too shall realize them."
"Thus it is, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas practice and bring forth this profound perfection of wisdom, the mass of merit generated by them in the mere time it takes to snap one's fingers surpasses the merit obtained by those bodhisattvas who, while adhering to the notion of attainment, practice generosity for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. How much more so for those who can do so for even a single day or half a day!"
These bodhisattvas will before long abide on the stage of non-retrogression and shall always be protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

If a multitude of bodhisattvas is protected and remembered by the Buddhas, they will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they will not fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they will definitely not be reborn in the evil destinies, and they will always be born among gods and humans, never being separated from the Buddhas.

If bodhisattvas, while practicing to bring forth the profound perfection of wisdom, recollect and contemplate the virtues of the Buddhas for even the duration of a finger-snap, they still obtain boundless merit and benefits; how much more so if they practice to bring forth the profound perfection of wisdom with courageous diligence for a single day, or more than a day, while recollecting and contemplating the virtues of the Buddhas!

"Just as with the fragrant elephants and others, the assembly of Bodhisattvas constantly practiced pure conduct in the presence of the Buddha Akṣobhya and were never separated from the Prajñāpāramitā.

When the Bhagavat had finished speaking this sūtra, the immeasurable assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, headed by Maitreya Bodhisattva, along with the venerable Subhūti, Śāriputra, and other great śrāvakas, as well as all the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced and, with faith and acceptance, put it into practice.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Sixty-five.
